docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Supplementary page

Periodicity is not a separate topic of Math I: Calculus. This page makes precise the word periodic used for the trigonometric functions and elsewhere on the wiki.

Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) and let \(f\colon D\to\mathbb{R}\) be a function. A number \(T>0\) is a period of \(f\) if, for every \(x\in D\), also \(x+T\in D\) and \(x-T\in D\), and

\[ f(x+T)=f(x). \]

The function \(f\) is periodic if it has a period. The smallest period, if one exists, is the fundamental period. The same definition is used for functions of a complex variable, where the period may be a nonzero complex number.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A periodic function repeats itself: its graph on any interval of length \(T\) determines the whole graph, by shifting copies \(T\) to the left and right. Periodic functions model cycles such as rotations, oscillations and seasonal patterns.

The graph is \(\sin(3x)\) from the Examples, whose fundamental period is \(T=2\pi/3\). The shaded window \([0,T]\) holds one period; every other part of the graph is a copy of it shifted by a multiple of \(T\). The two green points sit at some \(x\) and at \(x+T\) and have the same height, which is the defining equation \(f(x+T)=f(x)\).

Shift the graph by \(s\): the dashed copy \(x\mapsto f(x+s)\) lies exactly on the graph when \(s\) is a whole multiple of the fundamental period \(T\). The scale \(a\) puts \(ax\) in place of \(x\), which divides the period by \(a\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(T\) is a period of \(f\), then so is \(kT\) for every positive integer \(k\). So "the period" usually means the fundamental period.
  • If \(T\) is a period of \(f\) and \(a>0\), then \(g(x)=f(ax)\) has period \(T/a\), since \(g(x+T/a)=f(ax+T)=f(ax)\).
  • Sums and products of functions with a common period \(T\) also have period \(T\), though their fundamental period can be smaller: \(\sin^2x=\tfrac{1}{2}(1-\cos2x)\) has fundamental period \(\pi\), not \(2\pi\).
  • A continuous periodic function on \(\mathbb{R}\) is bounded and attains its maximum and minimum: by the extreme value theorem it does so on \([0,T]\), and every value is repeated there.
  • A periodic function need not have a fundamental period: a constant function has every \(T>0\) as a period, and the Dirichlet function has every positive rational number as a period, but no smallest one.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) have fundamental period \(2\pi\): \(\sin(x+2\pi)=\sin x\) and \(\cos(x+2\pi)=\cos x\) for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}\).
  • \(\tan\) has fundamental period \(\pi\): shifting by \(\pi\) changes the sign of both \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\), so \(\tan(x+\pi)=\tan x\) wherever \(\cos x\neq0\).
  • \(\sin(3x)\) has fundamental period \(2\pi/3\), by the scaling rule above.
  • The complex exponential is \(2\pi\mathrm{i}\)-periodic: by Euler's formula, \(\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}}=\cos2\pi+\mathrm{i}\sin2\pi=1\), so \(\mathrm{e}^{z+2\pi\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{e}^{z}\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{e}^{z}\) for every \(z\in\mathbb{C}\).
  • The fractional part \(x-\lfloor x\rfloor\) (floor function) has fundamental period \(1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A polynomial is a function formed by adding together finitely many monomials, and the highest degree of all monomials that appear in it is called the degree of the polynomial.

Equivalently, a polynomial is an expression that can be built from constants and symbols called variables by means of addition, multiplication and exponentiation to a nonnegative integer power, i.e.,

\[ P(x)=a_0+a_1x+a_2x^2+\cdots+a_n x^n, \]

where \(a_0,\,\dots,\,a_n\) are constants that are called the coefficients of the polynomial.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Polynomials are functions built from finite algebraic combinations of integer powers of the variable.

Change the coefficients \(a_0,\dots,a_3\) and count the real zeros: a polynomial of degree \(n\) has at most \(n\) of them, and setting \(a_3=0\) lowers the degree.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Polynomials are continuous, differentiable and smooth everywhere.
  • The degree of a polynomial controls its long-term behaviour.
  • Zeros of polynomials determine factorization.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x)=x^2-3x+2\) is a polynomial.
  • Nonzero constant functions are polynomials of degree zero; the zero polynomial is not assigned a degree.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. We say that \(A\) is a proper subset of \(B\text{,}\) denoted unambiguously by \(A\subsetneq B\text{,}\) if every element of \(A\) is also an element of \(B\text{,}\) but some element of \(B\) is not in \(A\text{.}\) Equivalently,

\[ \begin{aligned} A\subsetneq B \;&\iff\; A\subseteq B\text{ and }A\neq B\\ \;&\iff\; A\subseteq B\text{ and }\exists x\in B\\ &\qquad\text{such that }x\notin A. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A proper subset captures strict inclusion between sets.

It distinguishes between equality and containment.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every proper subset is a subset, but not conversely.
  • Proper inclusion is transitive, i.e., \(A\subsetneq B\) and \(B\subsetneq C\) implies \(A\subsetneq C\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\{1,\,2\}\subsetneq\{1,\,2,\,3\}\text{.}\)
  • A set is never a proper subset of itself.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) and let \(x_0 \in \mathbb{R}\text{.}\)

The point \(x_0\) is a limit point of \(X\) if, for every \(\delta>0\text{,}\) there is an \(x\in X\) with \(0<|x-x_0|<\delta\text{.}\) If \(x_0\in X\) is not a limit point of \(X\text{,}\) it is an isolated point of \(X\text{.}\)

For \(r>0\text{,}\) the set \((x_0-r,\,x_0+r)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon |x-x_0|<r\}\) is a neighbourhood of \(x_0\text{.}\) Removing \(x_0\) itself gives the punctured neighbourhood of \(x_0\text{,}\) which is any set of the form

\[ \{x \in \mathbb{R} \colon 0 < |x - x_0| < r\}, \]

for some \(r > 0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A punctured neighbourhood describes points arbitrarily close to a given point while excluding the point itself.

It isolates local behaviour without evaluating the function at the point.

This set is obtained from an open interval about \(x_0\) by removing \(x_0\). The absolute value expresses distance from the centre; \(0<|x-x_0|\) excludes the centre and \(|x-x_0|<r\) keeps the point inside the interval.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The definition of a limit at a point requires \(x_0\) to be a limit point of the domain, which is exactly what makes "\(x\) approaches \(x_0\)" meaningful.
  • The limit laws for functions are stated for functions defined on a punctured neighbourhood of \(x_0\text{.}\)
  • Excluding the centre point avoids any reliance on the value \(f(x_0)\text{.}\)
  • A function is never differentiable at an isolated point of its domain.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((-1,0)\cup(0,1)\) is a punctured neighbourhood of the origin.
  • Every point of \([0,1]\) is a limit point of \([0,1]\text{,}\) and so is every point of \((0,1)\text{.}\)
  • \(3\) is an isolated point of \([0,1]\cup\{3\}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
If the function is \(f\colon X\to Y\text{,}\) the range or image of \(f\) is the set

\[ \{f(x)\colon x\in X\}. \]

We call an output \(y=f(x)\) the dependent variable.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The range, or image, of a function describes all possible output values produced by the function.

It captures how the codomain is actually realized by the function.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The range is a subset of the codomain.
  • Different functions may share the same range.
  • Determining the range often requires solving equations or inequalities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The range of \(f(x)=x^2\) is \([0,+\infty)\text{.}\)
  • The range of \(f(x)=\sin x\) is \([-1,1]\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A rational function is the quotient of two polynomials when the denominator is not always equal to zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A rational function models relationships formed by ratios of polynomial expressions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Rational functions are undefined where the denominator vanishes.
  • The behaviour as \(x\to\pm\infty\text{,}\) including any horizontal asymptote, is determined by the degrees and leading coefficients of the two polynomials.
  • Discontinuities arise from zeros of the denominator.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}\) is a rational function.
  • \(f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1}\) is undefined at \(x=1\text{.}\)
  • \(f(x)=\dfrac{x^3-x^2+4x-5}{3x^2+1}\) is defined everywhere.

The denominator \(3x^2+1\) never vanishes, so the graph is one unbroken curve over all of \(\mathbb{R}\).

This rational function is a quotient of two polynomials of degree one. Move \(x_0\), \(L\) and \(k\): the zero of the denominator gives a vertical asymptote, and the ratio of leading coefficients the horizontal one.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A rational number is a number of the form

\[ \frac{a}{b}, \qquad a,b\in\mathbb{Z},\quad b\neq0. \]

Two such fractions represent the same rational number exactly when

\[ \frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad ad=bc, \]

where \(b,d\neq0\text{.}\) The set of all rational numbers is denoted by \(\mathbb{Q}\text{.}\) Math I: Calculus takes \(\mathbb{Q}\) and its usual arithmetic as given.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Rational numbers represent ratios of integers and enlarge \(\mathbb{Z}\) so that division by a nonzero number is possible.

Every integer is rational because \(a=a/1\text{,}\) so \(\mathbb{Z}\subsetneq\mathbb{Q}\text{.}\)

The fractions marked illustrate the density of \(\mathbb{Q}\): between any two distinct rational numbers lies another rational number.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every rational number has infinitely many representations.

  • For \(b,d\neq0\text{,}\)

    \[ \begin{gathered} \frac{a}{b}+\frac{c}{d}=\frac{ad+bc}{bd}, \qquad \frac{a}{b}\frac{c}{d}=\frac{ac}{bd},\\ -\frac{a}{b}=\frac{-a}{b}. \end{gathered} \]

  • Rational numbers are closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication, and under division by a nonzero rational number.

  • Between any two distinct rational numbers lies another rational number; this is the density of \(\mathbb{Q}\) in itself.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{2}{4}\text{.}\)
  • \(\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{5}{6}\text{.}\)
  • \(-\dfrac{3}{5}\) is a rational number.
  • \(\sqrt{2}\) is not a rational number.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The set of all real numbers, denoted by \(\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) is the complete ordered number system represented by the real number line. It contains the rational numbers, obeys the usual arithmetic and order rules, and has no gaps.

Completeness distinguishes \(\mathbb{R}\) from \(\mathbb{Q}\text{.}\) In this course it appears through the existence of suprema and through convergence theorems such as the monotone convergence theorem.

Each enlargement of the number systems removes a limitation of the previous one:

\[ \mathbb{N}\subsetneq\mathbb{Z}\subsetneq\mathbb{Q}\subsetneq\mathbb{R}. \]

Natural numbers support counting, integers support unrestricted subtraction, rationals support division by nonzero numbers, and real numbers fill the gaps on the number line.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Math I: Calculus uses \(\mathbb{R}\) and its arithmetic and order directly. Real numbers fill the gaps left by the rationals, allowing limits and geometric quantities to be represented exactly.

They allow limits and convergence to be treated as exact numerical objects.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every nonempty subset of \(\mathbb{R}\) that is bounded above has exactly one least upper bound; this existence statement is the defining advantage of \(\mathbb{R}\) over \(\mathbb{Q}\text{.}\)
  • Every real number is either rational or irrational.
  • The order on \(\mathbb{R}\) satisfies trichotomy and is preserved by addition and by multiplication with a positive number.
  • Between any two distinct real numbers lies a rational number; this is the density of \(\mathbb{Q}\) in \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\)
  • The Archimedean property says that for positive real numbers \(x\) and \(\varepsilon\text{,}\) there is a positive integer \(M\) with \(M\varepsilon>x\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\sqrt{2}\) is a real number but not rational: no rational number squares to \(2\text{,}\) yet a real number does.
  • \(\pi\text{,}\) the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, is real but not rational.
  • The approximations \(1.4,\,1.41,\,1.414,\,1.4142,\ldots\) have squares approaching \(2\text{,}\) but the number they approach is missing from \(\mathbb{Q}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The reciprocal of a nonzero rational number \(x\text{,}\) written \(x^{-1}\text{,}\) is the unique rational number satisfying

\[ x\,x^{-1}=1. \]

If \(x=a/b\) with \(a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}\text{,}\) then

\[ \left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{-1}=\frac{b}{a}. \]

The reciprocal of \(0\) is undefined. The same definition applies to nonzero real numbers.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The reciprocal of a number represents multiplicative inversion.

It formalizes the idea of undoing multiplication and plays a central role in division and rational expressions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The reciprocal of a nonzero number is unique.
  • \((x^{-1})^{-1}=x\) for every \(x\neq0\text{.}\)
  • \((xy)^{-1}=x^{-1}y^{-1}\) when \(x\) and \(y\) are nonzero.
  • For positive numbers, taking reciprocals reverses order: if \(0<x<y\text{,}\) then \(x^{-1}>y^{-1}\text{.}\)
  • Zero has no reciprocal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The reciprocal of \(2\) is \(1/2\text{.}\)
  • The reciprocal of \(-3/4\) is \(-4/3\text{.}\)
  • The reciprocal of \(1/5\) is \(5\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon [a,b]\to\mathbb{R}\) be a bounded function. We say that \(f\) is Riemann integrable on \([a,b]\) if there exists \(s\in\mathbb{R}\) such that, for every \(\varepsilon>0\text{,}\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that every partition \(P\) with mesh \(\lVert P\rVert<\delta\) and every choice of tags satisfy

\[ \begin{aligned} &|S(f,P)-s|\\ &\quad=\left|\,\sum_{i=1}^n f(x^*_i)(x_i-x_{i-1})-s\,\right|<\varepsilon. \end{aligned} \]

The number \(s\) is the Riemann integral of \(f\text{,}\) denoted by \(\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Riemann integral formalizes the idea of accumulation as the limit of Riemann sums.

It defines the total contribution of a function over an interval through approximation by rectangles.

Refine the partition: the upper and lower sums close in on each other, so every tagged sum \(S(f,P)\), wherever the tags sit, is pushed towards the same number \(\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Equivalent criterion. A bounded \(f\) is Riemann integrable if and only if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\text{,}\) there is a partition \(P\) with \(U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\varepsilon\text{;}\) the upper and lower sums then squeeze the same integral as the partition is refined.
  • Informally, \(\displaystyle\int_a^b f=\lim_{n\to\infty}S(f,P_n)\) along the regular subdivisions \(P_n\) into \(n\) equal pieces.
  • The integral value is independent of the choice of tags \(x_i^*\text{.}\)
  • Boundedness of the function is essential for integrability.
  • Every constant function is Riemann integrable with \(\displaystyle\int_a^b C\,\mathrm{d}x=C(b-a)\text{,}\) and so is every piecewise constant function on a bounded interval.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Continuous functions on a closed bounded interval are Riemann integrable.
  • Monotone functions on a closed bounded interval are Riemann integrable.
  • The Dirichlet function is bounded on \([0,1]\) but not Riemann integrable: every partition has \(U-L=1\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon [a,b]\to\mathbb{R}\) be a bounded function. Given a partition \(P=\{x_0,\ldots,x_n\}\) of \([a,b]\) and a tag \(x^*_i\in J_i=[x_{i-1},x_i]\) in each subinterval, the corresponding Riemann sum is

\[ S(f, P)=\sum_{i=1}^n f(x^*_i)(x_i-x_{i-1}), \]

where the tags may be chosen independently of one another.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Riemann sums approximate the accumulation of a function by finite weighted sums.

They provide the link between discrete approximations and continuous integration.

\(\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{4}f(t_i)\,(x_i-x_{i-1})\) is the shaded area: on each piece \([x_{i-1},x_i]\) a rectangle whose height is the value of \(f\) at a chosen point \(t_i\).

Move the tags with \(\theta\) and refine the partition: every tagged sum \(S(f,P)\) stays between \(L(f,P)\) and \(U(f,P)\), and the gap closes as \(n\) grows.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Riemann sums depend on both the partition and the choice of tags \(x^*_i\text{.}\)
  • On a regular subdivision, the tag \(x^*_i=x_{i-1}\) gives the left Riemann sum and \(x^*_i=x_i\) gives the right Riemann sum.

  • Because \(f\) is bounded, each subinterval has a finite supremum and infimum, so we may also form the upper and lower Riemann sums

    \[ \begin{aligned} U(f,P)&=\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\sup_{x\in J_i}f(x)\right)|J_i|,\\ L(f,P)&=\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\inf_{x\in J_i}f(x)\right)|J_i|, \end{aligned} \]

    which bracket every tagged Riemann sum on the same partition. These exist even when the extreme values are not attained. - As the mesh shrinks, the Riemann sums of an integrable function approach its integral, whatever tags are chosen. A single refinement need not improve a particular tagged sum, but it can only lower the upper sum and raise the lower sum.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Left and right Riemann sums approximate areas differently.
  • Regular subdivisions lead to uniform rectangle widths.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(a < b\) be real numbers, and consider a function \(f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) that is continuous on the interval \([a, b]\) and differentiable on \((a, b)\text{.}\) If we have \(f(a) = f(b)\text{,}\) then there exists a \(c\in (a, b)\) for which \(f'(c) = 0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Rolle’s theorem guarantees the existence of a stationary point when the function takes equal values at the endpoints, \(f(a)=f(b)\text{.}\)

It expresses the idea that a function returning to the same value must flatten somewhere in between.

Pick \(a\); the figure finds the next \(b\) with \(f(b)=f(a)\) and every \(c\in(a,b)\) with \(f'(c)=0\). The tent function is not differentiable at \(2\), and no horizontal tangent exists.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Continuity and differentiability are essential hypotheses.
  • The conclusion guarantees existence but not uniqueness.
  • Rolle’s theorem is a special case of the mean value theorem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=x^2-1\) on \([-1,1]\) satisfies Rolle’s theorem.
  • The sine function satisfies the hypotheses on suitable intervals.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: Let \(a < b\) be real numbers, and let \(f \colon (a, b) \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function which is twice-differentiable at its stationary point \(x_0\in(a,b)\text{.}\) Then \(x_0\) is a local maximum point of \(f\) if \(f''(x_0)<0\text{,}\) and it is a local minimum point of \(f\) if \(f''(x_0)>0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The second-order condition refines the first-order condition by analysing curvature.

It uses second derivatives to distinguish between local maxima and minima.

The figure marks every stationary point and its sign of \(f''\). The example \(2x^4-\frac13x^6\) has \(f''(0)=0\), so the condition is silent there, as are \(x^3\) and \(x^4\) at \(0\), one without and one with an extremum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A negative second derivative indicates local maximality.
  • A positive second derivative indicates local minimality.
  • A zero second derivative indicates that further analysis is needed.
  • The condition is sufficient but not necessary.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The function \(f(x)=2x^4-\frac{1}{3}x^6\) has three stationary points \(x=0\text{,}\) \(x=2\text{,}\) and \(x=-2\text{.}\) We plug \(x=0\text{,}\) \(2\text{,}\) and \(-2\) in \(f''(x)=24x^2-10x^4\) to find \(f''(2)=f''(-2)=-64<0\) and \(f''(0)=0\text{.}\) Then, we conclude that \(x=2\) and \(x=-2\) are local maximum points. Additionally, \(x=0\) has to be a local minimum point since it is the only stationary point between two local maximum points of a differentiable function.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Given an integer \(m\) (usually 0 or 1), a sequence \((a_n)_{n\geq m}\) is an ordered collection of elements \(a_n\) (e.g., numbers, vectors, functions):

\[ a_{m},\,a_{m+1},\,a_{m+2},\,\dots. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A sequence is an ordered list indexed by integers.

Order distinguishes sequences from sets and allows the study of limiting behaviour.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Sequences are functions defined on subsets of the integers.
  • Order matters in sequences.
  • Sequences may be finite or infinite.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) denotes an infinite sequence.
  • The sequence \((1,\,-1,\,1,\,-1,\,\dots)\) oscillates.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A set \(A\) is an unordered collection of objects. If \(x\) is an object, we say that \(x\) is an element of \(A\) or write \(x\in A\) if \(x\) lies in the collection; otherwise, we write \(x\notin A\text{.}\)

It provides the foundational language for all mathematical structures.

  • Sets may be finite or infinite.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The signum function \(\operatorname{sgn} \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) is defined by

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} \operatorname{sgn}(x)&=\begin{cases} \displaystyle \, \frac{|x|}{x},& x\neq 0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \, 0,& x= 0 \end{cases}\\[6pt] &=\begin{cases} \displaystyle \, 1,& x>0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \, 0,& x=0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \, -1,& x<0. \end{cases} \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The signum function extracts the sign information of a real number.

It compresses magnitude information into directional information.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The signum function takes values in \(\{-1,\,0,\,1\}\text{.}\)
  • It reflects the trichotomy of real numbers.
  • The function is discontinuous at zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{sgn}(3)=1\text{.}\)
  • \(\operatorname{sgn}(-2)=-1\text{.}\)
  • \(\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A point \(x_0\) is called a singularity of a function \(f\) if \(f\) fails to be defined or continuous at \(x=x_0\text{,}\) while being defined and continuous in a punctured neighbourhood of \(x_0\text{.}\)

Lecture 5 classifies these problem points by their one-sided limits:

  • Removable: the finite limit exists, but \(f(x_0)\) is missing or has the wrong value.
  • Jump: both one-sided limits are finite but unequal.
  • Infinite: at least one one-sided limit is \(+\infty\) or \(-\infty\text{.}\)
  • Oscillatory: a one-sided limit fails because of persistent oscillation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A singularity marks a point where a function fails to behave regularly, despite being well behaved arbitrarily close to that point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• At an interior point, \(f\) is continuous if and only if \(f(x_0^-)=f(x_0^+)=f(x_0)\text{;}\) a discontinuity is exactly a failure of this equality.
  • Several distinct things can go wrong at \(x_0\text{:}\) \(f(x_0)\) may be undefined while nearby values behave well; \(f\) may be defined but not continuous; nearby values may become unbounded; or nearby values may oscillate without approaching anything.
  • The word singularity returns in Lecture 12 for improper integrals: an integrand may be unbounded at an interior singularity, and the integral is then split there.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x) = (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1)\) has a removable discontinuity at \(x=1\text{.}\)
  • The piecewise function \(f(x)=x\) for \(x\leq 0\) and \(f(x)=x+1\) for \(x>0\) has a jump discontinuity at \(x=0\text{;}\) so does the signum function at the origin.
  • The function \(f(x)=1/x\) has an infinite discontinuity at \(x=0\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f(x) = \sin(1/x)\) has an oscillatory discontinuity at \(x=0\text{.}\)

The three graphs illustrate singularities at \(x=0\). The first is removable because changing the assigned value \(-1\) to the limit \(0\) restores continuity; the second has unequal one-sided limits \(0.5\) and \(1\); and the third, \(1/x\), has an infinite singularity.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Suppose that \(g(x)\leq f(x)\leq h(x)\) for every \(x\) sufficiently close to \(x_0\), except perhaps at \(x=x_0\) itself. If

\[ \lim_{x\to x_0}g(x)=\lim_{x\to x_0}h(x)=L, \]

then \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to x_0}f(x)=L\text{.}\)

For a one-sided limit, use the inequalities only on that side and replace all three limits by the matching one-sided limits.

The same statement holds for limits as \(x\to+\infty\) or \(x\to-\infty\): the inequalities need only hold for sufficiently large \(|x|\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The squeeze theorem shows that a function inherits its limit from two bounding functions.

The limits at the point of the lower and upper bounding functions must be the same finite value. Their common limiting band traps the middle function; a bound on its values alone would not force a limit.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The function must be bounded above and below by convergent functions.
  • Equality of the bounding limits forces convergence.
  • The theorem applies even when the middle function is difficult to analyse directly.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}x^2\sin(1/x)=0\) follows from squeezing between \(\pm x^2\text{.}\)

  • Oscillatory functions can converge when tightly bounded.

Zoom in on \(x_0=0\): however fast \(x^2\sin(1/x)\) oscillates, it stays between \(-x^2\) and \(x^2\), which both tend to \(0\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \((a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\text{,}\) \((b_n)_{n=1}^\infty\text{,}\) and \((c_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) be sequences of real numbers such that \(a_n\leq b_n\leq c_n\) for all \(n \geq 1\text{.}\) Suppose also that \((a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) and \((c_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) converge to the same limit \(L\text{.}\) Then \((b_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) also converges to \(L\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The squeeze theorem for sequences establishes convergence using termwise inequalities.

It reduces convergence questions to bounding arguments.

Shrink \(\varepsilon\): from the index where both \(a_n\) and \(c_n\) are inside the band, \(b_n\) is trapped inside too, so it converges to the same \(L\).

The inequalities keep each middle term between its lower and upper terms. Once both outer sequences enter a band about the common limit, the middle sequence lies in that same band.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The middle sequence \((b_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) must lie termwise between two convergent sequences.
  • Equality of outer limits enforces convergence of the middle sequence.
  • The theorem does not require monotonicity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(-1/n \le b_n \le 1/n\text{,}\) then \(b_n\to 0\text{.}\)
  • \(\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\left(n \cdot\sin(1/n)\right)= 1\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a differentiable function \(f\colon X\to\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) a stationary point of \(f\) is a point \(x_0\in X\) where its derivative is zero, i.e., \(f'(x_0)=0\text{;}\) the corresponding point \((x_0,f(x_0))\) on the graph of \(f\) is sometimes also called a stationary point.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A stationary point is where local change temporarily vanishes.

It identifies candidates for local extrema.

Every stationary point has a horizontal tangent. Most here are peaks or valleys, but \(x^3\) shows a stationary point that is neither.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Not every stationary point corresponds to an extremum.
  • Stationary points must be analysed further to determine behaviour.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=x^2\) has a stationary point at \(x=0\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f(x)=x^3\) has a stationary point that is not an extremum.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Where this appears in the course

Subsequences are not defined in the 2026-27 lectures. The definition is given inside the tutorial question that uses it (Tutorial 2), and this page records it in the same form.

Let \((a_n)_{n\ge m}\) be a sequence. A subsequence of \((a_n)\) is a new sequence \((a_{n_k})_{k\ge 1}\) obtained by selecting terms of \((a_n)\) along a strictly increasing sequence of indices \((n_k)_{k\ge 1}\) with \(n_k \ge m\):

\[ (a_{n_k})_{k\ge 1} = a_{n_1},\,a_{n_2},\,a_{n_3},\,\dots, \]

where \(m \le n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < \cdots.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A subsequence is what you get when you “thin out” a sequence while keeping the original order.

You are not allowed to reorder terms. You only choose some of them, further and further along the sequence.

Choose the indices \(n_k\): the even and odd subsequences of \(a_n=(-1)^n\left(1+\frac1n\right)\) converge to different limits, which is why the whole sequence diverges.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every subsequence of a sequence uses terms from the original sequence, but with a new index set \(n_1<n_2<\cdots\text{.}\)
  • If \(a_n \to L\text{,}\) then every subsequence \(a_{n_k}\) also converges to \(L\text{.}\)
  • Subsequence limits help detect non-convergence: if two subsequences converge to different limits, then the original sequence does not converge.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(a_n = (-1)^n\text{,}\) then \((a_{2k})_{k\ge 1} = 1,1,1,\dots\) and \((a_{2k-1})_{k\ge 1} = -1,-1,-1,\dots\) are subsequences.
  • If \(a_n = \dfrac{1}{n}\text{,}\) then \(a_{2k}=\dfrac{1}{2k}\) is a subsequence, and it still converges to \(0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\text{,}\) \(B\) be sets. We say that \(A\) is a subset of \(B\text{,}\) denoted \(A\subseteq B\text{,}\) if every element of \(A\) is also an element of \(B\text{,}\) i.e.,

\[ \text{for any object }x,\; x\in A \; \implies\; x\in B. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A subset describes containment between collections of objects.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every set is a subset of itself.
  • Subset relations are transitive, i.e., \(A\subseteq B\) and \(B\subseteq C\) implies \(A\subseteq C\text{.}\)
  • Proper subsets exclude equality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\{1,\,2\}\subseteq\{1,\,2,\,3\}\text{.}\)
  • \(\varnothing\) is a subset of every set.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The operation of subtraction \(x-y\) of two integers \(x\) and \(y\) is defined as

\[ x-y=x+(-y). \]

The result is called the difference between \(x\) and \(y\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Subtraction measures how one quantity differs from another.

It is defined using addition and negation to ensure algebraic consistency.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Subtraction is not commutative.
  • The difference \(x-y\) equals \(x+(-y)\text{.}\)
  • Subtraction extends addition within the integers.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(E\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be nonempty and bounded above. The supremum of \(E\) is its least upper bound, denoted by \(\sup E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The supremum captures the smallest value that bounds a set from above.

It allows precise description of upper limits even when no maximum exists.

Move the candidate \(u\): every number at or above \(\sup E\) is an upper bound, and for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some element of \(E\) lies within \(\varepsilon\) below it, which is what makes it the least one.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A supremum need not belong to the set.
  • By the least-upper-bound property (see real number) of \(\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) every nonempty subset of \(\mathbb{R}\) that is bounded above has a unique supremum.
  • In the extended real numbers, one uses the conventions \(\sup E=+\infty\) for a nonempty set with no upper bound and \(\sup\varnothing=-\infty\text{;}\) neither \(+\infty\) nor \(-\infty\) is a real number.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The supremum of \((0,1)\) is \(1\text{.}\)
  • The supremum of \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon x<2\}\) is \(2\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A function \(f\colon X\to Y\) is surjective if for every \(y \in Y\text{,}\) there exists an \(x \in X\) such that \(f (x) = y\text{.}\) In other words, a function is onto if its codomain is exactly its range.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Surjectivity describes how completely a function covers its codomain.

A surjective function ensures that no element of the codomain is left unused.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A function is surjective if every element of the codomain is attained.
  • Surjectivity depends on both the function rule and the chosen codomain.
  • Changing the codomain may change surjectivity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=x^3\) from \(\mathbb{R}\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) is surjective.
  • The function \(f(x)=x^2\) from \(\mathbb{R}\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) is not surjective.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For all real numbers \(x\) and \(y\text{,}\)

\[ |x+y|\leq |x|+|y|. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The triangle inequality bounds the size of a sum by the sizes of its components.

It formalizes the idea that direct paths are shorter than indirect ones.

In the top diagram, \(x\) and \(y\) have the same sign, so \(|x+y|=|x|+|y|\). In the bottom diagram their signs are opposite, so the displacements partly cancel. In general, equality holds precisely when \(xy\ge0\), including the case where either value is zero.

Walk \(x\), then \(y\): when they have the same sign the lengths add up exactly, and when the signs differ part of the walk is undone, so \(|x+y|<|x|+|y|\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Absolute values interact subadditively under addition.
  • The inequality provides fundamental bounds in analysis.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(|3+(-1)|\le |3|+|{-1}|\text{.}\)
  • \(|x-y|\le |x|+|y|\) for all real numbers \(x,y\text{.}\)

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For any two real numbers \(x\) and \(y\text{,}\) exactly one of the following is true: \(x<y\text{,}\) \(x=y\text{,}\) or \(x>y\text{.}\) Equivalently, for any real number \(x\text{,}\) exactly one of the following is true: \(x\) is zero, \(x\) is positive, or \(x\) is negative.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Trichotomy says that any two real numbers are comparable; together with transitivity of \(<\) it makes \(\mathbb{R}\) totally ordered.

It ensures that comparisons between real numbers are always decisive.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Exactly one of three relations holds between any two real numbers.
  • Trichotomy underpins order-based arguments.
  • Many proofs rely on splitting cases via trichotomy.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Complex numbers do not have this property: there is no compatible total order on \(\mathbb{C}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(x \in \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Consider the point \((\cos x, \sin x)\) on the unit circle \(\{(u,v)\in\mathbb{R}^2 \colon u^2+v^2=1\}\) obtained by rotating the point \((1,0)\) counterclockwise by an angle \(x\) (measured in radians). The functions \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\) are defined as the second and first coordinates of this point, respectively.

For all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) such that \(\cos x \neq 0\text{,}\) the tangent function is defined by \(\displaystyle \tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Trigonometric functions encode angular relationships using coordinates on the unit circle.

They provide periodic models for oscillatory behaviour.

The point at angle \(x\) on the unit circle is \((\cos x,\sin x)\): \(\cos x\) is its horizontal coordinate (red dashed), \(\sin x\) its vertical one (green dashed), and \(\tan x=\sin x/\cos x\).

Turn the angle \(x\) (or press play): the coordinates of the point on the unit circle trace out \(\cos x\) and \(\sin x\) on the right. Show \(\tan x\) to see it blow up where \(\cos x=0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Sine and cosine are defined for all real numbers.
  • Trigonometric functions are periodic.
  • Tangent is defined only where cosine is nonzero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\sin 0=0\) and \(\cos 0=1\text{.}\)
  • \(\tan x\) is undefined at \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}+\pi k\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Given two sets \(A\) and \(B\text{,}\) the union \(A\cup B\) of \(A\) and \(B\) is a set whose elements consist of all the elements which belong to \(A\) or \(B\) or both,

\[ \begin{aligned} x\in A\cup B \; &\iff \; x\in A \text{ or } x\in B\\ \;&\iff \; (x\in A)\lor (x\in B). \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The union of sets combines elements from multiple collections.

It formalizes logical disjunction in set-theoretic language.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Elements belong to the union if they belong to at least one set.
  • Union is commutative and associative, i.e., we have \(A\cup B=B\cup A\) and \(A\cup(B\cup C)=(A\cup B)\cup C\text{.}\)
  • The union with the empty set leaves a set unchanged.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(E\) be a subset of \(\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) and let \(M\) be a real number. We say that \(M\) is an upper bound for \(E\) if we have \(x \leq M\) for every element \(x\) in \(E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An upper bound limits a set from above without requiring attainment.

It formalizes constraints that restrict growth.

Every \(M\ge 1.1\) is an upper bound; the least one, \(\sup S=1.1\), is also \(\max S\).

The set \(E\) specifies which elements must be compared. The inequality \(x\le M\) must hold for every \(x\in E\); \(M\) need not belong to \(E\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A set may have many upper bounds.
  • Upper bounds need not belong to the set.
  • Upper bounds are not unique.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The set \((0,1)\) has upper bound \(1\text{.}\)
  • Any number greater than \(1\) is also an upper bound for \((0,1)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) The vertical line \(x=x_0\) is called a vertical asymptote of the curve \(y=f(x)\) if at least one of the following holds:

\[ \begin{aligned} \lim_{x\to x_0}f(x)&=+\infty,\\ \lim_{x\to x_0^+}f(x)&=+\infty,\\ \lim_{x\to x_0^-}f(x)&=+\infty,\\[6pt] \lim_{x\to x_0}f(x)&=-\infty,\\ \lim_{x\to x_0^+}f(x)&=-\infty,\\ \lim_{x\to x_0^-}f(x)&=-\infty. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A vertical asymptote describes unbounded behaviour near a finite input value.

\(f(x)\to+\infty\) as \(x\to1^+\) and \(f(x)\to-\infty\) as \(x\to1^-\): the line \(x=1\) is a vertical asymptote.

Shrink \(h\) and watch \(f(x_0-h)\) and \(f(x_0+h)\): the values run off to \(+\infty\) on one side and \(-\infty\) on the other. Change the sign of \(k\) to swap the sides.

Divergence to infinity at a finite input is the analytic condition behind the vertical line. At least one relevant one-sided limit must diverge; the two sides need not have the same sign.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Vertical asymptotes arise from divergence at finite points.
  • One-sided divergence is sufficient.
  • Vertical asymptotes are detected using limits.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=1/x\) has a vertical asymptote at \(x=0\text{.}\)
  • Rational functions often exhibit vertical asymptotes at zeros of the denominator.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A zero of a function (also called a root or \(x\)-intercept) is any input value that makes the function's output equal to zero

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Graphically, a zero of function is where the function's graph crosses or touches the \(x\)-axis.

The zeros of \(f\) are the \(x\)-intercepts of its graph: \(f(x_1)=f(x_2)=f(x_3)=0\) for \(f(x)=x^3-3x+1\).

Shift the graph with \(c\) and count the zeros: three crossings become a touch and then a single crossing. At a touching zero the graph meets the \(x\)-axis without crossing it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • A zero of a function is a solution to the equation \(f(x)=0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The zeros of the quadratic polynomial \(f(x)=x^2-1\) are \(x=1\) and \(x=-1\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f(x)=2^x\) does not have any zeros.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An algorithm is a prescribed sequence of computational rules for solving a problem. In the iterative methods considered in the course, these rules are applied repeatedly; each repetition is an iteration.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An algorithm replaces an unavailable closed-form answer with a sequence of manageable calculations. A stopping condition specifies when the required answer has been obtained.

For the optimization algorithms in this course, the optimization model specifies the objective to improve and the constraints that every acceptable answer must satisfy.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The simplex method, network algorithms, and dynamic programming use different problem structures.
  • An iteration need not strictly improve the objective: a degenerate simplex pivot can leave its value unchanged.
  • A heuristic is a solution procedure without a general guarantee of optimality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Simplex checks its objective-row sign condition; the shortest-path method settles vertices until the destination is reached; flow augmentation stops when no augmenting path remains; dynamic programming advances through stages.

  • A simplex iteration exchanges a basic and a nonbasic variable.
  • A spanning-tree algorithm repeatedly adds an eligible edge.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The ambulance location model selects a minimum number of station towns while ensuring that every town is within 18 minutes of a selected station. Let \(y_j=1\) if a station is placed at town \(j\), and let \(N_i=\{j\colon t_{ij}\le18\}\). Then

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_{j=1}^6y_j,\\ \sum_{j\in N_i}y_j\ge1\ (i=1,\ldots,6),\\ y_j\in\{0,1\}. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Each coverage constraint requires at least one sufficiently close station. A station may cover several towns and a town may be covered by several stations.

This is a binary integer program: each station decision is zero or one, and linear coverage constraints ensure that every town is served.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Include the town itself because its travel time to itself is zero.
  • The threshold includes exactly 18 minutes.
  • This is the set-covering structure illustrated by the exercise; no station-capacity limit is specified.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The dashed links indicate travel times at most 18 minutes; the displayed positions are schematic rather than a geographical scale.

  • Town 1 can be covered from towns 1 or 4, giving \(y_1+y_4\ge1\).
  • Town 3 can be covered from towns 3 or 5, giving \(y_3+y_5\ge1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An artificial variable \(R_i\ge0\) is introduced temporarily into an equality or a converted \(\ge\) constraint to construct an initial basis. It is added with coefficient \(+1\) and initially takes the nonnegative right-hand-side value while the other variables in that row are zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Artificial variables make the auxiliary starting problem feasible. They have no physical interpretation and must be driven to zero to satisfy the original equations.

Augmented form first expresses inequalities as equations with slack or surplus variables. Artificial variables then supply temporary basic columns when those genuine added variables do not provide a feasible starting basis.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• They differ from slack and surplus variables, which record genuine inequalities.
  • The first phase of the two-phase method maximizes the negative sum of artificial variables.
  • The original constraints are recovered when every artificial variable is zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, setting \(x_A=x_B=S_1=0\) gives the initial artificial basis \(R_1=R_2=6\). Minimizing \(R_1+R_2\) is equivalent to maximizing its negative, as used in Phase I.

  • \(2x_1+3x_2=6\) becomes \(2x_1+3x_2+R_1=6\).
  • \(3x_1-x_2\ge4\) becomes \(3x_1-x_2-S_1+R_2=4\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: In a square one-to-one assignment problem, adding a constant \(a_i\) to every cost in row \(i\), or a constant \(b_j\) to every cost in column \(j\), preserves the set of optimal assignments. Every complete assignment's cost changes by the same total \(\displaystyle \sum_i a_i+\sum_j b_j\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Every assignment uses each row and each column exactly once. Uniform changes along a row or column therefore change the baseline cost without changing which assignment is best.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Subtracting row and column minima is a valid transformation.
  • The Hungarian uncovered-entry adjustment is equivalent to suitable row and column changes.
  • For a maximum-profit assignment, negate profits and add a constant large enough to make the resulting costs nonnegative.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, subtracting \(a_1=2\) from row 1 lowers each complete assignment cost by 2. More generally, subtracting row amounts \(a_i\) and column amounts \(b_j\) changes every complete total by \(\displaystyle -\sum_i a_i-\sum_j b_j\).

Assignment pairs Original total Transformed total \((1,1),(2,3),(3,2)\) \(4+7+1=12\) \(2+7+1=10\) \((1,2),(2,1),(3,3)\) \(2+4+6=12\) \(0+4+6=10\) \((1,3),(2,2),(3,1)\) \(8+3+3=14\) \(6+3+3=12\)
  • If row minima are 2, 5, 6, and 4, subtracting them reduces every assignment cost by 17.
  • Transforming profits \(p_{ij}\) into costs \(M-p_{ij}\) changes a complete assignment objective to \(\displaystyle nM-\sum_i p_{i,\pi(i)}\), where \(\pi(i)\) is the column assigned to row \(i\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The assignment problem pairs \(n\) agents with \(n\) tasks so that each agent receives exactly one task and each task exactly one agent. If \(c_{ij}\) is the cost of assigning agent \(i\) to task \(j\), a binary model is

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^nc_{ij}x_{ij},\qquad \sum_jx_{ij}=1,\\ \sum_ix_{ij}=1,\qquad x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
One-to-one matching couples the choices: assigning a task to one agent removes that task from consideration for the others. The Hungarian algorithm solves this structure directly.

The displayed binary integer program uses a zero-or-one variable for each possible pair; its row and column equations enforce exactly one partner on each side.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Costs can represent execution times as well as monetary amounts.
  • Unequal numbers of agents and tasks can be handled with dummy entries.
  • Task quotas can be modelled by duplicating agent rows into separate slots.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated three-agent instance has \(3!=6\) complete assignments. The highlighted pairs have total cost \(4+7+1=12\), which is optimal. For this assignment formulation with integer data, an integral optimal solution exists even after relaxing the binary restrictions.

  • The main example assigns machines 1, 2, 3, 4 to jobs 1, 4, 2, 3, with cost 20.
  • Machines can be assigned to locations or players to field positions.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The augmented form of the course's initial LP models replaces each \(\le\) functional constraint by an equality with a nonnegative slack variable. For \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\le \boldsymbol{b}\), \(\boldsymbol{x}\ge0\), this gives

\[ \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{s}=\boldsymbol{b},\qquad \boldsymbol{x}\ge0,\quad \boldsymbol{s}\ge0, \]

with the same objective in the original variables.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Adding slacks changes the algebraic representation, not the allowed original decisions. Each original feasible vector determines exactly one vector of slack values.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Count auxiliary variables when determining the dimension of the equality system used for a basis.
  • For \(m\) independent equalities in \(n\) augmented variables, a basis contains \(m\) variables.
  • Artificial variables used for other constraint types require a feasibility phase; they cannot simply remain free in the final model.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, \(s_1\) measures unused finishing hours, \(s_2\) unused carpentry hours, and \(s_3\) unused soldier-demand allowance. The three equations contain five variables, so a basis sets two nonbasic variables to zero.

  • Two original variables and two slack variables give four augmented variables.
  • The constraints \(2x_1+x_2+s_1=10\) and \(x_1+3x_2+s_2=15\) have initial solution \((0,0,10,15)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The augmenting path algorithm starts with a feasible flow, initially zero in the course examples. Find a source-to-sink augmenting path, augment by its bottleneck \(\delta\), decrease each traversed residual capacity by \(\delta\), increase the opposite residual capacity by \(\delta\), and repeat. If no augmenting path remains, the current flow is maximum.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The residual network allows both new routing and correction of earlier routing. The stopping condition certifies that no further flow increase is possible.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Maintain flow conservation after every augmentation.
  • The integer capacities in the exercises allow integer augmentations and finite termination.
  • Recover original flows from the final residual values, taking edge directions into account.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
On an original forward edge the augmentation adds \(\delta\) to its flow; on a backward residual edge it subtracts \(\delta\). With integer capacities and an integral starting flow, each augmentation increases the value by at least 1, so only finitely many are possible.

  • The main example augments by \(5,2,1,4,1,2\), totalling 15.
  • The last residual network cannot reach the sink T from the source S through positive residual directions.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An augmenting path is a source-to-sink path in the residual network with strictly positive residual capacity in every traversed direction. Its residual capacity, or bottleneck, is

\[ \delta=\min_{e\text{ on the path}}r_e. \]

An additional \(\delta\) units of net source-to-sink flow can be assigned along it.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The smallest remaining capacity limits the whole path. A backward residual segment reduces an original flow while still increasing the total source-to-sink value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• All residual directions on the path must be feasible.
  • Augmenting by the bottleneck saturates at least one residual direction.
  • A path may use both forward and reverse directions relative to original edges.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated edge labels are flow/capacity. The red path \(A-C-E-F\) has residual capacities \(3,4,3\), so \(\delta=\min(3,4,3)=3\) increases total flow from 5 to 8. A feasible flow is maximum exactly when no source-to-sink augmenting path remains.

  • The first S-A-D-T augmentation in the video has bottleneck 5.
  • A later S-B-E-D-A-C-T path cancels part of the earlier A-D flow and adds two units overall.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A basic feasible solution is a basic solution of an equality-form LP with all its variables nonnegative. A basic solution with a negative variable is a basic infeasible solution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Simplex maintains this combination of algebraic structure and feasibility. It can then improve the objective without leaving the allowed region.

Each intersection of two boundaries corresponds to a basic solution. The feasible ones (filled) are the basic feasible solutions; the hollow ones are basic but infeasible.

A feasible solution satisfies the original restrictions. Here that test is applied after the nonbasic variables have been set to zero and the basic equations solved.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Nonbasic variables are set to zero; feasibility is checked through the resulting basic values.
  • A basic variable may be zero in a degenerate solution.
  • For the course LPs with a finite optimum, an optimal basic feasible solution exists.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The filled points in the illustrated region \(F\) are its feasible corners; the hollow boundary intersections violate at least one nonnegativity restriction in the augmented system.

  • \((x_1,x_2,s_1,s_2)=(0,0,10,15)\) is basic feasible in the main simplex example.
  • \((0,10,0,-15)\) is basic but infeasible.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For \(m\) independent linear equality constraints in \(n\) variables, a basic solution is obtained by choosing \(n-m\) variables to be nonbasic and setting them to zero, then uniquely solving for the other \(m\) variables. The chosen basic columns must be linearly independent.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Choosing a basis selects an algebraic candidate for a corner. Some choices fail to give a unique solution and some give negative values, so not every choice is a feasible candidate.

Augmented form supplies an equality system by including slack or surplus variables. A basis selects independent columns of that system, so the corresponding basic values can be solved uniquely.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• There are at most \(\binom{n}{m}\) basis choices.
  • A basic solution may be feasible or infeasible.
  • Different bases can represent the same degenerate solution.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated system has \(m=3\) equations and \(n=5\) variables:

\[ \begin{aligned} 2x_s+x_t+s_1&=100,\\ x_s+x_t+s_2&=80,\\ x_s+s_3&=40. \end{aligned} \]

Setting two nonbasic variables to zero gives the following basic solutions. The nonnegative solutions are corners of the shaded feasible region; negative slack values identify the red, infeasible points.

Variables set to zero \((x_s,x_t)\) \((s_1,s_2,s_3)\) Feasible? \(x_s,x_t\) \((0,0)\) \((100,80,40)\) Yes \(s_1,s_2\) \((20,60)\) \((0,0,20)\) Yes \(x_t,s_3\) \((40,0)\) \((20,40,0)\) Yes \(s_2,s_3\) \((40,40)\) \((-20,0,0)\) No \(x_t,s_1\) \((50,0)\) \((0,30,-10)\) No

There are at most \(\binom53=10\) basis choices for this system. The figure shows five of their corresponding basic solutions.

  • The four-variable example has at most \(\binom42=6\) bases.
  • Week 2 practice 4 has five variables and two equalities, but only eight basic solutions from ten candidate choices.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A basic variable belongs to the selected basis of an equality-form LP. Its value is obtained from the constraint equations after the nonbasic variables have been set to zero. With \(m\) independent equalities, the basis contains \(m\) variables.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Being basic describes a variable's role in the current representation. It does not mean the variable must have a positive value.

Constructing a basic solution fixes the nonbasic variables at zero; the remaining unknowns solved from the independent constraint equations are its basic variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In a canonical tableau, a basic variable has coefficient 1 in its row and 0 in the other rows, including the objective row.
  • A zero-valued basic variable makes the basic feasible solution degenerate.
  • A pivot replaces one member of the basis.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the illustrated canonical tableau, the basic variables are \(x_t,s_3,x_s\). Their unit columns let their values \(60,20,20\) be read from the right-hand side when \(s_1=s_2=0\).

  • The initial simplex example uses the two slacks as basic variables.
  • At the optimal basis, \(x_1=3\) and \(x_2=4\) are basic.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The bin packing problem assigns every item to a container, subject to a common capacity per container, and minimizes the number of containers used. If item \(i\) has weight \(w_i\) and a container has capacity \(C\), the weights assigned to each container must sum to at most \(C\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Combining items efficiently can reduce the number of containers. A simple packing rule is easy to apply, but need not find the best combination.

A packing is a feasible solution only if every item is assigned once and every container respects capacity. A heuristic can construct such a packing quickly, giving an upper bound even when optimality has not been proved.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Each item must be packed exactly once without splitting it.
  • Any feasible packing provides an upper bound on the minimum number of containers.
  • The total-weight bound is \(\displaystyle \lceil\sum_i w_i/C\rceil\); it need not be attainable. This follows by aggregating the capacity requirements.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure is a separate four-item illustration with weights \(15,30,20,35\) and capacity \(C=50\). Its lower bound is \(\lceil100/50\rceil=2\), attained by the displayed packing \(\{15,35\}\) and \(\{30,20\}\). This proves optimality for the illustrated instance, rather than for the 15-item course exercise.

  • The exercise has 15 items and container capacity 50.
  • First-fit uses five containers, while the solution sheet states that four suffice.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A binary integer program (BIP) is a linear optimization model in which all decision variables are binary. For variables \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\), the domain is \(y\in\{0,1\}^n\) before imposing the remaining constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
BIPs describe combinations of yes-or-no choices. Even a moderate number of choices creates many candidate combinations, motivating methods such as branch-and-bound.

Integer linear programming imposes integer restrictions on a linear model. Restricting every integer decision further to a binary variable gives the special zero-or-one model considered here.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• There are \(2^n\) binary assignments before functional constraints eliminate infeasible combinations.
  • Its LP relaxation replaces each binary restriction by \(0\le y_j\le1\).
  • The objective can count selected alternatives or weight them by costs or returns.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Project selection maximizes the return from projects under yearly budgets.
  • Ambulance location minimizes the number of selected station sites.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A bipartite matching pairs entities from two distinct groups, with each selected pair containing one member of each group and no entity used in more than one pair. A complete one-to-one assignment between equally sized groups is a perfect bipartite matching.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The separation into two groups distinguishes assignment from pairing odd-degree vertices in the Chinese postman problem (CPP). This special structure supports the Hungarian algorithm.

In the network representation, entities are vertices and allowed cross-group pairs are edges. A matching selects edges without sharing an endpoint.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Agents and tasks form the two groups in an assignment problem.
  • A matching need not use every entity unless completeness is required.
  • Maximum zero-cost matching can be represented as a unit-capacity flow problem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Grey edges are allowed pairs and green edges form the matching. It contains \(|M|=3\) pairs, equal to the number of jobs, so no larger matching is possible; the fourth worker remains unmatched. A perfect matching would cover every vertex on both sides and requires equal group sizes.

  • A machine-job pair connects the machine group to the job group.
  • The CPP odd-vertex pairing is nonbipartite because all paired vertices belong to one common set.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For a maximization integer program with incumbent value \(L\), a branch-and-bound node can be pruned if its LP relaxation is infeasible, its relaxed optimizer satisfies all integer restrictions, or its relaxed upper bound \(U\) satisfies \(U\le L\). In the integral case, update the incumbent if appropriate. For minimization, reverse the bound comparison.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Each condition proves that further subdivision of that node cannot improve the best known value. This is what makes the method more efficient than full enumeration.

The incumbent solution is the best integer-feasible answer already found. Its value supplies the threshold against which a node bound is tested before discarding that node.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For maximization, a valid global upper bound is the maximum of the incumbent value and the LP bounds of active unresolved nodes.
  • At completion the incumbent proves the optimal value.
  • Pruning equality with the incumbent is sufficient to find the optimum value, but can discard other equally optimal solutions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For minimization, prune a node when its relaxed lower bound \(z_R\), the optimal value of its LP relaxation, is at least the incumbent value.

  • A node with upper bound 3.3 can be discarded once the incumbent is 3.4.
  • In week 3 practice 9, the branch \(x_3\ge7\) is infeasible because \(x_2+3x_3\le20\) and \(x_2\ge0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Branch-and-bound solves an integer program by solving LP relaxations of subproblems, splitting subproblems when restricted variables are fractional, and discarding subproblems whose bounds cannot improve the best feasible integer solution. If \(x_j=v\) is fractional, branch into

\[ x_j\le\lfloor v\rfloor\qquad\text{and}\qquad x_j\ge\lceil v\rceil. \]

For a binary variable these branches fix it to 0 and 1.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The branches retain every possible integer solution while excluding the current fractional value. Bounds prevent unnecessary exploration of parts of the search tree.

Optimization bounds let the algorithm discard a subproblem without enumerating its integer solutions: its relaxed bound cannot improve the best feasible value already found.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Carry all ancestor branching constraints into each child.
  • Prune for infeasibility, an integral relaxed optimum, or an uncompetitive bound.
  • Continue until every remaining possibility is resolved or bounded by the incumbent.
  • Branching choices affect the work required but not the correctly proven optimum.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure branches on \(x_2=1.25\), giving \(x_2\le\lfloor1.25\rfloor=1\) or \(x_2\ge\lceil1.25\rceil=2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The bus scheduling model chooses nonnegative integer counts \(x_i\) of buses starting in each of six consecutive four-hour intervals. Each bus operates for two intervals. With requirements \(d=(4,8,10,7,12,4)\), the cyclic model is

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_{i=1}^6x_i,\\ x_{i-1}+x_i\ge d_i\ (i=1,\ldots,6),\\ x_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}, \end{gathered} \]

where \(x_0=x_6\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The variables count shift starts, while each coverage constraint counts all buses operating in an interval. The wrap-around term links the last daily shift to the first interval.

Linear program formulation turns shift counts into decision variables and coverage requirements into linear inequalities. Because every variable counts buses, the model is a pure integer program, not a continuous staffing approximation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Eight-hour operation covers exactly two consecutive four-hour intervals.
  • Coverage may exceed the minimum demand.
  • The repeating daily interpretation is the assumption used to formulate the midnight boundary.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The midnight-to-4 AM constraint is \(x_6+x_1\ge4\).
  • The 4 PM-to-8 PM requirement gives \(x_4+x_5\ge12\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The course's capacity expansion model uses a binary purchase variable \(y\) to switch additional capacity on or off. If existing capacity is 100 and a new machine supplies 50 more, the restriction is

\[ x_1+x_2\le100+50y,\qquad y\in\{0,1\}. \]

Here \(x_1,x_2\) are the production quantities that share this capacity, and \(y=1\) means the additional machine is purchased.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The capacity right-hand side becomes a linear expression in the purchase decision. This links operational quantities to a discrete investment choice.

The binary variable \(y\) encodes the purchase decision. The capacity constraint then permits production up to the old capacity plus the extra capacity exactly when \(y=1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With \(y=0\), the capacity limit is 100.
  • With \(y=1\), the capacity limit is 150.
  • Any specified acquisition cost must also be represented in the economic objective or budget; the isolated course example only demonstrates the capacity restriction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated point \(A=(50,40)\) uses capacity 90 and is allowed with \(y=0\); \(B=(70,50)\) uses 120 and requires \(y=1\).

  • A plan with total production 120 requires \(y=1\).
  • A plan with total production 90 satisfies the capacity restriction with \(y=0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Chinese postman problem (CPP) finds a minimum-length closed route traversing every edge at least once in a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths. To solve the course version, find a minimum-cost pairing of the odd-degree vertices using shortest-path distances, duplicate the corresponding paths, and construct an Euler tour in the resulting network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Every street must be covered. Repeated edges are necessary only to make a closed covering route possible, and the matching step chooses a minimum total extra length.

Vertex degree identifies the odd vertices preventing an Euler tour. A shortest path problem gives the least added length for each possible odd-vertex pair; minimum-weight perfect matching chooses those pairs jointly at minimum total added length.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If every vertex already has even degree, any Euler tour is optimal.
  • The optimal cost is the sum of original edge lengths plus the minimum pairing cost.
  • The shortest path between paired vertices can contain intermediate vertices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, \(A\) and \(C\) are the two odd-degree vertices. Their direct edge costs 4, compared with \(2+3=5\) via \(D\) or \(3+2=5\) via \(B\). Duplicating the direct edge gives route length \(14+4=18\). The dashed edge denotes this extra copy.

  • The five-vertex example has total edge length 25 and minimum pairing cost 7, giving CPP value 32.
  • Pairing A with D duplicates A-C-D, while pairing B with E duplicates B-E.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The classical EOQ model, based on the economic order quantity (EOQ), assumes deterministic constant demand rate \(D>0\), instantaneous batch replenishment, no shortages, fixed setup cost \(K>0\) per order, and holding cost \(h>0\) per unit per unit time. A constant unit purchasing price can be excluded when optimizing. For batch size \(y>0\), relevant total cost per unit time (TCU) is

\[ TCU(y)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Inventory repeatedly drops linearly from the batch size to zero. Large batches reduce setup frequency but increase average stock.

Move \(y\): the setup cost rate \(KD/y\) falls and the holding cost rate \(hy/2\) rises. The right panel shows the inventory sawtooth for this batch size.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Average stock is \(y/2\) and ordering cycle length is \(y/D\).
  • The cost is strictly convex for positive \(y\).
  • The model optimizes a continuous order quantity; discrete purchasing units require checking feasible nearby quantities.
  • Using a mean demand to approximate stochastic demand does not incorporate its variability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The phone data \(D=2\), \(K=605\), \(h=5\) give an optimal batch of 22.
  • The exercise uses average weekly demand 100 while explicitly omitting its standard deviation 10 from the EOQ calculation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An undirected network is connected if every pair of vertices can be joined by a path. It is disconnected if at least one pair cannot be joined.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Connectedness establishes that all parts of the network can be reached from one another. The spanning-tree and undirected routing problems in the course assume it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A disconnected network has no spanning tree covering all its vertices.
  • A tree is connected as well as cycle-free.
  • For a directed flow network, available directed routes must still be checked; undirected connectedness alone does not imply flow to the sink.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A chain of roads linking A to B and B to C connects all three towns.
  • Two groups of towns with no road between the groups are disconnected.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A constraint is a requirement that an allowed decision must satisfy. A linear functional constraint has the form

\[ a_{i1}x_1+\cdots+a_{in}x_n\le b_i, \]

or the corresponding equality or \(\ge\) inequality. The \(a_{ij}\) are constraint coefficients and \(b_i\) is the right-hand side.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Constraints translate capacity limits, demand requirements, and other restrictions into mathematics. Feasibility requires all constraints to hold together.

The objective function \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is the quantity to maximize (for example, profit) or minimize (for example, cost). Functional constraints describe what an allowed decision must satisfy, such as resource limits or demand requirements. Domain restrictions specify signs or integrality.

In the diagram, blue identifies decision variables, whose values the model determines; red identifies model parameters, the given data \(c_j\), \(a_{ij}\) and \(b_i\). In general, the model is \(\max/\min\ f(\boldsymbol{x})\) subject to \(\boldsymbol{x}\in F\), where the constraints define the feasible set \(F\). A solution assigns values to all variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A capacity limit commonly gives a \(\le\) constraint; a minimum requirement commonly gives a \(\ge\) constraint.
  • An equality represents an exact requirement or balance.
  • Multiplication by a negative number reverses an inequality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x_s+x_t\le80\) limits carpentry use in the Giapetto production model.
  • \(800x_A+1000x_B\ge8000\) requires enough calories in the diet problem, where \(x_A,x_B\) are the pounds of feeds A and B.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Contingent decisions are binary choices whose admissibility depends on other choices. If decision 2 is allowed only when decision 1 is yes, the implication is represented by

\[ y_2\le y_1,\qquad y_1,y_2\in\{0,1\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The inequality prohibits precisely the combination “decision 2 yes, decision 1 no.” It does not force decision 2 to be selected when decision 1 is selected.

A binary variable turns each yes-or-no choice into zero or one. Checking those four possible pairs shows that \(y_2\le y_1\) excludes exactly the forbidden implication outcome.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If decision 2 must be yes when decision 1 is no, use \(y_1+y_2\ge1\).
  • If decision 3 is allowed only when both decisions 1 and 2 are yes, use \(y_3\le y_1\) and \(y_3\le y_2\).
  • If \(y_1=1\) and \(y_2=0\) must imply \(y_3=0\), use \(y_1-y_2+y_3\le1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• With binaries \(W_{LA}=1\) if a warehouse is built at location LA and \(F_{LA}=1\) if a factory is built there, \(W_{LA}\le F_{LA}\) requires a local factory before a warehouse can be built.
  • \(y_1+y_2+y_3\le2\) rules out all three yes decisions together.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For continuous demand with finite mean and CDF \(F\), the newsvendor expected cost \(G(y)\) of ordering \(y\), with underage cost \(b\) and overage cost \(h\), satisfies

\[ G'(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b. \]

If \(F\) is continuous and strictly increasing through \(\beta=b/(b+h)\) and that quantile lies in the allowed quantity domain, the unique optimum is

\[ y^*=F^{-1}(\beta). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The optimal stock is a quantile of demand, determined by the cost balance. Continuity alone does not guarantee uniqueness if the CDF has a flat segment at the critical probability.

Where \(G'(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b\) is zero the CDF equals \(\beta\); read \(y^*=F^{-1}(\beta)\) off the right panel.

The critical ratio fixes the target demand probability from the relative underage and overage costs. The continuous rule selects a demand quantile at that probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For uniform demand on \([a,u]\), the optimum is \(a+(u-a)\beta\).
  • For the course normal demand approximation \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), it is \(\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(\beta)\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF.
  • A continuous demand approximation may give a noninteger answer even when actual items are indivisible.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Meal demand uniform on \([80,120]\) with \(\beta=0.6\) gives 104 meals.
  • Normal meal demand with mean 100 and standard deviation 20 gives about 105.07.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
If \(\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)},\ldots,\boldsymbol{x}^{(k)}\) are optimal solutions of the same LP and \(\alpha_j\ge0\) with \(\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_j=1\), then

\[ \boldsymbol{x}=\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_j\boldsymbol{x}^{(j)} \]

is also optimal. Such a weighted average is a convex combination.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Linear constraints are preserved by these weighted averages, and the linear objective remains equal to the common optimum. Two optimal corners therefore generate an entire optimal segment.

For any \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) the mixture \(\alpha \boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}+(1-\alpha)\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}\) of the two optimal corners is feasible and has the same optimal \(z\).

Multiple optimal solutions provide distinct feasible points with the same optimal objective value. Linear constraints preserve feasibility between them, and the linear objective preserves that value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Weights must be nonnegative and sum to one.
  • For two points use \(\alpha\) and \(1-\alpha\), with \(0\le\alpha\le1\).
  • The property concerns continuous LP feasibility; averaging integer solutions need not preserve integrality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated objective \(2x_s+2x_t\), the edge between \((0,80)\) and \((20,60)\) is optimal with value 160. The displayed combination \(\tfrac{1}{4}(0,80)+\tfrac{3}{4}(20,60)=(15,65)\) has the same value. In general, the combined value is \(\displaystyle \sum_j\alpha_jz^*=z^*\).

  • Combining \((5,0)\) and \((3,4)\) gives \((3+2\alpha,4-4\alpha)\), all with value 20.
  • Combining \((2,3)\) and \((0,6)\) gives \((2\alpha,6-3\alpha)\); \(\alpha=1/2\) gives \((1,9/2)\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For the LPs in the course with a nonempty feasible region in nonnegative variables, if a finite optimum exists, at least one feasible corner point attains it. Consequently, a unique optimal solution must be a feasible corner point. If a bounded feasible region has multiple optimal solutions, at least two of its corner points are optimal.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This result allows an LP to be solved without testing every point in its feasible region. Simplex uses the algebraic counterparts of these corners.

Turn the objective with \(c_1\) and \(c_2\): whenever a finite optimum exists, some feasible corner attains it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The existence of a finite optimum is essential.
  • The bounded-region qualification in the multiple-corner statement matters when the feasible region has rays.
  • Every convex combination of optimal corners is optimal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure evaluates \(z=3x_s+2x_t\) at its five feasible corners: the values are \(0,120,160,180,160\). The largest is 180 at \((20,60)\), and the orange line is the objective line through that point.

  • The manufacturing optimum \((2,5)\) is a feasible corner.
  • For the course LP with objective \(4x_1+2x_2\) and boundary \(2x_1+x_2\le11\), an entire feasible boundary segment attains 22.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In an LP with \(n\) decision variables, a corner point is a point determined by the intersection of constraint boundaries with \(n\) independent boundary equations. At least \(n\) constraints are therefore active there, counting nonnegativity boundaries. A corner point is feasible only if it satisfies all constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Corner points are the finite candidates exploited by the graphical and simplex methods in the course. Merely counting repeated or dependent constraints does not determine a corner.

Every intersection of two boundaries is a candidate corner. Filled points are feasible corners; hollow ones lie outside the region.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In two dimensions, two nonparallel active boundaries determine a corner.
  • Extra active constraints can occur at a degenerate corner.
  • Not every intersection of boundaries is feasible.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated feasible corner \((20,60)\) solves \(2x_s+x_t=100\) and \(x_s+x_t=80\). The boundary intersection \((50,0)\) is infeasible because it violates the soldier-demand limit; it is not an extreme point of the feasible set. Feasible corners correspond to basic feasible solutions of the augmented model.

  • The lines \(x_2=5\) and \(2x_1+x_2=9\) intersect at \((2,5)\).
  • The nonnegativity boundaries meet at the origin \((0,0)\).
