docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For newsvendor selling price \(p\), unit cost \(c\) and salvage value \(s\), with overage cost \(h=c-s>0\) and underage cost \(b=p-c>0\), the critical ratio is

\[ \beta=\frac{b}{b+h}=\frac{p-c}{p-s},\qquad 0<\beta<1. \]

It is the cumulative-demand probability used to select the optimal stock quantile.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A large underage cost justifies a higher demand quantile; a large overage cost justifies a lower one. The ratio balances the two marginal risks.

Change \(p\), \(c\) and \(s\): \(\beta=b/(b+h)\) moves, and the optimal stock is the demand quantile where the CDF reaches \(\beta\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For integer demand, increasing from \(y\) to \(y+1\) helps while \(F(y)<\beta\).
  • For the continuous strictly increasing CDFs used in the examples, the optimum solves \(F(y^*)=\beta\).
  • The ratio is not the expected fraction of demand served.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Newspapers with \(b=1.5\) and \(h=2\) have \(\beta=3/7\).
  • Meals with \(b=3.3\) and \(h=2.2\) have \(\beta=0.6\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the course's network terminology, a cycle or tour is a path that starts and ends at the same vertex. Because its path convention requires distinct edges, no edge is repeated within such a cycle.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Cycles return to their starting point. They are useful for routes that must return home and are excluded when constructing a tree.

docs.text:
• An Euler tour is a closed traversal using every edge exactly once.
  • A tree contains no cycles.
  • In the Chinese postman problem, “tour” is also used for a closed route that may repeat original edges; repeated copies are distinct in the augmented network.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The red cycle in the figure is \(B-D-E-C-B\). An undirected network with no cycles is a forest; when it is also connected, it is a tree.

  • Three edges \(A-B\), \(B-C\), and \(C-A\) form a cycle.
  • Adding an edge between two already connected vertices of a tree creates a cycle.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A decision variable represents a quantity or choice that the model is intended to determine. Its definition specifies its practical meaning, unit, and allowed values. A solution assigns a value to every decision variable.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A clear variable definition connects a mathematical expression to a real decision. It also determines whether fractions, negative values, or only yes-or-no choices make sense.

The objective function \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is the quantity to maximize (for example, profit) or minimize (for example, cost). Functional constraints describe what an allowed decision must satisfy, such as resource limits or demand requirements. Domain restrictions specify signs or integrality.

In the diagram, blue identifies decision variables, whose values the model determines; red identifies model parameters, the given data \(c_j\), \(a_{ij}\) and \(b_i\). In general, the model is \(\max/\min\ f(\boldsymbol{x})\) subject to \(\boldsymbol{x}\in F\), where the constraints define the feasible set \(F\). A solution assigns values to all variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The number of decision variables is the dimension of the original optimization problem.
  • Input data such as available hours are parameters rather than decisions.
  • Variable restrictions must be stated explicitly.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x_s\) denotes the number of wooden soldiers to produce in the Giapetto production model.
  • \(x_A\) denotes pounds of feed A in a pig diet problem.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A degenerate basic feasible solution has at least one basic variable equal to zero. A degenerate pivot has a zero step length (the minimum-ratio test gives \(\theta=0\), so the entering variable stays at zero) and can change the basis without changing the solution vector or objective value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
At a degenerate point, several constraints become active together. More than one basis may describe the same point, so a simplex iteration need not correspond to visible movement.

A zero ratio in the minimum-ratio test permits an entering variable to replace a basic variable without increasing the step size. This simplex pivot changes the basis while leaving the represented point and objective unchanged.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A tie for the minimum ratio can produce a degenerate basic feasible solution.
  • Zero ratios must be considered when the pivot-column coefficient is positive.
  • The basic/nonbasic distinction is determined by the basis, not by whether a value is zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
At the illustrated point \((20,60)\), \(s_1=s_2=s_4=0\). The augmented model has two nonbasic variables, so at least one of these three zeros is basic. Without an anti-cycling rule (a tie-breaking rule for the entering and leaving variables, such as Bland's smallest-index rule), repeated degenerate pivots can cause simplex to cycle, that is, return to an earlier basis and repeat indefinitely.

  • With \(x_1-x_2\le1\) and \(2x_1+x_2\le2\), increasing \(x_1\) gives tied ratios of 1.
  • At \((x_1,x_2,s_1,s_2)=(1,0,0,0)\), exchanging \(s_2\) for \(x_2\) leaves the point and \(z=3\) unchanged.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The course's diet problem chooses pounds \(x_A,x_B\) of two feeds to minimize daily feed cost while satisfying calorie, vitamin, and composition requirements:

\[ \begin{aligned} \min\quad &0.4x_A+0.8x_B\\ \text{subject to}\quad &800x_A+1000x_B\ge8000,\\ &140x_A+70x_B\ge700,\\ &2x_A-x_B\le0,\\ &x_A,x_B\ge0. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This is a minimum-cost mixture model. The composition restriction prevents cheap feed A from exceeding one-third of total feed weight.

Linear program formulation identifies feed amounts as variables, cost as the objective and nutritional requirements as constraints. The graphical method locates the cheapest feasible mixture by moving an objective line to its first contact with the feasible region.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The share constraint follows from \(x_A\le(x_A+x_B)/3\).
  • Nutrient requirements are lower bounds, so their inequalities point toward greater nutrient intake.
  • The optimal solution is \(x_A=20/7\), \(x_B=40/7\), with cost \(40/7\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure uses a simplified illustrative diet model, distinct from the course-data formulation above: minimize \(2x_A+3x_B\) subject to \(x_A+2x_B\ge6\), \(3x_A+x_B\ge6\) and \(x_A,x_B\ge0\). The variables still represent pounds of feeds A and B. Sliding the cost line towards the origin gives the illustrated optimum \((1.2,2.4)\) with cost 9.6.

  • The optimal mixture contains exactly one-third feed A.
  • At the optimum the calorie requirement is tight, while vitamin intake is \(800\ge700\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Dijkstra-Prim method constructs a minimum spanning tree in a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths. Let \(U\) be the set of vertices reached so far; start with \(U\) containing one arbitrary vertex and no selected edges. Repeatedly select a shortest edge joining a vertex in \(U\) to a vertex outside \(U\), add that edge, and add the outside endpoint to \(U\). Stop when every vertex belongs to \(U\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The method grows one connected tree. Each new edge connects one previously unreached vertex at the smallest available joining cost.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Compare edges crossing from the whole set \(U\), not only from the last added vertex.
  • Ties can be broken arbitrarily.
  • The starting vertex can change the construction order without changing the minimum total value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, each green edge label gives its weight and selection step in brackets. After reaching \(U=\{A,B,C\}\), \(BD=5\) is cheaper than \(CD=8\) or \(CE=10\); \(AB\) is ineligible because both endpoints are already in \(U\). The five selected edges have total length 13.

  • In the Euclidean example, starting with \(U=\{1\}\) selects edge \(1-7\) of length \(\sqrt{13}\).
  • The next edge is \(1-4\), of length 5.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A directed network is a network whose edges have specified orientations. An edge \(i\to j\) allows traversal or flow from \(i\) to \(j\); reverse traversal is not implied by its existence.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Direction represents asymmetric connections such as one-way movement or the order in which activities must occur.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Incoming and outgoing edges have different roles at a vertex.
  • Maximum-flow constraints respect the original edge directions.
  • A backward residual edge cancels assigned flow; it is not necessarily an original directed edge.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The red edge permits \(E\to D\), but there is no edge permitting \(D\to E\). Such orientations can represent one-way streets, pipe flows or activity precedence.

  • The maximum-flow network has outgoing edges at the source and incoming edges at the sink.
  • An activity edge \(i\to j\) points from its preceding event to its following event.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let demand be a nonnegative integer-valued random variable with CDF \(F\), finite mean, and newsvendor underage cost \(b>0\) and overage cost \(h>0\). Over nonnegative integer order quantities, a smallest optimal quantity is

\[ \begin{gathered} y^*=\min\{y\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\colon F(y)\ge\beta\},\\ \beta=\frac{b}{b+h}. \end{gathered} \]

For the expected cost \(G(y)\) of ordering \(y\), the marginal difference is

\[ G(y+1)-G(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Add another item while its expected lost-margin saving exceeds its expected leftover loss. Stop at the first CDF value reaching the critical ratio.

With integer demand, increase \(y\) while \(F(y)<\beta\): the first \(y\) with \(F(y)\ge\beta\) is optimal.

The positive part separates excess stock \((y-D)^+\) from unmet demand \((D-y)^+\). Comparing their expected costs for adjacent integer orders gives the discrete critical-probability rule.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(F(y)=\beta\), quantities \(y\) and \(y+1\) have equal expected cost.
  • All integer optimal quantities satisfy \(F(y-1)\le\beta\le F(y)\), taking \(F(-1)=0\).
  • Compute the expected cost with the actual discrete probabilities, not only the critical ratio.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The drawn CDF steps other than \(F(9)\) and \(F(10)\) are schematic; they do not specify additional probabilities for the dress example.

  • For the newspaper distribution, \(F(16)=0.25<3/7\le F(17)=0.50\), so the smallest optimum is 17; expected cost is 1.975.
  • The dress example has \(\beta=0.75\), optimal quantity 10, and expected cost 138.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A dummy assignment makes a rectangular assignment matrix square by adding fictitious agents or tasks with zero assignment costs. Add dummy agents when there are fewer agents than tasks; add dummy tasks when there are fewer tasks than agents.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An assignment to a dummy records an unfilled task or an unused agent. It allows the square Hungarian procedure to represent the intended rectangular problem.

The square assignment problem requires equally many agents and tasks. Dummy rows or columns balance unequal sets; their selected entries represent unused capacity or an unfilled task rather than a real assignment.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use zero dummy costs under the course assumption that leaving the corresponding entity unused has no additional penalty.
  • A dummy agent leaves its assigned real task unperformed.
  • A real agent assigned to a dummy task remains unused.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, one optimal assignment is \(A_1\to T_2\) at cost 2, \(A_3\to T_1\) at cost 3 and \(A_2\) to the dummy task. Thus \(A_2\) is idle and the total cost is 5.

  • Three agents and four tasks require one dummy-agent row.
  • Five machines and four jobs require one dummy-job column if machines are the rows.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The dynamic lot-size model chooses order quantities over \(n\) discrete periods with known varying demands, no shortages, and no lead time. In the detailed course notation, \(y_i\) is the period-\(i\) order, \(D_i\) demand, \(x_i\) starting stock, \(K_i\) setup cost, \(c_i(y_i)\) the variable ordering cost of \(y_i\) units, and \(h_i\) holding cost per unit carried to the next period. Then

\[ \begin{gathered} x_{i+1}=x_i+y_i-D_i\ge0,\\ C_i(y_i)=\begin{cases}0,&y_i=0,\\K_i+c_i(y_i),&y_i>0.\end{cases} \end{gathered} \]

Minimize \(\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n[C_i(y_i)+h_ix_{i+1}]\), with given \(x_1\) and terminal stock \(x_{n+1}=0\) in the course examples.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The model balances setup costs against carrying inventory into later periods. Unlike EOQ, demand and costs can change over the finite planning horizon.

An inventory policy specifies orders and stocks over the horizon. The production-inventory model supplies the period balance linking starting stock, replenishment, demand and ending stock (there \(I_{t-1}+P_t-d_t=I_t\), here \(x_i+y_i-D_i=x_{i+1}\)); setup costs make the timing of positive orders matter.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The course tables enumerate nonnegative integer order and stock quantities.
  • Variable ordering cost \(c_i(y_i)\) may depend nonlinearly on the batch size.
  • The model is introduced in the week 5 overview and developed in week 6.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the illustrated three-period policy, the period-2 order exceeds that period’s demand by one unit. Carrying it into period 3 gives the displayed total cost 79.

  • For demands \((2,1,3)\), the worked optimum orders \((2,2,2)\) at total cost 79.
  • Week 6 practice 2 has two optimal policies, \((4,0,4,0)\) and \((6,0,0,2)\), both costing 31.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Dynamic programming (DP) decomposes an optimization problem into related subproblems and computes their optimal values recursively. A state records the information needed to connect stages, and the optimum for a smaller subproblem becomes an input to the next calculation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Rather than enumerate every complete policy separately, the method reuses solutions to subproblems with the same state. In this course, periods are stages and inventory levels are states, as in the dynamic lot-size model.

The algorithm progresses through stages and stores solutions to smaller state problems. Its recursion reuses those values instead of repeatedly solving the same remaining-horizon problem.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Specify the state, decision, transition, cost, boundary conditions, and recursion.
  • Store minimizing decisions as well as costs to reconstruct an optimal policy.
  • Keep every minimizing decision if all optimal policies are required.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the figure’s forward calculation, each incoming arrow contributes its transition cost plus the preceding state value: \(f_2(\text{state})=\min_{\text{incoming arrows}}\{\text{arrow cost}+f_1(\text{previous state})\}\). The red arrows record the minimizing decisions used to reconstruct the policy.

  • \(f_i(x_{i+1})\) records the least cost through period \(i\) for a specified ending inventory.
  • The three-period calculation finds \(f_3(0)=79\) and then traces decisions backward.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Under the classical EOQ assumptions with \(D,K,h>0\), the unique order quantity minimizing the total cost per unit time (TCU) \(TCU(y)=KD/y+hy/2\) over \(y>0\) is

\[ y^*=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}},\qquad t_0^*=\frac{y^*}{D}=\sqrt{\frac{2K}{Dh}}. \]

The optimal policy orders \(y^*\) units when stock reaches zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The formula balances the two policy-dependent cost components. Demand and setup cost favour larger batches; expensive holding favours smaller ones.

Change \(D\), \(K\) and \(h\): the minimum of \(TCU(y)\) sits where the two cost rates are equal, at \(y^*=\sqrt{2KD/h}\).

The classical EOQ model gives average setup and holding costs as functions of order size. Minimizing their sum yields the economic order quantity below.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• At the optimum, \(KD/y^*=hy^*/2\).
  • The minimum relevant cost rate is \(\sqrt{2KDh}\).
  • Increasing demand raises the batch size but shortens the ordering cycle.
  • The formula follows from \(-KD/y^2+h/2=0\) and strict convexity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the illustrated phone shop, \(K=605\), \(D=2\) per day and \(h=5\) per unit per day give \(y^*=\sqrt{2\cdot605\cdot2/5}=22\). It orders every \(22/2=11\) days; setup and holding each cost \(55\) per day, giving relevant daily cost \(110\).
  • The snack bar obtains \(y^*=\sqrt{2(50)(10)/(3/7)}\approx48.30\) kilograms.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a repeating EOQ ordering cycle of length \(t_0^*>0\) and fixed lead time \(L\ge0\), the effective lead time is

\[ L_e=L-nt_0^*,\qquad n=\left\lfloor\frac{L}{t_0^*}\right\rfloor. \]

Thus \(0\le L_e<t_0^*\). The course's on-hand reorder level is \(DL_e\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The formula removes complete ordering cycles from the delay. It locates the ordering moment within a repeating stock cycle when orders from earlier cycles can still be in transit.

Whole cycles inside \(L\) do not matter for the reorder level: only \(L_e=L-nt_0^*\) does. Make \(L\) longer than a cycle to see orders overlap.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a lead time shorter than a cycle, \(L_e=L\).
  • The quantity \(L_e\) is a cycle remainder, not a shorter physical delivery delay.
  • If the delay is an exact multiple of the cycle, the remainder is zero; ordering and receipt events must be interpreted at that common cycle boundary.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the figure, time is measured in weeks. A cycle of \(t_0^*=7\) weeks gives \(y^*=7D\). With \(L=20\) weeks, \(n=2\) and \(L_e=20-2\cdot7=6\) weeks, so the reorder level is \(6D\). The order placed at week 1 arrives at week 21; two earlier orders are still in transit when it is placed.
  • The snack bar has \(L=12\) days and \(t_0^*\approx4.83\), giving \(L_e\approx2.34\) days.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
To require at least one of \(\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\le b\) and \(\boldsymbol{d}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\le e\), introduce \(y\in\{0,1\}\) and write

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}&\le b+My,\\ \boldsymbol{d}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}&\le e+M(1-y). \end{aligned} \]

The finite constant \(M\) must be large enough that the relaxed inequality imposes no unintended restriction over the relevant variable domain.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
One inequality is enforced while the other is allowed to relax. Both original inequalities may still hold, so this formulation expresses inclusive “or.”

A binary variable selects which branch is enforced. A valid big-M constraint relaxes the other branch without excluding a point allowed by the intended disjunction.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(y=0\), the first inequality is enforced; for \(y=1\), the second is enforced.
  • A valid value of \(M\) requires information about bounds on the expressions being relaxed.
  • This is a modelling device; it does not mean multiplying two decision variables.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The blue inequality is enforced when \(y=0\), and the red one when \(y=1\). The illustrated union is nonconvex, so it cannot be represented by one system of continuous linear inequalities in \(\boldsymbol{x}\) alone.

  • \(3x_1+2x_2\le18+My\) and \(x_1+4x_2\le16+M(1-y)\) implement the video example.
  • The week 3 exercise applies the same switch to two inequalities involving four variables.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the course's maximization simplex tableau, the entering variable rule selects a nonbasic variable with the most negative coefficient in the objective row. If several coefficients tie for most negative, any tied variable may be chosen.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Because the objective row is written with the objective on the left, a more negative coefficient corresponds to a higher improvement rate per unit increase of that variable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The selected variable defines the pivot column.
  • The greatest improvement rate is not necessarily the greatest total improvement, because allowable step sizes differ.
  • The ratio test determines how far the entering variable can increase while preserving feasibility.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated row is \(z-3x_s-2x_t=0\), so \(x_s\) has the largest objective improvement rate per unit, \(3>2\), and enters. Choosing the smallest index is one possible tie convention; it is not required by the course rule. A feasible canonical tableau with no negative nonbasic objective-row coefficient is already optimal.

  • From \(z-3x_1-2x_2=0\), choose \(x_1\).
  • From \(z-(1/2)x_2+(3/2)s_1=15\), choose \(x_2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The EOQ model with lead times retains constant known demand, no shortages, and the classical setup and holding costs, but an order arrives after a fixed delay \(L\ge0\). The optimal quantity remains \(y^*=\sqrt{2KD/h}\). In the course's repeating on-hand-stock convention, order when stock falls to \(DL_e\), where \(L_e\) is the effective lead time.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Lead time changes when an order must be placed so that replenishment arrives at the required moment. It does not change the EOQ under these deterministic assumptions.

Change the lead time \(L\): the batch size stays \(y^*\), but the order must be placed when stock reaches \(DL_e\) (dashed).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(L<t_0^*\), the reorder stock level is \(DL\).
  • If lead time exceeds an ordering cycle, several orders can be outstanding; use the course effective-lead-time construction.
  • The on-hand trigger describes steady-state cycles, not the initial setup of an empty supply pipeline.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated pencil inventory, demand is \(D=100\) per day, each order costs \(K=180\), and holding one pencil costs \(h=0.001\) per day. The optimal order quantity and relevant daily cost are

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} y^*&=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\cdot180\cdot100}{0.001}}\\ &=6000,\\ \sqrt{2KDh}&=6. \end{aligned} \]

The cycle lasts \(t_0^*=y^*/D=60\) days. With a 12-day lead time, the reorder level is \(DL=1200\): place the order on day 48 so that it arrives on day 60, when the stock runs out. The order quantity and cost remain unchanged.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The EOQ model with planned shortages allows all unmet demand to be backordered until instantaneous replenishment. With constant \(D>0\), setup \(K>0\), holding rate \(h>0\), and shortage cost (backlog penalty) \(p>0\), choose batch size \(y>0\) and stock just after replenishment \(0\le s\le y\). Maximum backlog is \(y-s\), and

\[ TCU(y,s)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hs^2}{2y}+\frac{p(y-s)^2}{2y}. \]

The optimum is

\[ \begin{aligned} y^*&=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}\sqrt{\frac{p+h}{p}},\\ s^*&=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}\sqrt{\frac{p}{p+h}}. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The policy deliberately balances periods with positive stock and periods with waiting customers. Replenishment first clears the backlog, leaving \(s\) units on hand.

Choose the batch size \(y\) and the stock \(s\) after replenishment. The level curves of \(TCU(y,s)\) (left) surround the optimum; the right panel shows stock and backlog.

The classical EOQ model balances setup and holding costs with no shortages. Adding shortage cost permits a planned backlog, so both order size and the division between stock and backlog must be chosen.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Order \(y^*\) when backlog reaches \(y^*-s^*\).
  • Ordering cycle length is \(y^*/D\); the fraction of time without shortage is \(p/(p+h)\).
  • The stock-phase mean \(s/2\) is not the whole-cycle average; the latter is \(s^2/(2y)\).
  • For finite positive \(p\), the optimal batch is larger than the classical EOQ.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the illustrated phone example, \(D=2\) per day, \(K=605\), \(h=5\) per phone per day and \(p=6\) per backlogged phone per day give \(y^*=22\sqrt{11/6}\approx29.79\) and \(s^*=22\sqrt{6/11}\approx16.25\). Order when the backlog reaches \(y^*-s^*\approx13.54\). The cycle lasts about \(14.9\) days: stock is positive for about \(8.1\) days and backlogged for about \(6.8\) days, with stock-positive fraction \(6/11\).
  • With \(p=h\), the model is out of stock for half the cycle.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The course's EOQ model with price breaks gives an all-unit discount: every ordered unit has price \(c_2<c_1\) when the batch meets a threshold \(q\). Following the “at least” convention of the worked examples,

\[ \begin{gathered} c(y)=\begin{cases}c_1,&0<y<q,\\c_2,&y\ge q,\end{cases}\\ TCU(y)=Dc(y)+\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}. \end{gathered} \]

Holding rate \(h\) is fixed across price levels; demand is constant, replenishment instantaneous, and shortages prohibited.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A larger batch may be worth buying to reduce the price of every unit. Purchasing cost must therefore be included in the comparison.

From the break \(q\) on, every unit costs \(c_2<c_1\), so the total cost curve jumps down. Compare the best quantity on each side of \(q\).

The economic order quantity gives a candidate within each constant-price range. Compare eligible candidates and price thresholds using total purchasing, setup and holding cost rather than comparing order sizes alone.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Let \(y_m=\sqrt{2KD/h}\). If \(y_m\ge q\), order \(y_m\) at the discount price.
  • If \(y_m<q\), compare the full costs at \(y_m\) and \(q\) and choose the cheaper; both are optimal at equality.
  • This page treats \(y=q\) as qualifying for the discount, as the worked examples do; check the convention when a problem states the threshold as \(y>q\).
  • The discount is all-unit, not a discount only on units above the threshold.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For phones, \(y_m=22\): cost at 22 is 450 per day, while cost at the qualifying 35 is about 442.07; order 35.
  • For the snack bar, the 100-kilogram threshold is not worthwhile; the optimal quantity remains about 48.30.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In the course's Euclidean network, cities have plane coordinates \((x_i,y_i)\), an edge may join every pair of cities, and its length is

\[ d_{ij}=\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}. \]

The resulting distances provide the weights for the minimum spanning tree problem.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Coordinates turn a location problem into a complete weighted network. Distances are straight-line lengths rather than road travel times.

An undirected network allows travel along either orientation of each edge. The Euclidean version assigns each edge the distance between its endpoints; the geometric coordinates determine its weight, not extra connections.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Distances are symmetric: \(d_{ij}=d_{ji}\).
  • Use sufficient precision when comparing close distances.
  • The usual spanning-tree algorithms apply once the distance matrix is computed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The red edge has length \(\ell_{12}=\sqrt{3^2+2^2}=\sqrt{13}\). Euclidean distances satisfy the triangle inequality and can also be used as routing costs.

  • Between \((13,6)\) and \((15,9)\) the distance is \(\sqrt{13}\approx3.61\).
  • The seven-city example has tree length about 27.29 using the displayed rounded distances.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: A finite connected undirected network has an Euler tour if and only if every vertex has even degree. Such a network is called an Euler network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Even degree is necessary because each arrival along an edge must be paired with a departure. The cycle-splicing construction of the Euler tour algorithm establishes sufficiency.

Vertex degree counts incident edges. On a closed edge-covering tour, arrivals and departures pair those incidences, explaining why each degree must be even.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• One odd-degree vertex is enough to rule out an Euler tour.
  • Connectedness is required to traverse all edges in one tour.
  • Parallel copies introduced by the Chinese postman construction are counted as separate edges.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The seven-bridge network violates the even-degree condition.
  • Duplicating suitable paths between odd-degree vertices makes their endpoint degrees even.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a connected undirected Euler network, the course's Euler tour algorithm starts at a vertex \(s\), follows unused edges until returning to \(s\), and calls the resulting cycle \(\Omega\). If unused edges remain, choose a vertex \(v\) on \(\Omega\) incident to an unused edge, build another closed unused-edge traversal \(\Omega_1\) from \(v\), and splice \(\Omega_1\) into \(\Omega\) at \(v\). Repeat until every edge is used.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The method builds a complete tour from smaller cycles. Even degree ensures that an unused-edge excursion can close at its starting vertex.

Euler network characterization supplies the connectedness and even-degree conditions under which the tour exists. The construction then joins closed edge-disjoint cycles until every edge has been used.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Keep track of used edge identities, especially with parallel copies.
  • The splice inserts one closed excursion into another without losing any previously used edge.
  • Arbitrary eligible choices can give different valid Euler tours.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An Euler tour is a closed traversal of a network that uses every edge exactly once. Vertices may be revisited. A network possessing an Euler tour is called an Euler network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The requirement concerns visiting edges, not visiting each vertex once. It models a route that covers every street without retracing an edge.

A cycle is a closed route that can be used as one component of the construction. An Euler tour may revisit vertices while covering every edge once; vertex degree determines whether a connected undirected network admits such a tour.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• At each vertex, arrivals and departures balance.
  • For connected undirected networks, an Euler tour exists exactly when every vertex has even degree.
  • In a weighted Euler network, every Euler tour has length equal to the sum of all edge lengths.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the illustrated Euler network, \(\deg A=4\) and every other degree is 2. The tour returns to its start while using every edge once.

  • The Königsberg bridge network has no Euler tour because its vertices have odd degree.
  • The course weighted Euler example has total edge length 24, so its Euler tours have length 24.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The feasible region is the set of all feasible solutions of a model:

\[ F=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{x}\text{ satisfies all constraints}\}. \]

For a two-variable LP it is obtained by intersecting the allowed half-planes and equality lines, including variable-domain restrictions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The feasible region shows the choices available before the objective is considered. Each extra constraint can retain or reduce this set.

Drag the decision point: it is feasible exactly when it satisfies every constraint, including \(x_s,x_t\ge0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Removing a constraint cannot shrink the feasible region.
  • An empty feasible region means the model is infeasible.
  • An unbounded feasible region does not by itself imply an unbounded objective value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated upper-bound model, \(F=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\le \boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\ge0\}\). It is an intersection of half-planes in two dimensions, or a convex polyhedron in \(\mathbb{R}^n\); an LP feasible set may be bounded, unbounded or empty.

  • \(x_1,x_2\ge0\) restrict the region to the first quadrant.
  • The diet requirements define the intersection of calorie, vitamin, and feed-share half-planes.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A feasible solution assigns values to all decision variables and satisfies every constraint, including their domain restrictions. A solution violating at least one constraint is infeasible.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Feasibility asks whether a decision is allowed. It must be checked before the decision's objective value can be used as a practical candidate.

Drag the point and read each constraint: a single violated inequality makes the decision infeasible, however good its objective value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An attractive objective value does not compensate for a violated constraint.
  • An LP-feasible fractional solution may be infeasible after integer restrictions are imposed.
  • Every optimal solution is feasible.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, \((15,40)\) satisfies \(70\le100\), \(55\le80\) and \(15\le40\); \((40,20)\) is also feasible. By contrast, \((30,50)\) requires \(2\cdot30+50=110>100\) finishing hours, and any \(x_s<0\) violates nonnegativity.

  • For \(x_1\le4\), \(x_2\le5\), \(2x_1+x_2\le9\), \(x_1,x_2\ge0\), \((2,5)\) is feasible.
  • In the same model, \((4,5)\) is infeasible because \(2(4)+5=13>9\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A linear expression can be restricted to one of the listed values \(d_1,\ldots,d_N\) by introducing binary variables \(y_i\) and writing

\[ \begin{gathered} a_1x_1+\cdots+a_nx_n=\sum_{i=1}^Nd_iy_i,\\ \sum_{i=1}^Ny_i=1,\qquad y_i\in\{0,1\}. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Exactly one indicator selects the allowed value of the expression. This avoids writing a separate alternative constraint for every possible value.

Mutually exclusive decisions ensure that exactly one value-selection indicator is active. The weighted sum of those indicators then returns one of the allowed values.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sum-to-one equality ensures that a value is actually selected.
  • The \(d_i\) are fixed data, so \(d_iy_i\) is linear.
  • Relaxing the indicators to continuous fractions would generally allow values between the listed values.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The light band shows intermediate totals made possible by fractional selector values; the binary selectors permit only the listed totals.

  • For allowed totals 3, 5, or 8, write \(x_1+x_2=3y_1+5y_2+8y_3\).
  • An even number of three yes decisions can take only the values 0 and 2.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The first-fit heuristic processes packing items in their given order. Place the current item into the first previously opened container with enough unused capacity. If no such container exists, open a new container and place the item there. Assume every item individually fits in a container.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The rule makes each placement using the current packing, without searching all arrangements. Both item order and container order affect its decisions.

The bin packing problem supplies the item weights and container capacity. First-fit maintains a feasible partial packing by putting the next item into the first existing container with enough remaining capacity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every produced packing respects capacity.
  • Its container count is an upper bound, not a proof of optimality.
  • The exercise gives this procedure without a name; first-fit is its conventional search name.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated order \(15,30,20,35\) with capacity 50 uses three containers under first fit. Two suffice with \(\{15,35\}\) and \(\{30,20\}\), so that first-fit result is not optimal. Reordering the same items as \(35,30,20,15\) makes first fit use two containers here.

  • In the course exercise, items 1, 2, 3, and 9 fill container 1 to weight 49.
  • Items 6, 7, and 8 fill another container to weight 49; the full heuristic packing uses five containers.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A forbidden assignment is an agent-task pair that is not allowed. In the course's Hungarian cost matrix, represent this pair by \(\infty\) and leave that entry infinite during all transformations.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The infinite cost acts as a prohibition rather than an expensive ordinary choice. A finite feasible complete assignment must avoid every prohibited pair.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Do not apply finite row or column adjustments as if they made an infinite entry available.
  • If no complete assignment avoiding forbidden pairs exists, the intended assignment problem is infeasible.
  • In a binary formulation, the equivalent restriction is \(x_{ij}=0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, prohibiting \((2,2)\) gives the highlighted assignment \(A_1\to T_1\), \(A_2\to T_3\), \(A_3\to T_2\) with cost \(2+4+6=12\), compared with diagonal cost \(2+3+2=7\) without the ban. A finite penalty \(M\) represents a prohibition only if it is sufficiently large and an allowed complete assignment exists; \(x_{22}=0\) enforces the ban directly.

  • A machine unable to process job 3 receives an infinite entry in that job's column.
  • A feasible assignment must choose another machine for that job.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Giapetto production model chooses wooden soldier production \(x_s\) and train production \(x_t\) to maximize profit. With the data in the course, the LP is

\[ \begin{aligned} \max\quad &z=3x_s+2x_t\\ \text{subject to}\quad &2x_s+x_t\le100,\\ &x_s+x_t\le80,\\ &x_s\le40,\\ &x_s,x_t\ge0. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The example shows how revenues, material costs, labour requirements, and sales limits become a complete production-planning LP.

The three resource constraints cut out the shaded region of production plans. Slide the profit line \(3x_s+2x_t=\bar z\) to find the best plan.

Linear program formulation turns toy-production quantities into variables, profit into an objective and resource availability into inequalities. The constraints distinguish profitable production from a physically feasible production plan.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The profit contribution is 3 per soldier and 2 per train.
  • Finishing and carpentry constrain the two products jointly.
  • The soldier demand limit constrains only \(x_s\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
At the illustrated plan \((x_s,x_t)=(20,60)\), the finishing and carpentry restrictions bind, while the soldier-demand restriction has slack because \(20<40\).

  • Producing 20 soldiers and 60 trains uses 100 finishing hours and 80 carpentry hours.
  • Producing 40 soldiers and 40 trains violates the finishing limit because it needs 120 hours.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Graphical integer programming solves a two-variable integer model by plotting its continuous constraints and considering only the lattice points satisfying all restrictions. Evaluate the objective at feasible integer points to identify the best value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The continuous feasible region helps locate the permitted integer points. Unlike an LP, the best integer point need not be a corner of that continuous region.

Only the lattice points count. The best integer point (ringed) need not be a corner of the continuous region: with the starting objective it lies on an edge, while in the static figure above it is an interior point.

Integer linear programming restricts feasible coordinates to integer values. The graphical method first draws the continuous feasible region, after which the eligible lattice points must be compared rather than merely rounding its best corner.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both coordinates must satisfy the stated integrality restrictions.
  • An LP-optimal fractional corner is not an integer-feasible decision.
  • For a small bounded example, explicit comparison of feasible lattice points proves optimality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure uses the illustrative model \(\max(3x_1+2x_2)\) subject to \(2x_1+2x_2\le9.5\), \(x_1\le3.5\) and \(\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^2\). Its best lattice point is \((3,1)\) with value 11; it is not a corner of the continuous polygon.

  • The integer work-order model uses \(3.2T+2.4S\le16\) and \(2T+3S\le15\).
  • Its best integer decision is \((T,S)=(0,5)\), with profit 750.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The graphical method solves a two-variable LP by drawing each constraint boundary, identifying the common feasible region, drawing a constant-objective line, and moving that line in the direction of improvement until the best feasible contact is reached. Intersecting the relevant boundary equations gives exact coordinates.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The method makes feasibility and optimality visible. It also reveals whether the best value is attained at one point or along a segment.

The numbered markers illustrate the method for the objective \(z=3x_s+2x_t\):

  1. Draw the boundaries \(2x_s+x_t=100\), \(x_s+x_t=80\) and \(x_s=40\).
  2. Shade their common feasible region, including the restrictions \(x_s,x_t\ge0\).
  3. Draw a constant-objective line, such as the dashed line \(3x_s+2x_t=90\).
  4. Move the line in the improving direction \((3,2)\) while it still touches the feasible region.
  5. The last contact is the optimum, here the corner \((20,60)\).

Push the objective line \(z=\bar z\) in the direction of the arrow until it last touches the feasible region; press the button to jump there. Here the last contact is the corner \((20,60)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Determine the allowed side of each boundary from the inequality; do not assume it is always below the line.
  • Check the direction of improvement from the objective, especially with negative coefficients.
  • Also allow for an empty feasible region or an objective that can improve without bound.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Maximizing \(x_1+2x_2\) with \(x_1\le4\), \(x_2\le5\), \(2x_1+x_2\le9\) gives \((2,5)\).
  • For \(z=2x_1-3x_2\), increasing \(z\) moves its objective line downward.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A heuristic is a solution method designed to obtain a good feasible solution without a general guarantee that it is optimal. In this course, a heuristic solution is required to satisfy the original problem's constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Heuristics are useful when finding an exact optimum is too difficult or time-consuming. A good feasible decision can be valuable even before its distance from optimality is known.

An optimal solution attains the best feasible objective value. A heuristic may return a feasible answer without proving that no better answer exists; a valid bound is needed to measure or certify the remaining gap.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For minimization, a feasible heuristic value is an upper bound on the optimum.
  • For maximization, a feasible heuristic value is a lower bound.
  • A relaxation can supply an opposing bound that measures solution quality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For maximization, improved incumbents raise the feasible lower bound. Resolving branch-and-bound nodes can reduce the global upper bound formed from the incumbent and the remaining open-node relaxation bounds.

  • In the vehicle routing problem, visiting each routing location separately from the depot gives a feasible starting plan.
  • First-fit packs items into the first container with enough remaining capacity.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A holding cost charges for inventory kept in stock. In the continuous-time EOQ model, \(h\) is the cost per unit held per unit of time. With average inventory \(\bar I\), the average holding cost rate is \(h\bar I\). In the discrete-time models, \(h_i\) charges each unit carried from period \(i\) to \(i+1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Holding cost makes early or large replenishment costly. Its time unit must match the demand rate and other rates in the calculation.

The average stock in the sawtooth is \(y/2\) (dashed line), so the holding cost rate is \(hy/2\). Raise \(h\) to see \(y^*\) fall.

An inventory policy determines stock over time. Holding cost charges that stock for the duration it is carried, so average inventory rather than order size alone determines the cost rate.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The shaded triangle has area \(yt_0/2\). Multiplying by \(h\) gives the holding cost of one cycle, \(hyt_0/2\); dividing by the cycle length \(t_0\) gives the cost rate \(hy/2\). Thus classical EOQ average inventory is \(y/2\).
  • With planned shortages, the full-cycle average positive stock is \(s^2/(2y)\), not \(s/2\).
  • Discrete-time exercises charge end-of-period stock.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The snack bar converts 3 per kilogram per week to \(3/7\) per kilogram per day.
  • The pencil example charges \(1/1000=0.001\) per pencil per day.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Hungarian algorithm solves the square minimum-cost assignment problem. Subtract each row minimum, then each column minimum. Cover all zeros of the resulting matrix with a minimum number of rows and columns. If \(n\) lines are needed, select \(n\) independent zeros, one per row and column. Otherwise let \(k\) be the smallest uncovered entry, subtract \(k\) from uncovered entries, add \(k\) to doubly covered entries, leave singly covered entries unchanged, and repeat the covering step.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The transformations preserve the optimal assignment while creating enough zero entries for a complete assignment. The final cost must be evaluated in the original matrix.

Assignment cost transformation subtracts row or column constants without changing the ordering of complete assignments. These transformations create zeros that can be searched for a complete matching.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The zero cover must use the minimum number of lines.
  • A set of independent zeros has no two in the same row or column.
  • The minimum line-cover size equals the maximum number of independent zero assignments in this construction.
  • Do not add together transformed zero costs to report the original objective value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, the smallest uncovered entry is 1: subtract 1 from uncovered entries, add 1 at double intersections, and leave singly covered entries unchanged. The final zero assignment \((1,1),(2,3),(3,2)\) has original cost \(4+7+1=12\).

  • The worked four-machine matrix initially needs three covering lines; an adjustment with k=2 enables a complete assignment.
  • The final original cost is \(2+5+6+7=20\).

docs.text: The incumbent solution in branch-and-bound is the best feasible solution of the original integer problem found so far. Its objective value supplies a lower bound for maximization and an upper bound for minimization.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An infeasible linear program has no decision vector satisfying all its constraints. Equivalently, its feasible region is empty. In the two-phase method, a negative optimal value of \(\displaystyle r=-\sum_iR_i\) proves infeasibility.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Conflicting requirements can make a model impossible even when each requirement is individually sensible. The objective cannot resolve this conflict.

The two constraints cannot hold together, so no decision is feasible. Lower \(b_2\) until the requirements become compatible.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An infeasible model has no optimal feasible solution.
  • A positive remaining artificial variable at the Phase I optimum indicates an unsatisfied original requirement.
  • Infeasibility differs from an unbounded objective, which requires feasible points.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(2x_1+x_2\le2\), \(3x_1+4x_2\ge12\), \(x_1,x_2\ge0\) is infeasible: the first constraint implies \(3x_1+4x_2\le8\).
  • A negative phase-I optimum, such as \(r^*=-4\), cannot be repaired by beginning Phase II.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An integer linear program (ILP) is a linear optimization model in which some or all decision variables must take integer values. The linear objective and functional constraints are retained, with restrictions such as \(x_j\in\mathbb{Z}\) added to the specified variables.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Integrality represents indivisible decisions and also supports modelling of logical conditions. It changes the feasible set and can make the problem substantially harder to solve.

Change the objective and compare the LP optimum with the best feasible lattice point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Pure integer programs require all decision variables to be integer.
  • Mixed integer programs include both integer and continuous variables.
  • Binary integer programs restrict every decision variable to 0 or 1.
  • Rounding an LP solution need not preserve feasibility or optimality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure uses the illustrative objective \(3x_1+2x_2\) and restrictions \(2x_1+2x_2\le9.5\), \(x_1\le3.5\), \(x\ge0\). Its continuous optimum \((3.5,1.25)\) has value 13, whereas requiring both variables to be integers gives \((3,1)\) with value 11. Branch-and-bound on LP relaxations is an exact method; arbitrary rounding is not.

  • A bus count must be a nonnegative integer.
  • A warehouse-opening decision uses a binary variable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An inventory policy specifies when to replenish stock and how much to order. Inventory theory constructs and analyses models to choose these decisions while accounting for demand and relevant costs.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Ordering frequently reduces stock held but increases the number of setups. Larger, less frequent orders reverse that trade-off. The appropriate model depends on the demand setting.

The optimization model specifies which inventory decisions are permitted and how their purchasing, setup, holding or shortage costs are evaluated. A policy supplies those decisions over time.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The EOQ models use a constant deterministic demand rate.
  • Dynamic lot sizing uses known demand varying by discrete period.
  • The newsvendor model uses stochastic demand for one selling period.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The job sequencing model orders jobs on one machine, each processed without interruption once started (nonpreemptive), to minimize total weighted tardiness penalties. Let \(s_i\ge0\) be job \(i\)'s start, \(p_i\) its duration, \(d_i\) its due date, \(T_i\ge0\) its tardiness, and \(w_i\) its penalty rate. Minimize \(\displaystyle \sum_iw_iT_i\) subject to \(T_i\ge s_i+p_i-d_i\). For each pair \(i<j\), impose

\[ \begin{gathered} s_i+p_i\le s_j+M(1-y_{ij}),\\ s_j+p_j\le s_i+My_{ij},\qquad y_{ij}\in\{0,1\}. \end{gathered} \]

Here \(y_{ij}=1\) means \(i\) precedes \(j\), and \(M\) must be valid for the scheduling horizon.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Pairwise alternatives prevent overlapping processing. Tardiness variables charge for finishing after the due date while imposing no penalty for early completion.

Either-or constraints choose which of two jobs precedes the other. Binary precedence choices and continuous start times coexist, making the schedule a mixed integer program.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For the supplied three jobs, total processing time is 40; a no-idle schedule starts at zero and lies within that horizon.
  • Nonnegative penalty rates make unnecessary idle time avoidable.
  • The formulation applies the either-or technique to the exercise's three jobs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The course has processing times \((5,20,15)\) and due dates \((24,22,35)\).
  • Sequence \(2,1,3\) completes at 20, 25, 40 and incurs \(12(0)+19(1)+34(5)=189\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
To require at least \(K\) of \(N\) inequalities \(\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\le d_i\), introduce binary relaxation indicators \(y_i\) and impose

\[ \begin{gathered} \boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\le d_i+My_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,N),\\ \sum_{i=1}^Ny_i\le N-K. \end{gathered} \]

Here \(0\le K\le N\) and \(M\) must validly relax each marked inequality. The video's equality \(\displaystyle \sum_i y_i=N-K\) gives the same allowed \(\boldsymbol{x}\) values when such relaxation is valid.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
At most \(N-K\) inequalities may be released, so at least \(K\) remain enforced. A released inequality is allowed to hold as well.

The big-M switch in either-or constraints releases one branch while enforcing another. Here the same release mechanism is applied to each inequality, and a bound on the number of released switches ensures that at least \(K\) remain enforced.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The formulation does not require exactly \(K\) original inequalities to be true.
  • The practice solution uses the inequality version; the video uses equality.
  • For \(K=N\), no constraint may be relaxed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure sets \(N=4\), \(K=2\): the binary bound \(y_1+y_2+y_3+y_4\le2\) allows at most two released inequalities, leaving at least two enforced. The constant \(M\) must be large enough to remove unintended restrictions from every released inequality.

  • At least two of four constraints can be enforced using \(y_1+y_2+y_3+y_4\le2\).
  • At least two of three constraints leave at most one relaxation indicator equal to 1.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Königsberg bridge problem asks whether a closed walk can cross each of the city's seven bridges exactly once. Represent each land region by a vertex and each bridge by an edge. The resulting four-vertex network asks whether an Euler tour exists.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Kruskal method constructs a minimum spanning tree by starting with no selected edges and repeatedly choosing a shortest unselected edge that does not create a cycle with the already selected edges. Stop once the selected edges connect all vertices.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The selected edges may initially form several separate pieces. The method joins those pieces while avoiding unnecessary loops.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Equivalently, inspect edges in nondecreasing order and reject any that create a cycle.

  • Equal-length eligible edges may be chosen in any order.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Linear program formulation converts a practical description into an LP by organizing the data, stating the objective in words, defining decision variables, writing the objective function, and writing all constraints including variable restrictions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The formulation should be understandable without guessing what its symbols mean. The main task is to translate the problem's choices and requirements accurately.

A model parameter is supplied data, such as a unit profit or available resource. Distinguishing those fixed coefficients from the decision variables prevents the optimizer from changing the problem data.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• State variable meanings before using them in formulas.
  • Use consistent measurement units in each constraint.
  • A percentage requirement can often be rearranged into a linear inequality.
  • Do not add integrality to a requested LP unless the intended model requires an integer program.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A linear program (LP) maximizes or minimizes a linear objective function subject to linear equality and/or inequality constraints. Its decision variables are continuous unless additional integer restrictions are imposed. For example,

\[ \begin{gathered} \max z=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jx_j,\\ \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j\le b_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\\ x_j\ge0. \end{gathered} \]

Other inequality directions and equalities are also allowed in an LP.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Linearity makes large planning models tractable by methods such as simplex. A model with indivisible decisions needs explicit integer restrictions to rule out fractional choices.

Change the objective coefficients \(c_1,c_2\): the feasible region stays put, and the optimum jumps from corner to corner.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Products of decision variables and powers such as \(x_j^2\) are not linear.
  • Negative coefficients are allowed.
  • The graphical method is useful for two variables; simplex handles larger models.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated Giapetto LP has objective \(3x_s+2x_t\) and attains value 180 at \((20,60)\). Its original quantities are continuous; no integrality restriction is included.

  • Giapetto maximizes \(3x_s+2x_t\) under linear labour and demand limits.
  • The diet problem minimizes cost under nutrient and composition requirements.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f_i(x_{i+1})\) be the minimum cost through period \(i\) of the dynamic lot-size model, including its ending-stock holding cost, conditional on stock \(x_{i+1}\). For given initial stock \(x_1\), the course's forward lot-size recursion is

\[ f_1(x_2)=C_1(D_1+x_2-x_1)+h_1x_2 \]

when the required order is nonnegative, and \(+\infty\) otherwise. For \(i\ge2\),

\[ \begin{aligned} &f_i(x_{i+1})\\ &\quad=\min_{0\le y_i\le D_i+x_{i+1}} \left\{C_i(y_i)+h_ix_{i+1}\right.\\ &\qquad\left.{}+f_{i-1}(x_{i+1}+D_i-y_i)\right\}. \end{aligned} \]

Use integer states and decisions in the course tables; unreachable predecessor states have value \(+\infty\). The required final value is \(f_n(0)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The previous stock level is inferred from the ending stock and current order. The recursion compares all feasible ways to reach the same ending state.

Dynamic programming compares an immediate cost plus the optimal remaining-stage cost. The dynamic lot-size model supplies the stock balance and feasible order sizes that define the transitions in this recursion.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The bound on \(y_i\) ensures nonnegative predecessor inventory.
  • Reconstruct from \(x_{n+1}=0\) using stored minimizers and \(x_i=x_{i+1}+D_i-y_i\).
  • In the course examples, states need not exceed the remaining future demand.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The three-period example gives \(f_2(1)=53\) and \(f_3(0)=26+53=79\).
  • Backward reconstruction gives \(y_3=2\), \(x_3=1\), \(y_2=2\), \(x_2=0\), \(y_1=2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The LP relaxation of an integer linear program removes its integrality requirements and keeps the objective and all other restrictions. In particular, a binary variable becomes a continuous variable satisfying \(0\le x_j\le1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The relaxation is easier to solve and includes every integer-feasible decision. Its optimum bounds the original integer optimum.

Dropping integrality enlarges the feasible set, so the relaxed optimum \(z_{LP}\) is an upper bound on the integer optimum \(z_{IP}\) for this maximization.

Integer linear programming restricts selected variables to integers. Dropping those restrictions enlarges the feasible set, so the relaxed optimum gives a bound in the appropriate objective direction.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Its value is an upper bound for maximization and a lower bound for minimization.
  • If a relaxed optimizer satisfies every original integrality restriction, it is also integer-optimal.
  • Do not drop binary upper bounds when dropping binarity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:

  • The project-selection relaxation allows \(x_3=0.2\) and obtains 3.52 at the root.
  • An integral relaxed solution such as \((1,0,1,1,0)\) is a feasible candidate for the original project model.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For the course network with only outgoing source edges and only incoming sink edges, the maximum flow LP (linear program) uses continuous variables \(x_{ij}\) and solves

\[ \begin{aligned} &\max\quad \sum_jx_{sj}\\ &\text{subject to}\\ &\quad\sum_jx_{ji}=\sum_jx_{ij}\quad(i\ne s,t),\\ &\quad0\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\\ &\qquad\text{for every directed edge }(i,j). \end{aligned} \]

Here \(c_{ij}\) is the edge capacity and sums run over existing edges.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The formulation separates the objective at the source from conservation at intermediate vertices. Capacities constrain individual directed flows.

The maximum flow problem specifies edge capacities and conservation at intermediate vertices. These are linear constraints, so maximizing the source-to-sink flow gives a linear programming formulation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Source outflow equals sink inflow by summing conservation equations.
  • No binary selection variable is needed: an edge may carry any feasible flow amount.
  • The formulation combines the capacity and flow-conservation conditions of the maximum flow problem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, maximize \(x_{AB}+x_{AC}\) with the displayed edge capacities. The intermediate balances are

\[ \begin{aligned}x_{AB}&=x_{BC}+x_{BD},\\x_{AC}+x_{BC}&=x_{CD}+x_{CE},\\x_{BD}+x_{CD}&=x_{DF},\\x_{CE}&=x_{EF}.\end{aligned} \]

The optimum is 8. For a maximum-flow formulation with integer capacities, an integral optimal flow exists; this is a property of this network formulation, not of arbitrary LPs with integer data.

  • The example objective is \(x_{SA}+x_{SB}\).
  • At A, conservation is \(x_{SA}=x_{AB}+x_{AC}+x_{AD}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The maximum flow problem assigns nonnegative flow \(x_{ij}\) to the edges of a directed network, subject to capacities \(x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\) and flow conservation (inflow equals outflow) at every intermediate vertex, that is, every vertex other than the source and the sink. The course assumes the source has only outgoing edges and the sink only incoming edges. The objective is to maximize total source outflow, equivalently total sink inflow.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Intermediate vertices pass flow through the network rather than create or consume it. Capacities limit how much can travel on each directed connection.

A capacity constraint bounds the flow on each edge, while conservation constraints balance incoming and outgoing flow at intermediate vertices. Together they prevent the objective from creating flow without a route through the network.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Flow into each intermediate vertex equals flow out.
  • The same maximum value can have several feasible edge-flow assignments.
  • Residual reverse capacity permits earlier routing choices to be revised.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated flow has source outflow \(3+5=8\), and each intermediate vertex passes on what it receives (for example, \(C\) receives 5 and sends \(2+3\)). A cut splits the vertices into a source side and a sink side; its capacity is the total capacity of the edges directed from the source side to the sink side, and no feasible flow value exceeds the capacity of any cut. The red dashed cut in the figure separates \(\{A,B,C,D,E\}\) from \(\{F\}\): only \(D\to F\) and \(E\to F\) cross it, with capacity \(5+3=8\), so no feasible flow can exceed 8. Attaining that cut bound certifies maximality.

  • A minimum cut need not be unique: the cut separating \(\{A,B,C,E\}\) from \(\{D,F\}\) is crossed by \(B\to D\), \(C\to D\) and \(E\to F\) and also has capacity \(3+2+3=8\).
  • Week 4 course examples (networks not shown on this page) use source \(S\) and sink \(T\): the main example has maximum flow 15, and Week 4 practice 7 reaches 16, with 9 entering \(T\) from \(D\) and 7 from \(E\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: Over the same feasible set, minimizing \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is equivalent to maximizing \(-f(\boldsymbol{x})\). The two problems have the same optimal solution vectors, and their optimal objective values have opposite signs.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The course presents simplex for maximization. Negating a minimization objective allows that procedure to be used while leaving the constraints unchanged.

Negating the objective function reverses all value comparisons while leaving the feasible set unchanged. Thus minimizers of the original objective are maximizers of its negative.

  • Recover the original optimal value by changing the sign back.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a feasible canonical tableau and an entering variable with constraint-column coefficients \(a_{ik}\) and right-hand sides \(b_i\ge0\), the minimum-ratio test selects

\[ \theta=\min_{i\colon a_{ik}>0}\frac{b_i}{a_{ik}}. \]

A row attaining the minimum supplies the leaving basic variable. Zero ratios are eligible; only the denominator must be strictly positive.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The test finds the first basic variable that reaches zero as the entering variable increases. A larger step would violate nonnegativity.

The entering variable rule first chooses an improving nonbasic variable. Starting from a basic feasible solution, the ratio test limits its increase so that none of the resulting basic values becomes negative.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Rows with zero or negative pivot-column coefficients do not restrict the increase.
  • A tie may be broken arbitrarily in the course procedure and can lead to degeneracy.
  • If there is no positive coefficient and the objective improves along this column, the objective is unbounded.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the illustrated tableau, increasing \(x_s\) gives \(s_1=100-2x_s\), \(s_2=80-x_s\) and \(s_3=40-x_s\). The limits \(50,80,40\) give step length 40, so \(s_3\) leaves.

  • The initial ratios \(10/2=5\) and \(15/1=15\) make \(s_1\) leave.
  • The next ratios are \(5/(1/2)=10\) and \(10/(5/2)=4\), so \(s_2\) leaves.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In the CPP construction, a minimum-weight perfect matching pairs the odd-degree vertices so that each belongs to exactly one pair and the sum of pair costs is minimized. The cost \(d_{ij}\) of a pair is its shortest-path distance. With a binary variable for each unordered pair,

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_{i<j}d_{ij}x_{ij},\\ \sum_{j<i}x_{ji}+\sum_{j>i}x_{ij}=1\\ \text{for each odd vertex }i. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This selects which odd vertices should be linked by duplicated paths. Pairing must be optimized jointly, since a locally cheap pair may leave expensive remaining pairs.

Vertex degree identifies the odd vertices to pair in the CPP construction. A shortest path problem supplies each pair cost, and the displayed binary integer program selects one partner for every such vertex.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Each pair variable is binary.
  • For four odd vertices there are three complete pairings to compare.
  • This is a nonbipartite matching problem because the vertices are not separated into two assignment groups.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated four odd vertices, the alternative pairing \(\{PR,QS\}\) costs 13. The minimum-cost pairing determines which shortest paths are duplicated in the CPP construction.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A minimum zero cover is a smallest set of matrix rows and columns (lines) that together cover all zero entries.

Zeros are independent if no two share a row or a column; a maximum independent zero assignment is a largest set of independent zeros. From such an assignment, a minimum zero cover is found by marking:

  1. Mark every row without an assigned zero.
  2. Mark every column that has a zero in a marked row.
  3. Mark every row whose assigned zero lies in a marked column.
  4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until nothing new is marked; then cover all marked columns and all unmarked rows.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This procedure supplies the minimum line cover required by the Hungarian algorithm. A merely maximal partial assignment is insufficient; use a maximum one.

Zero-cost matching via maximum flow finds the largest set of independent zero entries. Its minimum-cut construction determines an equally sized row-and-column cover of all zeros, which supplies the cover used for the next Hungarian adjustment.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For an \(n\times n\) matrix, \(n\) required covering lines indicate that a complete zero-cost assignment exists.
  • The cover size equals the size of the maximum independent zero assignment.
  • Rows and columns marked during the search are not the same as the final lines: the final rows are the unmarked ones.
  • If fewer than \(n\) lines are needed, subtract the smallest uncovered entry from all uncovered entries and add it to entries at intersections of covering lines. Repeat the assignment and covering steps until \(n\) lines are needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the illustrated matrix, the independent zeros at \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\) form a maximum assignment of size \(2\). Row 2 and column 2 cover every zero with two lines. Their equal sizes illustrate Kőnig's theorem: the largest number of independent zeros always equals the smallest number of lines covering all zeros (the matrix form of the bipartite matching duality). Since \(2<3\), the matrix still needs adjustment before a complete zero assignment is possible.
  • The marking finds this cover. Row 3 has no assigned zero, so it is marked; its zero in column 2 marks column 2; the zero assigned in column 2 is in row 1, so row 1 is marked; row 1 adds no new column. The cover is the marked column 2 and the unmarked row 2.
  • Course examples (matrices in the course materials, not reproduced here): Week 5 practice 5(b) covers columns 1 and 2 and rows 2 and 3; the ten-job example covers columns 1, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9 and rows 2, 10, eight lines in all.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A mixed integer program (MIP) is an integer linear program containing both integer-restricted decision variables and continuous decision variables. Binary variables may be used for the discrete decisions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A single model can select a discrete action and determine continuous quantities conditional on it. The domain of each variable must therefore be stated individually.

Integer linear programming supplies integrality restrictions; a mixed model retains those restrictions on some decisions while allowing the other decisions to vary continuously.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An LP relaxation removes integrality only from the restricted variables.
  • Continuous variables should not accidentally be forced to integer values.
  • Logical modelling often introduces auxiliary binary variables alongside quantities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A model parameter is a given numerical input to the optimization model. In the course's LP notation, parameters include objective coefficients \(c_j\), constraint coefficients \(a_{ij}\), and right-hand sides \(b_i\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Parameters describe the circumstances under which decisions are made. A parameter may be an estimate even though the optimization treats its supplied value as fixed.

The objective function \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is the quantity to maximize (for example, profit) or minimize (for example, cost). Functional constraints describe what an allowed decision must satisfy, such as resource limits or demand requirements. Domain restrictions specify signs or integrality.

In the diagram, blue identifies decision variables, whose values the model determines; red identifies model parameters, the given data \(c_j\), \(a_{ij}\) and \(b_i\). In general, the model is \(\max/\min\ f(\boldsymbol{x})\) subject to \(\boldsymbol{x}\in F\), where the constraints define the feasible set \(F\). A solution assigns values to all variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Changing parameters can change both the optimal decision and the optimal value.
  • Units must agree within an equation or inequality.
  • Sensitivity analysis investigates the effect of parameter changes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The coefficient \(3\) in \(3x_s+2x_t\) is profit per soldier.
  • The right-hand side \(100\) in \(2x_s+x_t\le100\) is available finishing time.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An optimization problem has multiple optimal solutions if distinct feasible decision vectors attain the same optimal objective value. In an LP, every convex combination of two optimal solutions is also optimal.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Different decisions can be equally good under the stated objective. In a two-variable LP, this often appears as an objective line coinciding with a feasible boundary segment.

The figure and the interactive example both use the feasible region of the Giapetto production model: \(x_s\) wooden soldiers and \(x_t\) trains, with finishing \(2x_s+x_t\le100\), carpentry \(x_s+x_t\le80\) and soldier demand \(x_s\le40\). Only the objective is changed, so that it becomes parallel to one edge.

With \(z=2x_s+2x_t\), every objective line \(x_s+x_t=z/2\) is parallel to the carpentry edge. Pushing the dashed line \(z=100\) outwards, it leaves the region along the whole edge from \((0,80)\) to \((20,60)\), where \(z=160\).

Here the objective is \(z=4x_s+2x_t\), parallel to the finishing line \(2x_s+x_t=100\), so the optimal edge runs from \((40,20)\) to \((20,60)\) with \(z=200\). Move \(\alpha\) along it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A zero objective-row coefficient for a nonbasic variable in an optimal simplex tableau suggests an alternative optimum.
  • A positive feasible movement in that direction produces a distinct optimum; a zero-length degenerate pivot alone does not establish a different decision vector.
  • Additional requirements can select one point from an optimal segment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the illustrated objective \(2x_s+2x_t\), the feasible part of \(x_s+x_t=80\) between \((0,80)\) and \((20,60)\) is optimal. It includes \((10,70)\); every point on the segment has value 160.
  • For the interactive objective \(4x_s+2x_t\), the five corners \((0,0)\), \((40,0)\), \((40,20)\), \((20,60)\), \((0,80)\) give \(0\), \(160\), \(200\), \(200\), \(160\), so the edge from \((40,20)\) to \((20,60)\) is optimal with value 200.
  • Adding the requirement \(x_s=30\) to that problem selects the single point \((30,40)\) of the optimal edge: \(2\cdot30+40=100\) and \(4\cdot30+2\cdot40=200\).
  • With the original Giapetto profit \(3x_s+2x_t\), the corner values are \(0,120,160,180,160\), so the optimum \((20,60)\) is unique.
  • The Week 3 course materials (data not reproduced here) give another LP in which \((5,0)\) and \((3,4)\) both attain \(4x_1+2x_2=20\); in practice exercise 3 of Week 3, imposing \(x_1=1\) selects \((1,9/2)\) from the optimal segment.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For binary variables \(y_1,\ldots,y_k\), mutually exclusive decisions allow at most one variable to equal 1:

\[ \sum_{j=1}^ky_j\le1. \]

If one alternative must be chosen, use \(\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^ky_j=1\) instead.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The inequality permits choosing none, while the equality requires one choice. This distinction matters when translating phrases such as “at most one” and “exactly one.”

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Binarity is essential to interpret the sum as the number of yes decisions.
  • Exactly one implies at most one, but the reverse is false.
  • This restriction concerns decisions, not an either-or condition on continuous inequalities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• With binaries \(W_{LA}\) and \(W_{SF}\) equal to 1 if a warehouse is built at location LA or SF, \(W_{LA}+W_{SF}\le1\) permits at most one warehouse.
  • \(y_1+y_2+y_3=1\) selects exactly one allowed quantity value.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The negative right-hand-side transformation multiplies an entire constraint by \(-1\) when its right-hand side is negative. An inequality reverses direction; an equality remains an equality.

docs.title: Interpretation

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Change every coefficient and the right-hand side.
  • A \(\le\) constraint can become a \(\ge\) constraint and consequently require a surplus and an artificial variable.
  • Changing only the right-hand side would change the problem.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A network consists of a set of vertices and edges connecting specified pairs of vertices. Vertices represent entities or locations; edges represent connections. Depending on the problem, edges may have directions and numerical values such as distances, costs, or capacities.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A network separates the connection structure of a problem from its physical setting. The same mathematical representation can describe roads, communication links, or project activities.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Vertices are also commonly called nodes.
  • An edge may be used only in its specified direction in a directed network.
  • The meaning of an edge value depends on the problem: distance and capacity are different quantities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure has vertices \(\{A,\ldots,F\}\) and edge labels denoting lengths.

  • A road network connects cities by roads.
  • A project network represents activities and their precedence relations.
