docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The newsvendor model chooses a single order quantity \(y\ge0\) before observing random demand \(D\). With unit purchase cost \(c\), selling price \(p>c\), and salvage value \(s<c\), define overage cost \(h=c-s\) and underage cost \(b=p-c\). Minimize

\[ G(y)=h\,\mathbb{E}[(y-D)^+]+b\,\mathbb{E}[(D-y)^+], \]

where \(u^+=\max\{u,0\}\) and the expectations are finite. Sales equal \(\min\{y,D\}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Too much stock leaves costly leftovers; too little misses profitable demand. The optimal quantity balances those risks through the demand distribution.

Move \(y\): the expected overage cost rises and the expected underage cost falls. Their sum \(G(y)\) is smallest at the \(\beta\)-quantile of demand (right).

The single-period inventory policy chooses stock before demand is known. The positive part records leftover stock and unmet demand separately, allowing their different unit costs to enter the expected objective.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Salvage value can be zero or negative.
  • \(G(y)\) is convex; an optimum occurs where increasing stock stops reducing expected cost.
  • \(G(y)\) measures overage and underage loss, not gross purchasing expenditure.
  • The model is introduced in the week 5 overview and developed in week 6.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated meal-demand example is uniform on \([80,120]\) with critical ratio \(\beta=0.6\). Its optimal stock is \(y^*=104\), for which \(F(104)=0.6\).

  • A newsvendor chooses newspaper stock before daily demand is known.
  • A shop chooses seasonal dress inventory; a canteen prepares meals before evening demand.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For a fixed integer quantity \(y\) and fixed purchase cost \(c\) and salvage value \(s<c\), newsvendor price sensitivity finds selling prices \(p>c\) for which \(y\) remains optimal. The condition is

\[ F(y-1)\le\frac{p-c}{p-s}\le F(y). \]

The endpoints include ties with neighbouring quantities.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A higher selling price raises the opportunity cost of unmet demand. The interval identifies how far the price can move before the chosen stock level stops being optimal.

Fix the quantity \(y\) and vary the price \(p\): \(y\) stays optimal while \(F(y-1)\le\frac{p-c}{p-s}\le F(y)\).

The discrete newsvendor rule selects the first integer quantity reaching the critical probability (the critical ratio \((p-c)/(p-s)\)). Changing the selling price changes that probability, so the optimal integer quantity can stay constant over a price interval and then jump.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The condition is for being an optimum, not necessarily the smallest optimum.
  • At the lower boundary, \(y-1\) can tie with \(y\).
  • This analysis holds the demand distribution fixed, as the exercise does.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
At \(p=250\), quantities 9 and 10 tie; at \(p=450\), quantities 10 and 11 tie. Increasing price past the upper endpoint calls for additional stock, with demand distribution held fixed.

  • The dress solution uses effective unit cost \(c=80+30=110\) and salvage \(s=50\).
  • For \(y=10\), \(F(9)=0.70\) and \(F(10)=0.85\) give \(250\le p\le450\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A nonbasic variable is a variable outside the chosen basis and is set to zero when the associated basic solution is read. For \(m\) independent equations in \(n\) variables, there are \(n-m\) nonbasic variables.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The method explores another basis by allowing a selected nonbasic variable to enter. The remaining basic values change to maintain the equations.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A zero value alone does not establish that a variable is nonbasic; basic variables can also be zero.
  • The objective row expresses the effect of changing nonbasic variables.
  • The entering variable becomes basic after a pivot.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated tableau has \(n-m=5-3=2\) nonbasic variables, \(s_1,s_2\). Raising \(s_1\) by 1 changes \(x_t\) and \(s_3\) by \(+1\), \(x_s\) by \(-1\) and \(z\) by \(-1\), while the displayed basis remains feasible.

  • The original decision variables are nonbasic at the initial slack-basis solution.
  • The final two-variable example sets \(s_1=s_2=0\) as its nonbasic variables.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Nonconvex region modelling represents a union of allowed regions using binary variables that select which region's inequalities are enforced. The selected region must satisfy all its defining inequalities; common constraints remain active for every selection.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A single system of continuous linear inequalities cannot describe separated allowed regions exactly. Binary switches can exclude the gaps between them.

The feasible region can be a union of separated pieces. Either-or constraints represent alternative pieces, while mutually exclusive decisions select exactly one when the model requires a unique alternative.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use one indicator per region and require exactly one selected region. With only two regions a single binary \(y\) suffices: \(1-y\) and \(y\) act as the two indicators.
  • Relax every inequality belonging only to an unselected region with a valid big-\(M\) constant, as in either-or constraints: \(M\) must be large enough that the relaxed inequality cuts off no point the model allows.
  • Keep nonnegativity and shared boundaries outside the switches.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated region, the course video example, is \(x_1,x_2\ge0\), \(x_1+x_2\le3\), with either \(x_2\le1\) or \(x_2\ge2\). Its switch is \(x_2\le1+My\), \(x_2\ge2-M(1-y)\), \(y\in\{0,1\}\). With \(y=0\) the lower piece \(x_2\le1\) is enforced and the second inequality becomes \(x_2\ge2-M\); with \(y=1\) the upper piece \(x_2\ge2\) is enforced and the first becomes \(x_2\le1+M\). Because \(0\le x_2\le3\) on the shared region, \(M=2\) is already large enough. The common restrictions \(x_1+x_2\le3\) and \(\boldsymbol{x}\ge\boldsymbol{0}\) remain active for both choices.

  • The practice region additionally selects \(x_1\in[0,1]\), \([2,3]\), or \([4,5]\) under \(2x_1+5x_2\le20\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A nonnegativity constraint requires a decision variable to satisfy \(x_j\ge0\). It excludes negative quantities while permitting zero. For a vector of variables, \(\boldsymbol{x}\ge0\) means \(x_j\ge0\) for every component \(j\). In the course's augmented simplex models, all original and auxiliary variables are nonnegative.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Production and shipment quantities are normally nonnegative. Variables representing signed quantities need a different domain or a transformation.

With two nonnegative variables \(x,y\ge0\) the feasible region lies in the first quadrant. Drag the peak of the objective to the left of the \(y\)-axis: the optimum moves onto the axis and the constraint \(x\ge0\) binds.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Nonnegativity is a constraint, not an automatic consequence of a variable name.
  • With two nonnegative variables, feasible points lie in the first quadrant.
  • Nonnegative continuous variables may still take fractional values.
  • At an optimum a nonnegativity constraint is either slack (\(x_j^\ast>0\)) or binding (\(x_j^\ast=0\)); in nonlinear problems this is what the Kuhn-Tucker conditions with nonnegativity constraints handle.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x_s\ge0\) prevents negative soldier production.
  • \(s_1\ge0\) ensures that a slack variable represents unused rather than exceeded capacity.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In the course's normal demand approximation, \(D\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with standard deviation \(\sigma>0\). If \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF, then

\[ \begin{gathered} F(y)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{y-\mu}{\sigma}\right),\\ y^*=\max\!\left\{0,\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(\beta)\right\}. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The mean sets the central demand level, while the standard deviation scales the distance to the required quantile. The examples use the normal model as an approximation to practical demand.

With \(D\sim N(100,20^2)\) the optimal stock is \(\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(\beta)\): above the mean when \(\beta>1/2\), below it when \(\beta<1/2\).

The continuous newsvendor rule requires the demand quantile at the critical ratio. Standardizing normal demand converts that quantile to a standard-normal quantile before restoring the original mean and scale.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use the standard deviation \(\sigma\), not the variance \(\sigma^2\), in the quantile formula.
  • The order quantity must satisfy \(y\ge0\). Use the normal quantile when it is nonnegative; otherwise the constrained optimum is \(y^*=0\).
  • The untruncated normal distribution allows negative values; the course examples retain that approximation.
  • The normal table gives rounded quantiles.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The shaded area in the figure is \(\mathbb{P}(D\le y^*)=0.6\). Table values \(\Phi(0.25)=0.5987\) and \(\Phi(0.26)=0.6026\) bracket the standardized quantile between 0.25 and 0.26.

  • Meal demand with \(\mu=100\), \(\sigma=20\) and \(\beta=0.6\) gives about 105.07.
  • For apples, \(\beta=1.8/2.2\approx0.8182\) and the source table approximation \(z\approx0.91\) gives 82.75 kilograms.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An objective coefficient range is an interval of values for one objective coefficient over which the current optimal basis remains optimal while all other data stay fixed. A report with coefficient \(c_j\), allowable decrease \(d_j\), and allowable increase \(u_j\) gives

\[ c_j-d_j\le c_j^{\mathrm{new}}\le c_j+u_j. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Within this interval the reported decision vector remains an optimum. Its objective value changes because the same quantity now earns a different unit return.

Change the profit per soldier \(c_s\): within the shown range the corner \((20,60)\) stays optimal and only \(z^*\) changes.

This sensitivity analysis changes one coefficient of the objective function while holding the other data fixed. The reported interval identifies changes that preserve optimality of the current basis, not changes that preserve its objective value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a change \(\Delta c_j\) within the range, the value changes by \(x_j^*\Delta c_j\).
  • At a range endpoint, additional optimal solutions may become available.
  • Separate reported ranges do not justify simultaneous changes automatically.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated objective \(c_1x_s+2x_t\), the coefficient \(c_1=3\) may decrease or increase by 1, giving \([2,4]\). The corner \((20,60)\) remains optimal, while its value becomes \(20c_1+120\); endpoint values may admit other optima.

  • The small-pipe profit coefficient 5 has allowable decrease 1 and increase 3, giving \([4,8]\).
  • Changing banana profit by \(-0.03\) with quantity 75 changes total profit by \(-2.25\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The objective function assigns a numerical value to a decision vector. The model specifies whether this value should be maximized or minimized. In an LP it has the form

\[ z=c_1x_1+\cdots+c_nx_n, \]

where the \(c_j\) are given objective coefficients.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The objective expresses the criterion used to compare feasible choices. Profit maximization and cost minimization are common, but the course also considers distance, time, and flow.

The objective function \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is the quantity to maximize (for example, profit) or minimize (for example, cost). Functional constraints describe what an allowed decision must satisfy, such as resource limits or demand requirements. Domain restrictions specify signs or integrality.

In the diagram, blue identifies decision variables, whose values the model determines; red identifies model parameters, the given data \(c_j\), \(a_{ij}\) and \(b_i\). In general, the model is \(\max/\min\ f(\boldsymbol{x})\) subject to \(\boldsymbol{x}\in F\), where the constraints define the feasible set \(F\). A solution assigns values to all variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An objective value is a number; an optimal solution is a vector of decisions.
  • In a profit objective, use revenues minus relevant costs.
  • The direction of optimization determines what constitutes an improvement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Giapetto maximizes \(z=3x_s+2x_t\).
  • The pig diet minimizes \(z=0.4x_A+0.8x_B\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a two-variable linear objective \(z=c_1x_1+c_2x_2\) with at least one nonzero coefficient, an objective line is the set of points giving a fixed value \(z=\bar z\). If \(c_2\ne0\), its slope-intercept form is

\[ x_2=-\frac{c_1}{c_2}x_1+\frac{\bar z}{c_2}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Changing the objective value translates the line without changing its slope. This is the geometric basis of the graphical solution method.

Change \(\bar z\) to translate the line and \(c_1,c_2\) to turn it: all lines for one objective are parallel, with slope \(-c_1/c_2\).

Holding the objective function at a fixed value produces a line. Changing that value moves a parallel line, so its last feasible contact identifies the graphical optimum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• All constant-objective lines for a fixed objective are parallel.
  • If \(c_2<0\), a larger objective value lowers the vertical intercept.
  • When \(c_2=0\), the objective lines are vertical.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Translating a line in the direction \((c_1,c_2)\) raises its objective value. When a finite maximum is attained, the last objective line meeting the feasible region identifies it.

  • \(z=x_1+2x_2\) gives \(x_2=-x_1/2+z/2\).
  • \(z=2x_1-3x_2\) gives \(x_2=2x_1/3-z/3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Operations research (OR) uses mathematical models and analytical solution methods to support optimal, or sufficiently good, decisions in practical situations. The decision problem includes an objective, available choices, and restrictions on those choices.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: OR turns a practical planning question into a problem that can be analysed systematically. The usefulness of the answer depends on how well the model represents the situation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Applications include production, transport, scheduling, maintenance, and inventory management.
  • An optimal model solution must still be checked against the practical situation.
  • Difficult problems may require a heuristic instead of an exact solution method.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Any stage of the OR study cycle can prompt a return to an earlier stage if validation shows that the simplified representation is inadequate.

  • Lecture scheduling allocates teaching activities to times and rooms.
  • A warehouse chooses replenishment quantities and ordering times.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a minimization problem with feasible set \(F\), a feasible vector \(\boldsymbol{x}^*\) is an optimal solution if

\[ f(\boldsymbol{x}^*)\le f(\boldsymbol{x})\quad\text{for every }\boldsymbol{x}\in F. \]

For maximization the inequality is reversed. The number \(z^*=f(\boldsymbol{x}^*)\) is the optimal value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Optimality compares a feasible decision with every allowed alternative. There may be several equally good decisions, even when the optimal value is fixed.

The objective function determines which feasible points are best. Feasibility alone only establishes admissibility; optimality also compares the objective value with every other feasible point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A model may have no feasible solution or no finite optimum.
  • The optimal value and the vector attaining it are different objects.
  • An optimum is relative to the specified objective, constraints, and input data.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated Giapetto objective, the optimal point \((20,60)\) has value \(3\cdot20+2\cdot60=180\).

  • The manufacturing example has \(x_1^*=2\), \(x_2^*=5\), and \(z^*=12\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Suppose an optimization problem has a finite optimal value \(z^*\). Let \(z_H\) be the value of a feasible solution and \(z_R\) the finite optimal value of a relaxation with the same objective. Then

\[ z_R\le z^*\le z_H\quad\text{for minimization}, \] \[ z_H\le z^*\le z_R\quad\text{for maximization}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The two bounds enclose the unknown optimum. Their difference limits how much the current feasible solution could still be improved.

A heuristic that returns a feasible answer supplies a bound from the feasible side: an upper bound for minimization or a lower bound for maximization. A relaxation supplies the opposite side.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a minimization problem, \(z_H-z^*\le z_H-z_R\).
  • If the feasible and relaxed values coincide, the feasible solution is proven optimal.
  • A feasible solution of a relaxation alone is not generally an opposing bound; its optimal value is needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For maximization, improved incumbents raise the feasible lower bound. Resolving branch-and-bound nodes can reduce the global upper bound formed from the incumbent and the remaining open-node relaxation bounds.

  • The routing example gives \(202\le z^*\le214\), so the remaining improvement is at most 12 miles.
  • A 232-mile route is also an upper bound, but 214 is tighter.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An optimization model specifies decision variables \(\boldsymbol{x}\), an objective function \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) to maximize or minimize, and constraints defining the allowed decisions. Writing the feasible set as \(F\), its form is

\[ \min_{\boldsymbol{x}\in F} f(\boldsymbol{x})\qquad\text{or}\qquad\max_{\boldsymbol{x}\in F} f(\boldsymbol{x}). \]

The coefficients and other given inputs are model parameters.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The model states what can be chosen, what counts as better, and which choices are allowed. Solving it selects the best allowed decision according to the chosen objective.

The objective function \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is the quantity to maximize (for example, profit) or minimize (for example, cost). Functional constraints describe what an allowed decision must satisfy, such as resource limits or demand requirements. Domain restrictions specify signs or integrality.

In the diagram, blue identifies decision variables, whose values the model determines; red identifies model parameters, the given data \(c_j\), \(a_{ij}\) and \(b_i\). In general, the model is \(\max/\min\ f(\boldsymbol{x})\) subject to \(\boldsymbol{x}\in F\), where the constraints define the feasible set \(F\). A solution assigns values to all variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The objective and constraints need not be linear in a general OR model.
  • Some simple models have a closed-form solution; many require an algorithm.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\min\{x^2+bx+c\colon x\ge d\}\), the optimum is \(x^*=\max\{-b/2,d\}\).
  • Giapetto chooses soldier and train production to maximize profit under labour limits.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The OR study cycle moves from a real situation to an assumed representation of it, then to a mathematical model, a solution, validation, and implementation. Validation checks whether the model and its solution adequately represent the practical decision problem.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A mathematically correct answer can be unsuitable if the modelling assumptions omit an essential feature. Model building and validation therefore belong to the same decision process.

Operations research links a practical decision to formal analysis. The optimization model is one stage of that cycle; interpreting, validating and implementing its solution remain separate stages.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Additional detail may improve realism but also increase data requirements and solution difficulty.
  • The required data must be available or obtainable.
  • Validation can reveal a need to revise assumptions before implementation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Any stage can prompt a return to an earlier stage if validation shows that the simplified representation is inadequate.

  • A route model may initially approximate travel distances by straight lines.
  • Road layout and time-dependent traffic may require a more detailed route model.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In the constant-demand EOQ setting, the ordering cycle length \(t_0\) is the time between consecutive orders. If each order contains \(y\) units and demand occurs at rate \(D>0\), then

\[ t_0=\frac{y}{D}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A batch supports exactly one cycle's demand in the repeating policy. The same identity holds with planned backorders because each batch still covers total demand over a cycle.

One batch of \(y\) units lasts \(t_0=y/D\): change \(y\) or \(D\) and watch the sawtooth's teeth stretch or shrink.

A repeating inventory policy determines the time between orders. With constant demand, dividing order quantity by demand rate gives that cycle length.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Orders per unit time equal \(D/y\).
  • Cycle length and lead time are different: one measures spacing of orders, the other order-to-receipt delay.
  • Convert demand and time consistently.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Ordering 22 phones at demand two per day gives an 11-day cycle.
  • In the figure, time is measured in days. Ordering \(6{,}000\) pencils at demand \(D=100\) per day gives a \(60\)-day cycle and \(D/y=1/60\) orders per day.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The overage cost in the newsvendor model is the net loss on one unit ordered but not sold at its regular price:

\[ h=c-s>0, \]

where \(c\) is its unit cost and \(s\) its salvage value. Total expected overage cost at order quantity \(y\) is \(h\mathbb{E}[(y-D)^+]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The salvage recovery offsets part of the cost of excess stock. A negative salvage value represents an additional disposal cost.

Each unsold unit loses \(h=c-s\). A low or negative salvage value \(s\) pushes \(y^*\) down.

The positive part \((y-D)^+\) counts units left over after demand. Multiplying it by the overage cost converts excess stock into the realized overage loss.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Only leftover units incur overage loss.
  • Increasing salvage value lowers overage cost.
  • This is a single-period per-unit loss, whereas EOQ holding cost is charged per unit per unit time.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated newspaper data give overage cost \(h=2\) and underage cost \(b=1.5\), hence critical ratio \(\beta=1.5/3.5=3/7\). These are single-period per-unit losses, rather than EOQ cost rates.

  • Newspapers costing 3.50 and salvaged for 1.50 have \(h=2\).
  • Meals costing 2.20 with zero salvage have \(h=2.20\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For three binary decisions \(y_1,y_2,y_3\), requiring an even number of yes decisions is equivalent to

\[ y_1+y_2+y_3=2x,\qquad x\in\{0,1\}. \]

The sum can therefore be 0 or 2, the only even values possible for three binary decisions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An auxiliary variable encodes the allowed count. The equality imposes a logical restriction using only linear expressions.

Each binary variable selects or rejects an item. A separate integer variable counts pairs, so the selected total can be constrained to an even or odd value as required.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• When \(x=0\), all three decisions are no.
  • When \(x=1\), exactly two decisions are yes.
  • Allowing \(x\) to be continuous would remove the parity restriction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((y_1,y_2,y_3)=(1,1,0)\) is allowed with \(x=1\).
  • \((1,1,1)\) is excluded because it would require \(x=3/2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the course's terminology, a path is a sequence of distinct edges connecting a starting vertex to an ending vertex, with consecutive edges joined through their shared vertices. For directed edges, traversal respects their directions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A path describes a connected route through a network. The course definition requires distinct edges; it does not add a requirement that all visited vertices be distinct. In graph theory such an edge-distinct walk is usually called a trail, and path is kept for walks that also visit every vertex at most once; this course uses path for the edge-distinct version.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The length of a weighted path is the sum of the lengths of the traversed edges.
  • The course convention corresponds to what some texts call a trail.
  • A path whose first and last vertices coincide is called a cycle or tour in the terminology video.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a real number \(u\), its positive part is

\[ u^+=\max\{u,0\}=\begin{cases}u,&u\ge0,\\0,&u<0.\end{cases} \]

In the newsvendor model, \((y-D)^+\) is leftover stock and \((D-y)^+\) is unmet demand.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The operator keeps a positive excess and replaces a negative excess with zero. It allows the two different demand cases to be expressed in a single formula.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both leftover and shortage quantities are nonnegative.
  • For a fixed realized demand, at least one of them is zero.
  • For discrete demand, expectations are computed by probability-weighting the positive parts for every demand outcome.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Defining the negative part by \(u^-=\max\{-u,0\}\) gives the identity \(u=u^+-u^-\).

  • If \(y=10\) and \(D=7\), leftovers are 3 and unmet demand is zero.
  • If \(y=10\) and \(D=12\), leftovers are zero and unmet demand is 2.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(y_m=\sqrt{2KD/h}\) and \(TCU_j(y)=Dc_j+KD/y+hy/2\), with \(c_1>c_2\). The price-break indifference quantity \(Q>y_m\) solves

\[ TCU_2(Q)=TCU_1(y_m), \]

or equivalently

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &Q^2+\frac{2(c_2D-TCU_1(y_m))}{h}Q\\ &\quad+\frac{2KD}{h}=0. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The larger root marks how far the qualifying order threshold can exceed the ordinary EOQ before extra holding costs outweigh the purchasing discount.

\(Q\) is where the discounted cost curve climbs back to the best cost without discount, \(TCU_1(y_m)\). Move \(q\) past \(y_m\) and past \(Q\) to see the three cases.

EOQ with price breaks requires comparing total costs across price ranges. The indifference quantity solves equality between competing cost expressions; it is a comparison threshold, not automatically a stationary EOQ.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With the worked-example convention that \(q\) qualifies, a threshold \(y_m<q<Q\) favours ordering \(q\).
  • For \(q>Q\), retain \(y_m\); for \(q<y_m\), \(y_m\) already receives the discount.
  • At \(q=Q\), the two candidates tie.
  • Directly comparing candidate costs avoids solving for \(Q\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The snack-bar exercise gives \(Q\approx89.07\) kilograms; its threshold 100 is too high.
  • For the phone example, \(Q\approx39.86\), and threshold 35 lies between \(y_m=22\) and \(Q\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A production-inventory model chooses production \(P_t\) and end-of-period stock \(I_t\) to meet known demands \(d_t\) across periods. With given initial stock \(I_0\), unit production costs \(c_t\), and end-of-period holding costs \(h_t\), the course problem is represented by

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_{t=1}^T(c_tP_t+h_tI_t),\\ I_{t-1}+P_t-d_t=I_t,\qquad P_t,I_t\ge0. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Production in a cheaper month may be stored for a later month. The inventory balance ensures that every unit sold comes from current production or previously held stock.

Linear program formulation introduces production and inventory decisions, balance equations and capacity restrictions. Its objective weights production and carried stock by their period costs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Nonnegative inventory rules out shortages.
  • The PDF charges 8 per window per month on end-of-month inventory.
  • The six-month exercise does not specify initial stock; taking \(I_0=0\) is an explicit modelling assumption.
  • With positive production and holding costs and no required final stock, surplus final inventory is unnecessary.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Month 1 requires 100 windows; producing 120 from zero stock leaves 20.
  • Producing a month-3 window in month 2 costs 45 plus 8 holding, compared with 55 in month 3.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The course's project longest path model uses a directed acyclic activity network with start \(S\) and finish \(T\). Each edge has an activity duration; an outgoing activity may start only after all activities entering its starting vertex finish. Under these precedence rules and without additional resource restrictions, project duration is the length of a longest \(S\)-to-\(T\) path.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The longest chain of dependent activities determines the earliest possible project completion. The exercise models this chain with binary edge-selection variables.

A directed network records precedence from an earlier activity to a later one. The shortest path binary formulation provides the path-balance equations; reversing the objective direction selects a longest path in the stated acyclic project network.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Maximize the sum of selected activity durations.
  • Use one unit of source-to-sink binary flow with balance at intermediate vertices.
  • Acyclicity matters: in a general cyclic network, flow balance alone could allow unrelated selected cycles.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure’s critical path \(S-2-3-T\) has duration \(2+5+2=9\), compared with 8 for \(S-2-T\). Negating the activity lengths turns this acyclic longest-path calculation into a shortest-path calculation; the lack of cycles permits the negative lengths.

  • In the exercise, \(S-A-D-F-T\) has duration \(5+2+6+4=17\).
  • \(S-B-D-F-T\) has duration \(3+3+6+4=16\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The project selection model chooses complete projects under resource budgets. Let \(y_j=1\) if project \(j\) is selected, \(r_j\) be its return, \(a_{tj}\) its expenditure in year \(t\), and \(B_t\) that year's budget. Then

\[ \begin{gathered} \max\sum_jr_jy_j,\\ \sum_ja_{tj}y_j\le B_t\ \text{for every }t,\\ y_j\in\{0,1\}. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A project uses resources in each relevant year and contributes its full return only when selected. Fractional project funding is excluded in this model.

The binary integer program sets each project variable to one if selected and zero otherwise. Annual budget inequalities couple the choices across the projects competing for those resources.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A separate budget constraint is needed for each year.
  • The later development-project example uses one capital budget.
  • Relaxing a binary variable to a fraction supplies a bound but not an implementable partial project.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The green columns in the figure represent selected projects, \(y_j=1\); each budget row sums only their expenditures.

  • The week 2 exercise has five projects and a budget of 25 in each of three years.
  • The development-project example has capital 20 and an optimal return of 3.4 from projects 1, 3, and 4.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The purchasing cost is the amount paid per inventory unit, multiplied by the quantity purchased. If its constant unit price is \(c\) and all demand is met at constant rate \(D\), the long-run purchasing cost rate is \(cD\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A constant unit price adds the same cost rate to every feasible EOQ policy. Quantity discounts change this because the chosen order size affects the unit price.

An inventory policy determines the quantities acquired. Multiplying those quantities by the applicable unit prices gives purchasing cost; price breaks can make the chosen timing or batch size affect that total.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A constant \(cD\) can be omitted when finding the classical EOQ, but retained when reporting full costs.
  • All-unit price breaks require comparing purchasing cost as well as setup and holding costs.
  • Purchasing cost is different from the fixed cost of initiating an order.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A pure integer program is an integer linear program in which every decision variable is restricted to integer values. Nonnegativity, upper bounds, and other restrictions remain separate model constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This model type fits decisions consisting entirely of counts. A linear objective alone does not permit fractional values once integrality has been imposed.

Integer linear programming permits integrality restrictions on selected decisions. In the pure case every decision variable has such a restriction.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• All \(n\) decision variables are integer-restricted, whereas a mixed integer program restricts only some of them.
  • Binary integer programs are a special case with the additional bounds 0 and 1.
  • Dropping integrality gives its LP relaxation.

The figure uses the illustrative model \(\max(3x_1+2x_2)\) subject to \(2x_1+2x_2\le9.5\), \(x_1\le3.5\) and \(\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^2\). Its best lattice point is \((3,1)\) with value 11; it is not a corner of the continuous polygon.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the course's maximization sensitivity report, the reduced cost of a currently zero-valued variable is the marginal change in the objective when that variable is increased and the other variables adjust through the current basis. If the tableau row is \(z+q_jx_j+\cdots=z_0\), the corresponding reduced cost is \(-q_j\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The number measures the opportunity cost of forcing an unused activity into the plan. A negative value means that a small forced increase reduces profit.

In sensitivity analysis, reduced cost describes the local objective effect of introducing a nonbasic variable while adjusting the basic variables to maintain the equations. Interpret its sign using the displayed tableau convention.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Do not confuse a reported reduced cost with the original objective coefficient.
  • The sign is opposite to the coefficient in the course maximization tableau.
  • The interpretation is local and relies on a feasible basis adjustment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, a third product \(x_c\) earns 4 and uses 3 finishing and 2 carpentry hours. At shadow prices 1 and 1, its reduced cost is \(4-(3\cdot1+2\cdot1)=-1\). A small forced increase therefore costs 1 unit of profit per unit produced while the basis remains feasible. Raising its profit by 1 removes that marginal disadvantage; a tie need not force it into every optimal solution.

  • Sheets have reported reduced cost -3.3 in the pipes-and-sheets example.
  • Their profit coefficient is 4 and its allowable increase is 3.3 before the current optimal basis can cease to be optimal.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A relaxation retains a problem's objective and removes or weakens constraints to obtain an easier problem. If \(F\) and \(F_R\) are the original and relaxed feasible sets, then \(F\subseteq F_R\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The larger feasible set gives a benchmark that may be unattainable in the original problem. Its optimum helps assess a feasible solution obtained by another method.

The optimization model fixes the original feasible set and objective. Removing a restriction enlarges that set, so its optimal solution can improve on the original optimum and supplies a bound rather than necessarily a feasible original answer.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For minimization, the relaxed optimum is no greater than the original optimum; for maximization, it is no smaller.
  • A relaxed optimum that is also feasible for the original problem is optimal for the original problem.
  • An infeasible relaxed optimizer need not have a strictly better value; equality can occur.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated objective \(4x_s+x_t\), dropping \(x_s\le40\) changes the optimum from \((40,20)\) with value 180 to \((50,0)\) with relaxed value 200.

  • Ignore the 100-mile refuelling limit in the routing example.
  • Remove integrality restrictions from an integer program while keeping its other constraints.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For an original directed edge \(i\to j\) with capacity \(c_{ij}\) and assigned flow \(x_{ij}\), its residual capacities are \(c_{ij}-x_{ij}\) in the forward direction and \(x_{ij}\) in the reverse direction. The residual network records these possibilities for increasing or cancelling current flow.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Reverse residual movement revises an earlier flow assignment. It is essential because a good final routing may require undoing part of an initially chosen path.

The maximum flow problem supplies the current arc flows and capacities. Forward residual capacity permits extra flow, while reverse residual capacity permits cancelling some previously assigned flow.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The course draws a connection with two directional residual labels; it must not be interpreted as equal capacity in both directions.
  • Only directions with positive residual capacity can be used by an augmenting path.
  • A forward augmentation decreases forward residual capacity and increases reverse residual capacity by the same amount.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
A saturated original edge has no forward residual capacity; its backward residual direction permits cancelling its assigned flow.

  • Capacity 6 and flow 2 on A-B give residual capacities 4 forward and 2 backward.
  • Cancelling one unit changes those residual capacities to 5 forward and 1 backward.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A right-hand-side sensitivity range is the interval for one constraint's right-hand side over which the current optimal basis remains feasible and optimal, with other parameters fixed. Within this range, its shadow price gives the exact linear change in optimal value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The same basis can represent different production quantities as a resource changes. Thus a valid shadow price does not imply an unchanged solution vector.

Change the finishing hours \(b_1\): inside the shaded range the same constraints stay binding, and \(z^*\) grows linearly in \(b_1\) (right).

Sensitivity analysis varies one right-hand side while keeping the basis fixed. Within the feasibility range, the shadow price gives the corresponding objective change; outside it, that basis-based formula need not apply.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use \(b_i-d_i\le b_i^{\mathrm{new}}\le b_i+u_i\) from the report.
  • A slack resource can often be reduced by its unused amount without affecting the current decision.
  • A change beyond the range cannot generally be valued by multiplying the full change by the old shadow price.

With the illustrated objective, the shadow price is 1 per added finishing hour throughout the range.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A rounding heuristic solves an integer program's LP relaxation and converts fractional variable values to nearby integers. The rounded vector is only a candidate: all original constraints must be checked before accepting it as a feasible solution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Rounding is simple and may be useful when quantities are large. Coupled constraints can make the nearest rounded decisions infeasible or substantially worse than an integer optimum.

The four lattice points around the LP optimum are the rounding candidates. Some violate a constraint, and none needs to be optimal.

This is a heuristic because rounding an LP answer need not preserve feasibility or attain the best integer objective. Every rounded candidate must be checked against the original restrictions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Rounding up can violate resource upper bounds.
  • Rounding down can violate minimum requirements or equalities.
  • Even a feasible rounded solution need not be optimal.
  • The video's numerical rounding illustration has inconsistent written constraints and a plotted feasible region; its claimed optimum is not used here.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Rounding \((2.6,1.6)\) upward to \((3,2)\) violates \(4x_1+x_2\le12\) because the left-hand side is 14.
  • The nearby vector \((2,2)\) satisfies that capacity inequality, but its objective value alone does not prove optimality.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Sensitivity analysis examines how changes in model parameters affect an LP's optimal solution and optimal value. The course studies changes to objective coefficients and resource right-hand sides using final simplex tableaux and Excel sensitivity reports.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Inputs may be estimates, and additional resources may be purchasable. Sensitivity information helps assess whether the current decision remains suitable after an input changes.

Vary one objective coefficient at a time and watch when the optimal corner changes.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The reported allowable ranges apply to one parameter change at a time.
  • Changing an objective coefficient can preserve the solution vector while changing profit.
  • Changing a right-hand side can change the solution vector even while the same basis and shadow prices remain valid.
  • Outside a valid range, reoptimization may be needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated objective with \(c_2>0\), \((20,60)\) remains optimal when \(1\le c_1/c_2\le2\). Changing the finishing right-hand side (RHS) from 100 to 110 instead moves the optimum to \((30,50)\) while preserving the basis. Within the applicable one-parameter range, \(\Delta z=y_i^*\Delta b_i\).

  • A change in banana ice-cream profit from 0.95 to 0.92 leaves the given production plan optimal.
  • Losing three gallons of cream changes the ice-cream quantities and reduces optimal profit by 3.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A setup cost is a fixed charge incurred whenever an order is placed, regardless of the order quantity. In the EOQ model it is denoted by \(K\). With demand rate \(D\) and batch size \(y\), its average rate is

\[ \frac{K}{y/D}=\frac{KD}{y}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Larger orders spread one fixed charge over more units and reduce ordering frequency. This saving must be balanced against extra holding cost.

Each order costs \(K\) and there are \(D/y\) orders per unit time, so setups cost \(KD/y\). Raise \(K\) to make larger batches worthwhile.

An inventory policy determines when positive orders occur. If each ordering cycle contains one setup, dividing the setup cost by cycle length gives the average setup-cost rate.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The charge is per order, not per inventory unit.
  • A period with no order incurs no setup in the dynamic lot-size model.
  • Increasing \(K\) increases the classical optimal order size.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated phone shop, \(K=605\) per order and \(D=2\) per day. The two panels cover the same \(33\) days:

Batch size Number of setups Setup cost per day \(y=11\) (left) \(6\) \(KD/y=1210/11=110\) \(y=22\) (right) \(3\) \(KD/y=1210/22=55\)

Doubling the batch size halves the setup frequency and its cost rate, but doubles average stock.

  • The snack bar pays 50 per order in addition to a per-kilogram purchase price.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The shadow price \(y_i^*\) of resource \(i\) is the rate of change of the optimal objective value when its right-hand side \(b_i\) increases slightly. Within the applicable sensitivity range,

\[ z^*(b_i+\Delta)=z^*(b_i)+y_i^*\Delta. \]

For the course's maximization LPs with \(\le\) resource constraints, it equals the coefficient of slack \(s_i\) in the final objective row.

The same marginal value is defined for nonlinear problems as the shadow price in constrained optimization, where it is given by a Lagrange multiplier; the linear-programming case is the one treated here.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A shadow price measures the marginal value of more resource under the current model. It can be compared with the cost of acquiring that resource.

The slope of \(z^*(b_1)\) on the right is the shadow price \(y_1^*\). It is valid only within the range where the basis stays the same.

Sensitivity analysis separates small parameter changes that preserve the current basis from changes that require reoptimization. The shadow price gives the objective response to a right-hand-side change over that valid range.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The rate is valid only over its allowable right-hand-side range.
  • At a degenerate optimum the rates for increasing and for decreasing \(b_i\) can differ, so the tableau value is then only a one-sided shadow price.
  • An unused resource has zero marginal value in the illustrated resource-allocation setting.
  • A binding constraint does not by itself guarantee a positive shadow price.
  • The tableau sign interpretation must be adjusted if the model or objective convention changes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Malt and barley have shadow prices 1, while hops has shadow price 0 in the beer-and-ale example.
  • In the drinks example, an additional unit of sugar is worth 0.5 within the valid range.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A shortage cost penalizes unmet demand. In the EOQ model with planned shortages, customers wait for replenishment and the parameter \(p\) charges each outstanding unit per unit of waiting time. With maximum backlog \(y-s\), the average shortage cost rate is

\[ p\frac{(y-s)^2}{2y}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The penalty permits a trade-off between holding stock and making customers wait. This time-based backlog penalty differs from the single-period lost-margin measure in the newsvendor model.

An inventory policy may allow a backlog instead of satisfying all demand immediately. Unlike holding cost, which charges positive stock, shortage cost charges the size and duration of the unmet demand.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The red triangle has area \((y-s)^2/(2D)\). Multiplying by \(p\) gives shortage cost \(p(y-s)^2/(2D)\) per cycle; dividing by \(t_0=y/D\) gives the cost rate \(p(y-s)^2/(2y)\).
  • Demand is backordered and later filled: the arriving batch first clears the backlog \(y-s\) and leaves \(s\) units on hand.
  • Use the same time unit for \(p\), \(h\), and \(D\).
  • In the newsvendor notation, \(p\) instead denotes selling price; symbols must be interpreted within their model.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The phone shop compensates waiting customers by 6 per phone per day.
  • The EOQ practice exercise permits planned shortages at 10 per unit per week.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For nonnegative edge lengths, the course's shortest path algorithm sets \(d(s)=0\) and \(U=\{s\}\). Repeatedly choose an edge \(u-v\) with \(u\in U\), \(v\notin U\) minimizing

\[ d(u)+\ell_{uv}. \]

Set \(d(v)\) equal to this value, record predecessor \(u\), and add \(v\) to \(U\). Stop when the destination is added, or continue to obtain distances to all vertices.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Vertices enter the settled set in order of their shortest distance from the origin. Predecessors recover the actual route after the distance has been computed.

The shortest path problem defines the origin, destination and route-length objective. The algorithm stores best-known distances and updates them using eligible connecting edges.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Compare complete distances from the origin, not just individual edge lengths.
  • Ties can be broken arbitrarily when one shortest path is sufficient.
  • Backtrack from the destination through predecessors and reverse the sequence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure settles vertices in the order \(A,C,B,D,E,F\). The recorded predecessor edges form a shortest-path tree rooted at \(A\).

  • The worked labels are \(d(B)=2\), \(d(A)=3\), \(d(D)=6\), \(d(C)=7\), \(d(E)=8\), \(d(T)=12\).
  • The predecessor chain \(T,E,D,A,B,S\) recovers the route of length 12.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A shortest path binary formulation assigns \(x_{ij}=1\) if a directed edge is selected. For the undirected course network, create both directed orientations of each edge. With origin \(s\), destination \(t\), and edge lengths \(\ell_{ij}\), use

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_{(i,j)}\ell_{ij}x_{ij},\\ \sum_jx_{ij}-\sum_jx_{ji}=\begin{cases}1,&i=s,\\-1,&i=t,\\0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\\ x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}. \end{gathered} \]

Sums include only existing directed orientations.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A unit of selected flow connects the origin to the destination. The objective chooses its least-cost route. This is the formulation derived from the video exercise.

The shortest path problem supplies the endpoint and arc-length data. A binary integer program then selects arcs, with flow balances connecting the origin to the destination.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With strictly positive lengths as in the exercise, an optimum contains no unnecessary cycle.
  • If zero-cost edges are allowed, an optimal binary solution may contain removable zero-cost cycles.
  • The balances alone must not be claimed to prohibit every possible cycle.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For a feasible network with nonnegative edge lengths, the unit-flow LP relaxation admits an integral optimal solution. Removing any zero-cost cycles leaves a shortest path; arbitrary optimal flow representations need not themselves be cycle-free.

  • The route S-B-A-D-E-T selects its five directed edges and has cost 12.
  • At A on that route, \(x_{BA}=x_{AD}=1\) balances one incoming and one outgoing edge.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The course's shortest path problem is defined on a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths, a specified origin, and a specified destination. It asks for a path between those vertices whose sum of edge lengths is minimum.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Silver-Meal heuristic chooses consecutive periods to cover with each order when the variable unit ordering cost is constant and identical across periods. For an order in period \(i\) covering through \(t\), define

\[ \begin{gathered} TC(i,t)=K_i+\sum_{j=i+1}^tD_j\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}h_k,\\ TCU(i,t)=\frac{TC(i,t)}{t-i+1}. \end{gathered} \]

Starting at the first uncovered period, extend coverage while average cost decreases, select the first local minimum, order \(\displaystyle \sum_{j=i}^{t^*}D_j\), and restart at \(i=t^*+1\). Stop at the horizon; on a flat tie, selecting the first local minimum is the convention used here.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The rule compares setup-plus-holding cost per covered period. It is simpler than full dynamic programming but does not guarantee the optimum.

The dynamic lot-size model supplies period demand, setup cost and stock-carrying cost. Silver-Meal is a heuristic: its local average-cost stopping rule does not compare every future ordering pattern and therefore does not prove global optimality.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Purchasing cost is omitted from the comparisons because the common unit price gives the same total for every complete demand-covering policy.
  • Add that constant purchasing cost when reporting a total that includes it.
  • At the start or end of the horizon, use only available neighbouring average-cost comparisons.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure’s first order covers \(D_1+D_2+D_3\); the rule then restarts at period 4. The displayed values are illustrative rather than the complete course exercise data.

  • The six-period video orders \((32,0,0,20,13,25)\), with setup and holding cost 122.
  • Week 6 practice 4 orders \((9,22,0,0)\) and costs 169 including purchases; the exact DP cost is 152.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The simplex method solves an LP by moving between basic feasible solutions through basis exchanges. In the course's maximization tableau convention, start with a feasible basis, test the objective row (optimality test), select an improving entering variable, apply the minimum-ratio test to select a leaving variable, pivot, and repeat until optimality or unboundedness is established.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Simplex uses the structure of an LP instead of enumerating all possible corners. Algebraic row operations implement movement between feasible corners.

Step through the iterations: starting from the slack basis at the origin, each pivot moves along an edge to a better corner until no improving variable is left.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The elementary starting form uses equality constraints, nonnegative right-hand sides, and nonnegative variables.
  • A slack basis starts the method for \(\le\) constraints with nonnegative right-hand sides.
  • The two-phase method supplies a feasible basis when one is not immediately available.
  • Degenerate pivots can change the basis without moving the decision vector.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For maximization, a feasible pivot does not decrease the objective. Degenerate pivots may leave it unchanged; an anti-cycling rule is needed to guarantee termination rather than relying only on the finite number of bases.

  • The two-variable example visits \((0,0)\), \((5,0)\), and \((3,4)\), with values 0, 15, and 17.
  • The three-variable example ends at \((0,5,4)\) with value 33.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For a maximization LP with a feasible canonical tableau written as \(\displaystyle z+\sum_{j\in N}q_jx_j=z_0\), if \(q_j\ge0\) for every nonbasic variable, the current basic feasible solution is optimal. Here \(N\) is the nonbasic index set and every variable is nonnegative.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Every allowed increase of a nonbasic variable then leaves the objective unchanged or reduces it. The tableau therefore certifies that the current value cannot be exceeded.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sign test depends on the course objective-row convention.
  • Feasibility and canonical form are required before applying the test.
  • A negative coefficient calls for further simplex analysis; degeneracy means it does not alone prove that a strictly better feasible vector exists.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, \(z=180-s_1-s_2\) and \(s_1,s_2\ge0\) certify \(z\le180\). Setting both nonbasic slacks to zero gives \(x_s=20\), \(x_t=60\), \(s_3=20\), attaining 180. A zero nonbasic objective coefficient can indicate an alternative optimum, but a distinct solution requires a positive feasible movement; a degenerate zero-length pivot is insufficient.

  • \(z+(7/5)s_1+(1/5)s_2=17\) proves \(z\le17\).
  • \(z-(1/2)x_2+(3/2)s_1=15\) still has a negative coefficient to investigate.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A simplex pivot replaces the leaving basic variable with the entering variable. Divide the selected pivot row by the nonzero pivot element, then subtract appropriate multiples of that normalized row from every other row, including the objective row, so that the pivot column is a unit column.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
These Gauss-Jordan operations preserve the equations while expressing them in terms of a new basis. The updated tableau can be used for the next iteration.

Each pivot exchanges one basic variable for another; geometrically it moves to an adjacent corner of the feasible region.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The pivot element is the intersection of the entering column and leaving row.
  • Update all coefficients and the right-hand side during each row operation.
  • Update the basic-variable label as well as the numerical entries.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the illustrated Giapetto pivot, the row operations are

\[ \begin{aligned}R_{s_3}&\leftarrow R_{s_3}/1,\\R_z&\leftarrow R_z+3R_{s_3},\\R_{s_1}&\leftarrow R_{s_1}-2R_{s_3},\\R_{s_2}&\leftarrow R_{s_2}-R_{s_3}.\end{aligned} \]

The new point is \((x_s,x_t)=(40,0)\) with \(z=120\); the next entering variable is \(x_t\).

  • Take the objective row \(z-3x_1-2x_2=0\) with the constraints of the augmented-form example. Then \(x_1\) enters and the minimum-ratio test picks the row of \(s_1\), so divide the pivot row \(2x_1+x_2+s_1=10\) by 2.
  • Add three times that normalized row to \(z-3x_1-2x_2=0\) to eliminate \(x_1\) from the objective row.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A simplex tableau records the variable coefficients, right-hand sides, and basic-variable labels of the current simplex equations. In the course convention, the first row writes the objective as

\[ z+\sum_jq_jx_j=z_0. \]

In canonical form (also called proper form), basic-variable columns form unit columns and have zero objective-row coefficients.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The tableau stores the equations compactly so that each pivot can be performed through row operations. It also makes the current solution and improvement directions easy to read.

Each basic variable has a unit column in a canonical tableau. Setting the other variables to zero then makes its value directly readable from the corresponding right-hand side.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Set nonbasic variables to zero and read basic values from the solution column.
  • The objective-row right-hand side is the current objective value.
  • A negative nonbasic coefficient indicates an improving direction for maximization.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated system is \(2x_s+x_t+s_1=100\), \(x_s+x_t+s_2=80\), \(x_s+s_3=40\), with objective \(z-3x_s-2x_t=0\). The orange objective row places coefficients on the left, and the blue basic columns form the identity. Setting \(x_s=x_t=0\) gives \(s_1=100\), \(s_2=80\), \(s_3=40\), \(z=0\).

  • \(z-3x_1-2x_2=0\) gives initial objective coefficients \(-3,-2\).
  • The final main-example row is \(z+(7/5)s_1+(1/5)s_2=17\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a constraint \(\displaystyle \sum_ja_{ij}x_j\le b_i\), a slack variable \(s_i\) converts it into

\[ \sum_ja_{ij}x_j+s_i=b_i,\qquad s_i\ge0. \]

Thus \(\displaystyle s_i=b_i-\sum_ja_{ij}x_j\) measures the unused allowance in the inequality.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The equality records both the amount used and the amount left over. This lets simplex work with equalities while preserving the original feasible choices.

Drag the decision point: \(\displaystyle s_i=b_i-\sum_j a_{ij}x_j\) is the unused amount of resource \(i\). A slack of \(0\) means the constraint is binding.

The nonnegativity constraint on the slack preserves the direction of the original inequality: \(s_i=b_i-\sum_j a_{ij}x_j\ge0\) holds exactly when the used amount does not exceed the allowance.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A zero slack means the constraint is binding at that solution.
  • The introduced slack has zero coefficient in the original objective.
  • With nonnegative right-hand sides, slack variables can form an initial feasible basis.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(2x_1+x_2\le10\) becomes \(2x_1+x_2+s_1=10\).
  • At \((x_1,x_2)=(3,4)\) this slack equals zero.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A spanning tree of a connected undirected network contains every original vertex and a subset of its edges that forms a tree. If the network has \(n\) vertices, every spanning tree has \(n-1\) edges.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: All locations remain connected, but enough edges are removed to eliminate every cycle. Different edge selections may produce different spanning trees.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Spanning refers to including all vertices, not all edges.
  • Adding another original edge to a spanning tree creates a cycle.
  • The minimum spanning tree problem compares the total lengths of spanning trees.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A network with seven vertices needs six edges in each spanning tree.
  • The Euclidean example selects \(1-7\), \(1-4\), \(4-3\), \(3-6\), \(6-2\), and \(6-5\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A surplus variable \(S_i\ge0\) transforms a lower-bound constraint into an equality:

\[ \begin{gathered} \sum_ja_{ij}x_j\ge b_i\\ \Longleftrightarrow\\ \sum_ja_{ij}x_j-S_i=b_i,\quad S_i\ge0. \end{gathered} \]

It measures the excess of the left-hand side over the required minimum.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A surplus is subtracted because it represents an amount above the minimum requirement. This differs from the added slack used for an upper-bound constraint.

The nonnegativity constraint on the surplus preserves the original lower bound: the excess \(S_i=\sum_j a_{ij}x_j-b_i\) must be at least zero.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The course uses capital \(S_i\) for surplus and lower-case \(s_i\) for slack.
  • A surplus variable alone generally does not produce an initial feasible slack-style basis.
  • An artificial variable may be added for the first simplex phase.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In task quota assignment, each task is assigned to exactly one agent and agent \(i\) must receive exactly \(q_i\) tasks. For binary assignment variables \(x_{ij}\) and times or costs \(c_{ij}\), the model is

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_i\sum_jc_{ij}x_{ij},\qquad \sum_ix_{ij}=1,\\ \sum_jx_{ij}=q_i,\qquad x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}. \end{gathered} \]

The quotas sum to the number of tasks.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Quotas impose a workload distribution while the objective minimizes the combined cost or time. The household exercise assigns two tasks to each person.

The binary integer program selects agent-task pairs. The task equations assign every task once, while the agent equations impose each workload quota rather than one task per agent.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In the later Hungarian-method treatment, duplicate each agent row \(q_i\) times to represent its available task slots.
  • Each task remains assigned exactly once.
  • Minimizing summed execution time is different from minimizing the latest completion time.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Eve receives marketing and dishwashing; Steven receives cooking and laundry, totalling 18.4 hours.
  • In week 5 practice 3, two identical rows per machine represent its two required jobs.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The transportation problem chooses shipments \(x_{ij}\ge0\) from plants \(i\) to distribution centres \(j\) to minimize total transport cost. With unit costs \(c_{ij}\), plant capacities \(s_i\), and required deliveries \(d_j\), a formulation is

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_i\sum_j c_{ij}x_{ij},\\ \sum_jx_{ij}\le s_i\ \text{for every }i,\\ \sum_ix_{ij}=d_j\ \text{for every }j. \end{gathered} \]

The demand constraints can also be written as \(\sum_ix_{ij}\ge d_j\): when every unit cost \(c_{ij}\) is positive, an optimal plan never delivers more than required, so both versions have the same optimal solutions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Each shipment consumes origin capacity and contributes to one destination's demand. The course example has more total production capacity than required demand, so unused capacity is permitted.

Linear program formulation identifies route shipments as variables and transport cost as the objective. Supply and demand constraints account for each origin and destination separately.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The decision variables are shipment quantities on routes.
  • Plant capacities are upper bounds rather than mandatory production amounts.
  • With positive unit costs, allowing deliveries above demand (\(\ge d_j\) instead of \(=d_j\)) cannot improve the optimum.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The diagram is a separate balanced illustration with total supply and demand both 50. Its unit costs are \(2,3,1\) from \(P_1\) to \(C_1,C_2,C_3\) and \(5,4,8\) from \(P_2\). Green-edge labels mean shipment quantity @ unit cost; their total is \(15\cdot2+15\cdot1+20\cdot4=125\). The plan is optimal: moving one unit of a customer's delivery from \(P_2\) to \(P_1\) saves \(5-2=3\) for \(C_1\), \(4-3=1\) for \(C_2\) and \(8-1=7\) for \(C_3\), so \(P_1\)'s 30 units go to \(C_3\) (15) and then \(C_1\) (15), and \(P_2\) supplies \(C_2\). Because total supply equals total demand, every plant here also ships its full supply. For a feasible transportation LP with integer supplies and demands, an integral optimal shipment plan exists.

  • Week 2 course data: three plants with capacities 5,000, 6,000 and 2,500 (13,500 in total) serve destinations whose demands total 12,000, so at least 1,500 units of capacity stay unused. The course's unit-cost table is not reproduced here, so its reported optimal cost of 35,000 cannot be checked on this page.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A tree is a connected undirected network containing no cycles. In the course, a tree can be formed by choosing a subset of the vertices and edges of a larger network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A tree connects its selected vertices without redundant loops. This makes it the basic structure for minimum-cost connection problems.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A finite tree with \(n\) vertices has \(n-1\) edges.
  • There is exactly one path between any two distinct vertices of a tree.
  • A spanning tree additionally includes every vertex of the original network.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The edges A-B and B-C form a tree on three vertices.
  • A tree on 77 vertices has 76 edges, as reinforced by the final-week statements exercise.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The two-phase method initializes and solves an LP using artificial variables \(R_i\ge0\). Phase I maximizes

\[ r=-\sum_iR_i \]

subject to the augmented constraints. If its optimum is negative, the original LP is infeasible. If its optimum is zero, restore the original objective, remove artificial variables from the working model, put the objective row in canonical form for the resulting feasible basis, and apply simplex in Phase II.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The first phase finds a point satisfying the original constraints. The second phase improves the objective from that feasible starting point.

The simplex tableau stores the auxiliary objective and its current basic columns in Phase I. Before Phase II, its objective row must be restored and reduced to canonical form for the basis obtained.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Eliminate basic artificial variables from the initial Phase I objective row before pivoting.
  • The phase-I objective can never exceed zero.
  • A zero-valued artificial variable still in the basis needs basis cleanup before its column is removed; the supplied worked example avoids this case.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(x_1+x_2\le10\) and \(2x_1+3x_2=25\), Phase I finds \((0,25/3)\).
  • Phase II for objective \(3x_1+2x_2\) reaches \((5,5)\) and value 25.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A maximization LP has an unbounded objective if feasible solutions attain objective values greater than any prescribed finite bound. For minimization, feasible values can be arbitrarily negative. In a feasible maximization tableau, an improving entering column with no strictly positive constraint coefficient certifies unboundedness.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
There is no finite best value: a feasible improvement can continue indefinitely. In a practical model, this can point to a missing restriction.

The region is open towards the upper right, and \(z=x_1+x_2\) keeps improving along it. Change the objective or add a constraint to get a finite optimum.

The minimum-ratio test normally limits an improving entering variable to keep basic values nonnegative. If no positive column coefficient provides a finite bound on that increase, the feasible objective can improve indefinitely.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An unbounded feasible region can still have a finite optimum for a particular objective.
  • The simplex certificate requires an improving objective coefficient and an unrestricted feasible increase together.
  • Do not confuse unboundedness with infeasibility.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure maximizes \(x_1+x_2\) subject to \(2x_1+x_2\ge40\) and \(\boldsymbol{x}\ge0\). Taking \(x_1=t\), \(x_2=0\) for \(t\ge20\) gives feasible values growing without bound. In an applied model, such a result can indicate a missing restriction rather than automatically proving a modelling error.

  • In week 2 practice 1(c), \(x_1=0\), \(x_2=t\ge0\) satisfies \(3x_1-2x_2\le8\) and gives \(z=t\).
  • In the week 3 example, \(x_1=x_2=t\) is feasible and yields \(2x_1+x_2=3t\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The underage cost in the newsvendor model is the foregone margin on one unit of demand that cannot be served:

\[ b=p-c>0, \]

where \(p\) is selling price and \(c\) is unit cost. Expected underage cost is \(b\mathbb{E}[(D-y)^+]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A stockout loses the opportunity to earn the margin, rather than the full selling price. The purchase cost that would have been paid must be subtracted.

Each unit of unmet demand loses the margin \(b=p-c\). Raise \(p\) and watch \(y^*\) move up.

The positive part \((D-y)^+\) counts demand that exceeds available stock. Multiplying it by the lost unit margin gives the realized underage loss.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Only demand above the available quantity contributes to underage loss.
  • Increasing selling price increases underage cost when unit cost is fixed.
  • The course assumes no additional per-unit stockout penalty beyond the lost margin.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated newspaper data give overage cost \(h=2\) and underage cost \(b=1.5\), hence critical ratio \(\beta=1.5/3.5=3/7\). These are single-period per-unit losses, rather than EOQ cost rates.

  • Newspapers sold for 5 and purchased for 3.50 have \(b=1.50\).
  • Meals sold for 5.50 and costing 2.20 have \(b=3.30\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An undirected network is a network in which edges have no prescribed orientation. An edge joining vertices \(i\) and \(j\) may be traversed in either direction.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This represents connections whose availability is symmetric. The course uses undirected networks for spanning trees, Euler tours, the Chinese postman problem, and shortest paths.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The pair \(i-j\) describes one undirected connection.
  • A path can traverse its edges in either direction.
  • Connectedness requires a path between every pair of vertices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
An undirected edge may be written \(\{i,j\}\); roads, cables and other symmetric links provide examples. The degree counts incident edge ends.

  • A two-way road connects two towns.
  • A cable connecting two sites can be selected as part of a spanning tree.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The course's uniform demand model assumes \(D\) is uniformly distributed on a known interval \([a,u]\), with \(0\le a<u\). Its CDF inside the interval is \(F(y)=(y-a)/(u-a)\), with values 0 below \(a\) and 1 above \(u\). Thus the continuous newsvendor quantity is

\[ y^*=a+(u-a)\beta. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Demand is spread uniformly across the stated interval. The relevant inventory calculation is a linear interpolation to the critical quantile.

With demand uniform on \([50,150]\) the optimal stock interpolates linearly: \(y^*=a+(u-a)\beta\).

The continuous newsvendor rule sets \(F(y^*)=\beta\). Solving the uniform CDF equation gives the linear interpolation between the two demand endpoints.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The distribution is used as an application of probability prerequisites; the course does not develop a general distribution theory.
  • For \(\beta=1/2\), the quantity is the midpoint.
  • The quantile lies within the demand interval.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For meal demand on \([80,120]\) and \(\beta=0.6\), order 104.
  • For that same interval, \(F(100)=0.5\) and \(F(104)=0.6\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An unrestricted variable \(x_j\) can be replaced everywhere by the difference of two nonnegative variables:

\[ x_j=x_j^+-x_j^-,\qquad x_j^+,x_j^-\ge0. \]

If \(x_j\le0\) is required, use \(x_j=-x_j^-\) with \(x_j^-\ge0\) instead.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The substitution allows simplex to use nonnegative variables while preserving the original variable's ability to take negative values. Recover the original decision after solving.

Linear programming keeps the objective and constraints linear after replacing \(x_j\) by \(x_j^+-x_j^-\). The nonnegativity constraint on each component allows simplex to work with nonnegative variables without restricting the sign of their difference.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Apply the substitution to both the objective and every constraint.
  • The difference representation is not unique; it is not necessary to impose a nonlinear restriction preventing both parts from being positive.
  • The optimal original variable is the difference of the computed parts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The two replacement columns are opposites and hence linearly dependent. They cannot both belong to one basis, although a nonbasic feasible representation may have both component values positive.

  • \(x_2^+=0\) and \(x_2^-=10\) give \(x_2=-10\).
  • The other-model-forms exercise transforms its nonpositive \(x_1\) as \(-x_1^-\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The vehicle routing problem asks for a minimum-distance set of vehicle routes that start and end at a depot, visit every required location, and respect the vehicle's restrictions. In the course example, one depot serves eight required locations. The vehicle can travel at most 100 miles between refuelling stops, and refuelling is possible only at the depot.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The fuel limit may require several depot-to-depot trips. This example illustrates how a feasible heuristic and a relaxed problem give complementary information.

The optimization model specifies both route coverage and the fuel restriction. A relaxation removing the fuel limit can produce a shorter route and a lower bound, but that route may be infeasible for the original vehicle.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every required location must be visited and every trip must respect the fuel limit.
  • Joining successive visits can improve a plan if feasibility is retained.
  • Removing the fuel limit gives a lower bound, not automatically a feasible route for the original problem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Separate visits from the depot produce the stated 232-mile heuristic plan.
  • The improved plan has length 214; the relaxed optimum has length 202.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The degree of a vertex in the undirected networks considered in the course is the number of edges incident to it. Parallel edges are counted separately. A vertex has even or odd degree according to the parity of that count.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Degree counts how many edge ends meet at a vertex. Its parity determines whether a closed traversal can use every incident edge exactly once.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• At a vertex on an Euler tour, arrivals and departures pair the incident edges.
  • Duplicating a path reverses degree parity at its endpoints and preserves it at internal vertices.
  • Odd-degree vertices are the vertices matched in the Chinese postman construction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, the degrees sum to \(\displaystyle \sum_v\deg v=2|E|=18\), since each of the nine edges contributes two ends. Thus the number of odd-degree vertices is even; the illustrated odd vertices are \(B\) and \(E\).

  • In the introduction network, A has degree 3 and C has degree 5.
  • In the five-vertex Chinese postman example, A, B, D, and E are odd-degree vertices.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Weibull demand distribution in the exercise has shape \(k>0\), scale \(\lambda>0\), and nonnegative support. For \(x\ge0\),

\[ \begin{gathered} F(x)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-(x/\lambda)^k},\\ f(x)=\frac{k}{\lambda}\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^{k-1}\mathrm{e}^{-(x/\lambda)^k}. \end{gathered} \]

For the newsvendor critical ratio \(0<\beta<1\), inversion gives

\[ y^*=\lambda[-\ln(1-\beta)]^{1/k}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The exercise supplies the density and CDF, so the required task is to solve the CDF equation at the cost-based probability. No broader Weibull theory is needed for this application.

The continuous newsvendor rule sets the supplied demand CDF equal to the critical ratio. Inverting that equation gives the Weibull order quantity without requiring a separate optimization over all stock levels.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use the given shape and scale parametrization.
  • The CDF is zero below zero.
  • The scale parameter has the same units as demand.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Bananas have \(k=2\), \(\lambda=50\), \(b=1.3\), \(h=0.2\), so \(\beta=13/15\).
  • The optimum is \(50\sqrt{-\ln(2/15)}\approx70.97\) kilograms.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: To obtain a maximum zero-cost matching, create a source \(S\), one vertex for each matrix row, one for each column, and a sink \(T\). Add source-to-row edges, row-to-column edges exactly where the matrix entry is zero, and column-to-sink edges. Give every edge capacity 1 and compute an integral maximum flow.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A unit of flow selects a zero-cost row-column pair. Unit capacities ensure that no row or column is assigned twice.

A bipartite matching selects row-column pairs without repeating a row or column. Unit capacities enforce precisely those non-repetition restrictions in the flow construction.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The maximum flow value is the maximum number of simultaneous zero-cost assignments.
  • Read selected pairs from row-to-column edges carrying flow 1.
  • The augmenting path algorithm starting at zero preserves integrality for these integer capacities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure’s zero pairs are \((1,2),(2,1),(2,2),(2,3),(3,2)\). Its integral maximum flow is 2, so only two independent zeros can be assigned, fewer than the three required for a complete assignment. The minimum cut also determines a minimum zero cover; further Hungarian adjustment is needed.

  • The five-job practice matrix admits four zero-cost pairs.
  • One such matching is jobs 1, 2, 3, 4 to machines 1, 4, 3, 2.
