docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a linear operator or square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\), a nonzero vector \(\boldsymbol{p}\) and scalar \(\lambda\) satisfying \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda \boldsymbol{p}\) give an eigenvector \(\boldsymbol{p}\) and corresponding eigenvalue \(\lambda\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The vector space supplies both the vectors and the scalar multiplication in \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda\boldsymbol{p}\); this equation compares two vectors in that same space.

For a real eigenvector with a real eigenvalue, the line it spans is invariant under the transformation. A positive eigenvalue preserves its direction, a negative eigenvalue reverses it, and a zero eigenvalue maps it to the zero vector. The equation \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda \boldsymbol{p}\) also defines eigenvectors and eigenvalues over the complex numbers.

\(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda \boldsymbol{p}\) with \(\boldsymbol{p}\neq\boldsymbol{0}\): \(\boldsymbol{A}\) only rescales \(\boldsymbol{p}\), by the eigenvalue \(\lambda\). Here \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\) has \(\lambda_1=3\) on \(\boldsymbol{p}_1=\binom11\) and \(\lambda_2=1\) on \(\boldsymbol{p}_2=\binom1{-1}\); a vector \(\boldsymbol{v}\) off these lines is turned.

Turn the unit vector \(\boldsymbol{x}\) with \(\varphi\): usually \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\) points elsewhere, but on the dashed eigenvector lines \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\lambda \boldsymbol{x}\). A quarter turn has no real eigenvector.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The zero vector is excluded from being an eigenvector.
  • Eigenvalues of triangular or diagonal matrices are their diagonal entries.
  • For a real-valued matrix, nonreal complex eigenvalues and eigenvectors occur in complex conjugate pairs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\), \((1,0)\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(2\).
  • For the same matrix, \((0,1)\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(3\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For any square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) with entries in a field \(\mathbb{F}\), the eigenvalues of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) are exactly the roots in \(\mathbb{F}\) of its characteristic polynomial \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The determinant vanishes exactly when the shifted square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I}\) is singular. Its nontrivial kernel then provides an eigenvector, linking a polynomial root to the eigenvalue equation.

The eigenvalue equation \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda \boldsymbol{p}\) has a nonzero solution \(\boldsymbol{p}\) exactly when \(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I}\) is singular, that is, when \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})=0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue if and only if \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})=0\).
  • Every eigenvalue has at least one corresponding eigenvector.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a diagonal matrix, the roots are precisely the diagonal entries.
  • For \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\), the eigenvalues are \(1\pm2\mathrm{i}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An elementary row operation is one of three reversible operations on a system or matrix: adding a multiple of one row to another, interchanging two rows, or multiplying a row by a nonzero scalar.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Elementary row operations transform a system without changing its solution set.

Each operation is undone by another of the same kind, so the transformed system is equivalent to the original. Each operation can also be written as multiplication on the left by an elementary matrix, the matrix obtained by applying the same operation to the identity matrix.

Replace \(\boldsymbol{R}_2\) by \(\boldsymbol{R}_2+k\boldsymbol{R}_1\): the second line swings about the solution, which never moves. The button picks the \(k\) that eliminates \(x_1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Elementary row operations preserve equivalence of systems.
  • Gauss-Jordan elimination consists of applying elementary row operations until reduced row echelon form is reached.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Replace \(\boldsymbol{R}_2\) by \(\boldsymbol{R}_2-3\boldsymbol{R}_1\).
  • Swap \(\boldsymbol{R}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{R}_3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An equivalence relation on a set \(A\) is a relation \(\sim\) on \(A\) such that, for all \(a,b,c\in A\), it is:

  1. reflexive: \(a\sim a\);
  2. symmetric: if \(a\sim b\), then \(b\sim a\);
  3. transitive: if \(a\sim b\) and \(b\sim c\), then \(a\sim c\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An equivalence relation formalizes when different objects should be treated as the same for a particular purpose.

The relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so its equivalence classes \([0],[1],[2]\), where \([x]=\{y\in A\colon y\sim x\}\), partition the set \(A=\{0,1,\ldots,8\}\). Every element lies in exactly one class, and \([x]=[y]\) if and only if \(x\sim y\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Equal cardinality is an equivalence relation on sets.
  • A bijection is the main tool for proving that two sets have the same cardinality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Congruence modulo \(n\) is an equivalence relation on integers.
  • The natural numbers \(\mathbb{N}\) are the standard example of a countably infinite set.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Two systems of equations are equivalent if they have the same solution set.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Equivalent systems contain the same mathematical information even if their equations look different.

The two systems have the same solution set \(\{(2,1)\}\) although their equations, and hence their lines, differ. The elementary row operations are reversible, so they preserve the solution set.

Every \(k\) gives a different-looking system with the same solution set: the systems are equivalent.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Elementary row operations produce equivalent systems.
  • Solving a system by elimination means replacing it by easier equivalent systems.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x+y=2\), \(x-y=0\) is equivalent to \(x=1\), \(y=1\).
  • Swapping the order of equations gives an equivalent system.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Euclidean distance between two points \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}\|=\sqrt{(x_1-y_1)^2+\cdots+(x_n-y_n)^2}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Euclidean distance is the ordinary straight-line distance inherited from the Euclidean norm.

The Euclidean distance is \(d(\boldsymbol{P},\boldsymbol{Q})=\|\boldsymbol{Q}-\boldsymbol{P}\|=\sqrt{(q_1-p_1)^2+\cdots+(q_n-p_n)^2}\). In the figure, \(d(\boldsymbol{P},\boldsymbol{Q})=\sqrt{3^2+2^2}=\sqrt{13}\).

Drag the points \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\): the distance is the length of \(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}\), the hypotenuse of a right triangle with the coordinate differences as legs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The distance between two points is the length of the vector connecting them.
  • The distance from a point to a line is the minimum Euclidean distance from the point to points on the line.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A Euclidean space is a pair \((V,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) of a real vector space \(V\) with \(\dim V<\infty\) and an inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\colon V\times V\to\mathbb{R}\); in other words, a finite-dimensional real inner product space.

The standard example, and the one meant by the Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\), is the real coordinate space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with the dot product \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}=x_1y_1+\cdots+x_ny_n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Euclidean space is the setting for ordinary geometric intuition in linear algebra.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The inner product induces the norm \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\langle \boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}\rangle}\) and the distance \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}\|\); on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with the dot product these are the Euclidean norm and the Euclidean distance.
  • The inner product also defines the angle between vectors and orthogonality.
  • Every \(n\)-dimensional Euclidean space is isomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with the dot product by a linear bijection that preserves the inner product: write each vector in coordinates with respect to an orthonormal basis, a basis of mutually orthogonal unit vectors.
  • Lines, planes, and hyperplanes are geometric objects in Euclidean spaces.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the dot product is the Euclidean plane; \(\mathbb{R}^3\) with the dot product is ordinary three-dimensional Euclidean space.
  • \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with \(\langle \boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle=2x_1y_1+x_2y_2\) is also a Euclidean space; its unit circle \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\langle \boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}\rangle=1\}\) is an ellipse in the usual picture of the plane.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For any \(z\in\mathbb{C}\), we have \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}z}=\cos z+\mathrm{i}\sin z.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The complex exponential and complex sine and cosine are defined by convergent power series in a complex number. Separating the even and odd terms of the exponential series gives the identity. For real \(\theta\), the polar coordinates of the complex plane identify \(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta\) as the point of modulus one and angle \(\theta\).

Euler's formula connects complex exponentials to trigonometry.

\(|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}|=1\) for every real \(\theta\): the exponential of an imaginary number is a rotation, not a stretch.

Move the real angle \(\theta\): \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}\) runs round the unit circle, with real part \(\cos\theta\) and imaginary part \(\sin\theta\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• We have \(|\mathrm{e}^z| = \mathrm{e}^{\operatorname{Re}(z)}\) and \(\arg(\mathrm{e}^z) = \operatorname{Im}(z) + 2\pi k .\)
  • We have \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta} + \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}}{2}\) and \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta} - \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}}{2\mathrm{i}}.\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • When \(z=\pi\), we get the well-known Euler's identity.

docs.title: Corollary
docs.text: Setting \(z=\pi\) in Euler's formula gives \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}+1=0.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The equality is an identity of complex numbers, with imaginary part zero when the angle is \(\pi\). In the polar coordinates of the complex plane, modulus one and angle \(\pi\) identify the negative real point \(-1\).

For a real angle \(\theta\), \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}=\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta\) is the point on the unit circle at angle \(\theta\). Taking \(\theta=\pi\) makes a half-turn from \(1\) to \(-1\). Euler's identity writes this as \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}+1=0\).

At \(\theta=\pi\) the point \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}\) has made half a turn from \(1\) to \(-1\), so \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}+1=0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Euler's identity involves three basic arithmetic operations exactly once: addition, multiplication, and exponentiation.
  • It also links five fundamental mathematical constants: the additive identity \(0\), the multiplicative identity \(1\), the fundamental circle constant \(\pi\), the base of the natural exponential \(\mathrm{e}\), and the imaginary unit \(\mathrm{i}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Substitute \(\theta=\pi\) into Euler's formula: \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}=\cos\pi+\mathrm{i}\sin\pi=-1+\mathrm{i}\cdot0=-1\). Adding \(1\) gives \(0\). Thus multiplication by \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}\) sends \(z=2+3\mathrm{i}\) to \((-1)(2+3\mathrm{i})=-2-3\mathrm{i}\), a half-turn about the origin.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A field is an algebraic structure \((F,+,\cdot)\) in which addition and multiplication behave like ordinary arithmetic: addition makes \(F\) an Abelian group, multiplication is associative and commutative and has an identity \(1\neq0\), every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse, and multiplication distributes over addition.

When a vector space is defined over a field \(F\), the elements of \(F\) are called scalars.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A field is a commutative ring with an identity \(1\ne0\) in which every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse. The ring laws supply distributivity; the inverse condition additionally permits division by any nonzero scalar.

Fields are the number systems over which vector spaces are built. In this course, the most important examples are \(\mathbb{R}\) and \(\mathbb{C}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In a vector space over \(F\), scalar multiplication uses elements of \(F\).
  • The real numbers and complex numbers are fields; the integers are not a field because most nonzero integers do not have integer multiplicative inverses.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{R}\) with ordinary addition and multiplication is a field.
  • \(\mathbb{C}\) with ordinary addition and multiplication is a field.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A vector space \(V\) over a field \(\mathbb{F}\) is finite-dimensional if it has a finite spanning list: there are vectors \(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_n\in V\) such that

\[ V=\operatorname{span}(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_n). \]

Equivalently, every \(\boldsymbol{v}\in V\) is a linear combination \(\boldsymbol{v}=a_1\boldsymbol{v}_1+\cdots+a_n\boldsymbol{v}_n\) with coefficients in \(\mathbb{F}\). The zero vector space is included and has dimension zero. A vector space that is not finite-dimensional is called infinite-dimensional.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Finitely many vectors suffice to generate every vector in the space. This does not mean that the space contains only finitely many vectors: \(\mathbb{R}^2\) contains infinitely many vectors, but two coordinate directions span it. Every basis has the same finite length, called the dimension, so each vector is described by a fixed number of coordinates.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A finite spanning list can be reduced to a basis.
  • Relative to a basis, every vector has a unique expression as a linear combination of the basis vectors.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The coordinate vectors \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) span \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
  • The space \(\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})\) of polynomials of degree at most two is spanned by \((1,x,x^2)\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: The fundamental theorem of algebra states that every nonconstant polynomial with complex number coefficients has at least one root in \(\mathbb{C}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The theorem says that \(\mathbb{C}\) is large enough to solve all nonconstant single-variable polynomial equations over \(\mathbb{C}\).

\(z^5-1\) has exactly \(5\) roots in \(\mathbb{C}\) (only \(z=1\) is real): a degree-\(n\) polynomial always has \(n\) complex roots, counted with multiplicity.

Change the coefficients, even to complex ones: a polynomial of degree \(n\) always has exactly \(n\) roots in \(\mathbb C\), counted with multiplicity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every complex polynomial of degree \(n\geq1\) has exactly \(n\) roots when counted with multiplicity.
  • Every complex polynomial of degree \(n\geq1\) can be factored into linear factors over \(\mathbb{C}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x^2+1\) has roots \(\mathrm{i}\) and \(-\mathrm{i}\) in \(\mathbb{C}\).
  • \(x^3\) has the root \(0\) with multiplicity \(3\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space and let \(\boldsymbol{A} \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\) be a linear map. Then

\[ \dim(\ker \boldsymbol{A}) + \dim(\operatorname{range} \boldsymbol{A}) = \dim V. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The range consists of the output vectors that can actually be reached. Its dimension counts the independent output directions, while the kernel counts the input directions sent to zero.

A linear map splits the dimension of its domain into directions lost to the kernel and directions visible in the range.

The rank-nullity formula is \(\dim(\ker \boldsymbol{A})+\dim(\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A})=\dim V\). In the figure, \(1+2=3\): one input dimension is collapsed to zero and two survive in the image.

However you set \(\boldsymbol{A}\), \(\dim(\ker \boldsymbol{A})+\dim(\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A})=2\): what the kernel takes away, the range loses.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The theorem is also called the rank-nullity theorem: the rank of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is \(\dim(\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A})\) and its nullity is \(\dim(\ker \boldsymbol{A})\).
  • It connects injectivity, surjectivity, and dimension for finite-dimensional vector spaces.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol{A}\colon\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^2\) has a one-dimensional kernel, then its range has dimension \(2\).
  • If \(\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathcal{L}(V)\) and \(\ker \boldsymbol{A}=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\), then \(\boldsymbol{A}\) has full range and is bijective.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text: Gauss-Jordan elimination is the algorithm that applies elementary row operations to an augmented matrix until it reaches reduced row echelon form.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
It solves linear systems by transforming them into equivalent systems whose solutions can be read off directly.

The forward elimination uses the row additions \(\boldsymbol{R}_2+\tfrac{3}{2}\boldsymbol{R}_1\), \(\boldsymbol{R}_3+\boldsymbol{R}_1\), and \(\boldsymbol{R}_3-4\boldsymbol{R}_2\). Scaling the pivots to \(1\) and clearing the entries above them gives reduced row echelon form, from which \(\boldsymbol{x}=(2,3,-1)\) can be read without back substitution. Stopping at row echelon form and then solving by back substitution is called Gaussian elimination.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Gauss-Jordan elimination preserves the solution set of the system.
  • If the coefficient side of an augmented matrix becomes the identity matrix, the right side gives the unique solution.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The system \(3x+y-z=-4\), \(x+z=0\), \(3x-2y=-3\) reduces to \(x=-1\), \(y=0\), \(z=1\).
  • Gauss-Jordan elimination can also be used to compute inverse matrices by augmenting with \(\boldsymbol{I}_n\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A generalized eigenvector of a square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) for eigenvalue \(\lambda\) is a nonzero vector \(\boldsymbol{v}\) such that \((\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})^k \boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}\) for some positive integer \(k\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The identity matrix makes \(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I}\) subtract \(\lambda\boldsymbol{v}\) from the image of \(\boldsymbol{v}\). The defining equation places \(\boldsymbol{v}\) in the kernel of a power of this shifted matrix, even when it is not in the kernel of the first power.

Generalized eigenvectors replace missing ordinary eigenvectors for defective matrices.

A nonzero vector \(\boldsymbol{v}\) is a generalized eigenvector for \(\lambda\) if \((\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})^k\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}\) for some positive integer \(k\). The vector \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\) is an ordinary eigenvector, while the chain \(\boldsymbol{v}_3\to \boldsymbol{v}_2\to \boldsymbol{v}_1\to\boldsymbol{0}\) supplies further basis vectors for the defective matrix.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every ordinary eigenvector is a generalized eigenvector with \(k=1\).
  • Generalized eigenvectors are used to construct Jordan normal form.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \((\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}\), then \(\boldsymbol{v}\) is an eigenvector and a generalized eigenvector.
  • If \((\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})^2\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}\) but \((\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{v}\neq\boldsymbol{0}\), then \(\boldsymbol{v}\) is generalized but not ordinary.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A group is a set \(A\) together with a binary operation \(\star\) such that:

  1. \(\star\) is associative;
  2. \(\star\) has an identity element;
  3. every element has an inverse element.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Associativity allows parentheses to move in \(a\star b\star c\) without changing the result. This makes repeated group operations unambiguous; it does not allow the factors to be reordered.

Groups capture the algebra of reversible operations.

The table shows addition modulo \(4\), which is associative and has identity \(0\). Each row contains a green \(0\), exhibiting an additive inverse; for example, \(1+3=0\) and \(2+2=0\). Each row and column is a permutation of \(\{0,1,2,3\}\). The symmetry of the table also shows that this group is Abelian.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every group is a monoid.
  • If the operation is also commutative, the group is Abelian.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((\mathbb{Z},+)\) is a group. \((\mathbb{N},+)\) is not a group because positive natural numbers do not have additive inverses in \(\mathbb{N}\).
  • \((\mathbb{R},+)\) is a standard example where the operation is ordinary addition.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Over \(\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{C}\), a linear system \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) is homogeneous if \(\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{0}\). It is inhomogeneous if \(\boldsymbol{b}\neq \boldsymbol{0}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The standard matrix form gathers all equations into \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\). Homogeneity is the special choice in which the right-hand side is the zero vector, so the zero vector is automatically a solution.

A homogeneous system asks which vectors are mapped to zero. An inhomogeneous system asks which vectors are mapped to a specified nonzero right-hand side.

\(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\) (here \(x_1+2x_2=0\)): the solutions form the subspace \(\ker \boldsymbol{A}\), so \(\boldsymbol{0}\) is always a solution and solutions can be added and scaled; for \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) (here \(x_1+2x_2=3\)) the solution set is \(\boldsymbol{x}_p+\ker \boldsymbol{A}\), for any one particular solution \(\boldsymbol{x}_p\), or empty.

With \(\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{0}\) both lines pass through the origin, so \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\) always solves the system. Make the rows parallel for infinitely many solutions, or switch \(\boldsymbol{b}\) on.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A homogeneous system always has at least the trivial solution \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\).
  • If a homogeneous system has more than one solution, then it has infinitely many solutions.
  • An inhomogeneous system may have no solution, one solution, or infinitely many solutions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\) is homogeneous.
  • \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) with \(\boldsymbol{b}\neq \boldsymbol{0}\) is inhomogeneous.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(V\) be a vector space of dimension \(n\ge1\).

  • A linear hyperplane of \(V\) is a subspace \(H\) of dimension \(n-1\).
  • An affine hyperplane of \(V\) is a translate \(\boldsymbol{p}+H=\{\boldsymbol{p}+\boldsymbol{h}\colon \boldsymbol{h}\in H\}\) of a linear hyperplane \(H\), where \(\boldsymbol{p}\in V\).

In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) the affine hyperplanes are exactly the sets

\[ \begin{gathered} \{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon a_1x_1+\cdots+a_nx_n=d\}\\ \text{with }\boldsymbol{a}=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\neq\boldsymbol{0}, \end{gathered} \]

and such a hyperplane is linear exactly when \(d=0\), that is, when it passes through the origin. Used without a qualifier in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), "hyperplane" usually means an affine hyperplane; some linear algebra texts reserve it for linear hyperplanes, so the qualifier is worth stating.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Hyperplanes generalize lines in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and planes in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

In \(\mathbb R^2\) the hyperplane \(a_1x_1+a_2x_2=d\) is a line with normal vector \(\boldsymbol{n}=(a_1,a_2)\). Change \(d\) to shift it; drag \(\boldsymbol{x}\) to see which side it is on.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The vector \(\boldsymbol{a}=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) is a normal vector of the hyperplane \(a_1x_1+\cdots+a_nx_n=d\): it is orthogonal to every difference \(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}\) of two of its points.
  • An affine hyperplane \(\boldsymbol{a}\cdot \boldsymbol{x}=d\) divides \(\mathbb{R}^n\) into the two closed half-spaces \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon \boldsymbol{a}\cdot \boldsymbol{x}\le d\}\) and \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon \boldsymbol{a}\cdot \boldsymbol{x}\ge d\}\), which meet exactly in the hyperplane.
  • The hyperplanes of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) are the lines and those of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) are the planes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x+y=1\) is an affine hyperplane of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) that is not linear, since it misses the origin.
  • \(x+y+z=0\) is a linear hyperplane of \(\mathbb{R}^3\).
  • The \(xy\)-plane \(\{(x,y,z)\colon z=0\}\) is a linear hyperplane of \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An idempotent matrix, or projection matrix, is a real square matrix \(\boldsymbol{P}\) satisfying \(\boldsymbol{P}^2=\boldsymbol{P}\).

Such a matrix projects onto its range: it maps every vector into the subspace \(\operatorname{range}(\boldsymbol{P})\) and leaves every vector of that subspace unchanged. A projection matrix that is also symmetric, \(\boldsymbol{P}^{\top}=\boldsymbol{P}\), is an orthogonal projection matrix; the others are oblique projections. In statistics and econometrics "projection matrix" usually means the orthogonal case, such as the hat matrix \(\boldsymbol{X}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{X})^{-1}\boldsymbol{X}^{\top}\) of least squares, for \(\boldsymbol{X}\) of full column rank.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The square \(\boldsymbol{P}^2\) is a matrix product, representing two successive applications of the same linear map. Idempotence says this composition equals one application.

Applying an idempotent matrix twice has the same effect as applying it once: projecting a vector that already lies in the subspace leaves it where it is.

\(\boldsymbol{A}^2=\boldsymbol{A}\): \(\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v})=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\), so vectors of \(\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A}\) stay fixed (\(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{w}=\boldsymbol{w}\)) and \(\ker \boldsymbol{A}\) is killed (\(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{k}=\boldsymbol{0}\)). Every \(\boldsymbol{v}\) splits as \(\boldsymbol{w}+\boldsymbol{k}\) with \(\boldsymbol{w}\in\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A}\), \(\boldsymbol{k}\in\ker \boldsymbol{A}\) (a direct sum). The eigenvalues are \(0\) and \(1\) only; the projection need not be orthogonal (here it is oblique).

For every \(a\) and direction \(d\) the matrix \(\boldsymbol{P}\) satisfies \(\boldsymbol{P}^2=\boldsymbol{P}\). The orthogonal case is also symmetric; the oblique one is not.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The zero square matrix and identity matrix are idempotent.
  • If an idempotent matrix is invertible, then it equals the identity matrix.
  • If \(\boldsymbol{P}\) is idempotent, then every vector splits as \(\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{v}+(\boldsymbol{v}-\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{v})\) with \(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{v}\in\operatorname{range}(\boldsymbol{P})\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}-\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{v}\in\ker(\boldsymbol{P})\), so the space is the direct sum \(\operatorname{range}(\boldsymbol{P})\oplus\ker(\boldsymbol{P})\): \(\boldsymbol{P}\) projects onto its range along its kernel.
  • If \(\boldsymbol{P}\) is idempotent, so is \(\boldsymbol{I}-\boldsymbol{P}\); it projects onto \(\ker(\boldsymbol{P})\) along \(\operatorname{range}(\boldsymbol{P})\).
  • The only possible eigenvalues of an idempotent matrix are \(0\) and \(1\).
  • An orthogonal projection matrix is symmetric and idempotent; then \(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{v}\) is the point of \(\operatorname{range}(\boldsymbol{P})\) closest to \(\boldsymbol{v}\), and \(\boldsymbol{v}-\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{v}\) is orthogonal to \(\operatorname{range}(\boldsymbol{P})\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\boldsymbol{I}_n^2=\boldsymbol{I}_n\), so \(\boldsymbol{I}_n\) is idempotent: it projects every vector onto the whole space.
  • \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) is idempotent and symmetric: the orthogonal projection onto the \(x\)-axis.
  • \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) is idempotent but not symmetric: an oblique projection onto the \(x\)-axis along the line spanned by \((1,-1)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An identity element for a binary operation \(\star\) on \(A\) is an element \(e\in A\) such that

\[ a\star e=e\star a=a \]

for all \(a\in A\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The identity element leaves every element unchanged under the operation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If an identity element exists, it is unique.
  • Associativity, identity elements, and inverse elements determine which algebraic structure is present.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(0\) is the identity for addition; \(1\) is the identity for multiplication.
  • \((\mathbb{R},+)\) is a standard example where the operation is ordinary addition.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The identity matrix \(\boldsymbol{I}_n\) is the \(n\times n\) matrix with \(1\) on the main diagonal and \(0\) everywhere else.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The identity matrix acts like the number \(1\) for matrix multiplication.

The identity matrix leaves every vector unchanged: \(\boldsymbol{I}\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{v}\). It satisfies \(\boldsymbol{I}\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{I}=\boldsymbol{A}\), \(\det \boldsymbol{I}=1\), and \(\boldsymbol{I}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{I}\), and its columns are the standard basis vectors \(\boldsymbol{e}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{e}_n\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For every \(m\times n\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\), \(\boldsymbol{I}_m\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{A}\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{I}_n=\boldsymbol{A}\).
  • The identity matrix is diagonal, symmetric, triangular, idempotent, and a permutation matrix.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\boldsymbol{I}_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{I}_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The imaginary unit, symbolized as \(\mathrm{i}\), is characterized by its square being \(-1\), i.e., \(\mathrm{i}^2 = -1.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Integer powers mean repeated multiplication, so \(\mathrm{i}^2=-1\) implies \(\mathrm{i}^3=-\mathrm{i}\) and \(\mathrm{i}^4=1\). Higher powers therefore repeat in a cycle of length four.

The imaginary unit \(\mathrm{i}\) is a solution, not the solution, to the equation \(x^2+1=0\) since \(-\mathrm{i}\) is also a solution.

The choice of \(\mathrm{i}\) over \(-\mathrm{i}\) as the "principal" square root of \(-1\) is largely a matter of convention, similar to how we choose the positive square root of a positive number as its principal square root.

\(\mathrm{i}^2=-1\): multiplying by \(\mathrm{i}\) is a rotation by \(90^\circ\), so four multiplications return to the start (\(\mathrm{i}^4=1\)).

Drag \(z\): multiplying by \(\mathrm{i}\) turns it a quarter turn, and doing it twice gives \(\mathrm{i}^2z=-z\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Complex numbers extend the real numbers by adding a solution of \(x^2=-1\).
  • The complex numbers form a field, so they can be used as scalars in complex vector spaces.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathrm{i}^3 = \mathrm{i}^2 \cdot\mathrm{i} = (-1) \cdot \mathrm{i} = -\mathrm{i}, \quad \mathrm{i}^4 = \mathrm{i}^3 \cdot \mathrm{i} = (-\mathrm{i})\cdot \mathrm{i} = 1, \quad \mathrm{i}^5 = \mathrm{i}^4 \cdot \mathrm{i} =\mathrm{i}.\)
  • The roots of \(x^2+x+1=0\) are \(x_{1,2}=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt{3}\mathrm{i}}{2}\).
  • For \(z=3+4\mathrm{i}\), the real part is \(3\), the imaginary part is \(4\), and \(|z|=5\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For vectors \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the dot product, or standard inner product, is

\[ \boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}=x_1y_1+x_2y_2+\cdots+x_ny_n. \]

More generally, an inner product on a real vector space \(V\) is a function \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\colon V\times V\to\mathbb{R}\) that is

  • symmetric: \(\langle \boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle=\langle \boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{x}\rangle\);
  • linear in the first argument, \(\langle \alpha \boldsymbol{x}+\beta \boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{z}\rangle=\alpha\langle \boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{z}\rangle+\beta\langle \boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{z}\rangle\), and hence, by symmetry, in the second;
  • positive definite: \(\langle \boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}\rangle>0\) for every \(\boldsymbol{x}\neq\boldsymbol{0}\).

The dot product is an inner product on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and it is the one meant when Math II speaks of the inner product of two vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The inner product measures how much two vectors point in the same direction and allows definitions of length, angle, and orthogonality.

The dot product satisfies, with \(\theta\) the angle between the vectors and \(\|\cdot\|\) the Euclidean norm, \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}=x_1y_1+\cdots+x_ny_n=\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\,\|\boldsymbol{y}\|\cos\theta\). For nonzero \(\boldsymbol{x}\), it is \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\) times the signed length of the projection of \(\boldsymbol{y}\) onto \(\boldsymbol{x}\): positive for an acute angle, zero for a right angle, and negative for an obtuse angle.

Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\): \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}\) is positive when they point roughly the same way, zero at a right angle and negative when they point apart. The thick segment is the shadow of \(\boldsymbol{x}\) on the line of \(\boldsymbol{y}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{x}\geq0\), and \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{x}=0\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\).
  • For real vectors, \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{y}\cdot \boldsymbol{x}\).
  • Together with linearity, these are the defining properties of an inner product, so everything proved from them alone, such as the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, holds for every inner product.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((1,2)\cdot(3,4)=11\).
  • \((1,0)\cdot(0,1)=0\), so the vectors are orthogonal.
  • \(\langle \boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle=2x_1y_1+x_2y_2\) is an inner product on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) different from the dot product.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathcal{L}(V)\) be a linear operator. A subspace \(U\subseteq V\) is an invariant subspace under \(\boldsymbol{A}\) if \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}\in U\) for every \(\boldsymbol{u}\in U\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An invariant subspace is a part of the vector space that the operator never sends outside itself.

The illustrated matrix is \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\). A subspace \(U\) is invariant under \(\boldsymbol{A}\) when \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}\in U\) for every \(\boldsymbol{u}\in U\). Eigenvector lines, \(\ker \boldsymbol{A}\) and \(\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A}\) are invariant subspaces.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\), \(V\), \(\ker \boldsymbol{A}\), and \(\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A}\) are basic invariant subspaces.
  • If \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda \boldsymbol{p}\), then \(\operatorname{span}(\boldsymbol{p})\) is invariant under \(\boldsymbol{A}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a diagonal matrix, each coordinate axis is invariant.
  • The kernel of any linear operator is invariant under that operator.

docs.title: Definition

Let \(\star\) be a binary operation on \(A\) with identity element \(e\). An inverse element of \(a\in A\) is an element \(a^{-1}\in A\) such that

\[ a\star a^{-1}=a^{-1}\star a=e. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: An inverse undoes the effect of an element with respect to the operation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A right inverse satisfies \(a\star a^{-1}=e\).
  • A left inverse satisfies \(a^{-1}\star a=e\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Under addition, the inverse of \(a\) is \(-a\). Under multiplication, the inverse of nonzero \(a\) is \(1/a\).
  • \((\mathbb{R},+)\) is a standard example where the operation is ordinary addition.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\), an inverse matrix is a matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\) such that

\[ \boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{I}. \]

If such a matrix exists, then \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is invertible, nonsingular, or nondegenerate. If no inverse exists, then \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is singular, non-invertible, or degenerate.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The defining equalities use matrix products, which represent composition of linear transformations. The identity matrix represents leaving every vector unchanged, explaining why both products must equal \(\boldsymbol{I}\).

An inverse matrix reverses the action of a linear transformation. Singular matrices are precisely those whose action cannot be reversed: they send some nonzero vector to \(\boldsymbol{0}\), so different inputs share an output.

\(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{I}\): \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v})=\boldsymbol{v}\) for every \(\boldsymbol{v}\); \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is invertible \(\iff\det \boldsymbol{A}\neq0\iff\) the parallelogram is not flattened.

\(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\) sends \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\) back to \(\boldsymbol{x}\) (ringed). Choose the singular example: two different vectors go to the same place, and no inverse exists.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and \(\boldsymbol{B}\) are invertible, then \((\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B})^{-1}=\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\).
  • A square matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is nonzero, if and only if it has full rank.
  • If \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is invertible, then \((\boldsymbol{A}^{\top})^{-1}=(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1})^{\top}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) is its own inverse.
  • \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\) is singular because its rows are dependent.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A Jordan block \(\boldsymbol{J}(\lambda)\) is a square matrix with eigenvalue \(\lambda\) on the main diagonal, \(1\)s immediately above the diagonal, and \(0\)s elsewhere.

A Jordan chain for eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of a square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is a sequence of generalized eigenvectors connected by

\[ \boldsymbol{v}_{r-1}=(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{v}_r, \]

ending with an ordinary eigenvector and then \(\boldsymbol{0}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Jordan blocks are the building pieces of Jordan normal form. Jordan chains explain where those blocks come from and how generalized eigenvectors are ordered.

The block has one eigenvalue and one independent eigenvector \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\), together with a Jordan chain \(\boldsymbol{v}_3\to \boldsymbol{v}_2\to \boldsymbol{v}_1\to\boldsymbol{0}\). The entries \(1\) immediately above the diagonal record the shift along that chain.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A Jordan block is upper triangular and has one eigenvalue on its diagonal.
  • The length of a Jordan chain corresponds to the size of the associated Jordan block.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\0&4\end{pmatrix}\) is a \(2\times2\) Jordan block.
  • If \((\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{v}_2=\boldsymbol{v}_1\) and \((\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{v}_1=\boldsymbol{0}\), then \((\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2)\) is a Jordan chain of length \(2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A Jordan normal form of a square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is a block diagonal matrix \(\boldsymbol{J}_{\boldsymbol{A}}=\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{P}\) whose diagonal blocks are Jordan blocks, where \(\boldsymbol{P}\) is invertible and its columns are chains of generalized eigenvectors of \(\boldsymbol{A}\). Every square matrix has a Jordan normal form over \(\mathbb{C}\) (more generally, whenever its characteristic polynomial splits into linear factors); it is unique up to the order of the blocks.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Jordan normal form is an almost diagonal form that still works when a matrix is not diagonalizable.

Over \(\mathbb{C}\), every square matrix is similar to a Jordan normal form, that is, \(\boldsymbol{J}=\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{P}\) for some invertible \(\boldsymbol{P}\), unique up to the order of its blocks. In the figure, \(\lambda_1\) has algebraic multiplicity \(3\) (its diagonal count) and geometric multiplicity \(2\) (the number of its blocks).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Jordan normal form is upper triangular with eigenvalues on the diagonal and possible \(1\)s above the diagonal.
  • If a matrix is diagonalizable, its Jordan normal form is diagonal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&1\\0&\lambda\end{pmatrix}\) is a \(2\times2\) Jordan block.
  • A diagonal matrix is already in Jordan normal form.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathcal{L}(V,W)\) be a linear map. The kernel or null space of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is \(\ker \boldsymbol{A}=\{\boldsymbol{v}\in V\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}\}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The kernel contains all input vectors that the linear map sends to the zero vector.

The matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) projects onto the first coordinate axis. Its kernel is \(\ker \boldsymbol{A}=\{\boldsymbol{v}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}\}=\operatorname{span}(\boldsymbol{e}_2)\). In general, a linear map is injective if and only if its kernel is \(\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\).

Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}\) onto the dashed line: there \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\). The kernel is \(\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\) only when \(\det(\boldsymbol{A})\neq0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The kernel of a linear map is a subspace of the domain.
  • A linear map is injective exactly when its kernel is \(\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\boldsymbol{A}(x,y)=(x,0)\), the kernel is \(\{(0,y)\colon y\in\mathbb{R}\}\).
  • The kernel of the identity map is \(\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \((\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_k)\) be a collection of vectors and let \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\ldots,\alpha_k\) be scalars. A linear combination is a vector of the form

\[ \alpha_1\boldsymbol{v}_1+\alpha_2\boldsymbol{v}_2+\cdots+\alpha_k\boldsymbol{v}_k. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Scalar multiplication forms each \(\alpha_i\boldsymbol{v}_i\); vector addition combines these scaled vectors into a single vector in the same space.

A linear combination is built by scaling vectors and adding the results.

To form \(\alpha_1\boldsymbol{v}_1+\alpha_2\boldsymbol{v}_2+\cdots+\alpha_k\boldsymbol{v}_k\), scale each vector by its coefficient and then add the results. Every point of the illustrated plane is a linear combination of \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}_2\).

Choose \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\): the combination \(\alpha_1\boldsymbol{v}_1+\alpha_2\boldsymbol{v}_2\) is reached by walking \(\alpha_1\boldsymbol{v}_1\) and then \(\alpha_2\boldsymbol{v}_2\). Drag \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}_2\) to change the grid.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Linear combinations are the building blocks of span, linear dependence, and bases.
  • Many questions about the concept reduce to solving equations involving linear combinations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(2\boldsymbol{v}_1-3\boldsymbol{v}_2\) is a linear combination of \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}_2\).
  • In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), vectors such as \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) illustrate the concept concretely.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A collection \((\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_k)\) of vectors is linearly dependent if there exist scalars \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k\), not all zero, such that

\[ \alpha_1\boldsymbol{v}_1+\alpha_2\boldsymbol{v}_2+\cdots+\alpha_k\boldsymbol{v}_k=\boldsymbol{0}. \]

The collection is linearly independent if this can only happen when

\[ \alpha_1=\alpha_2=\cdots=\alpha_k=0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Linear dependence means that at least one vector is redundant because it can be written using the others. Linear independence means that no vector in the collection is redundant.

Drag \(\boldsymbol{v}_2\) onto the line through \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\) (or press the button): then a combination with coefficients not all zero gives \(\boldsymbol{0}\), and the collection is dependent.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A collection is linearly independent if and only if every vector in its span has a unique expression as a linear combination of the collection.
  • Any collection containing the zero vector, a repeated vector, or a scalar multiple of another vector is linearly dependent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) are linearly independent.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), \((1,0)\) and \((2,0)\) are linearly dependent, since \((2,0)=2(1,0)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(\mathbb{F}\) be a field, and let \(V\) and \(W\) be vector spaces over \(\mathbb{F}\). A linear map \(\boldsymbol{A}\colon V\to W\) is a function satisfying additivity \(\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{u}+\boldsymbol{v})=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}+\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\) and homogeneity \(\boldsymbol{A}(\lambda \boldsymbol{u})=\lambda \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}\) for all \(\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v}\in V\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb{F}\). The set of all linear maps from \(V\) to \(W\) is denoted \(\mathcal{L}(V,W)\).

docs.title: Basic linear maps and operations
docs.text:
Two canonical examples are the zero map \(\boldsymbol{0}\colon V\to W\), defined by \(\boldsymbol{0}(\boldsymbol{v})=\boldsymbol{0}_W\), and the identity map \(\boldsymbol{I}\colon V\to V\), defined by \(\boldsymbol{I}(\boldsymbol{v})=\boldsymbol{v}\). If \(\boldsymbol{A},\boldsymbol{B}\in\mathcal{L}(V,W)\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb{F}\), then the sum and scalar multiple of linear maps are defined by

\[ \begin{aligned} (\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{B})(\boldsymbol{v})&=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}+\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{v},\\ (\lambda \boldsymbol{A})(\boldsymbol{v})&=\lambda(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}). \end{aligned} \]

These operations make \(\mathcal{L}(V,W)\) itself a vector space.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A linear map preserves the linear structure of a vector space: it respects vector addition and scalar multiplication.

The illustrated map satisfies \(\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{u}+\boldsymbol{v})=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}+\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}(\lambda \boldsymbol{v})=\lambda \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\). Its grid remains parallel and evenly spaced, and \(\boldsymbol{0}\) maps to \(\boldsymbol{0}\). A linear map is determined by its images of a basis; here \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_2\) are the matrix columns.

Drag the images \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_2\) of the basis vectors: they decide where the whole grid goes, and \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=x_1\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_1+x_2\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_2\). Move \(t\) to slide from the identity to \(\boldsymbol{A}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A linear map is completely determined by what it does to a basis of its domain.
  • The set \(\mathcal{L}(V,W)\) of all linear maps from \(V\) to \(W\) is itself a vector space.
  • A function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k\) is linear if and only if \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\) for some \(k\times n\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\), and then \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is unique: its \(j\)-th column is \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{e}_j)\). In particular a linear map sends \(\boldsymbol{0}\) to \(\boldsymbol{0}\), so a function \(\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b}\) with \(\boldsymbol{b}\ne\boldsymbol{0}\) is not linear but affine.
  • Linear map and linear transformation are synonyms. A linear map from a space to itself is also called a linear operator.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The zero map \(\boldsymbol{0}(\boldsymbol{v})=\boldsymbol{0}\) is linear.
  • The derivative map \(\boldsymbol{D}(p)=p'\) on polynomials is linear.
  • \(f(x,y)=x+y\) is a linear map \(\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\); \(g(x,y,z)=x-y+2z+1\) is not, since \(g(0,0,0)=1\ne0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A linear operator is a linear map from a vector space to itself, so it has the form \(\boldsymbol{A}\colon V\to V\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Linear operators transform vectors while staying inside the same vector space, which makes repeated application and matrix powers meaningful.

The illustrated operator is a rotation by \(30^\circ\), represented by \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos30^\circ&-\sin30^\circ\\\sin30^\circ&\cos30^\circ\end{pmatrix}\). Its domain and codomain are the same space, so powers such as \(\boldsymbol{A}^2,\boldsymbol{A}^3,\ldots\) represent repeated application.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The set of linear operators on \(V\) is denoted \(\mathcal{L}(V)=\mathcal{L}(V,V)\).
  • Eigenvalues, determinants, inverses, and diagonalization are concepts for linear operators or their square matrix representations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The identity map \(\boldsymbol{I}(\boldsymbol{v})=\boldsymbol{v}\) is a linear operator on \(V\).
  • The derivative \(\boldsymbol{D}\colon p\mapsto p'\) is a linear operator on the vector space of polynomials.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The linear span of a collection \(\mathcal{V}=(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_k)\) is the set of all linear combinations of vectors in the collection, with scalars from the field \(\mathbb{F}\) of the vector space:

\[ \operatorname{span}(\mathcal{V})=\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_i\boldsymbol{v}_i\colon \alpha_i\in\mathbb{F}\Big\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The span is everything that can be reached using the given vectors and scalar coefficients.

The span \(\operatorname{span}(\mathcal{V})\) consists of all linear combinations of the vectors in \(\mathcal{V}\). It is the smallest subspace containing those vectors and always contains \(\boldsymbol{0}\).

Animate \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\) to see which points are reached. One vector spans a line; two vectors span the whole plane unless they lie on one line.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The span of any collection of vectors is a vector space.
  • A collection spans \(V\) if its span equals \(V\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The span of one nonzero vector in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is a line through the origin.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), vectors such as \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) illustrate the concept concretely.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An LU decomposition factors a matrix, after possible row permutations, as \(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{U}\), where \(\boldsymbol{P}\) is a permutation matrix, \(\boldsymbol{L}\) is lower triangular, and \(\boldsymbol{U}\) is upper triangular.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
LU decomposition records the forward phase of Gaussian elimination (row reduction to row echelon form) as a matrix factorization.

The figure factors

\[ \boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\4&3&3\\-2&1&3\end{pmatrix}. \]

Subtracting \(2\) times row 1 from row 2, adding row 1 to row 3 (multiplier \(-1\)), and then subtracting \(2\) times the new row 2 from row 3 leaves \(\boldsymbol{U}\); the multipliers \(2\), \(-1\), \(2\) fill \(\boldsymbol{L}\) below its diagonal of ones.

To solve \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\), first solve \(\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{b}\) by forward substitution, then \(\boldsymbol{U}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{y}\) by back substitution. When no row swaps are needed, \(\boldsymbol{P}=\boldsymbol{I}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If no row interchanges are needed, the factorization is \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{U}\).
  • LU decomposition helps solve \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) efficiently by forward and back substitution.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\2&4&8\\3&9&27\end{pmatrix}\), subtract \(2\) and \(3\) times row 1 from rows 2 and 3, then \(3\) times the new row 2 from row 3. This gives \(\boldsymbol{U}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\0&2&6\\0&0&6\end{pmatrix}\), the multipliers fill \(\boldsymbol{L}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\2&1&0\\3&3&1\end{pmatrix}\), and \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{U}\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{U}\) includes pivoting through the permutation matrix \(\boldsymbol{P}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an \(m\times n\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}=(a_{ij})\):

  • the main diagonal consists of the entries \(a_{ii}\) with \(i\le\min(m,n)\);
  • the anti-diagonal of a square matrix (\(m=n\)) consists of the entries \(a_{n+1-i,i}\);
  • the off-diagonal entries are all entries \(a_{ij}\) with \(i\neq j\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The main diagonal runs from top-left to bottom-right, the anti-diagonal runs from bottom-left to top-right, and the off-diagonal entries are everything outside the main diagonal.

The main diagonal (shaded) holds the entries \(a_{ii}\) with \(i=j\); it exists for non-square matrices too. For square \(\boldsymbol{A}\), \(\displaystyle \operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol{A}=\sum_i a_{ii}\), and diagonal and triangular matrices are defined by it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Diagonal entries are central in definitions of diagonal matrices, triangular matrices, and the trace.
  • A square matrix is diagonal exactly when all off-diagonal entries are zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\), the main diagonal is \((1,4)\) and the anti-diagonal is \((3,2)\).
  • In \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&4\end{pmatrix}\), all off-diagonal entries are zero.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: If \(\boldsymbol{A}\) has size \(m\times n\) and \(\boldsymbol{B}\) has size \(n\times k\), the matrix product \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}\) is the \(m\times k\) matrix with entries \(\displaystyle (\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B})_{ij}=\sum_{r=1}^n a_{ir}b_{rj}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Matrix multiplication combines rows of the left matrix with columns of the right matrix and represents composition of linear maps.

The entry \(c_{22}=a_{21}b_{12}+a_{22}b_{22}+a_{23}b_{32}\) is obtained by multiplying row \(2\) of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) by column \(2\) of \(\boldsymbol{B}\). In general, \(\displaystyle (\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B})_{ij}=\sum_{r=1}^n a_{ir}b_{rj}\), provided the inner dimensions agree.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The product \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}\) is defined only when the number of columns of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) equals the number of rows of \(\boldsymbol{B}\).
  • Matrix multiplication is associative and distributive, but not generally commutative.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A \(2\times3\) matrix times a \(3\times4\) matrix gives a \(2\times4\) matrix.
  • \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}11\\4\end{pmatrix}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A matrix is a rectangular array of elements of a field, arranged in rows and columns. A matrix with \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns has size \(m\times n\).

Two matrices are equal if and only if they have the same size and all corresponding entries are equal. A square matrix is a matrix with the same number of rows and columns.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Matrices store coefficients, describe linear maps in coordinates, and organize data in a way that supports algebraic operations.

A matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is a rectangular array and is square when \(m=n\). The green entry \(a_{23}\) lies in row \(2\) and column \(3\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Rows are listed first and columns second: an \(m\times n\) matrix has \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns.
  • A matrix can be viewed as a list of vertical or horizontal vectors; an \(n\times1\) matrix is a column vector and a \(1\times n\) matrix is a row vector.
  • Matrices of different sizes cannot be equal; matrices of the same size are equal exactly when their corresponding entries match.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\) is a \(2\times2\) square matrix.
  • \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\end{pmatrix}\) is a \(2\times3\) matrix and is not square.

docs.title: Examples

  • \((\mathbb{R},+)\) is a standard example where the operation is ordinary addition.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A normal vector to a plane is a nonzero vector perpendicular to every direction vector in the plane.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A normal vector describes the inclination of a plane.

The vector \(\boldsymbol{n}\) is perpendicular to the independent directions \(\boldsymbol{v}\) and \(\boldsymbol{w}\), so \(\boldsymbol{n}\cdot \boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{n}\cdot \boldsymbol{w}=0\) and it is perpendicular to their plane. In \(\mathbb{R}^3\), one can take the cross product \(\boldsymbol{n}=\boldsymbol{v}\times \boldsymbol{w}=(v_2w_3-v_3w_2,\,v_3w_1-v_1w_3,\,v_1w_2-v_2w_1)\). Any nonzero multiple of a normal vector is again normal.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A point and a normal vector determine a plane in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).
  • If \(\boldsymbol{n}\) is normal to a plane and \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is a point of the plane, then \(\boldsymbol{n}\cdot(\boldsymbol{B}-\boldsymbol{A})=0\) for every point \(\boldsymbol{B}\) on the plane.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the \(xy\)-plane, \((0,0,1)\) is a normal vector.
  • If a plane has direction vectors \(\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{w}\), then a normal vector is orthogonal to both \(\boldsymbol{v}\) and \(\boldsymbol{w}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The origin of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is the vector whose coordinates are all zero:

\[ \boldsymbol{0}=(0,0,\ldots,0). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The origin is the zero vector of the real coordinate space \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Position vectors are often drawn as arrows starting at the origin.
  • Many questions about the concept reduce to solving equations involving linear combinations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), the origin is \((0,0)\).
  • In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), vectors such as \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) illustrate the concept concretely.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Two vectors \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\) are orthogonal if their inner product is zero: \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}=0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Orthogonal vectors meet at a right angle in Euclidean geometry.

The illustrated vectors are orthogonal because \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}=3\cdot(-1)+1\cdot3=0\), so the angle between them is \(90^\circ\). Pythagoras therefore gives \(\|\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{y}\|^2=\|\boldsymbol{x}\|^2+\|\boldsymbol{y}\|^2\).

Turn \(\boldsymbol{y}\) until \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}=0\), or press the button: the shadow of \(\boldsymbol{x}\) on \(\boldsymbol{y}\) disappears and the vectors meet at a right angle.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Orthogonality is equivalent to a \(90^\circ\) angle for nonzero real vectors.
  • If \(\boldsymbol{y}\) has unit length, then \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}\) gives the signed length of the projection of \(\boldsymbol{x}\) onto \(\boldsymbol{y}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) are orthogonal.
  • \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\) are orthogonal.

docs.title: Parametric Representations of Lines and Planes
Definition
docs.text:
A parametric representation of a line in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) has the form

\[ \boldsymbol{\ell}(t)=\boldsymbol{A}+t\boldsymbol{v}, \]

where \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is a point on the line, \(\boldsymbol{v}\neq\boldsymbol{0}\) is a direction vector, and \(t\in\mathbb{R}\).

A parametric representation of a plane has the form

\[ \boldsymbol{P}(s,t)=\boldsymbol{A}+s\boldsymbol{v}+t\boldsymbol{w}, \]

where \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is a point on the plane and \(\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{w}\) are linearly independent direction vectors.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Scalar multiplication turns the parameters into displacements \(t\boldsymbol{v}\), \(s\boldsymbol{v}\) and \(t\boldsymbol{w}\). Their linear combinations, added to the starting point \(\boldsymbol{A}\), trace out the line or plane.

The parameters describe movement from a starting point along one direction for a line, or along two independent directions for a plane.

In \(\boldsymbol{\ell}(t)=\boldsymbol{A}+t\boldsymbol{v}\), \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), the point \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{\ell}(0)\) lies on the line and \(\boldsymbol{v}\ne\boldsymbol{0}\) is its direction. Equally spaced parameter values give equally spaced points. Choosing another point on the line or a nonzero multiple of \(\boldsymbol{v}\) gives another representation of the same line.

Move \(t\): \(\boldsymbol{\ell}(t)=\boldsymbol{A}+t\boldsymbol{v}\) walks along the line, through \(\boldsymbol{A}\) at \(t=0\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{v}\) at \(t=1\). Drag \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and the tip of \(\boldsymbol{v}\) to move the line.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A point lies on the line or plane exactly when it is obtained for some parameter value or parameter pair.
  • Two distinct points determine a line, while three non-collinear points determine a plane.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\boldsymbol{\ell}(t)=(4,2)+t(1,1)\) represents a line through \((4,2)\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{P}(s,t)=(1,0,0)+s(1,1,0)+t(0,1,1)\) represents a plane in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A permutation matrix is a square matrix with exactly one entry equal to \(1\) in each row and each column, and all other entries equal to \(0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
It is fundamentally formed by rearranging, or permuting, the rows or columns of an identity matrix. Multiplying by it carries out the corresponding reordering.

The entries of \(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{x}\) are the entries of \(\boldsymbol{x}\) reshuffled: \(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{A}\) permutes the rows of \(\boldsymbol{A}\), \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{P}\) its columns; \(\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{P}^{\top}\) and \(\det \boldsymbol{P}=\pm1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The identity matrix is a permutation matrix.
  • The product of two permutation matrices is a permutation matrix.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) swaps two rows when multiplied on the left.
  • \(\boldsymbol{I}_3\) represents the permutation that changes nothing.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A permutation of a set \(A\) is a bijective function

\[ \pi\colon A\to A. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A permutation rearranges the elements of a set without losing or duplicating any element.

\(\pi=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3&4\\3&1&4&2\end{pmatrix}=(1\,3\,4\,2)\) (cycle notation: \(1\mapsto3\mapsto4\mapsto2\mapsto1\)) is bijective: every element is hit exactly once, and \(\pi^{-1}=(1\,2\,4\,3)\) reverses the arrows.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The composition of two permutations is again a permutation.
  • A finite set with \(n\) elements has \(n!\) permutations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Swapping two elements and leaving the rest fixed is a permutation.
  • On \(A=\{1,2,3\}\), the map \(\pi(1)=2\), \(\pi(2)=3\), \(\pi(3)=1\) is a permutation. The map \(f(n)=2n\) on \(\mathbb{N}\) is injective but not surjective, so it is not a permutation of \(\mathbb{N}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A pivot of a nonzero row is the first nonzero entry in that row.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A matrix arranges the coefficients into rows and columns; finding the first nonzero entry of a row identifies its pivot position and the corresponding column.

Pivots mark the leading variables and structure of an echelon form.

Blue columns hold a pivot: \(x_1,x_3,x_4\) are basic (pivot) variables; the orange column has none: \(x_2\) is a free variable, which can take any value, and the basic variables are then determined by it. The number of pivots is the rank; in echelon form each pivot sits to the right of the one above.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In row echelon form, each pivot lies to the right of the pivot in the row above.
  • In reduced row echelon form, every pivot is a leading \(1\) and is the only nonzero entry in its column.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \((0,0,5,2)\), the pivot is \(5\).
  • In \((1,3,0)\), the pivot is \(1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A plane is a two-dimensional geometric object described by a point \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and two linearly independent direction vectors \(\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{w}\) as \(\boldsymbol{P}(s,t)=\boldsymbol{A}+s\boldsymbol{v}+t\boldsymbol{w}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The displacement \(s\boldsymbol{v}+t\boldsymbol{w}\) is a linear combination of the two direction vectors. Their independence ensures that the two parameters describe genuinely different directions rather than a single line.

A plane needs two independent directions, so it is described by two parameters.

The parametrization \(\boldsymbol{P}(s,t)=\boldsymbol{A}+s\boldsymbol{v}+t\boldsymbol{w}\), \(s,t\in\mathbb{R}\), starts at \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and moves along the independent directions \(\boldsymbol{v}\) and \(\boldsymbol{w}\). It gives a plane, with \(\boldsymbol{P}(1,1)=\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{v}+\boldsymbol{w}\) in the figure.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Three non-collinear points determine a plane.
  • If two direction vectors are scalar multiples, they do not determine a unique plane.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\boldsymbol{P}(s,t)=(0,0,0)+s(1,0,0)+t(0,1,0)\) is the \(xy\)-plane.
  • The plane through three non-collinear points \(\boldsymbol{A},\boldsymbol{B},\boldsymbol{C}\) can be written \(\boldsymbol{P}(s,t)=\boldsymbol{A}+s(\boldsymbol{B}-\boldsymbol{A})+t(\boldsymbol{C}-\boldsymbol{A})\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The point-normal equation of a plane through \((x_0,y_0,z_0)\) with normal vector \(\boldsymbol{n}=(a,b,c)\) is \(a(x-x_0)+b(y-y_0)+c(z-z_0)=0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The inner product \(\boldsymbol{n}\cdot(\boldsymbol{P}-\boldsymbol{P}_0)\) tests whether a displacement is orthogonal to the normal. Setting it to zero and expanding its coordinate sum gives the displayed plane equation.

The equation says that the displacement from the fixed point to any point on the plane is perpendicular to the normal vector.

For \(\boldsymbol{P}_0=(x_0,y_0,z_0)\) and \(\boldsymbol{P}=(x,y,z)\): \(\boldsymbol{n}\cdot(\boldsymbol{P}-\boldsymbol{P}_0)=0\iff a(x-x_0)+b(y-y_0)+c(z-z_0)=0\). The plane is the set of points whose displacement from \(\boldsymbol{P}_0\) is orthogonal to \(\boldsymbol{n}\); expanding gives \(ax+by+cz=d\) with \(d=\boldsymbol{n}\cdot \boldsymbol{P}_0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• It can be rewritten as \(ax+by+cz=d\), where \(d=ax_0+by_0+cz_0\).
  • The normal vector is read from the coefficients of \(x,y,z\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A plane through \((0,0,0)\) with normal \((0,0,1)\) has equation \(z=0\).
  • For \(\boldsymbol{A}=(0,0,0)\), \(\boldsymbol{B}=(1,0,-3)\) and \(\boldsymbol{C}=(0,1,7)\), a normal \(\boldsymbol{n}=(a,b,c)\) satisfies \(\boldsymbol{n}\cdot(\boldsymbol{B}-\boldsymbol{A})=a-3c=0\) and \(\boldsymbol{n}\cdot(\boldsymbol{C}-\boldsymbol{A})=b+7c=0\). Taking \(c=1\) gives \(\boldsymbol{n}=(3,-7,1)\) and the plane \(3x-7y+z=0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The polar coordinate system specifies a given point in the plane \(\mathbb{R}^2\) (see real coordinate space) by using two coordinates:

  • the point's distance from a reference point called the pole,
  • the point's direction from the pole relative to the direction of the polar axis, a ray drawn from the pole.

The distance from the pole is called the radius, and the angle is called the polar angle.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Cartesian product \([0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}\) supplies pairs \((r,\theta)\); different angle values can represent the same point. The trigonometric functions convert the radius and direction to Cartesian coordinates through \(x=r\cos\theta\) and \(y=r\sin\theta\).

The polar coordinate system locates a point on a plane by saying how far away it is from a centre point and what angle it makes from a fixed direction.

Using the 2-argument arctangent for the angle, for the nonzero point in the figure, \(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) and \(\theta=\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)\). Constant \(r\) gives a circle and constant \(\theta\) gives a ray of the polar grid.

Set the radius \(r\) and the polar angle \(\theta\), or drag the point: \(x=r\cos\theta\) and \(y=r\sin\theta\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Conversion to Cartesian coordinates: \(x = r \cos \theta\), \(y = r \sin \theta.\)
  • Conversion from Cartesian coordinates: \(r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\), \(\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x).\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• With \(r\ge0\), \(\theta=\pi/4\) describes the ray from the pole at angle \(\pi/4\) to the polar axis: \((x,y)=(r/\sqrt{2},r/\sqrt{2})\).
  • \(r = 1\) is a unit circle centred at the pole.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A greatest common divisor (GCD) of two polynomials \(a(x)\) and \(b(x)\), not both zero, is a polynomial of greatest possible degree that divides both \(a(x)\) and \(b(x)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Polynomial long division produces the quotient and smaller-degree remainder at each step. Replacing \((a,b)\) by \((b,r)\) preserves their common divisors and eventually yields the last nonzero remainder.

The polynomial GCD can be found using the Euclidean algorithm: repeatedly divide and replace the pair by divisor and remainder until the remainder is zero.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The last nonzero remainder is a GCD.
  • The GCD is often normalized to be monic (leading coefficient \(1\)), which makes it unique.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The GCD of \(x^2-1\) and \(x-1\) is \(x-1\).
  • Euclidean algorithm: \(x^3-1=x\,(x^2-1)+(x-1)\) and \(x^2-1=(x+1)(x-1)+0\), so the last nonzero remainder \(x-1\) is the GCD of \(x^3-1\) and \(x^2-1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Polynomial long division is the procedure that computes the quotient and remainder in the division algorithm for polynomials: for nonzero polynomials \(a(x),b(x)\in\mathbb{F}[x]\), the polynomials with coefficients in a field \(\mathbb{F}\), there are unique polynomials \(q(x)\) and \(r(x)\) such that

\[ a(x)=q(x)b(x)+r(x), \]

with \(r(x)=0\) or \(\deg(r)<\deg(b)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The coefficients lie in a field, so the nonzero leading coefficient of the divisor has an inverse. Dividing by that coefficient lets each step cancel the highest remaining term of the dividend.

It is the polynomial analogue of integer division with quotient and remainder.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The quotient and remainder are uniquely determined.
  • Polynomial division gives a quotient and remainder with the remainder of smaller degree.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Dividing \(x^2-1\) by \(x-1\) gives quotient \(x+1\) and remainder \(0\).
  • Dividing \(x^3+2x+1\) by \(x^2+1\) gives quotient \(x\) and remainder \(x+1\): \(x^3+2x+1=x\,(x^2+1)+(x+1)\), with \(\deg(x+1)=1<2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The power set of a set \(A\), denoted \(2^A\) or \(\mathcal{P}(A)\), is the set of all subsets of \(A\):

\[ 2^A = \{B \colon B \subseteq A\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The power set collects every possible choice of elements from \(A\), including the empty choice and the full set itself.

\(\mathcal{P}(\{a,b,c\})\) has \(2^3=8\) elements (each element is in or out); lines show inclusion, \(\varnothing\) at the bottom and the whole set at the top.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(A\) is finite with \(n\) elements, then \(2^A\) has \(2^n\) elements.
  • Cantor's theorem shows that for any set \(A\), the power set \(2^A\) has strictly larger cardinality than \(A\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(A=\{a,b\}\), then \(2^A=\{\varnothing,\{a\},\{b\},\{a,b\}\}\).
  • If \(A=\varnothing\), then \(2^A=\{\varnothing\}\), so the power set of the empty set has one element.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A quadratic form on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a function \(Q\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) of the form

\[ Q(\boldsymbol{v})=\boldsymbol{v}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}v_iv_j, \]

where \(\boldsymbol{A}=(a_{ij})\) is a real \(n\times n\) matrix and \(\boldsymbol{v}\) a column vector. Equivalently, \(Q\) is a polynomial in \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) whose terms all have degree exactly two (a homogeneous polynomial of degree two, the zero polynomial included, which comes from \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{0}\)). The matrix can always be chosen symmetric, and the symmetric choice is unique: it is called the matrix of \(Q\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The transpose turns the column vector \(\boldsymbol{v}\) into a row; the matrix products \(\boldsymbol{v}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\) then have size \(1\times1\). Expanding those products yields the scalar sum of terms \(a_{ij}v_iv_j\).

A quadratic form turns a vector into a second-degree expression determined by a symmetric matrix.

The shading shows \(\boldsymbol{v}^T\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\) over the plane: colour for positive values, the other colour for negative ones. Change the entries of the symmetric matrix and drag \(\boldsymbol{v}\).

Change \(a_{11}\), \(a_{12}\), \(a_{22}\) and turn the surface: the sign of \(\boldsymbol{v}^T\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\) in each direction shows up as a bowl, a cap or a saddle.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Different matrices can give the same form: \(\boldsymbol{v}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{v}^{\top}\bar{\boldsymbol{A}}\boldsymbol{v}\) for \(\bar{\boldsymbol{A}}=\tfrac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{A}^{\top})\), because \(\boldsymbol{v}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{v}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{v}\). The symmetric matrix \(\bar{\boldsymbol{A}}\) is the only symmetric one with this form.
  • In terms of the symmetric matrix, the coefficient of \(v_i^2\) is \(a_{ii}\) and the coefficient of \(v_iv_j\) (\(i\ne j\)) is \(2a_{ij}\).
  • Quadratic forms are used to define definiteness of symmetric matrices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{I}_n\), then \(\boldsymbol{v}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}=\|\boldsymbol{v}\|^2\).
  • For \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\), \(\boldsymbol{v}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}=x^2-y^2\).
  • \(Q(x,y)=3x^2+4xy+5y^2\) has the symmetric matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\2&5\end{pmatrix}\); the non-symmetric \(\begin{pmatrix}3&4\\0&5\end{pmatrix}\) gives the same form.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathcal{L}(V,W)\) be a linear map. The range or image of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is \(\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A}=\{\boldsymbol{w}\in W\colon\exists \boldsymbol{v}\in V, \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{w}\}=\{\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\colon\boldsymbol{v}\in V\}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The range is the part of the codomain that is actually reached by the map.

The matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\) sends \(\boldsymbol{v}\) to \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}=v_1\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}+v_2\begin{pmatrix}2\\4\end{pmatrix}\). Its outputs are all multiples of \((1,2)\), so its range is the line spanned by its columns. A linear map into \(W\) is surjective precisely when \(\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A}=W\).

Every \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\) lands in the shaded range. For a rank-one \(2\times2\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) it is a line; move \(t\) to watch the plane collapse onto it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The range of a linear map is a subspace of the codomain.
  • A linear map is surjective exactly when its range equals the codomain.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\boldsymbol{A}(x,y)=(x,0)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\), the range is the \(x\)-axis.
  • The range of the zero map is \(\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\).
