docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a nonnegative random variable with survival function \(S_X(t)=\mathbb{P}(X>t)\), also written \(\overline F_X(t)\). A half-life is a time \(h\) such that

\[ S_X(h)=\frac{1}{2}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Half-life is the time by which survival or remaining amount has fallen to half. It gives an easily understood summary of decay or waiting time.

For an exponential lifetime, the half-life \(h\) satisfies \(S_X(h)=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda h}=1/2\), hence \(h=\ln2/\lambda\). Each additional interval of length \(h\) halves the surviving proportion: \(S_X(kh)=2^{-k}\) for integers \(k\ge0\).

Change the rate \(\lambda\): the half-life \(h=\ln 2/\lambda\) is where survival drops to \(\frac12\), and each further \(h\) halves it again.

The exponential distribution has survival \(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\). The logarithm and logarithmic function inverts the equation \(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}=1/2\), giving \(t=\log(2)/\lambda\) in this model.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For exponential decay with rate \(\lambda\), the half-life is \(\log(2)/\lambda\).
  • Half-life is a median survival time in exponential waiting models.
  • Shorter half-life corresponds to faster decay or faster event occurrence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If a drug concentration decays exponentially, the half-life is the time until the concentration is halved.
  • In radioactive decay, half-life summarizes how quickly unstable atoms decay.
  • For an exponential component lifetime, the half-life is the time by which half of components are expected to have failed.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let a population contain \(N\) objects, of which \(K\) are successes (\(0\le K\le N\)), and suppose \(n\) objects (\(0\le n\le N\)) are drawn without replacement. A random variable \(X\) has a hypergeometric distribution if \(X\) counts the number of successes in the draw, with

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathbb{P}(X=k)=\frac{\binom Kk\binom{N-K}{n-k}}{\binom Nn},\\ \max(0,\,n-N+K)\le k\le\min(n,K), \end{gathered} \]

and \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)=0\) for all other \(k\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A hypergeometric distribution counts successes when sampling without replacement. The trials are dependent because each draw changes what remains.

The diagram counts successes in a sample of \(n=6\) objects drawn without replacement from \(N=20\) objects, of which \(K=8\) are successes. The PMF is \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)=\binom8k\binom{12}{6-k}/\binom{20}6\) for \(0\le k\le6\). Its mean is \(6\cdot\tfrac{8}{20}=2.4\), and its variance \(1.44\cdot\tfrac{14}{19}\approx1.061\) is smaller than the variance \(6(0.4)(0.6)=1.44\) of \(\operatorname{Bin}(6,0.4)\), the corresponding model with replacement.

Change \(N\), \(K\) and \(n\): drawing without replacement gives mean \(nK/N\), like the binomial, but a smaller variance because each draw changes what remains.

A combination counts an unordered selection without replacement. Counting the chosen successes and failures separately and dividing by all samples gives the hypergeometric probabilities.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The hypergeometric distribution models sampling without replacement.
  • Unlike the binomial distribution, the trials are dependent.
  • Its mean is \(nK/N\) when \(K\) successes are in a population of size \(N\) and \(n\) items are drawn.

  • Its variance is

    \[ \operatorname{Var}(X)=n\frac{K}{N}\left(1-\frac{K}{N}\right)\frac{N-n}{N-1}. \]

    This is the binomial variance with \(p=K/N\) times the finite population correction \(\frac{N-n}{N-1}\), which is below \(1\) when \(n\ge2\) and close to \(1\) when the population is much larger than the sample.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The number of aces in a five-card hand has a hypergeometric distribution.
  • The number of defective items in a sample drawn without replacement from a shipment is hypergeometric.
  • The number of red balls drawn from an urn without replacement is hypergeometric.

docs.title: Independent and Identically Distributed Random Variables
Definition
docs.text: A sequence \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) is independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) if it is mutually independent and all its variables have the same distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Being i.i.d. means that the observations share one distribution and do not influence each other probabilistically. Both requirements are needed in the course’s weak and strong laws of large numbers and CLT.

Each variable in the diagram has the PMF of a fair die. Independence gives \(\mathbb{P}(X_1=a,X_2=b,X_3=c)=\mathbb{P}(X_1=a)\mathbb{P}(X_2=b)\mathbb{P}(X_3=c)\), so these rolls form an i.i.d. sample.

A random variable assigns numerical values to outcomes. Saying that several such variables are identically distributed concerns their individual laws, while independence concerns their joint law; neither condition alone implies the other.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For i.i.d. \(X_i\), \(\mathbb{P}(X_1\in A_1,\ldots,X_n\in A_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n\mathbb{P}(X_i\in A_i)\) for every finite collection.
  • Identical marginal distributions alone do not imply independence; pairwise independence alone does not establish mutual independence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Repeated independent fair die rolls are i.i.d., all with the discrete uniform law on \(\{1,\ldots,6\}\).
  • If \(X_1=X_2=Z\) with \(Z\sim\operatorname{Bern}(1/2)\), the margins match but the observations are not i.i.d.: \(\mathbb{P}(X_1=1,X_2=0)=0\) rather than \(1/4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be events. The inclusion-exclusion principle for two events states that

\[ \mathbb{P}(A\cup B)=\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B)-\mathbb{P}(A\cap B). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Inclusion-exclusion corrects double counting. When two events overlap, the overlap is counted twice unless it is subtracted once.

The labels show how many times each region is counted by \(\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B)+\mathbb{P}(C)\). Subtracting the pairwise intersections and adding the triple intersection gives

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &\mathbb{P}(A\cup B\cup C)\\ &=\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B)+\mathbb{P}(C)\\ &\quad-\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)-\mathbb{P}(A\cap C)\\ &\quad-\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)+\mathbb{P}(A\cap B\cap C). \end{aligned} \]

Grow the overlap: \(\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B)\) counts \(A\cap B\) twice, so it is subtracted once to give \(\mathbb{P}(A\cup B)\).

Union and intersection of events identifies outcomes counted in several events at once. The probability function is additive on disjoint pieces, so subtracting intersections corrects the repeated counting of their probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For two events, inclusion-exclusion subtracts the overlap once.
  • For three events, the triple overlap must be added back after pairwise overlaps are subtracted.
  • The principle works for both counting and probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• To count students taking mathematics or statistics, add both course counts and subtract students taking both.
  • In card problems, the probability of drawing a heart or a face card requires subtracting heart face cards once.
  • To compute the chance of at least one of several alarms sounding, inclusion-exclusion adjusts for simultaneous alarms.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent if

\[ \mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B). \]

For a collection of events, mutual independence requires the product identity for every finite subcollection; pairwise independence alone is insufficient.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Two events are independent when knowing one happened leaves the probability of the other unchanged.

In the illustrated example, \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=0.6\cdot0.5=0.3=\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B)\) \(\iff\) \(A\) and \(B\) independent equivalently \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\): inside \(B\) the band \(A\) still takes up \(60\%\).

Make \(B\) fill the same share of \(A\) as of its complement: then \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B)\) and the events are independent.

Each event is a subset of outcomes. Independence is a property of the probability function on those subsets: their joint probability factors into their individual probabilities, rather than merely depending on whether the sets overlap.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\), independence is equivalent to \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\).
  • Independence of \(A,B\) implies independence of \(A^c,B\) and of \(A^c,B^c\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Heads on two independent fair tosses have intersection probability \(1/4=(1/2)(1/2)\).
  • On one fair die, \(\{1\}\) and \(\{2\}\) are disjoint but not independent: \(0\ne(1/6)(1/6)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Real-valued random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &\mathbb{P}(X\in A,Y\in B)\\ &\quad=\mathbb{P}(X\in A)\mathbb{P}(Y\in B) \end{aligned} \]

for every pair of intervals \(A,B\); equivalently, for every pair of Borel sets \(A,B\). For a finite family, mutual independence requires the analogous product formula for every selection of intervals (one for each variable) and every subfamily, rather than merely for pairs.

For discrete variables with a joint PMF, this is equivalent to \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_X(x)p_Y(y)\) for every \(x,y\). For a pair with a joint density, it is equivalent to \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_X(x)f_Y(y)\) for all \((x,y)\) except possibly on a set of zero area, for example along finitely many lines. In either case, conditional laws agree with the corresponding marginal laws wherever the conditioning denominator is positive (with density identities allowed to fail on a set of zero length or area).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Independent variables supply separate sources of randomness: learning one variable does not change the distribution of the other. PMF and PDF factorization are two ways to check the same property.

Every cell is the product of its row and column marginal, e.g. \(\mathbb{P}(X=1,Y=1)=0.5\cdot0.6=0.30\): \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, \(\mathbb{P}(X\in A,\,Y\in B)=\mathbb{P}(X\in A)\mathbb{P}(Y\in B)\) for all \(A,B\); knowing \(Y\) does not change the distribution of \(X\).

The threshold events generated by the variables must be independent events for every selection of thresholds. This condition factors the joint law, rather than comparing only the marginal distributions or one pair of events.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For arbitrary real-valued \(X,Y\), independence is equivalent to \(F_{X,Y}(x,y)=F_X(x)F_Y(y)\) for every \(x,y\).
  • If \(X,Y\) are independent and integrable, then \(XY\) is integrable and \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=\mathbb{E}X\,\mathbb{E}Y\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Two independent fair dice have \(p_{X,Y}(i,j)=1/36=(1/6)(1/6)\) for all \(i,j\in\{1,\ldots,6\}\).
  • The joint density \(2\) on \(0<x<y<1\) has marginals \(f_X(x)=2(1-x)\) and \(f_Y(y)=2y\) on \((0,1)\). At \((x,y)=(1/4,3/4)\) their product is \(9/4\), rather than \(2\), and this discrepancy persists on a whole neighbourhood, which has positive area; hence the density does not factor.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For an event \(A\), the indicator random variable \(\indicator_{A}\) equals \(1\) if \(A\) occurs and \(0\) otherwise.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An indicator turns an event into a numerical yes-or-no observation. Counting how many events occur becomes adding random variables: the number of the events \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\) that occur is \(\indicator_{A_1}+\cdots+\indicator_{A_n}\).

An event \(A\) identifies the outcomes where the indicator equals one. Membership in that event is converted to a numerical variable, allowing probabilities to be handled through expectations.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\indicator_A\sim\operatorname{Bern}(\mathbb{P}(A))\).
  • \(\indicator_{A\cap B}=\indicator_A\indicator_B\) and \(\indicator_{A^c}=1-\indicator_A\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A fair-toss heads indicator is \(1\) on heads and \(0\) on tails.
  • The number of heads in three tosses is \(\indicator_{A_1}+\indicator_{A_2}+\indicator_{A_3}\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: A sum of indicators counts the number of events that occur, even when those events are dependent.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(\{B_i\}\) be a finite or countable partition of the sample space into events. For every event \(A\),

\[ \mathbb{P}(A)=\sum_{i\colon\mathbb{P}(B_i)>0}\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i)\mathbb{P}(B_i). \]

Null partition events contribute zero to \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) and are omitted so that no undefined conditional probability is used.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Compute a probability by conditioning on each possible case and weighting by how likely that case is.

The diagram splits \(A\) into the disjoint pieces \(A\cap B_1\), \(A\cap B_2\) and \(A\cap B_3\). Their probabilities add to \(\mathbb{P}(A)\); each positive-probability case contributes \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i)\mathbb{P}(B_i)\).

Split the sample space into three cases and set \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i)\) in each: \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) is the total shaded area, a weighted average of the three.

A partition of a set divides the sample space into disjoint blocks covering every outcome. Additivity of the probability function sums the contributions from \(A\) within those blocks, and conditional probabilities express each contribution as a block probability times a within-block probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \mathbb{P}(A)=\sum_i\mathbb{P}(A\cap B_i)\) for a countable partition.
  • Only terms with \(\mathbb{P}(B_i)>0\) need conditional probabilities; zero-probability cases contribute zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If factories supply \(60\%\) and \(40\%\) of products with defect rates \(0.01\) and \(0.03\), the defect probability is \(0.6(0.01)+0.4(0.03)=0.018\).
  • For a fair die, conditioning on odd or even gives \(\mathbb{P}(X=6)=0(1/2)+(1/3)(1/2)=1/6\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For integrable random variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) and real constants \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\), linearity of expectation states

\[ \mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n a_iX_i\right]=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\mathbb{E}X_i. \]

Independence is not required. In particular, \(\mathbb{E}[aX+bY]=a\mathbb{E}X+b\mathbb{E}Y\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The average of a finite linear combination is the same linear combination of averages. Dependence does not affect this rule.

The independent variables shown have means \(2\) and \(4\), so their sum has mean \(6\). Here the sum takes the values \(3\), \(5\), \(7\) and \(9\), each with probability \(1/4\); the identity for the means itself does not require independence.

Addition and sum forms the finite weighted sum of the variables. Expectation then averages it: distributing the probability weights across its summands explains why taking this average commutes with the finite sum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For integrable \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\), \(\displaystyle \mathbb{E}[\sum_ia_iX_i]=\sum_ia_i\mathbb{E}X_i\).
  • \(\mathbb{E}[a+bX]=a+b\mathbb{E}X\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(\mathbb{E}X=2\) and \(\mathbb{E}Y=5\), then \(\mathbb{E}[3X-Y]=1\) regardless of dependence.
  • If \(Y=X\) and \(\mathbb{E}X=4\), then \(\mathbb{E}[X+Y]=8\) despite perfect dependence.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(Y\) be normally distributed with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). The random variable \(X=\mathrm{e}^Y\) has a lognormal distribution with parameters \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A lognormal distribution models positive quantities created by multiplicative effects. Taking logarithms turns it into a normal distribution.

In the illustrated example, \(X=\mathrm{e}^{Y}\) with \(Y\sim N(0,0.5^2)\): \(\ln X\) is normal, so \(X>0\). The density is right-skewed, with mode \(<\) median \(<\) mean (the three dashed lines, from left to right).

Change \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) of the underlying normal \(Y\): the density of \(X=\mathrm e^Y\) is skewed to the right, and more so as \(\sigma\) grows.

The exponential function transforms a real-valued normal variable into a positive value. Taking the logarithm reverses that transformation, which explains why a lognormal variable is characterized through a normal logarithm.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A lognormal random variable is always positive.
  • If \(X\) is lognormal, then \(\log X\) is normal.
  • Lognormal models often arise from products of many positive random factors.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Household income is often modelled with a lognormal-type distribution.
  • Multiplicative investment growth can lead to lognormal returns over time.
  • Repair times that are positive and right-skewed may be approximated by a lognormal model.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(g\) be a Borel-measurable real function (preimages of Borel sets are Borel sets), so that \(g(X)\) is a random variable. If \(\mathbb{E}|g(X)|<\infty\), the law of the unconscious statistician (LOTUS) gives

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[g(X)]&=\sum_x g(x)p_X(x)\\ &\qquad\text{for discrete }X,\\[4pt] \mathbb{E}[g(X)]&=\int_{\mathbb{R}}g(x)f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\\ &\qquad\text{when }X\text{ has a density}. \end{aligned} \]

The formulas also hold as extended nonnegative expectations when \(g\ge0\). A finite signed result requires absolute integrability; no distribution of \(g(X)\) has to be computed first.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
To average a transformed variable, apply the transformation to each possible value and weight using the original distribution. This avoids deriving a new distribution merely to compute an expectation.

For the transformation \(g(x)=x^2\) shown, \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]=1(0.1)+0(0.3)+1(0.4)+4(0.2)=1.3\). The values of \(g\) are weighted by the PMF of \(X\), without deriving the PMF of \(g(X)\).

A function of a random variable changes the value on each outcome from \(X\) to \(g(X)\). LOTUS averages those transformed values using the original law of \(X\), avoiding a separate derivation of the distribution of \(g(X)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Choosing \(g(x)=x^k\) computes the \(k\)th moment when it exists; in particular \(g(x)=x^2\) gives the second moment.
  • Choosing \(g(x)=\indicator_{\{x\in A\}}\) gives \(\mathbb{P}(X\in A)\) by a sum or an integral.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]=(1+4+9+16+25+36)/6=91/6\).
  • For \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\), \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{-X}]=\int_0^\infty2\mathrm{e}^{-3x}\,\mathrm{d}x=2/3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a random variable with distribution function \(F_X\). A median of \(X\) is a real number \(m\) such that

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(X\le m)&\ge \frac{1}{2}\quad\text{and}\\ \mathbb{P}(X\ge m)&\ge \frac{1}{2}. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A median is a central value that splits the distribution into two balanced parts. It is often less sensitive to extreme values than the mean.

For the illustrated density \(f(x)=x\mathrm{e}^{-x}\) on \(x\ge0\), the median is approximately \(1.68\) and the mean is \(2\). Each shaded region has probability \(1/2\) in this continuous example.

Move the candidate \(m\) and check both conditions. For the skewed density the median is unique; for \(\operatorname{Bin}(3,\frac12)\) every \(m\in[1,2]\) is a median.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A median need not be unique: the medians of a distribution form an interval, which contains more than one point exactly when the CDF equals \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) on a whole stretch (for a fair die, every point of \([3,4]\) is a median). If the CDF jumps from below \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) to above \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) at a point, that point is the unique median.
  • For a continuous strictly increasing CDF, the median is the point where the CDF equals one half.
  • The median is robust to extreme values compared with the mean.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The median of a symmetric normal distribution is its centre.
  • For waiting times, the median is the time by which half of cases have occurred.
  • In income data, the median can better describe a typical person than the mean when there are extreme high incomes.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A nonnegative waiting time is memoryless if, once it has lasted a certain time, the time still to wait has the same distribution as the original waiting time. For a nonnegative integer-valued \(G\) this means that for all nonnegative integers \(m,n\)

\[ \mathbb{P}(G\ge m+n\mid G\ge m)=\mathbb{P}(G\ge n). \]

For an absolutely continuous nonnegative \(T\) it means that for all \(s,t\ge0\)

\[ \mathbb{P}(T>s+t\mid T>s)=\mathbb{P}(T>t). \]

The conditioning events must have positive probability. The property also works in reverse. Suppose the waiting time is finite with probability \(1\) and all its tail probabilities are positive. Then a memoryless \(G\) has a \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) distribution for some \(0<p<1\) (counting the failures before the first success), and a memoryless \(T\) has an \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\) distribution for some \(\lambda>0\). For the first-success distribution, which counts trials and takes the values \(1,2,\dots\), the same condition is written with strict tails: \(\mathbb{P}(X>m+n\mid X>m)=\mathbb{P}(X>n)\) for all nonnegative integers \(m,n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
For a memoryless waiting time, surviving the elapsed waiting period leaves the same distribution for the remaining waiting time.

The blue curve shows the original survivor function; the red curve restarts it at time \(s\). For an exponential waiting time \(T\), the conditional probability is

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &\mathbb{P}(T>s+t\mid T>s)\\ &=\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda(s+t)}}{\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda s}}=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}=\mathbb{P}(T>t). \end{aligned} \]

Thus surviving until \(s\) leaves the same distribution for the remaining wait. The continuous and discrete characterizations, including their assumptions, are stated in the definition above.

After waiting \(s\), the wide pale band shows the conditional survival of the remaining wait, shifted back to \(0\): it coincides with the original curve. The discrete version does the same for \(G\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(G\sim\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) counting failures, \(\mathbb{P}(G\ge m+n\mid G\ge m)=(1-p)^n\) for admissible nonnegative integers \(m,n\).
  • For \(T\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\), \(\mathbb{P}(T>s+t\mid T>s)=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\) for \(s,t\ge0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(G\sim\operatorname{Geo}(1/4)\), \(\mathbb{P}(G\ge5\mid G\ge2)=(3/4)^3=27/64\).
  • For \(T\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\), \(\mathbb{P}(T>4\mid T>3)=\mathrm{e}^{-2}=\mathbb{P}(T>1)\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be independent exponential random variables with rates \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\). Then \(\min(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) is exponentially distributed with rate \(\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The minimum is the first waiting time among several independent clocks. The more clocks are running, the faster the first one tends to ring.

The minimum exceeds \(t\) only if both do: \(\mathbb{P}(\min(X_1,X_2)>t)=\mathrm{e}^{-t}\,\mathrm{e}^{-2t}=\mathrm{e}^{-3t}\), again exponential, with the rates added. Moreover \(\mathbb{P}(X_1\text{ is the minimum})=\dfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}=\tfrac{1}{3}\).

Multiply the survival curves: the minimum survives only if both clocks do, which gives rate \(\lambda_1+\lambda_2\). The simulation agrees with the exponential density.

The minimum of a set exceeds \(t\) only when every waiting time exceeds \(t\). Independent random variables allow those survival probabilities to multiply; the exponential distribution makes that product another exponential survivor function, with the rates added.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The minimum of independent exponentials is exponential with rate equal to the sum of the rates.
  • The probability that a particular clock is first is its rate divided by the total rate.
  • This result connects competing risks with Poisson process arrivals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If two repair teams respond independently, the first response time can be modelled as the minimum of two exponential times.
  • In competing failure modes, the first failure time has rate equal to the sum of mode-specific rates.
  • If buses from two routes arrive independently, the next bus time can be the minimum of the two route waiting times.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(Z\) be a random index taking finitely or countably many values, and let the conditional distribution of \(X\) given \(Z=i\) be specified for each \(i\) with \(\mathbb{P}(Z=i)>0\). The distribution of \(X\) is a mixture distribution if it is obtained by averaging these conditional distributions using the probabilities of the values of \(Z\). A continuous mixing index instead requires integration against its mixing distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A mixture distribution combines several simpler distributions. It represents a situation where the population is made of different hidden groups.

First pick the component \(Z\) (with \(\mathbb{P}(Z=1)=0.4\)), then draw \(X\) from that component. The density of \(X\) is the weighted average of the component densities.

Change the weight and the two group means: the mixture density is the weighted average of the group densities, and its mean is the weighted average of their means.

Conditional probability gives the component law after the component is selected. The law of total probability averages those laws with the selection probabilities to obtain the unconditional mixture.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A mixture distribution is a weighted average of component distributions.
  • The weights are nonnegative and sum to one.
  • Mixtures can produce multimodal shapes even when each component is unimodal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Customer spending can be modelled as a mixture of business and leisure customer distributions.
  • Machine lifetime may be a mixture of lifetimes from old and new machines.
  • Exam scores can form a mixture if two preparation groups are present.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X\) be a random variable. A mode of \(X\) is a value at which the probability mass function or probability density function attains its maximum.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A mode is the most likely or most densely represented value. A distribution may have one mode, several modes, or no unique mode.

For the illustrated density \(f(x)=x\mathrm{e}^{-x}\) on \(x\ge0\), the mode is \(1\), the median is approximately \(1.68\) and the mean is \(2\). The Poisson example has two modes, at \(2\) and \(3\).

For the lognormal density, change \(\sigma\) and watch mode, median and mean drift apart. For the Poisson distribution, set \(\lambda\) to a whole number to get two modes.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A mode is a maximizer of the mass function or density function.
  • A distribution may have more than one mode.
  • For continuous distributions, density height is not itself probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A fair die has every face as a mode because all faces are equally likely.
  • A normal distribution has one mode at its centre.
  • A mixture of two separated normal distributions can be bimodal, with two peaks; both peaks are modes in the strict sense only when they have equal height.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be random variables with finite expectations. If \(X\le Y\) almost surely (that is, \(\mathbb{P}(X\le Y)=1\)), then monotonicity of expectation states that

\[ \mathbb{E}[X]\le \mathbb{E}[Y]. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Monotonicity says that a random variable that is always no larger has no larger average. It matches the ordinary idea that bigger outcomes lead to a bigger mean.

The inequality \(X\le Y\) holds outside an event of probability zero. Averaging the nonnegative difference \(Y-X\) cannot give a negative value, so the same ordering holds between their finite expectations.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(X\le Y\) almost surely, then \(\mathbb{E}[X]\le \mathbb{E}[Y]\) when expectations exist.
  • Strict inequality is not guaranteed unless the ordering is strict with positive probability.
  • Monotonicity is often used to bound expectations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If a premium service always costs at least as much as a basic service, its expected cost is at least as large.
  • If one policy always pays no more than another, its expected payout is no larger.
  • Truncating losses from above produces a random variable with no larger expectation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider a compound experiment made of two stages. If the first stage has \(a\) possible outcomes and, for each of them, the second stage has \(b\) possible outcomes, then the compound experiment has

\[ a\cdot b \]

possible outcomes. This is the multiplication rule for counting. For \(k\) successive stages with \(n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_k\) choices it gives \(n_1n_2\cdots n_k\) ordered outcomes; in set notation, \(|A\times B|=|A|\,|B|\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The multiplication rule counts ordered outcomes stage by stage: in a tree diagram, the number of leaves is the product of the numbers of branches at each level. The same tree carries probabilities, and multiplying along a path gives the probability of that path.

Counting the ordered outcomes gives \(52\cdot51=2652\) ordered draws, \(4\cdot3=12\) of them two aces, so \(\tfrac{12}{2652}=\tfrac{1}{221}\). Probabilities multiply along a path in the same way: \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\,\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\).

The Cartesian product records an ordered choice from each stage. If every first-stage choice permits the same \(b\) second-stage choices, counting the pairs gives \(|A\times B|=|A||B|\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The number of choices at a stage must not depend on the outcomes of earlier stages, although the choices themselves may.
  • Probability version: for events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(\mathbb{P}(A)>0\), \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\); for several events the rule becomes a product of successive conditional probabilities.
  • For independent events, the conditional factor reduces to the marginal probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A code of two letters followed by three digits can be formed in \(26^2\cdot10^3=676\,000\) ways.
  • Two dice give \(6\cdot6=36\) ordered outcomes, and \(n\) distinct objects can be ordered in \(n(n-1)\cdots1=n!\) ways.
  • Two cards drawn without replacement are both aces with probability \(\frac{4}{52}\cdot\frac{3}{51}=\frac{1}{221}\): the chance of the first ace times the conditional chance of the second. In counts, \(4\cdot3=12\) of the \(52\cdot51=2652\) ordered draws.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(S\) be a finite sample space whose outcomes are equally likely. For an event \(A\subseteq S\), the naive probability of \(A\) is

\[ \mathbb{P}(A)=\frac{|A|}{|S|}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Naive probability counts favourable outcomes and divides by all possible outcomes. It works only when the outcomes are equally likely.

For two independent fair dice, all 36 ordered outcomes are equally likely and six have sum \(7\). Thus \(\mathbb{P}(\text{sum}=7)=6/36=1/6\).

Cardinality counts favourable outcomes and all possible outcomes. Their ratio is a probability only under the stated equal-likelihood assumption.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Naive probability applies only when all outcomes in the sample space are equally likely.
  • It is computed as favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
  • Counting errors in either numerator or denominator lead directly to probability errors.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The probability of rolling an even number on a fair die is three favourable faces out of six.
  • The probability of drawing an ace from a well-shuffled deck is four favourable cards out of fifty-two.
  • If a random PIN is chosen uniformly from all four-digit PINs, naive probability can compute the chance of a repeated digit pattern.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(r\) be a positive integer and \(p\in(0,1]\). A random variable \(X\) has a negative binomial distribution if \(X\) counts the number of trials needed to obtain the \(r\)th success in independent Bernoulli trials with success probability \(p\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
In this trial-count convention, a negative binomial distribution generalizes the first success distribution. Instead of waiting for the first success, it waits for a fixed later success.

The diagram uses \(r=3\) and \(p=0.4\). For \(k\ge r\), \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)=\binom{k-1}{r-1}p^r(1-p)^{k-r}\): the first \(k-1\) trials have \(r-1\) successes, and trial \(k\) is the \(r\)th success.

Change \(r\) and \(p\): the distribution of the trial of the \(r\)th success starts at \(r\) and has mean \(r/p\). With \(r=1\) it is the first success distribution.

Independent random variables describe the successive trial results. Their probabilities multiply for any fixed success-and-failure sequence, after which counting the sequences that place the final success at the specified trial gives the mass function.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• It counts waiting time until a fixed number of successes.
  • For \(r=1\), \(X\) has the first success distribution. The shifted variable \(X-1\) has the geometric distribution used in this course.
  • The failure-count convention uses \(X-r\) instead of \(X\). For \(k=r,r+1,\ldots\), the trial-count probability is \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)=\binom{k-1}{r-1}p^r(1-p)^{k-r}\); the final trial is a success, and the preceding \(k-1\) trials contain exactly \(r-1\) successes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The number of sales calls needed to close five sales can be negative binomial.
  • The number of coin tosses needed to obtain three heads follows a negative binomial model.
  • The number of inspected items until the tenth defective item can be modelled this way under independent constant defect probability.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\mu\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(\sigma>0\). A continuous random variable \(X\) has a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), written \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), if its density is

\[ f_X(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A normal distribution is the familiar bell-shaped distribution. It is widely used because many sums and averages of independent variables behave approximately normally, by the central limit theorem.

The curve is symmetric about its mean \(\mu\), and its variance is \(\sigma^2\). Approximately \(68\%\) of its probability lies within \(\mu\pm\sigma\), and \(95\%\) lies within \(\mu\pm2\sigma\).

Move \(\mu\) to shift the bell and \(\sigma\) to widen it. The interval \((\mu-\sigma,\mu+\sigma)\) always holds about \(68\%\) of the probability.

As a continuous random variable, the normal variable assigns probabilities by areas under the density. The exponential function applied to the negative squared standardized deviation gives its bell-shaped decay.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A normal distribution is determined by its mean and variance.
  • Standardizing a normal random variable gives a standard normal random variable.
  • Sums of independent normal random variables are normal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Measurement error is often approximated by a normal distribution.
  • The average of many small independent effects is often modelled as normal.
  • Manufacturing deviations from a target dimension are frequently modelled with a normal distribution.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be random variables and let \(X_{(1)}\le\cdots\le X_{(n)}\) be the ordered values. The random variable \(X_{(k)}\) is called the \(k\)th order statistic.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Order statistics describe positions in a sorted sample. They include the minimum, maximum, and sample median.

The diagram relabels the same five values by rank. For i.i.d. observations with CDF \(F\), \(\mathbb{P}(X_{(n)}\le x)=F(x)^n\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X_{(1)}>x)=(1-F(x))^n\): the maximum is at most \(x\) exactly when every observation is, and the minimum exceeds \(x\) exactly when every observation does.

Sort a uniform sample and pick the \(k\)th smallest. Over many samples \(X_{(k)}\) clusters around \(k/(n+1)\): the minimum near \(0\), the maximum near \(1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The first order statistic is the sample minimum and the last is the sample maximum.
  • Order statistics are functions of a sample.
  • They are central in quantile estimation and reliability calculations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The smallest of five component lifetimes is the first order statistic.
  • The median of a sample of odd size \(n\) is the middle order statistic \(X_{((n+1)/2)}\); for \(n=5\) it is \(X_{(3)}\).
  • The maximum daily demand in a month is the largest order statistic of the daily demands.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(S\) be a sample space. An outcome is an element \(\omega\in S\) representing one possible result of the random experiment.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An outcome is one possible result of an experiment. It is the most detailed result considered by the chosen model.

In the diagram, the realized die outcome is \(4\). Thus the event \(\{2,4,6\}\) occurs and \(\{1,2\}\) does not: an event occurs exactly when it contains the realized outcome.

A set represents all possible results in the sample space. An individual outcome is an element of that set; it is distinct from an event, which can contain several outcomes.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An outcome is a single element of the sample space.
  • The level of detail in an outcome depends on how the experiment is modelled.
  • Events are collections of outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For one die roll, the outcome can be the face that appears.
  • For two coin tosses, an outcome can record the ordered pair of heads and tails.
  • For a customer-order experiment, an outcome might include purchase amount, item type, and delivery time.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A partition of a set \(E\) is a family \(\{B_i\colon i\in I\}\) of nonempty subsets satisfying

\[ B_i\cap B_j=\varnothing\quad(i\ne j),\qquad\bigcup_{i\in I}B_i=E. \]

In probability, take \(E=\Omega\) and require the blocks to be events. The elementary total-probability sums use finite or countable partitions. A nonempty event can still have probability zero; omit such blocks from formulas that divide by their probability.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A partition separates every outcome into exactly one case. This lets a probability or expectation be calculated case by case.

In the illustrated example, \(B_i\cap B_j=\varnothing\) for \(i\neq j\) and \(B_1\cup\cdots\cup B_4=S\), so \(\mathbb{P}(B_1)+\cdots+\mathbb{P}(B_4)=1\); a partition splits any question into cases: \(\displaystyle \mathbb{P}(A)=\sum_i \mathbb{P}(A\cap B_i)\) (law of total probability).

Disjoint events ensure that no outcome belongs to two probability blocks. Union and intersection of events expresses the two requirements: pairwise intersections are empty and the union covers the whole sample space.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every outcome belongs to exactly one partition event.
  • For any event \(A\), the events \(A\cap B_i\) are disjoint and have union \(A\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, the odd and even outcomes partition \(\{1,\ldots,6\}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(A\) be a finite set with \(n\) elements and let \(0\le k\le n\). A \(k\)-permutation of \(A\) is an ordered selection \((a_1,\ldots,a_k)\) of \(k\) distinct elements of \(A\). For \(k=n\) it is an ordering of all of \(A\), which corresponds to a bijection \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\to A\); when \(A=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) this is a permutation of \(A\) in the Math II sense of a bijection from \(A\) onto itself.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
\(k\)-permutations count selections in which order matters: changing the order gives a different selection. Counting texts often say permutation for both cases; the \(k\) makes clear which one is meant.

An ordered selection of \(k\) objects from \(n\) distinct objects can be made in \(n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)=n!/(n-k)!\) ways. For example, there are \(4\cdot3=12\) ordered pairs from four letters.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The number of \(k\)-permutations of \(n\) distinct objects is \(n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)=n!/(n-k)!\).
  • In particular there are \(n!\) orderings of \(n\) distinct objects.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The number of possible podium finishes among eight runners is a permutation count.
  • Arranging five books on a shelf uses full permutations.
  • Assigning three distinct tasks to three ordered time slots is a permutation problem.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A distribution has a point mass, or atom, at \(a\in\mathbb{R}\) when \(p_a=\mathbb{P}(X=a)>0\). Here \(X\) is a real-valued random variable with that distribution. The CDF has a jump of size \(p_a\) at \(a\):

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} p_a&=F_X(a)-F_X(a^-),\\ F_X(a^-)&=\lim_{x\uparrow a}F_X(x). \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A point mass assigns positive probability to one exact value. It can be one part of a distribution that also has a density component. It does not mean that all probability is concentrated at that value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Suppose \(X=0\) with probability \(0.3\) and, with probability \(0.7\), \(X\) is drawn from the uniform distribution on \((0,1)\). Then \(F_X(0^-)=0\) and \(F_X(0)=0.3\): there is a point mass \(0.3\) at zero. The remaining probability is spread over the interval.

This differs from a constant random variable, for which the point mass at its only possible value is one. An absolutely continuous distribution has no point masses.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\lambda>0\). A discrete random variable \(X\) has a Poisson distribution with parameter \(\lambda\), written \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\), if, for \(k=0,1,2,\ldots\),

\[ \mathbb{P}(X=k)=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}, \]

and the PMF is zero elsewhere. The extension \(\lambda=0\) gives the constant-zero distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A Poisson variable models a nonnegative count with a parameter equal to its mean count.

Change \(\lambda\): it is both the mean and the variance. Small \(\lambda\) piles the mass near \(0\); large \(\lambda\) gives a wider, more symmetric hump.

This discrete random variable takes nonnegative integer counts. The factorial \(k!\) and the exponential function supply the mass-function weights; the exponential-series identity makes their total probability equal one.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}X=\operatorname{Var}(X)=\lambda\).
  • MGF \(M_X(t)=\exp(\lambda(\mathrm{e}^t-1))\) for every real \(t\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\lambda=2\), \(\mathbb{P}(X=0)=\mathrm{e}^{-2}\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X=1)=2\mathrm{e}^{-2}\).
  • A Poisson count with mean \(5\) has variance \(5\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt{5}\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: Independent Poisson counts add to a Poisson count with the sum of their parameters. A binomial model converges to this law when the number of trials tends to infinity and the success probabilities shrink so that their product tends to a fixed parameter.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\lambda>0\). A process \(\{N_t\colon t\ge 0\}\) with \(N_0=0\), in which \(N_t\) counts the arrivals in \([0,t]\), is a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\) if it has independent increments (arrival counts in disjoint time intervals are independent) and

\[ N_{t+s}-N_s\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda t) \]

for all \(s,t\ge 0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A Poisson process models random arrivals over time. It assumes arrivals occur independently and at a constant average rate.

The count \(N_t\) records arrivals in \([0,t]\). For a Poisson process of rate \(\lambda\), \(N_{t+s}-N_s\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda t)\) and disjoint increments are independent. The interarrival times, that is, the waiting times between consecutive arrivals, are i.i.d. exponential \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\) variables, with \(\lambda\) expected arrivals per unit time.

Each press of the button draws new arrivals at rate \(\lambda\). The number in the window \((s,s+t]\) varies from draw to draw like a \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda t)\) variable.

A stochastic process consists of variables indexed by time. The Poisson distribution specifies each interval count, while independent random variables describe counts on disjoint intervals; both properties are needed to specify the process, not just its one-time law.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A Poisson process has independent increments.
  • The number of arrivals in an interval depends only on the interval length.
  • Interarrival times in a Poisson process are independent exponential random variables.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Customer arrivals to a store can be approximated by a Poisson process during a stable period.
  • Particle emissions from a radioactive source are often modelled as a Poisson process.
  • Requests to a server may be modelled as a Poisson process over short intervals.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A probability density function of an absolutely continuous \(X\) is a nonnegative integrable function satisfying

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathbb{P}(X\in A)=\int_Af_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\\ \int_{\mathbb{R}}f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=1. \end{gathered} \]

Densities that agree except possibly on a set of zero length, for example at finitely many points, describe the same distribution. This qualification is called almost everywhere here: values on the exceptional set do not affect the integrals. It does not require two densities to agree at every point.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A density describes how probability is spread over the real line. Areas under it are probabilities; the height at a point is not a probability.

Probabilities are areas under the density. The narrow uniform density reaches height \(2\), which is fine: only areas, never heights, are probabilities.

For the course's continuous random variable convention, the density is integrated to obtain interval probabilities. The definite integral measures that area; for the piecewise continuous densities used in the examples, Riemann integral calculations evaluate it. Density height itself is not point probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(a<X\le b)=\int_a^bf_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  • \(F_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^xf_X(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\), so \(F_X'=f_X\) except possibly on a set of zero length.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f_X(x)=2x\) on \((0,1)\) and zero elsewhere, \(\mathbb{P}(X\le1/2)=1/4\).
  • The uniform density on \((0,1/2)\) has height \(2\), total area \(1\), and \(\mathbb{P}(X=1/4)=0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(S\) be a sample space and let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a sigma-algebra of events, that is, a collection of events containing \(S\) and closed under complements and countable unions. A probability function is a function \(P\colon\mathcal{F}\to[0,1]\) that assigns probabilities to events and satisfies the axioms of probability.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A probability function is the rule that assigns chances to events. It turns a sample space into a usable probability model.

For the fair die in the diagram, the disjoint events \(\{1,3\}\) and \(\{6\}\) have probabilities \(1/3\) and \(1/6\). Their union therefore has probability \(1/2\). Different events can have the same probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A probability function assigns numbers to events according to the probability axioms.
  • The full sample space has probability one.
  • Disjoint unions are handled by adding probabilities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, the probability function assigns probability one sixth to each single-face event.
  • In a reliability model, the probability function assigns a probability to the event that the system fails.
  • For a deck of cards, the probability function assigns probabilities to events such as drawing a heart.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable. The probability mass function of \(X\) is the function \(p_X\) defined by

\[ p_X(x)=\mathbb{P}(X=x). \]

It is zero except on the countable set of values that \(X\) can take.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A PMF assigns a probability to each discrete value. Its nonnegative masses account for all outcomes.

The diagram shows \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(3,1/2)\), with masses \(1/8\), \(3/8\), \(3/8\) and \(1/8\), which sum to \(1\). The two red bars give \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge2)=3/8+1/8=1/2\).

Each bar is a value of \(p_X(x)=\mathbb{P}(X=x)\); together they add up to \(1\). Set \(c\) and \(d\) to add the masses of a range of values.

A discrete random variable has countably many possible values. Applying the probability function to each generated event \(\{X=x\}\) gives its mass; summing the masses over a set of values gives the probability of that set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(p_X(x)\ge0\) and \(\displaystyle \sum_xp_X(x)=1\).
  • \(\displaystyle F_X(t)=\sum_{x\le t}p_X(x)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, \(p_X(3)=1/6\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X\le3)=3/6\).
  • If \(p_X(0)=0.7\) and \(p_X(1)=0.3\), then \(\mathbb{P}(X>0)=0.3\).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The prosecutor's fallacy is the error of confusing the probability of observing evidence under a hypothesis with the probability that the hypothesis is true given the evidence.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This fallacy reverses a conditional probability. It can make evidence sound much stronger than it actually is.

In the illustrated population, one culprit matches and about ten innocent people match. Thus \(\mathbb{P}(\text{innocent}\mid\text{match})\approx10/11\approx0.91\), despite \(\mathbb{P}(\text{match}\mid\text{innocent})=0.00001\). The fallacy confuses these conditional probabilities and overlooks the large number of innocent people.

A tiny chance of an innocent match, spread over a large population, still produces several innocent matches. Compare \(\mathbb{P}(\text{match}\mid\text{innocent})\) with \(\mathbb{P}(\text{innocent}\mid\text{match})\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The fallacy confuses \(\mathbb{P}(E\mid H)\) with \(\mathbb{P}(H\mid E)\).
  • Bayes' rule shows that posterior probabilities require prior probabilities and alternative explanations.
  • Rare evidence is not automatically decisive if it can also occur under competing hypotheses.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A rare DNA match probability is not the same as the probability that a defendant is innocent.
  • A rare disease test result is not the same as the probability of disease without considering prevalence.
  • A suspicious transaction pattern must be compared against both fraud and non-fraud explanations.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a CDF \(F\) and \(0<u<1\), its generalized inverse is

\[ F^{-1}(u)=\inf\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon F(x)\ge u\}. \]

It need not be an ordinary inverse: \(F\) can have flat portions or jumps. Endpoint values at \(u=0,1\) are irrelevant when using a continuous uniform input.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The generalized inverse converts a probability level into a threshold. Applied to a uniform input, it simulates a variable with the desired distribution.

In this diagram, the generalized inverse is written \(Q(u)=\inf\{x\colon F(x)\ge u\}\) reads the CDF backwards: the smallest value whose CDF reaches the probability \(u\). \(Q(0.5)\) is the median and \(Q(0.25)\), \(Q(0.75)\) are the quartiles.

Pick a level \(u\) and read the CDF backwards. At a jump many levels share one quantile, and where \(F\) is flat the infimum picks the left end.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(0<u<1\), \(F^{-1}(u)\le x\) if and only if \(u\le F(x)\).
  • Consequently, if \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), \(\mathbb{P}(F^{-1}(U)\le x)=F(x)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\operatorname{Exp}(2)\), \(F^{-1}(u)=-\log(1-u)/2\).
  • For \(\operatorname{Bern}(0.3)\), \(F^{-1}(u)=0\) for \(0<u\le0.7\) and \(1\) for \(0.7<u<1\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: The median is a quantile at probability level \(1/2\). Other probability levels define percentiles. The generalized inverse is useful even when an ordinary inverse does not exist.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be random variables with \(A\le B\). A random interval is an interval whose endpoints are random, such as \([A,B]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A random interval is an interval that changes from one outcome to another. It is useful when uncertainty affects the bounds rather than just a single value.

In the illustrated example, \(A\le B\) are random, so \([A,B]\) changes from run to run. \(\mathbb{P}(A\le\theta\le B)\) is the probability that the random interval covers the fixed \(\theta\) (the idea behind confidence intervals); here \(5\) out of \(6\) runs cover it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A random interval has endpoints that are random variables.
  • Events can be formed from statements about whether a fixed value lies inside the interval.
  • Random intervals are useful for uncertainty bands and coverage statements.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A confidence interval computed from data is a random interval before the data are observed.
  • The interval between two random arrival times is random.
  • A forecast range with random lower and upper bounds is a random interval.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(S\) be a sample space. A random variable is a function \(X\colon S\to\mathbb{R}\) that assigns a real number to each outcome in \(S\), subject to the measurability condition that \(\{\omega\in S\colon X(\omega)\le x\}\) is an event for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A random variable converts outcomes into numerical values. It lets probability questions be studied using functions and distributions.

The diagram counts heads in two independent fair coin tosses: \(X(HH)=2\), \(X(HT)=X(TH)=1\) and \(X(TT)=0\). The outcome probabilities give \(\mathbb{P}(X=1)=\mathbb{P}(\{HT,TH\})=1/2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A random variable is a function from outcomes to real numbers.
  • Random variables generate events such as threshold events.
  • The distribution of a random variable describes probabilities of its numerical values or ranges.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a die roll, the displayed face is a random variable.
  • For a customer order, the order value is a random variable.
  • For a machine, the time until failure is a random variable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\sigma>0\). A continuous random variable \(X\) has a Rayleigh distribution with parameter \(\sigma\) if its density is

\[ f_X(x)=\frac{x}{\sigma^2}\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),\qquad x\ge 0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A Rayleigh distribution often describes the magnitude of a two-dimensional random vector. It appears naturally when two independent normal components are combined into a distance.

For independent \(Y_1,Y_2\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma>0\), the radius \(X=\sqrt{Y_1^2+Y_2^2}\) has density \(f_X(x)=\frac{x}{\sigma^2}\exp(-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2})\) for \(x\ge0\). The dashed lines mark its mode and mean, respectively.

Change \(\sigma\): the density peaks at \(x=\sigma\) and the mean sits a little further out, at \(\sigma\sqrt{\pi/2}\).

This is a continuous random variable, so probabilities are density integrals over nonnegative intervals. Its density is zero on negative values, and its total integral over the nonnegative line is one.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The Rayleigh distribution is supported on nonnegative values.
  • It arises as the magnitude of a two-dimensional random vector with independent, centred normal components of equal variance.
  • Its density starts at zero, rises to a peak, and then decays.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Wind speed magnitude can sometimes be modelled with a Rayleigh distribution.
  • The distance error from two independent normal coordinate errors can be Rayleigh.
  • Signal envelope amplitudes in some noise models follow a Rayleigh distribution.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be a finite set of \(n\) distinct objects, and draw \(k\) of them one at a time.

  • With replacement: each drawn object is put back before the next draw, so the same object can be drawn more than once.
  • Without replacement: drawn objects are removed, so all \(k\) drawn objects are distinct and \(k\le n\).

A sample is ordered if the order of the draws is recorded, and unordered if only which objects were drawn (with their multiplicities) matters.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The two choices give four counting problems. Ordered samples are counted with the multiplication rule; an unordered sample without replacement is a combination, obtained from the ordered count by dividing out the \(k!\) orders of the same \(k\) objects.

The table places the four counts of the first example, \(k=3\) draws from \(n=10\) tickets, in a grid: the columns say whether drawn tickets are put back, the rows whether the order is recorded. Only in the column without replacement does every unordered sample come from exactly \(3!=6\) ordered ones, so dividing \(720\) by \(3!\) gives \(\binom{10}{3}=120\). With replacement the same division fails, because \(1000/3!\) is not even an integer: a sample with repeats has fewer than \(3!\) orders, which is why the \(220\) unordered samples with replacement are not equally likely.

With replacement, every draw faces the same \(n\) objects, so the history of earlier draws changes nothing; in the language of Week 2, the draws are independent with the same distribution. Without replacement, each draw changes what remains, so the draws are dependent: after a red ball is removed, a second red ball is less likely.

Draw \(n\) balls from an urn with \(N\) balls, \(K\) of them white, and count the white balls drawn. Both counts have mean \(nK/N\), but without replacement the variance carries the extra factor \((N-n)/(N-1)\). Make \(N\) large compared with \(n\) and the two distributions merge.

Two common slips are worth naming. First, "without replacement" does not by itself mean "unordered": dealing cards one by one is ordered sampling without replacement, and a hand of cards is the unordered version of the same experiment. Second, the unordered samples with replacement must not be treated as equally likely, as the Key Results explain.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
The number of possible samples of size \(k\) from \(n\) distinct objects is:

  • ordered, with replacement: \(n^k\);
  • ordered, without replacement: \(n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)=n!/(n-k)!\), the number of \(k\)-permutations; it is \(0\) when \(k>n\);
  • unordered, without replacement: the binomial coefficient \(\binom{n}{k}\);
  • unordered, with replacement: \(\binom{n+k-1}{k}\), by stars and bars.

In the first three cases every sample is equally likely when each draw is uniform, so naive probability applies. The unordered samples with replacement are not equally likely, so probabilities should be computed from ordered samples instead.

  • Each ordered sample without replacement corresponds to exactly \(k!\) orderings of one unordered sample, so \(\binom{n}{k}=\dfrac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}\).
  • Without replacement, the \(j\)th draw on its own is still uniform over all \(n\) objects: by symmetry, as many ordered samples have a given object in place \(j\) as in place \(1\). Only the joint behaviour of the draws differs from sampling with replacement.
  • A particular object is included in the sample with probability \(k/n\) without replacement and \(1-(1-1/n)^k\) with replacement; the latter is smaller for \(k\ge2\), because repeats waste draws.
  • With replacement, all \(k\) draws are distinct with probability \(n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)/n^k\), the ratio of the two ordered counts.

Looking ahead to Week 3: if \(n\) balls are drawn from an urn with \(N\) balls, \(K\) of them white, the number of white balls drawn has the binomial distribution \(\operatorname{Bin}(n,K/N)\) with replacement and the hypergeometric distribution without replacement. Both have mean \(nK/N\); sampling without replacement has the smaller variance, and the two are close when \(N\) is large compared with \(n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Choosing \(3\) of \(10\) numbered tickets gives \(10^3=1000\) ordered samples with replacement, \(10\cdot9\cdot8=720\) ordered samples without replacement, \(\binom{10}{3}=120\) unordered samples without replacement, and \(\binom{12}{3}=220\) unordered samples with replacement.
  • In the same setting, ticket number \(7\) is among the three draws with probability \(3/10=0.3\) without replacement, and \(1-0.9^3=0.271\) with replacement.
  • An urn holds \(20\) balls, \(8\) of them red, and \(6\) are drawn. The probability of no red ball is \(0.6^6\approx0.0467\) with replacement, but \(\binom{12}{6}/\binom{20}{6}=924/38760\approx0.0238\) without replacement.
  • From the same urn, two balls are drawn without replacement. Of the \(20\cdot19=380\) ordered pairs, \(8\cdot7=56\) are red–red and \(12\cdot8=96\) are non-red–red, so the second ball is red with probability \(152/380=0.4=8/20\), the same as the first.
  • Two draws with replacement from \(\{1,2\}\) give the \(\binom{3}{2}=3\) unordered samples \(\{1,1\}\), \(\{1,2\}\) and \(\{2,2\}\), but with probabilities \(\tfrac{1}{4},\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{4}\): the mixed sample arises from the two ordered samples \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\).
  • In the birthday problem, assigning birthdays to \(k\) people is ordered sampling with replacement from \(365\) days (\(365^k\) outcomes), and all birthdays distinct is ordered sampling without replacement. Hence
\[ \mathbb{P}(\text{no match})=\frac{365!/(365-k)!}{365^k}. \]

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A random variable \(Z\) has the standard normal distribution, written \(Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\), if its density is \(\phi\); its CDF is \(\Phi\):

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} \phi(z)&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\mathrm{e}^{-z^2/2},\\ \Phi(z)&=\int_{-\infty}^z\phi(t)\,\mathrm{d}t. \end{aligned} \]

In \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\) the second parameter is the variance.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The standard normal law provides the reference scale for normal approximations: a centred value is measured in standard deviations.

In this diagram, \(Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) has density \(\varphi(z)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\mathrm{e}^{-z^2/2}\) and CDF \(\Phi(z)=\mathbb{P}(Z\le z)=\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{z}\varphi(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\), the shaded area. By symmetry, \(\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)\).

Move \(c\) and \(d\) and read probabilities as differences \(\Phi(d)-\Phi(c)\); try \(c=-1.96\), \(d=1.96\).

The normal distribution allows arbitrary mean and positive variance. Choosing mean zero and variance one gives the reference density and CDF used to evaluate probabilities after standardization.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}Z=0\), \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=1\), and \(\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)\).
  • If \(Y\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma>0\), then \((Y-\mu)/\sigma\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\).
  • Quantiles transform the same way: the \(p\)-quantile of \(Y\) is \(\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(p)\). Printed normal tables list the left-tail probabilities \(\Phi(z)\), so a quantile is read off the table in reverse and then transformed back.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(Z\le1)=\Phi(1)\approx0.8413\).
  • For \(Y\sim\mathcal{N}(10,4)\), \(\mathbb{P}(Y\le12)=\Phi((12-10)/2)=\Phi(1)\approx0.8413\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a random variable with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma>0\). The standardization of \(X\) is

\[ Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Standardization expresses a value relative to its mean and spread. It makes variables with different units or scales easier to compare.

The illustrated calculation gives \(Z=\dfrac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\). Subtracting \(\mu\) centres the distribution at \(0\) and dividing by \(\sigma\) rescales the spread to \(1\), so \(\mathbb{E}[Z]=0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=1\). The \(z\)-score measures the distance from the mean in units of \(\sigma\).

Change \(\mu\), \(\sigma\) and \(x\): the standardized value \(z=(x-\mu)/\sigma\) cuts off exactly the same probability under the standard normal.

Expectation supplies the centring value \(\mu\). Subtracting that value gives mean zero; dividing by the positive standard deviation then gives variance one without asserting that the transformed law is normal.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Standardization subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation.
  • The standardized variable has mean zero and variance one when the original mean and variance exist.
  • For normal variables, standardization produces a standard normal variable.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A student's score can be standardized relative to the class mean and standard deviation.
  • A product weight can be standardized to see how many standard deviations it lies from the target.
  • Standardizing normal measurement errors allows probabilities to be computed from a standard normal table.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Let \(n,k\in\mathbb{N}\). Stars and bars is a counting method for the number of ways to distribute \(k\) identical objects among \(n\) distinct boxes, often by representing objects as stars and dividers as bars.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Stars and bars turns a problem of distributing identical objects among boxes into an arrangement problem. It is useful when objects are identical and only the counts in each box matter.

The six stars and two bars in the figure represent \((x_1,x_2,x_3)=(2,1,3)\). Every arrangement of six stars and two bars corresponds to one nonnegative integer solution of \(x_1+x_2+x_3=6\). Choosing the two bar positions among eight positions gives \(\binom{8}{2}=28\) distributions. In the general notation below, \(k\) objects and \(n\) boxes require \(n-1\) bars.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Stars and bars counts nonnegative integer solutions to \(x_1+\cdots+x_n=k\).
  • The number of such solutions is \(\binom{k+n-1}{n-1}\).
  • Positive integer solutions can be counted by first giving one object to each box.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The number of ways to distribute ten identical candies among four children is a stars-and-bars count.
  • The number of nonnegative solutions to \(x_1+x_2+x_3=8\) is counted by stars and bars.
  • Allocating identical spare parts among labelled warehouses can use stars and bars.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(T\) be an index set. A stochastic process is a collection of random variables \(\{X_t\colon t\in T\}\) defined on a common probability space, that is, one sample space with one probability function.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A stochastic process describes randomness that evolves over an index such as time. Instead of one random value, it studies a whole family of related random values.

In this diagram, \(\{X_t\colon t\in T\}\) lives on one probability space. Fixing \(t\) gives a random variable (the vertical slice); fixing the outcome \(\omega\) gives a sample path \(t\mapsto X_t(\omega)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A stochastic process is a family of random variables indexed by time or another set.
  • The index set may be discrete or continuous.
  • Sample paths describe how one realization of the process evolves across the index set.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Daily demand over a year can be modelled as a discrete-time stochastic process.
  • The number of arrivals up to time \(t\) in a queue is a continuous-time stochastic process.
  • Stock prices observed over time form a stochastic process.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be independent random variables. The sum of independent random variables is the random variable \(X+Y\), whose distribution is determined by combining the distributions of \(X\) and \(Y\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Sums of independent random variables combine separate sources of randomness. Many important distributions arise from adding independent components.

For the independent fair dice shown, convolution gives \(\mathbb{P}(X+Y=7)=6/36\). Their sum has mean \(\mathbb{E}[X]+\mathbb{E}[Y]=7\). Independence also gives \(\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).

Add dice one at a time: each new distribution is a convolution of the previous one with a single die. Means and variances add, and the shape becomes bell-like.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The distribution of a sum of independent variables is obtained by convolution in many common settings.
  • Means add whenever expectations exist.
  • Variances add for independent variables with finite variances.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The total number of heads from two independent sets of tosses is a sum of independent binomial variables.
  • The total waiting time for independent service stages is a sum of waiting-time variables.
  • The total claim amount from independent claims is a sum of independent losses.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X\) be a random variable with a distribution. Summary measures of a distribution are numerical quantities, such as centre, spread, and shape measures, that describe important features of that distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Summary measures condense a distribution into interpretable numbers. They help compare distributions without listing every probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Location measures describe centre.
  • Spread measures describe variability.
  • Shape measures describe asymmetry, tail weight, or modality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Mean and median summarize the centre of delivery times.
  • Variance and standard deviation summarize variability in demand.
  • Skewness and kurtosis summarize shape features of a loss distribution.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The course uses \(\{x\colon p_X(x)>0\}\) for a discrete support and a positive-density region for standard continuous models. The topological support, which depends only on the distribution, is

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{supp}(X)=\{x\colon{}&\mathbb{P}(|X-x|<\varepsilon)>0\\ &\text{ for every }\varepsilon>0\}. \end{aligned} \]

For the usual continuous densities, this is the closure of the positive-density region. If a density has been changed on a set of zero length, for example at finitely many points, use the neighbourhood definition: such changes do not change the support.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The support records where values with positive probability occur, or where probability can be found arbitrarily nearby. It prevents using a PMF or PDF outside its intended range.

A random variable generates probabilities on the numerical values it can take. Its support is a set of values whose every neighbourhood has positive probability; this definition depends on the law, rather than a chosen version of its density.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The course discrete support is \(\{x\colon p_X(x)>0\}\).
  • The topological support consists of points whose every open neighbourhood has positive probability, including boundary and accumulation points.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\operatorname{Bern}(p)\) with \(0<p<1\), the support is \(\{0,1\}\).
  • For \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), a positive-density region is \((0,1)\), while the topological support is \([0,1]\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X\) be a random variable and let \(a\in\mathbb{R}\). The distribution of \(X\) is symmetric about \(a\) if \(X-a\) and \(a-X\) have the same distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A symmetric distribution has matching behaviour on both sides of its centre. The left and right sides mirror each other in probability.

The illustrated density is symmetric about \(a\), so \(f_X(a-t)=f_X(a+t)\) and the two shaded tails have equal probability. The value \(a\) is a median and is the mean when it exists; any finite odd central moment is zero.

Pick a centre \(a\) and a distance \(t\): the distribution is symmetric about \(a\) when the two tails match for every \(t\). The exponential distribution fails for every \(a\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Symmetry about a centre means left and right deviations have the same distribution.
  • For many symmetric distributions, mean and median coincide when they exist.
  • A symmetric distribution need not be normal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A normal distribution is symmetric about its mean.
  • A fair die distribution is symmetric around three and a half.
  • A two-point distribution with equal mass at negative one and one is symmetric about zero.

docs.title: Transformation of a Continuous Random Variable
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(X\) have a density on an interval \(I\). Suppose \(g\colon I\to J\) is a continuously differentiable bijection with \(g'(x)\ne0\) on \(I\). For the transformed variable \(Y=g(X)\) and \(y\in J\),

\[ f_Y(y)=f_X(g^{-1}(y))\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}y}g^{-1}(y)\right|, \]

and the density is zero outside \(J\). Density values at endpoints do not affect probabilities. The absolute derivative accounts for interval stretching; non-strict monotonicity alone is insufficient for this formula. For transformations with suitable monotone branches, add the contributions from each inverse branch.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A monotone transformation changes a density by stretching or compressing intervals. The absolute inverse derivative compensates for this change of scale.

In the illustrated example, \(f_Y(y)=f_X\big(g^{-1}(y)\big)\Big|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}y}g^{-1}(y)\Big|=1\cdot\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt y}\) on \((0,1]\) for \(g(x)=x^2\). The derivative factor rescales the density so that each strip keeps its probability and the total area stays \(1\).

A small interval of \(X\) and its image under \(g\) carry the same probability. Where \(g\) stretches intervals, the density of \(Y\) drops by the factor \(\left|\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dy}g^{-1}(y)\right|\).

A continuous random variable assigns probabilities through a probability density function. Integration by substitution type 1 transfers those probabilities through the change of variable. Derivative and differentiability describes local interval stretching, and the inverse function theorem gives the reciprocal derivative of the inverse when the derivative of \(g\) is nonzero.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(Y=a+bX\) with \(b\ne0\), then \(f_Y(y)=f_X((y-a)/b)/|b|\).
  • For a suitable finite collection of monotone branches, sum \(f_X(x)/|g'(x)|\) over the preimages \(g(x)=y\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(Y=2X+1\), then \(f_Y(y)=1/2\) on \((1,3)\).
  • If \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(Y=X^2\), then \(f_Y(y)=1/(2\sqrt y)\) on \((0,1)\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: The transformed density integrates to one. In higher-dimensional transformations, a Jacobian determinant provides the corresponding volume adjustment.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For real numbers \(a<b\), a random variable \(X\) has the uniform distribution on \((a,b)\), written \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(a,b)\), if its density is

\[ f_X(x)=\begin{cases}1/(b-a),&a<x<b,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} \]

Including the endpoints in the density interval does not change the distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A continuous uniform variable has constant density over an interval. Equal-length subintervals have equal probability.

Widen or narrow \((a,b)\): the density height \(1/(b-a)\) adjusts so that the total area stays \(1\), and equal-length subintervals get equal probability.

The interval \((a,b)\) specifies the range over which this continuous random variable is spread. Its constant probability density function has height \(1/(b-a)\), so an interval inside that range has probability equal to its length divided by \(b-a\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}X=(a+b)/2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=(b-a)^2/12\).
  • For \(a\le c\le d\le b\), \(\mathbb{P}(c<X<d)=(d-c)/(b-a)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(2,6)\), \(\mathbb{P}(3<X<5)=2/4=1/2\).
  • For \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), \(\mathbb{E}X=1/2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1/12\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A distribution is unimodal if its probability mass function or density function has a single peak (one local maximum), and multimodal if it has several separated peaks; with two peaks it is called bimodal. Here every peak is called a mode, although only the highest peak is a mode in the strict sense of a global maximizer.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A unimodal distribution has one main peak. A multimodal distribution has several peaks, which may indicate several groups or mechanisms.

Pull the two group means apart, or shrink \(\sigma\): at some point a single peak splits into two.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A unimodal distribution has a single peak, which is then its mode.
  • A multimodal distribution has several peaks; they need not be equally high.
  • Mixtures can create multimodal distributions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A normal distribution is unimodal.
  • A mixture of weekday and weekend demand distributions may be bimodal.
  • Exam scores from two very different preparation groups can form a multimodal distribution.
