docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be events in a sample space. The union \(A\cup B\) is the event that at least one of \(A\) or \(B\) occurs, and the intersection \(A\cap B\) is the event that both \(A\) and \(B\) occur.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The union combines events by allowing either event to happen. The intersection focuses only on outcomes shared by both events.

Adding the probabilities of the two discs counts their overlap twice, so its probability must be subtracted once. De Morgan's identities relate these operations to complements: \((A\cup B)^c=A^c\cap B^c\) and \((A\cap B)^c=A^c\cup B^c\).

Union of sets collects outcomes belonging to at least one of the events. Intersection of sets retains only outcomes shared by both; treating those sets as events connects set operations with probabilistic statements.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(A\cup B\) occurs when at least one of the events occurs.
  • \(A\cap B\) occurs when both events occur.
  • Inclusion-exclusion connects the probability of a union to the probabilities of the two events and their intersection.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The event 'draw a heart or a king' is a union of two events.
  • The event 'draw a red king' is an intersection of two events.
  • The event that a customer buys online and uses a coupon is an intersection.

docs.title: Universality of the Uniform and CDF Realizability
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(F\colon\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]\) be nondecreasing and right-continuous, with \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty}F(x)=0\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}F(x)=1\). Let \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and define \(Q(u)=\inf\{x\colon F(x)\ge u\}\) for \(0<u<1\). Then \(X=Q(U)\) satisfies

\[ \mathbb{P}(X\le x)=F(x)\quad\text{for every }x. \]

Thus every function satisfying the CDF conditions is realizable as a distribution, and a uniform input can generate that distribution. The construction allows jumps and flat portions of \(F\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A uniform draw selects a probability level; the quantile function converts it into an outcome. This both proves that valid CDFs describe genuine random variables and provides inverse transform simulation.

The equally spaced probability levels map to quantiles \(x=Q(u)\). These quantiles are closer together where \(F\) is steep, illustrating how a uniform input produces the target distribution.

Press the button to draw uniform levels \(U\): pushed through \(Q\), they produce a sample whose histogram follows the target distribution, including the jumps of a discrete one.

The uniform distribution on \((0,1)\) assigns probability \(v\) to the interval \((0,v]\). The quantile construction turns \(\{Q(U)\le x\}\) into \(\{U\le F(x)\}\), so that probability becomes \(F(x)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The monotonicity, right-continuity, and endpoint-limit conditions are necessary and sufficient for a function to be a CDF.
  • For \(0<u<1\), \(Q(u)\le x\) exactly when \(u\le F(x)\), so \(\mathbb{P}(Q(U)\le x)=\mathbb{P}(U\le F(x))=F(x)\).
  • Conversely, if \(X\) has a continuous CDF \(F\), then \(F(X)\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\); this direction is the probability integral transform. It fails when \(F\) has jumps, because \(F(X)\) then takes some values with positive probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the step CDF \(F(x)=0\) when \(x<c\) and \(F(x)=1\) when \(x\ge c\), \(Q(u)=c\) and the construction gives \(X=c\) almost surely, that is, with probability \(1\).
  • For \(F(x)=0\) when \(x<0\) and \(F(x)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-2x}\) when \(x\ge0\), the construction gives \(X=-\log(1-U)/2\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a random variable with \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]<\infty\), and let \(\mu=\mathbb{E}X\). The variance of \(X\) is

\[ \operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2]=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mu^2, \]

and the standard deviation is \(\sigma_X=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Variance measures average squared distance from the mean. Its square root measures spread in the original units.

The arrows mark one standard deviation on either side of the mean for each curve. Standard deviation has the same units as \(X\), whereas variance uses squared units.

Spread the mass out and the variance grows; shift the whole distribution and it hardly changes. Darker bars contribute more to \(\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2]\).

Expectation supplies both the mean used to centre \(X\) and the average squared deviation from it. Expanding that square and averaging gives the second-moment formula for variance.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{Var}(a+bX)=b^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=0\) if and only if \(X=\mathbb{E}X\) almost surely, that is, \(\mathbb{P}(X=\mathbb{E}X)=1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\operatorname{Bern}(0.3)\), the variance is \(0.3(0.7)=0.21\).
  • If \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=4\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(5-3X)=36\) and its standard deviation is \(6\).

docs.title: Accumulation Point in a Metric Space
Definition
docs.text:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(E\subseteq X\). A point \(x\in X\) is called an accumulation point (or cluster point, limit point) of \(E\) if every metric ball around \(x\) contains a point of \(E\) different from \(x\), i.e.,

\[ \forall \varepsilon>0,\quad \left(B_d(x,\varepsilon)\setminus\{x\}\right)\cap E\neq\varnothing. \]

Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \((x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) be a sequence in \(X\). A point \(x\in X\) is called an accumulation point (or cluster point) of \((x_n)\) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist infinitely many \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) such that \(x_n\in B_d(x,\varepsilon)\), i.e., for every \(\varepsilon>0\),

\[ \left|\{n\in\mathbb{N}\colon x_n\in B_d(x,\varepsilon)\}\right|=\infty. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An accumulation point of a set is a location you can approach arbitrarily closely using other points from the set.

For a sequence, it is a value that the sequence visits infinitely often, no matter how tight a neighbourhood you pick.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • A limit point can be characterized as an adherent point that is not an isolated point (a point \(x\in E\) such that some ball \(B_d(x,\varepsilon)\) meets \(E\) only in \(x\)).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(E=\{1,\,1/2,\,1/3,\, \dots,\}\), the only accumulation point is \(0\). Each point \(1/n\) is isolated.
  • The sequence \(a_n=(-1)^n\) has accumulation points 1 and -1. It does not converge.

  • Consider the sequence \((a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) that is defined by \(a_n=\sin n\). We can show that any number \(A\in[-1,1]\) is an accumulation point of this sequence.

    Among the first \(50\) terms, four lie in the band \([0.4,0.6]\) (red); infinitely many terms fall in every band around \(0.5\), so \(0.5\) is an accumulation point.

docs.title: Adherent Point and Closure of a Set
Definition
docs.text: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(E\) be a subset of \(X\). A point \(x_0\) in \(X\) is termed an adherent point of \(E\) if, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), the ball \(B(x_0, \varepsilon)\) intersects \(E\) nonemptily. The set of all adherent points of \(E\) constitutes the closure of \(E\), denoted as \(\overline{E}\) or \(\operatorname{cl}E\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An adherent point of a set is one that you can get arbitrarily close to from inside the set.

The closure is the original set together with all its adherent points, meaning everything you can touch or approach.

An adherent point has every ball meeting \(E\): the points of the closed disc and the isolated point \(\boldsymbol p\). Switching the metric does not change the answer.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• We have \(\overline{E} = \operatorname{int}E \cup \partial E = E \cup \partial E = X \setminus \operatorname{ext}E.\)
  • A set is closed if and only if it contains all its adherent points.
  • The closure of a set \(E\) is the intersection of all closed sets which contain \(E\), or equivalently, the smallest closed set that contains \(E\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The closure of \((0,1)\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is \([0,1]\). The endpoints \(0\) and \(1\) are adherent points even though they are not in the open interval.
  • If \(E = \{1/n \colon n \in \mathbb{N}^+\}\) in \(\mathbb{R}\), the closure is \(E \cup \{0\}\). Zero is an adherent point approached by the sequence.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(n,\,k \in\mathbb{N}^+\). A function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to \mathbb{R}^k\) is an affine map (or affine transformation) if there are a \(k\times n\) real matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and a vector \(\boldsymbol{b}\in\mathbb{R}^k\) such that

\[ \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{A} \boldsymbol{x}+ \boldsymbol{b}\qquad\text{for all }\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n. \]

A real-valued affine map \(f\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to \mathbb{R}\) (\(k=1\)) is an affine function:

\[ \begin{aligned} &f(x_1,\,x_2,\,\dots,\,x_n)\\ &\quad=a_1x_1+a_2x_2+\cdots+a_nx_n+b. \end{aligned} \]

An affine map is a linear map exactly when \(\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{0}\), that is, when \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{0})=\boldsymbol{0}\).

Terminology

The Math III lecture notes, like much of economics and calculus, call an affine function a linear function and reserve linear transformation for the case \(\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{0}\). In linear algebra linear always means \(\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{0}\), so this wiki says affine for the general case.

As a Function between Spaces, the map assigns one output vector to each input vector. The Vector Space operations make the expression \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b}\) meaningful: first apply the matrix, then add the translation vector.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An affine map is a linear map followed by a shift: if one argument is increased by \(c\) units, the value changes by \(c\) times a fixed vector, wherever the starting point is.

The blue linear map \(f(x)=2x\) passes through the origin. The red affine map \(g(x)=f(x)+1\) is shifted upwards by \(1\), so \(g(0)=1\) rather than \(0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The graph \(\{(\boldsymbol{x},f(\boldsymbol{x}))\colon\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\}\) of an affine function on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is an affine hyperplane of \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\); it passes through the origin exactly when \(b=0\text{.}\)
  • The level sets \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})=c\}\) of a non-constant affine function are parallel affine hyperplanes of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
  • A composition of affine maps is affine.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x + 2y - 1\) is affine but not linear, since \(f(0,0)=-1\); \(x+2y\) is both.
  • \(g(x,y) = x + xy\) and \(h(x,y) = 2^x + \sin y\) are not affine.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider two functions \(f\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(g\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Let \(a\in[-\infty,+\infty]\).

  • We say that \(f(x)\) is big-\(O\) of \(g(x)\) as \(x\) tends to \(a\text{,}\) and write \(f(x)=O(g(x))\) as \(x\to a\text{,}\) if there is a constant \(M>0\) such that \(|f(x)|\le M\,|g(x)|\) for all \(x\) near \(a\text{:}\) for \(0<|x-a|<\delta\) (a punctured neighbourhood of \(a\)) when \(a\) is finite, for \(x>N\) when \(a=+\infty\text{,}\) and for \(x<-N\) when \(a=-\infty\text{,}\) for some \(\delta>0\) or \(N\text{.}\)
  • Assume that \(g(x)\neq0\) for all \(x\) near \(a\) in the same sense. We say that \(f(x)\) is little-\(o\) of \(g(x)\) as \(x\) tends to \(a\text{,}\) and write \(f(x)=o(g(x))\) as \(x\to a\text{,}\) if \(\displaystyle \lim\limits_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=0\text{.}\)

The constant \(M\) gives an Upper Bound on the relative size of \(f\) near \(a\). For little-\(o\), use a Limit at a Point when \(a\) is finite and a Limit at Infinity when \(a=\pm\infty\) to test whether \(f/g\) tends to zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: • Big-\(O\) means that near \(a\) the size of \(f\) is at most a constant multiple of the size of \(g\text{;}\) little-\(o\) means that \(f\) is negligible compared with \(g\) near \(a\text{.}\) When \(g\to0\text{,}\) this reads: \(f\) goes to zero at least as fast as \(g\) (big-\(O\)), or faster than \(g\) (little-\(o\)).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The little-\(o\) notation makes a stronger assertion than the big-\(O\) notation: every function that is little-\(o\) of \(g\) is also big-\(O\) of \(g\text{,}\) but not all functions that are big-\(O\) of \(g\) are little-\(o\) of \(g\text{.}\)
  • If \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) are asymptotically equivalent as \(x\) tends to \(a\text{,}\) i.e., \(f(x)\sim g(x)\) as \(x\to a\text{,}\) then we have \(f(x)=O(g(x))\) and \(g(x)=O(f(x))\text{,}\) as \(x\to a\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• As \(x\to 0\), \(x^2\) is both \(O(x)\) and \(o(x)\) since \(\displaystyle \lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{x^2}{x} = 0\).
  • As \(x\to 0\), \(\sin (x^2)\) is \(O(x^2)\) but not \(o(x^2)\) since \(\displaystyle \lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{\sin(x^2)}{x^2} = 1\).

  • In the following graph, we have \(g(x)=o(f(x))\) and \(g(x)=o(h(x))\) as \(x\to 0\):

    Near \(0\) the parabola \(g\) is much flatter than \(f\) and \(h\): \(g(x)/f(x)\to0\) and \(g(x)/h(x)\to0\) as \(x\to0\).

Zoom in towards \(0\): \(f=O(g)\) when some \(M\) keeps \(|f|\le M|g|\) near \(0\); \(f=o(g)\) when the ratio \(f/g\) (right) tends to \(0\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Each bounded sequence in the Euclidean space \((\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)\) has a convergent subsequence.

Equivalently, a subset \(E\) of the Euclidean space is sequentially compact if and only if it is both closed and bounded.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Even if a sequence wanders around without settling down, as long as it stays within a bounded region you can always pick out a subsequence that eventually homes in on some point.

In Euclidean space, closedness and boundedness guarantee enough crowding to force a convergent subsequence.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The limit of a convergent subsequence is an accumulation point of the original sequence.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), every Cauchy sequence is bounded, so by Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem it has a convergent subsequence. A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence must itself converge. This gives another proof that \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is complete.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The sequence \(x_n = (-1)^n\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is bounded between \(-1\) and \(1\). It does not converge, but it has two convergent subsequences: the even terms \(x_{2n}=1\) converge to \(1\), and the odd terms \(x_{2n-1}=-1\) converge to \(-1\).
  • The sequence \(x_n = 1/n\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is bounded in \([0,1]\). It already converges to \(0\), so every subsequence also converges to \(0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a metric space \((X,d)\text{,}\) and a subset \(E \subseteq X\text{,}\) a point \(x_0\) is a boundary point of \(E\) if it's neither an interior nor an exterior point of \(E\text{.}\) We denote the set of boundary points of \(E\) as \(\partial E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The boundary is the dividing line between inside and outside.

The boundary consists of points that are neither interior nor exterior: \(\partial E=\overline{E}\setminus\operatorname{int}(E)\).

On the unit circle, and at the isolated point \(\boldsymbol p\), every ball meets both \(E\) and its complement, however small \(\varepsilon\) is.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A boundary point \(x_0\) of \(E\) may or may not be in \(E\text{.}\)
  • For a boundary point \(x_0\) of \(E\text{,}\) any balls centred at \(x_0\) will contain points both inside and outside \(E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The boundary of \((0,1)\) is \(\{0,1\}\). Every neighbourhood around \(0\) contains points in \((0,1)\) and points not in \((0,1)\).
  • The boundary of \(\mathbb{Q}\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is all of \(\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Bounded Set in a Metric Space
Definition
docs.text: Given a metric space \((X,d_{X})\text{,}\) a set \(E\subseteq X\) is termed bounded if there exists \(M>0\) such that the ball \(B_{(X,d_{X})} (x,M)\) contains \(E\text{.}\) Here, \(x\) can be any point in \(X\) (usually chosen to be the origin or a particular point in \(E\)).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A bounded set is one that fits entirely inside some large enough ball.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A nonempty set is bounded if and only if \(\displaystyle \sup_{x,y\in E} d_{X}(x,y)\) is finite.
  • Any subset of a bounded set is bounded.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A unit sphere \(\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon x^2+y^2+z^2=1\}\) is bounded.
  • A parabola curve \(\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon y=x^2\}\) is unbounded.

docs.title: Cauchy Sequence in a Metric Space
Definition
docs.text: A sequence of points \((x_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) in a metric space \((X,d)\) is called a Cauchy sequence if, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists an integer \(N\geq 1\) such that the distance \(d(x_j,x_k)<\varepsilon\) for all \(j, k \geq N\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
It is the same idea as a Cauchy sequence of real numbers, but with the absolute value replaced by a general metric.

The terms get closer to each other, but a Cauchy sequence need not converge to a point of \(X\) unless the space is complete.

Raise \(N\) until all tail points lie within \(\varepsilon\) of each other, without using the limit at all.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • While all convergent sequences are Cauchy, not every Cauchy sequence converges because a sequence can cluster together (Cauchy property) around a limit that does not exist within the current space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Take the rational numbers \(\mathbb{Q}\) with the usual metric \(d(x,y)=|x-y|\). The sequence \(a_n=\left(1+\dfrac{1}{n}\right)^n\) consists of rational numbers and converges in \(\mathbb{R}\) to \(\mathrm{e}\), so it is Cauchy. Since \(\mathrm{e}\) is irrational, it does not converge to any point of \(\mathbb{Q}\): the space \((\mathbb{Q},d)\) is not complete.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a metric space \((X,d)\), a point \(x_0\) in \(X\), and \(r > 0\), the closed metric ball \(\overline{B}_{(X,d)}(x_0,r)\) in \(X\), centred at \(x_0\) with radius \(r\) in metric \(d\), is defined as the following set:

\[ \overline{B}_{(X,d)}(x_0,r) = \{x \in X \colon d(x, x_0) \leq r\}. \]

The ball is a subset of the ambient space \(X\): its members are selected by the distance condition, not by adding new points to \(X\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A closed metric ball is the set of all points whose distance from the centre is less than or equal to the radius.

The closed ball also contains its sphere \(\{d(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol x_0)=r\}\). Drag \(\boldsymbol x\) onto the boundary to see the difference.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The closed metric ball is a closed set.
  • In a normed vector space, in particular in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with any \(p\)-metric, the closed metric ball is the closure of the open metric ball with the same centre and radius. This can fail for a metric that is merely topologically equivalent to these, such as \(\min(|x-y|,1)\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) with radius \(1\).
  • In a general metric space, we do not have \(\overline{B}_{(X,d)}(x_0,\varepsilon)=\overline{B_{(X,d)}(x_0,\varepsilon)}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the usual distance, \(\overline{B}((0,0),1)\) is the closed disc of radius \(1\) centred at the origin. Points with \(x^2 + y^2 \leq 1\) are elements of this ball.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider a space \(X\) in which open sets are defined. A subset \(E\) of \(X\) is called compact if every open cover of \(E\) has a finite subcover.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: No matter how you try to cover a compact set with open patches, you only ever need finitely many of them to do the job.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The set \(E\subseteq \mathbb{R} ^n\) is compact if and only if it is both closed and bounded.
  • Let \(E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\text{,}\) \(\boldsymbol{f} \colon E \to \mathbb{R}^k\) be a function, and \(X \subseteq E\) be a compact set. If \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is continuous on \(X\text{,}\) then the image \(\boldsymbol{f}(X)\) is also compact. This result is known as continuity preserves compactness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The closed unit ball \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\in \mathbb{R}^n\colon \|\boldsymbol{x}\|\leq 1\}\) is compact.
  • Any finite set in any metric space is compact. You can always pick one open set for each point; finitely many suffice.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A metric space \((X, d)\) is termed complete if each Cauchy sequence contained within converges in \((X, d)\). When a complete normed vector space is encountered, it's also referred to as a Banach space.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A complete metric space is one with no “missing points”: every sequence that looks like it should converge actually lands inside the space.

The displayed Cauchy sequence converges to \(\sqrt{2}\) in \(\mathbb{R}\). It has no limit in \(\mathbb{Q}\) because \(\sqrt{2}\notin\mathbb{Q}\), illustrating the incompleteness of the rational numbers.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • In any metric space every convergent sequence is a Cauchy sequence; in a complete metric space the converse also holds, so a sequence converges if and only if it is Cauchy.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a complete normed vector space.
  • The open interval \((0,1)\) with the usual metric \(d(x,y)=|x-y|\) is not complete: \((1/n)_{n\ge2}\) is a Cauchy sequence whose limit \(0\) does not belong to \((0,1)\text{.}\)
  • The \(n\)-dimensional real coordinate space equipped with the discrete metric is complete: a Cauchy sequence is eventually constant, because \(d(\boldsymbol{x}_j,\boldsymbol{x}_k)<\tfrac{1}{2}\) forces \(\boldsymbol{x}_j=\boldsymbol{x}_k\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider a space \(X\) in which openness is defined. A subset \(E \subseteq X\) is called disconnected if it has an open cover \(\{V,W\}\) such that \(E \subseteq V\cup W\) and the intersections \(E\cap V\) and \(E\cap W\) are disjoint and nonempty. Thus \(E\cap V\cap W=\varnothing\); the ambient sets \(V\) and \(W\) may overlap outside \(E\). If \(E\) is nonempty and not disconnected, it is connected.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A set is disconnected if you can split it into two nonempty open pieces that do not touch each other.

A set is connected if it comes in one piece without such a split.

On the left, the dark set \(E\) meets both disjoint open sets \(U\) and \(V\) and is contained in their union, so it is disconnected. The right-hand set cannot be split into two nonempty disjoint intersections with an open cover, so it is connected.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The only type of connected subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\) is interval.
  • Consider metric spaces \((X,d_{X})\) and \((Y,d_{Y})\text{.}\) Let \(f\colon X\to Y\) be a continuous function, and let \(E\) be a connected subset of \(X\text{.}\) Then \(f(E)\) is a connected subset of \(Y\text{.}\) This result is known as continuity preserves connectedness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any singleton set is connected.
  • \(\mathbb{Q}\) is a disconnected subset of \(\mathbb{R}\).
  • In a discrete metric space, any set with at least two points is disconnected because each singleton is open.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider two metric spaces \((X,d_{X})\) and \((Y,d_{Y})\text{,}\) and a function \(f\colon E\to Y\) where \(E\subseteq X\text{.}\) Let \(x_0\in X\text{.}\) Assume there exists an \(r>0\) such that \(B_{(X,d_{X})}(x_0,r)\subseteq E\text{.}\) We say that \(f\) is continuous at \(x=x_0\) if, for any \(\varepsilon > 0\text{,}\) there exists a \(0<\delta \leq r\) such that whenever \(d_{X}(x,x_0)<\delta\text{,}\) we have \(d_{Y}(f(x),f(x_0))<\varepsilon\text{.}\)

We say that \(f\) is continuous on \(E\) (or simply continuous) if it is continuous at every point of \(E\text{.}\) At a point \(x_0\in E\) that has no such ball inside \(E\) (a boundary point of \(E\)), the same condition is required only for \(x\in E\text{.}\)

The condition says that the intersection of the domain with a sufficiently small open metric ball around \(x_0\) is mapped into the \(\varepsilon\)-ball around \(f(x_0)\). With the usual real distance \(|x-y|\), this is the familiar definition of continuity.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A function is continuous at a point if you can make the outputs as close as you want to the value at that point by taking inputs sufficiently close to it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(f(x)\) tends to two different values as \(x\) approaches \(x_0\) in two different ways (for example along two different lines, or along two sequences converging to \(x_0\)), then the limit of the function at that point does not exist, so the function is not continuous there. More generally, if for some sequence \(x_k\to x_0\) the values \(f(x_k)\) do not tend to \(f(x_0)\text{,}\) then \(f\) is not continuous at \(x_0\text{.}\)
  • A vector-valued function into \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with its usual Euclidean metric is continuous if and only if each real component function is continuous.
  • Most properties of real-valued functions of one real variable are preserved under continuity. In particular, continuity is preserved under addition, subtraction, multiplication, division (where the denominator is nonzero), as well as taking the maximum, minimum, and composition of functions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). At \((0,0)\), if you want \(f\) within \(\varepsilon\) of \(0\), choose \(\delta=\sqrt{\varepsilon}\). Then \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}<\delta\) gives \(x^2+y^2<\varepsilon\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given a metric space \((X, d)\), a sequence \((x_{i})_{i=1}^\infty\) and a point \(x\) in \(X\), the sequence is said to converge to \(x\) under metric \(d\) if \(\displaystyle \lim_{i\to\infty}d(x_i, x) = 0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This is just like convergent sequences of real numbers, but with a general notion of distance.

For each \(\varepsilon\) there is an \(N\) after which every \(\boldsymbol x_i\) lies in the \(\varepsilon\)-ball around the limit. Change the metric: \(N\) changes, the limit does not.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • A convergent sequence in a metric space must be a Cauchy sequence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The sequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_{i})_{i=1}^\infty\) where \(\boldsymbol{x}_i = (1/i, 1/i)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) converges to \((0,0)\) under the Euclidean metric \(d_2\).
  • The sequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_{i})_{i=1}^\infty\) where \(\boldsymbol{x}_i = (1/i, 1/i)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) also converges to \((0,0)\) under the taxicab metric \(d_1\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Consider a power series \(\displaystyle f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) with a radius of convergence \(R > 0\text{.}\) For any chosen \(r\) such that \(0 < r < R\):

  • The series converges pointwise on the open interval \((a-R, a+R)\text{.}\)
  • It converges uniformly on the closed interval \([a-r, a+r]\text{.}\)
  • The limit function \(f\) is differentiable on \((a-R, a+R)\text{.}\)
  • The derivative series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty nc_n (x-a)^{n-1}\) converges uniformly to the derivative, \(f'\text{,}\) on \([a-r, a+r]\text{.}\)

The smaller closed Interval \([a-r,a+r]\) stays strictly inside the convergence interval, which is why one uniform tail estimate works there; the endpoints \(a\pm R\) need separate tests.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The derivative of a power series within its radius of convergence can be found by differentiating each term individually, and the resulting series converges to the correct derivative.

For every \(0<r<R\), the power series and its termwise derivative converge uniformly on \([a-r,a+r]\): \(\displaystyle \sum_n c_n(x-a)^n\rightrightarrows f(x)\) and \(\displaystyle \sum_{n\ge1}nc_n(x-a)^{n-1}\rightrightarrows f'(x)\).

On every closed interval \([a-r,a+r]\) with \(r<R\) the partial sums approach the sum uniformly; near the ends of the interval they need many more terms.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Term-by-term differentiation is valid inside the radius of convergence.
  • Locally (on \([a-r,a+r]\)), a power series behaves like a polynomial: it is smooth and uniformly controlled.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n(-2)^n (x-3)^n\) with \(R = 1/2\) centred at \(a = 3\text{,}\) converges pointwise on \((5/2, 7/2)\) and uniformly on any closed interval within it.
  • The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{n^2} (x+2)^n\) with \(R = 0\) centred at \(a = -2\text{,}\) converges solely at its centre \(x = -2\text{.}\)
  • The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{-n^2} (x+2)^n\) with \(R = +\infty\) centred at \(a = -2\text{,}\) converges pointwise over the entire real line \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Uniform convergence for this series over \(\mathbb{R}\) needs further analysis.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider a (topological) space \(X\text{.}\) Let \(E\) be a subset of \(X\text{,}\) and let \(\mathcal{C}=\{G_i\colon i\in I\}\) be a collection of subsets \(G_i\) of \(X\) indexed by an arbitrary index set \(I\text{.}\) The collection \(\mathcal{C}\) is called a cover of \(E\) if \(\displaystyle E \subseteq \bigcup_{i\in I} G_i\text{.}\)

  • An open cover is a cover where each "patch" \(G_i\) is open.
  • A finite cover consists of a collection \(\{G_i\colon i\in I\}\) where \(I\) is finite. A cover is called a countable cover when \(I\) is a countable set, e.g., \(\mathbb{N}\text{.}\)
  • A subcover is a cover that is a subset of another cover.

The Union of Sets collects all points lying in at least one patch \(G_i\); the inclusion requires every point of \(E\) to occur in that union.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A cover is just a collection of sets that together contain the set you care about.

Think of it as laying patches over the set so every point is under at least one patch.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Any set \(E\subseteq X\) is covered by the space \(X\). So covers always exist.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The set \((0,1)\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) can be covered by the collection of open sets \(\{(1/n,1-1/n)\colon n\geq 3\}\). This is an infinite open cover.
  • The set \(\{1,2,3\}\) is covered by the three singletons \(\{1\}\), \(\{2\}\), \(\{3\}\). That is a finite cover.
  • The set of rational numbers \(\mathbb{Q}\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) can be covered by open intervals centred at each rational with radius \(1\). That's a countable cover because \(\mathbb{Q}\) is countable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider a subset \(E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) and a function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon E\to\mathbb{R}^k\). Let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) be an interior point of \(E\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}\) be a unit vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (note: some authors only require \(\boldsymbol{v}\) to be a nonzero vector). If the limit

\[ \lim_{t\to 0^+}\frac{\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0+t\boldsymbol{v})-\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)}{t} \]

exists, then \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is said to be differentiable in the direction \(\boldsymbol{v}\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\). This limit is termed the directional derivative and is denoted by \(\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}} \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\).

Here unit length is measured by the Euclidean Norm, \(\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_2=1\). Equivalently, the Inner Product satisfies \(\langle\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{v}\rangle=1\), so \(t\) measures distance travelled along the chosen direction.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The directional derivative measures the instantaneous rate of change of a function as you move from a point in a specific direction.

It generalizes the one-sided derivative to functions of several variables by looking at how the function changes along a straight line in that direction.

For a differentiable \(f\) and a unit direction \( oldsymbol{v}\), the directional derivative is \(D_{ oldsymbol{v}}f( oldsymbol{x}_0)= oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}_0)\cdot oldsymbol{v}\). For the nonzero gradient drawn, it is largest when the direction follows the gradient and zero in a tangent direction to the level curve.

Turn the direction \( oldsymbol v\) with \( heta\): the slope of \(f\) along \( oldsymbol v\) is \( oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol x_0)\cdot oldsymbol v\), largest along the gradient and zero along the level curve.

Turn \( oldsymbol v\): the slice of the graph through \( oldsymbol x_0\) in direction \( oldsymbol v\) has slope \(\mathrm{D}_{ oldsymbol v}f( oldsymbol x_0)= oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol x_0)\cdot oldsymbol v\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is totally differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\text{,}\) then the directional derivative \(\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) exists for every direction \(\boldsymbol{v}\) and equals the total derivative at \(\boldsymbol{v}\text{,}\) \(\mathrm{D} \boldsymbol{f}_{\boldsymbol{x}_0}(\boldsymbol{v})\text{.}\)
  • A function is totally differentiable at a point implies that this function is directionally differentiable in any direction. The converse is incorrect.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • For the function \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)=(x^2,y^2)\), consider \(\boldsymbol{x}_0=(1,2)\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}=(3/5,4/5)\). We have \(\displaystyle \mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) =\left(\frac{6}{5},\frac{16}{5}\right)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider the space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with its elements \( oldsymbol{x}\) and \( oldsymbol{y}\). We define a discrete metric \(d_{\mathrm{disc}}\) as:

\[ d_{\mathrm{disc}}( oldsymbol{x}, oldsymbol{y}) = egin{cases} \displaystyle \;1, & ext{if } oldsymbol{x} eq oldsymbol{y}, \[2pt] \displaystyle \;0, & ext{if } oldsymbol{x} = oldsymbol{y}. \end{cases} \]

Although the example uses the Real Coordinate Space \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the same formula works on any set. It satisfies the Metric and Metric Space axioms: in particular, if \(x e z\), at least one of \(x e y\) and \(y e z\) holds, giving the triangle inequality.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The discrete metric is the simplest possible distance: distinct points are always exactly 1 unit apart, and a point is 0 units from itself.

It treats every pair of different points as equally far.

The discrete distance is \(0\) between a point and itself, and \(1\) between distinct points. A ball of radius less than \(1\), such as the radius \(1/2\) drawn around \(\boldsymbol{x}\), contains only its centre, so every point is isolated and every subset is open.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The discrete metric is not strongly equivalent to any of the \(p\)-metrics.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(d_{\mathrm{disc}}(2,5)=1\) since \(2\neq 5\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \((X,d_{X})\) and \((Y,d_{Y})\) be metric spaces, and let \(f\colon X\to Y\) be a function. The following statements are equivalent:

  • \(f\) is continuous.
  • For every \(x_0\in X\) and every convergent sequence \((x_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) in \((X,d_{X})\) converging to \(x_0\), its image under \(f\), \(f(x_i)_{i=1}^\infty\), also converges to \(f(x_0)\).
  • The preimage of any open set in \((Y,d_{Y})\) is open in \((X,d_{X})\).
  • The preimage of any closed set in \((Y,d_{Y})\) is closed in \((X,d_{X})\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A function is continuous if and only if the preimage operation preserves openness and closedness.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • At a fixed point \(x_0\text{,}\) the sequential condition is equivalent to continuity at \(x_0\text{.}\) In metric spaces it is often the easiest to work with when proving discontinuity. To show \(f\) is not continuous at a point, find one sequence converging to that point whose image does not converge to the function value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A continuous function \(f\) might map an open set \(V\) to a non-open set \(f(V)\). For example, let \(V=(0,1)\) with \(f(x)=1\) for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). Then \(f(V)=\{1\}\) isn't open under usual metrics.
  • A continuous function \(f\) might map a closed set \(F\) to a non-closed set \(f(F)\). For example, let \(F=[1,+\infty)\) and \(f(x)=1/x\) for all \(x>0\). Then \(f(F)=(0,1]\) isn't closed under usual metrics.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Two norms \(\|\cdot\|_p\) and \(\|\cdot\|_q\) on a vector space \(V\) (the subscripts are just labels for two arbitrary norms, not necessarily \(p\)-norms) are termed equivalent if there exist constants \(a, b > 0\) such that for every \(\boldsymbol{v} \in V\), we have:

\[ a \|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p \leq \|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q \leq b \|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p. \]

For example, the Euclidean Norm and maximum norm on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \(\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_\infty\le\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_2\le\sqrt n\,\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_\infty\). These constants show precisely how their lengths are comparable.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Equivalent norms are different ways of measuring length that are comparable up to fixed scaling factors.

On \(\mathbb{R}^2\), the illustrated norms satisfy \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty\le\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_2\le\sqrt{2}\,\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty\), so they are equivalent.

Pick \(p\) and \(q\): the \(q\)-circles of radius \(a\) and \(b\) squeeze the \(p\)-unit circle between them, so \(a\|\boldsymbol v\|_p\le\|\boldsymbol v\|_q\le b\|\boldsymbol v\|_p\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Any two norms \(\|\cdot\|_p\) and \(\|\cdot\|_q\) on a finite-dimensional vector space \(V\) are equivalent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The Euclidean norm and the taxicab norm are equivalent.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a metric space \((X,d)\text{,}\) and a subset \(E \subseteq X\text{,}\) a point \(x_0\) is an exterior point of \(E\) if \(B(x_0,\varepsilon) \cap E = \varnothing\) for some \(\varepsilon > 0\text{.}\) We denote the set of exterior points of \(E\) as \(\operatorname{ext} E\text{.}\)

The Open Metric Ball is a neighbourhood that avoids \(E\); the empty Intersection of Sets expresses that no point lies in both the neighbourhood and \(E\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An exterior point is one that has a ball around it completely missing the set.

The ambient space is the disjoint union \(X=\operatorname{int}(E)\cup\partial E\cup\operatorname{ext}(E)\). The exterior is \(\operatorname{ext}(E)=\operatorname{int}(X\setminus E)\).

Outside the closed disc (and away from \(\boldsymbol p\)) a small enough ball misses \(E\) entirely.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • An exterior point \(x_0\) of \(E\) can never be in \(E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(E = (0,1) \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), the point \(x = 2\) is an exterior point. A small ball around \(2\), say \((1.9,2.1)\), avoids \((0,1)\).
  • For \(E = \{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x^2 + y^2 \leq 1\}\), the point \((3,0)\) is an exterior point. A small disc around it stays entirely outside the unit disc.

docs.title: Extreme Value Theorem on Compact Sets
Theorem
docs.text: Let \(E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\text{,}\) \(f \colon E \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function, and \(X \subseteq E\) be a nonempty compact set. If \(f\) is continuous on \(X\text{,}\) then \(f\) attains both its maximum and minimum on \(X\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A continuous function on a compact set cannot sneak off to infinity or skip its highest and lowest values. It must actually hit both a maximum and a minimum somewhere inside that set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If the domain is not compact, the conclusion may fail. For example, \(f(x)=1/x\) on \((0,1)\) is continuous but has no maximum (it blows up as \(x\to0^+\)) and no minimum (its values decrease towards \(1\) as \(x\to1^-\text{,}\) but \(1\) is never attained, since \(1\notin(0,1)\)).
  • This theorem is used to prove existence of solutions in optimization problems.
  • Together with the intermediate value theorem, it gives a complete picture of the range of a continuous real-valued function on a connected compact set: the range is the closed interval \([m,M]\) between the minimum \(m\) and the maximum \(M\). (In \(\mathbb{R}\), a connected compact set is itself a closed bounded interval.)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The function \(f(x,y)=x+y\) on the closed unit disc \(\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x^2+y^2\leq 1\}\) attains maximum \(\sqrt{2}\)​ at \((1/\sqrt{2},1/\sqrt{2})\) and minimum \(-\sqrt{2}\)​ at \((-1/\sqrt{2},-1/\sqrt{2})\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider a function \(f\colon X \to Y\) where \(X\) is set in an \(n\)-dimensional space (e.g., \(\mathbb{R}^n\)) and \(Y\) in an \(k\)-dimensional space (e.g., \(\mathbb{R}^k\)). We have the following terminologies:

  • it is called a univariate function (also known as single variable function, function of one variable) if \(n=1\);
  • it is called a bivariate function (also known as function of two variables) if \(n=2\);
  • it is called a multivariable function (also known as multivariate function, function of several variables) if \(n\geq 2\);
  • it is called a real-valued function if its codomain is a subset of \(\mathbb{R}\);
  • it is called a vector-valued function if \(k\geq 2\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A function is classified by how many numbers go in and how many come out.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • A multivalued function (a rule that may assign several outputs to one input, such as \(x\mapsto\pm\sqrt{x}\)) is not a function in the sense used here, so it is neither a multivariable function nor a vector-valued function.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2\) from \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) is a bivariate real valued function.
  • \(\boldsymbol{F}(x,y) = (x+y, x-y, xy)\) from \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is a multivariable vector valued function.

Let \(E\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(f \colon E \to \mathbb{R}\) be a real-valued function. If \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is an interior point of \(E\) and all first partial derivatives exist there, the gradient \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} f (\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) of \(f\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is given as the \(n\)-dimensional column vector:

\[ \begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{\nabla} f (\boldsymbol{x}_0) &= \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}(\boldsymbol{x}_0),\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}(\boldsymbol{x}_0),\right.\\ &\qquad\left.\ldots,\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\right)^{\top}. \end{aligned} \]

docs.text:
When \( oldsymbol{ abla} f ( oldsymbol{x}_0)= oldsymbol{0}\), we say that \( oldsymbol{x}_0\) is a stationary point of \(f\) (possibly a local extremum point).

When \(f\) is totally differentiable at \( oldsymbol{x}_0\) and \( oldsymbol{ abla} f ( oldsymbol{x}_0) eq oldsymbol{0}\), the gradient gives two things: the direction \( oldsymbol{u}= oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}_0)/\| oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}_0)\|\) of steepest ascent, and the maximal rate of increase \(\| oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}_0)\|=\max_{\| oldsymbol{u}\|=1}\mathrm{D}_{ oldsymbol{u}}f( oldsymbol{x}_0) ext{,}\) by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.

The gradient arrows point uphill, perpendicular to the level curves, and are longer where the curves are close together. Drag \( oldsymbol x_0\) to a stationary point.

The red path climbs the surface along \( oldsymbol{ abla} f\); on the floor it crosses the level curves at right angles.

\[ \boldsymbol{\nabla} f (\boldsymbol{x}_0) \cdot \boldsymbol{v} = \mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0). \]

docs.text:
• Let \(f(x,y) = \mathrm{e}^{x+y}\). Then \(\displaystyle \boldsymbol{\nabla} f(x,y) = \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{e}^{x+y} \\ \mathrm{e}^{x+y} \end{pmatrix}\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(E\) be a subset of the Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\text{.}\) The set \(E\) is compact if and only if it is both closed and bounded.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A set in Euclidean space is compact exactly when it contains all its limit points and stays within some finite distance from the origin. Closedness keeps the boundary in, boundedness keeps it from running off to infinity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The continuous image of a compact set is compact. This yields the extreme value theorem.
  • Any closed subset of a compact set in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is itself compact.
  • Finite unions of compact sets are compact. The intersection of any nonempty family of compact subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact; the intersection itself may be empty.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A closed metric ball \(\overline{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r) = \{\boldsymbol{x} \in X \colon d_2(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}_0) \leq r\}\) in the Euclidean space is closed and bounded, so compact.
  • Any finite set \(\{\boldsymbol{x}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{x}_k\}\subset \mathbb{R}^n\) is closed (finite sets are closed) and bounded, so compact.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(a < b\) be real numbers, and consider a function \(f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) that is continuous on \([a, b]\text{.}\) Then, \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \([a, b]\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• A continuous function on a closed interval can’t "escape" or behave wildly near the edges because the interval includes its endpoints.
  • This prevents sudden jumps or unbounded growth, ensuring that the function's small changes near one point apply uniformly across the whole interval.

Because \(f\) is continuous on the compact interval \([a,b]\), it is uniformly continuous. For any prescribed vertical tolerance, one horizontal tolerance works at every point, as illustrated by windows of the same width and height.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• This theorem has a generalized version if \([a,b]\) is replaced by a compact set.
  • This theorem does not imply that uniform continuity holds only on closed intervals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=\dfrac{x^2+\sin x}{\mathrm{e}^x}\) is uniformly continuous on any closed interval since we know it is continuous everywhere.
  • The function \(g(x)=x\) is uniformly continuous on \((0,1)\) though \((0,1)\) is not a closed interval. This does not contradict with the theorem since the "closed interval" condition is sufficient but not necessary.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(n,\,k \in\mathbb{N}^+\) and \(m\in \mathbb{Z}\). A function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to \mathbb{R}^k\) is homogeneous of degree \(m\) if

\[ \boldsymbol{f}(cx_1,\dots,cx_n)=c^m \boldsymbol{f}(x_1,\dots,x_n) \]

for every \((x_1,\,x_2,\,\dots,\,x_n)\) and \(c\neq 0\). In economics one often uses the variant with domain \(\mathbb{R}^n_{++}=(0,+\infty)^n\), only \(c>0\), and any real degree \(m\); for example, \(f(x,y)=x^{1/2}y^{1/2}\) is homogeneous of degree \(1\) in this sense.

The definition treats \(\boldsymbol{f}\) as a Function between Spaces: scaling an input vector changes its assigned output by the prescribed scalar factor.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
If each of the homogeneous function's arguments is multiplied by the same scalar, then the function's value is multiplied by some power of this scalar.

Scale the point by \(c\): the value is multiplied by \(c^m\), so the level curves are scaled copies of each other along rays from the origin.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(f\) is homogeneous of degree \(m\) and differentiable, then each partial derivative is homogeneous of degree \(m-1\).
  • The sum of two functions that are homogeneous of the same degree \(m\) is homogeneous of degree \(m\text{;}\) the product of functions homogeneous of degrees \(m\) and \(\ell\) is homogeneous of degree \(m+\ell\text{,}\) and the composition of functions homogeneous of degrees \(m\) and \(p\) is homogeneous of degree \(mp\text{.}\) A sum of homogeneous functions of different degrees, such as \(xy+x\text{,}\) is not homogeneous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 + xy\) is homogeneous as \(f(cx, cy) = c^2 f(x,y)\).
  • \(g(x,y) = xy + x\) is said to be inhomogeneous.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A polynomial on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is called homogeneous of degree \(k\) if all of its nonzero terms have degree \(k\). Such a polynomial is also called a (algebraic) form.

Every degree-\(k\) monomial acquires the same factor \(c^k\) when its variables are scaled by \(c\). Their sum therefore satisfies the defining identity of a Homogeneous Function.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A homogeneous polynomial is one where every term has the same total degree.

Scaling all variables by a factor scales the polynomial by that factor raised to that degree.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sum of two homogeneous polynomials of the same degree is homogeneous of that degree.
  • The product of a homogeneous polynomial of degree \(k\) and one of degree \(\ell\) is homogeneous of degree \(k+\ell\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(P(x) = 2x^5\) is a homogeneous polynomial of degree 5.
  • \(P(x,y) = x^2 + xy + y^2\) is homogeneous of degree 2. Each term has total degree 2.

docs.title: Image and Preimage of a Set
Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be sets (in this course usually subsets of metric spaces), and let \(f\colon X\to Y\) be a function. Let \(C\) be a subset of the domain \(X\), the image of \(C\) under \(f\) is defined as:

\[ \begin{aligned} &f(C)=\{y\in Y\colon \text{there exists some }\\ &\qquad x\in C \text{ such that } y=f(x)\}. \end{aligned} \]

Let \(V\) be a subset of the codomain \(Y\), the preimage of \(V\) under \(f\) includes all points in the domain that give results in \(V\):

\[ f^{-1}(V)=\{x\in X\colon f(x)\in V\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Image is the set of all outputs you actually get from the function when you put in points from a specific set.

Preimage is the set of all inputs that the function sends into a chosen target set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(V\) only needs to be a part of the codomain of \(f\). This means there might be some \(y\) in \(V\) that doesn't match any \(x\) in the domain \(X\).
  • We have \(C \subseteq f^{-1}(f(C))\) and \(f(f^{-1}(V)) \subseteq V\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let \(f\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(f(x,y)=x+y\). Image of the unit square \([0,1]\times[0,1]\) under \(f\) is \([0,2]\). Preimage of \(\{0\}\) under \(f\) is the line \(y=-x\).
  • Let \(f\colon \mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(f(x,y)=x\). Image of the disc \(\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x^2+y^2 \leq 1\}\) under \(f\) is \([-1,1]\). Preimage of \([2,3]\) under \(f\) is the vertical strip \([2,3]\times\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider a sequence of functions \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) from \(X\) to \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) If the sequence of partial sums \(\displaystyle S_N(x) = \sum_{n=1}^N f_n(x)\) converges to \(f\colon X \to \mathbb{R}\) pointwise or uniformly on \(X\) as \(N \to \infty\text{,}\) then we say the infinite series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n\) converges pointwise/uniformly to \(f\) on \(X\text{,}\) denoted as \(\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The infinite sum of functions is defined by its partial sums, and if these partial sums converge to a function, we say the series itself converges to that function.

Raise \(N\): the partial sums \(\displaystyle S_N(x)=\sum_{n=1}^N f_n(x)\) settle on the limit function (dashed).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(f_n\)'s are (continuously) differentiable, \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n \rightarrow f\text{,}\) and \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f'_n\rightrightarrows g\) on \((a,b)\text{,}\) then \(f\) is (continuously) differentiable on \((a, b)\) with \(f' = g\text{,}\) i.e., for every \(x_0\in(a,b)\),
\[ \sum_{n=1}^\infty f'_n(x_0)=\left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n\right)'(x_0). \]
  • On a finite closed interval \([a,b]\) with \(a<b\), if every \(f_n\) is Riemann integrable and \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n\) converges uniformly, then its sum is Riemann integrable and
\[ \int_a^b \left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\right) \, \mathrm{d}x = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \int_a^b f_n(x) \, \mathrm{d}x. \]

The finite interval matters: the integral of a uniform error is at most \((b-a)\) times that error. Uniform convergence alone does not provide this bound for an improper integral on an unbounded interval.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The series \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n/n!\) converges uniformly (by the Weierstrass \(M\)-test) on every fixed interval \([-R,R]\), where \(R>0\): \(|x^n/n!|\le R^n/n!\), and \(\displaystyle \sum_n R^n/n!=\mathrm{e}^R\). It converges pointwise on \(\mathbb{R}\), but not uniformly there; for each finite partial sum, the difference from \(\mathrm{e}^x\) is unbounded as \(x\to+\infty\).
  • The geometric series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n\) converges uniformly on \([-r,r]\) for every fixed \(0<r<1\), because \(|x^n|\le r^n\) and \(\displaystyle \sum_n r^n<\infty\). On \((-1,1)\) it converges pointwise to \(1/(1-x)\), but not uniformly: the remainder \(x^{N+1}/(1-x)\) is unbounded as \(x\to1^-\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a metric space \((X,d)\text{,}\) and a subset \(E \subseteq X\text{,}\) a point \(x_0\) is an interior point of \(E\) if there exists some \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that \(B(x_0,\varepsilon) \subseteq E\text{.}\) We denote the set of interior points of \(E\) as \(\operatorname{int} E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An interior point is one that has a little ball around it completely contained in the set.

The green ball lies entirely inside \(E\), so its centre \(x_0\) is an interior point. Every ball around the red edge point leaves \(E\), so that point is not interior. The interior is the largest open subset of \(E\).

\(E\) is the open unit disc together with one extra point \(p\). Drag \(x_0\) and shrink \(\varepsilon\): an interior point has some ball inside \(E\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An interior point \(x_0\) of \(E\) is always in \(E\) since balls centred at \(x_0\) include \(x_0\text{.}\)
  • The interior of \(E\) is the largest open subset of \(E\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(E = (0,1) \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), every point in \((0,1)\) is interior. Pick a small enough interval around any point and it stays inside \((0,1)\).
  • For \(E = \{1,2,3\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), no point is interior. Any ball around \(1\) contains numbers other than \(1,2,3\).

docs.title: Intermediate Value Theorem on Connected Sets
Theorem
docs.text: Let \(f\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) be a continuous real-valued function. Let \(E\) be any connected subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\text{,}\) and let \(\boldsymbol{a}\) and \(\boldsymbol{b}\) be any two points in \(E\text{.}\) If \(y\) is a real number between \(f(\boldsymbol{a})\) and \(f(\boldsymbol{b})\text{,}\) then there exists a \(\boldsymbol{c} \in E\) such that \(f(\boldsymbol{c}) = y\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A continuous function on a connected set cannot skip values: if it takes two different numbers, it must also take every number in between.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Continuous image of a connected set is connected.
  • If \(E\) is path‑connected, the theorem can be proved by composing \(f\) with a path and applying the one‑dimensional intermediate value theorem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let \(E\) be the closed unit disk in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\)​. The image is \([0,1]\) which is also a connected set.
  • Let \(E\) be the unit sphere in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) and \(f(x,y,z)=z\) (height). The image is \([-1,1]\).

docs.text:
Suppose \(E\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is an interior point of \(E\). For a function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon E\to\mathbb{R}^k\) that each of its partial derivatives exists at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\), the following \(k\times n\) matrix

\[ \begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{\mathrm{J}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)&=\begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_1}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) & \cdots & \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_n}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\\[8pt] \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\[4pt] \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial x_1}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) & \cdots & \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial x_n}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) \end{pmatrix}\\[10pt] &=\begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\nabla} f_1 (\boldsymbol{x}_0)^{\top}\\ \vdots\\ \boldsymbol{\nabla} f_k (\boldsymbol{x}_0)^{\top} \end{pmatrix}\\[10pt] &=\left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_1}(\boldsymbol{x}_0),\,\cdots,\,\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_n}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\right) \end{aligned} \]

is called the derivative matrix or the Jacobian matrix.

Each row is the Gradient of one scalar component \(f_i\). When the function is totally differentiable, multiplying this matrix by an increment gives the Linear Map that approximates the output change; the existence of partial derivatives alone does not guarantee that approximation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The Jacobian matrix is a matrix that stacks all the partial derivatives of a vector-valued function, showing how each output changes with each input.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The total derivative of a differentiable function is represented by the Jacobian matrix: the Jacobian is the matrix of this linear map with respect to the standard bases.
  • The existence of the Jacobian matrix does not necessarily imply the total differentiability of the function.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y) = (x^2, xy)\). Then \(\dfrac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x} = (2x, y)\), \(\dfrac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial y} = (0, x)\), so
\[ \boldsymbol{\mathrm{J}}\boldsymbol{f}(x,y) = \begin{pmatrix} 2x & 0 \\ y & x \end{pmatrix}. \]

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon X \to \mathbb{R}\) be a real-valued function defined on a set \(X\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\). A level set is defined as the preimage of a singleton set \(\{k\}\), i.e.,

\[ \begin{aligned} L_k(f)&=f^{-1}(\{k\})\\ &=\{(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\in X\colon\\ &\qquad f(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)=k\}. \end{aligned} \]

When the number of independent variables is two, a level set is called a level curve, also known as contour line.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A level curve is the set of all real-valued solutions of an equation in two variables \(x_1\) and \(x_2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Different level sets for distinct values are disjoint, and the union over all possible values covers the entire domain where the function is defined.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let \(f\colon \mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\). Level sets are circles centred at the origin for \(k>0\), a single point \((0,0)\) for \(k=0\), and empty for \(k<0\).

    The level curves \(x^2+y^2=k\) are circles of radius \(\sqrt k\) for \(k>0\). They appear in red on the graph of \(f\) and in blue in the \(xy\)-plane.

Move \(k\) to highlight the level curve \(L_k(f)\). Drag \(\boldsymbol x_0\) to read off \(f\); nearby level curves crowd together where \(f\) changes fast.

Move \(k\): the plane \(z=k\) cuts the graph along the level curve \(L_k(f)\), drawn again on the floor.

  • Let \(f\colon \mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(f(x,y)=x+y\). Level sets are straight lines of slope \(-1\): \(x+y=k\). All level sets are parallel lines.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n=0}^{\infty}\) be a sequence. For each \(N\in\mathbb{N}\text{,}\) consider the supremum and infimum of the terms from \(a_N\) onward: \(\displaystyle s_N = \sup_{n\geq N} a_n\) and \(\displaystyle i_N = \inf_{n\geq N} a_n\text{.}\) The limit superior and limit inferior of \((a_n)_{n=0}^{\infty}\) are defined as:

\[ \begin{aligned} \limsup_{n\to \infty}a_n &:= \lim_{N\to\infty} s_N = \inf_{N\geq 0} s_N\\ &=\inf_{N\geq 0}\sup_{n\geq N} a_n, \\ \liminf_{n\to \infty}a_n &:= \lim_{N\to\infty} i_N = \sup_{N\geq 0} i_N\\ &=\sup_{N\geq 0}\inf_{n\geq N} a_n. \end{aligned} \]

Apply the definition of a Limit of a Sequence to the tail suprema \(s_N\) and infima \(i_N\). Their monotonicity ensures extended-real limits; if the original sequence has an ordinary limit, both tail limits equal it.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The limit superior and limit inferior describe the largest and smallest "long-run" accumulation points of a sequence, essentially capturing its eventual upper and lower bounds.

Move \(N\): \(s_N=\sup_{n\ge N}a_n\) can only decrease and \(i_N=\inf_{n\ge N}a_n\) can only increase. Their limits are \(\limsup a_n\) and \(\liminf a_n\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The limit superior and limit inferior of a real sequence always exist in the extended real numbers \([-\infty,+\infty]\).
  • A sequence converges if and only if its \(\limsup\) and \(\liminf\) are equal and finite; otherwise, it's divergent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(a_n = (-1)^n\): \(\limsup\limits_{n\to \infty}a_n = 1\text{,}\) \(\liminf\limits_{n\to \infty}a_n = -1\text{.}\)
  • For \(a_n = 1/2^n\): \(\limsup\limits_{n\to \infty}a_n = \liminf\limits_{n\to \infty}a_n = 0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The maximum norm of \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) in an \(n\)-dimensional real coordinate space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with fixed Cartesian coordinate system is:

\[ \|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_i|. \]

Correspondingly, the Chebyshev distance between \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_n)\) is calculated as:

\[ d_\infty(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_i-y_i|. \]

This is a norm because it is zero only at the zero vector, scales with absolute scalar size, and obeys the triangle inequality coordinate by coordinate. The induced distance is a metric distance. Comparison with the Euclidean Norm gives \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty\le\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_2\le\sqrt n\,\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The maximum norm is the limiting case of the \(p\)-norm when \(p\to+\infty\).

With \(\|\boldsymbol x\|_\infty=\max(|x_1|,|x_2|)\) the unit circle is a square. Drag \(\boldsymbol x\) and compare the three norms.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The closed unit ball in the maximum norm is an axis-aligned hypercube
\[ \overline{B}_{d_\infty}(\boldsymbol{0},1)=[-1,1]^n. \]

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A metric space \((X, d)\) consists of a set of points \(X\) and a distance function (or metric) \(d\colon X \times X \to [0,+\infty)\) that maps pairs of points to nonnegative real values. The metric adheres to the following properties:

  1. Nonnegativity: \(d(x,y) \geq 0\) for any \(x, y \in X\text{.}\)
  2. Identity of indiscernibles: \(d(x,y) = 0\) if and only if \(x=y\text{.}\)
  3. Symmetry: \(d(x,y) = d(y,x)\) for any \(x, y \in X\text{.}\)
  4. Triangle inequality: \(d(x,z) \leq d(x,y) + d(y,z)\) for any \(x, y, z \in X\text{.}\)

The Triangle Inequality requires a direct distance to be no greater than a journey through an intermediate point. The absolute-value inequality \(|x-z|\le|x-y|+|y-z|\) is its real-line instance.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A metric space is just a set of points with a clear and reasonable rule for measuring the distance between any two of them.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Metrics are always nonnegative. The only point at a zero distance from a point \(x\) is \(x\) itself.
  • Metrics are symmetric and adhere to the triangle inequality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Euclidean distance in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is defined as \(\displaystyle d(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}) = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - y_i)^2\right)^{1/2}\text{.}\)
  • The complex numbers \(\mathbb{C}\) with the distance function (based on modulus) \(d(z,w) = |z-w|\) form a metric space.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A monomial on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a function from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) given by a product of real coefficients and variables raised to nonnegative integer powers, i.e., a monomial has the general expression

\[ f(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n) = a x_1^{k_1} x_2^{k_2} \cdots x_n^{k_n}, \]

with constant \(a \in \mathbb{R}\) and exponents \(k_1,\, \dots,\, k_n \in \mathbb{N}\). The total degree of a monomial on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is the sum of the exponents of all variables appearing in that monomial, i.e., \(k_1+\cdots+k_n\).

For \(n=1\) this is the usual Monomial; for several variables it is a Function between Spaces from an input tuple to one real output.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A monomial is a simple expression made by multiplying a constant with each variable raised to a whole number power.

Its total degree is the sum of those powers, telling you how many factors of variables appear in total.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The product of two monomials is again a monomial. The exponents add componentwise, and the constant multiplies.
  • Every monomial is a homogeneous function whose degree equals its total degree.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y)=-2x^2y\)  is a monomial with exponents \(k_1=2\), \(k_2=1\), total degree \(3\).
  • The monomial \(f(x,y)=x^4\) has \(k_1=4\), \(k_2=0\), total degree \(4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A norm on a vector space \(V\) over the scalar field \(\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{C}\) (in this course \(\mathbb{R}\)) is a function \(\|\cdot\|\colon V\to[0,+\infty)\) that adheres to the following criteria:

  1. Nonnegativity and definiteness: For any \(\boldsymbol{x} \in V\), \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\| \geq 0\), and \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\| = 0\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{0}\).
  2. Absolute homogeneity (absolute scalability): For any scalar \(c \in \mathbb{F}\) and any \(\boldsymbol{x} \in V\), \(\|c\boldsymbol{x}\| = |c|\cdot\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\), where \(|c|\) is the absolute value (modulus) of \(c\).
  3. Triangle inequality: For any \(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y} \in V\): \(\|\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{y}\| \leq \|\boldsymbol{x}\| + \|\boldsymbol{y}\|\).

A normed vector space \((V, \|\cdot\|)\) is a vector space \(V\) over \(\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{C}\), equipped with a norm \(\|\cdot\|\).

The norm version of the Triangle Inequality bounds the length of a sum by the sum of the lengths. The Euclidean Norm \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_2=\sqrt{x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2}\) is the standard example satisfying all three axioms.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A norm is a rule that assigns a length to every vector in a consistent way.

A normed vector space is just a vector space where every vector has such a length, and scaling or adding vectors behaves as you would expect.

Each \(p\ge1\) gives a norm on \(\mathbb R^2\) with its own unit circle; all of them are convex and symmetric about \(\boldsymbol 0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Given a normed vector space \((V, \|\cdot\|)\), one can define the metric as \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) = \|\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{y}\|,\) making \((V, d)\) inherently a metric space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The real line \(\mathbb{R}\) with the absolute-value norm forms a normed vector space over \(\mathbb{R}\).
  • The plane \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the Euclidean norm is similarly a normed vector space. Using the taxicab norm, \(\mathbb{R}^2\) remains a normed vector space.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of bounded functions on \(X\). We say the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\) is normally convergent if the series of uniform norms of the terms of the series converges, i.e., \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \|f_n\|_\infty<+\infty.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Normal convergence means the functions are so well controlled that their worst-case contributions are summable.

\(\displaystyle \sum_n\|f_n\|_\infty=\sum_n 1/n^2\) converges, so the partial sums stay within the shrinking band around the limit.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Normal convergence implies uniform absolute convergence (the series \(\sum_n|f_n(x)|\) converges uniformly), which in turn implies uniform convergence, which in turn implies pointwise convergence, i.e.,
\[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{n=1}^\infty \|f_n\|_\infty<+\infty &\implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty |f_n(x)|\rightrightarrows g\\ &\implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\rightrightarrows f\\ &\implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\to f. \end{aligned} \]

Here \(g\) is the sum of the absolute series; it differs from \(f\) unless every \(f_n\ge0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Uniform absolute convergence does not imply normal convergence. On \(X=\mathbb{N}\), consider

\[ f_n(x)=\begin{cases} 1/n, &x=n,\\[2pt] 0, &x\neq n. \end{cases} \]

The absolute series converges uniformly: its tail after the first \(N\) terms has supremum \(1/(N+1)\), which tends to zero. However, \(\|f_n\|_\infty=1/n\), so the series of uniform norms is the harmonic series and diverges.

docs.title: Open and Closed Sets in a Metric Space
Definition
docs.text:
For a metric space \((X,d)\) and its subset \(E\):

  • \(E\) is closed if it includes all of its boundary points, i.e., \(\partial E \subseteq E\).
  • \(E\) is open if it doesn't include any of its boundary points, i.e., \(\partial E \cap E = \varnothing\).
  • \(E\) is neither open nor closed if it includes some but not all of its boundary points.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Open sets keep their boundaries out. Closed sets keep their boundaries in. Sets that include some boundary points but not others are neither open nor closed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A set \(E\) is open if and only if \(E = \operatorname{int}E\).
  • A set \(F\) is closed if and only if every convergent sequence \((x_i)_{i=1}^{\infty}\) within \(F\) converges to a limiting point lying in \(F\).
  • A set \(E\) is open if and only if its complement \(E^\complement=X\setminus E\) is closed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The open metric ball \(B(x_0, \varepsilon)\) is open.
  • \(\varnothing\) is both open and closed. It has no boundary points to include or exclude.
  • Under the discrete metric, every set is both open and closed. Each singleton set has a ball containing only itself.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a metric space \((X,d)\), a point \(x_0\) in \(X\), and \(r > 0\), the open metric ball \(B_{(X,d)}(x_0,r)\) in \(X\), centred at \(x_0\) with radius \(r\) in metric \(d\), is defined as the following set:

\[ B_{(X,d)}(x_0,r) = \{x \in X \colon d(x, x_0) < r\}. \]

If the context is clear, we'll abbreviate this as \(B_d(x_0,r)\) or simply \(B(x_0,r).\)

A ball is a subset of \(X\) selected by the distance condition; the ambient space matters, so a real-line ball and a plane ball have different members.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An open metric ball is the set of all points whose distance from the centre is strictly less than the radius.

It is the basic building block for defining open sets and continuity in metric spaces.

Change the centre, the radius \(r\) and the metric: the ball contains the points at distance less than \(r\). Points on the dashed sphere are not included.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Open balls are open sets.
  • A subset of a metric space is open if and only if it can be written as a union of open balls.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the usual distance, \(B((0,0),1)\) is the open disc of radius \(1\) centred at the origin. Points with \(x^2 + y^2 < 1\) are elements of this ball.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the taxicab metric \(d_1\), \(B((0,0),1)\) is a diamond shape with vertices at \((\pm1,0)\) and \((0,\pm1)\).
  • In any set with the discrete metric, \(B(x,1) = \{x\}\) and \(B(x,0.5) = \{x\}\), but \(B(x,2)\) is the whole space.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,x_2, \ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n\). For \(p\in[1,+\infty)\), the \(p\)-norm, denoted \(\|\cdot\|_p\), is defined on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) by:

\[ \|\boldsymbol{x}\|_p = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n |x_i|^p\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}. \]

For \(p=+\infty\) one sets \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty=\max\limits_{1\le i\le n}|x_i|\), which is the limit of \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_p\) as \(p\to+\infty\).

Correspondingly, the \(p\)-metric \(d_p\) is defined as \(d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}\|_p\), that is,

\[ \begin{aligned} d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})&=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n |x_i-y_i|^p\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}\\ &\qquad(1\le p<+\infty),\\ d_\infty(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})&=\max_{1\le i\le n}|x_i-y_i|. \end{aligned} \]

The formula uses Exponentiation and Power twice: raise the coordinate magnitudes to \(p\), then take the \(1/p\) power of their sum. The value \(+\infty\) is an Extended Real Number indexing the separate maximum-norm limit, not a finite exponent to substitute directly. Setting \(p=2\) recovers the Euclidean Norm.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The \(p\)-norm is a way of measuring the size of a vector by raising each coordinate's absolute value to the \(p\)-th power, summing them, and taking the \(p\)-th root.

The figure compares the unit balls \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_p\le1\}\) for \(p=1,2,4,\infty\). As \(p\) increases, these balls expand from the diamond towards the square.

Move \(p\): the unit circle \(\{\boldsymbol x:\|\boldsymbol x\|_p=1\}\) swells from the diamond at \(p=1\) through the circle at \(p=2\) towards the square at \(p=\infty\). Drag \(\boldsymbol x\) to compare its norms.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The smallest permissible value for \(p\) in the \(p\)-norm is \(1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Euclidean distance \(d_2\) is a particular \(p\)-metric when \(p=2\).
  • The taxicab distance \(d_1\) is a particular \(p\)-metric when \(p=1\).
  • The maximum norm \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\) is a particular \(p\)-norm when \(p=+\infty\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) and consider a function \(\boldsymbol{f} \colon E \to \mathbb{R}^k\). For an interior point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) of \(E\) and an integer \(1 \leq j \leq n\), the partial derivative of \(\boldsymbol{f}\) with respect to the \(x_j\)-variable at \(\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{x}_0\), denoted by \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\), is given by

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) &= \lim_{{t\to0}} \frac{\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0 + t\boldsymbol{e}_j) - \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)}{t}\\ &= \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0 + t\boldsymbol{e}_j)\,\right|_{t=0}, \end{aligned} \]

where \(\boldsymbol{e}_j\) represents the unit vector in the positive direction of the \(j\)-th coordinate, provided the limit exists.

The partial derivative changes only the \(j\)th coordinate, so it is the Directional Derivative along the coordinate vector \(\boldsymbol{e}_j\) when the corresponding two-sided limit exists.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The partial derivative measures how the function changes when you nudge only one coordinate while keeping all others fixed.

It is like taking an ordinary derivative in the direction of that coordinate axis.

Choose \(j\): along the line \(\boldsymbol x_0+t\boldsymbol e_j\) the function becomes a one-variable function (right), and \(\partial f/\partial x_j\) is its slope at \(t=0\).

Freeze one variable: the graph is cut along a line through \(\boldsymbol x_0\), and \(\partial f/\partial x_j\) is the slope of that slice. Edit \(f\) to try your own function.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The partial derivative \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) exists if and only if both \(\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{e}_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) and \(\mathrm{D}_{-\boldsymbol{e}_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) exist and are negatives of each other. In such a scenario, we have \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{e}_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0).\)
  • If \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is totally differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\text{,}\) then for every unit vector \(\displaystyle \boldsymbol{v} = (v_1,\,\ldots,\,v_n)= \sum_{j=1}^n v_j\boldsymbol{e}_j\) we have \(\displaystyle \mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) = \sum_{j=1}^n v_j \frac{\partial }{\partial x_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0).\) Without total differentiability this can fail even when all partial derivatives exist.
  • If all the partial derivatives are both existent within a neighbourhood and continuous at the centre, then \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is totally differentiable at this point.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The partial derivative of \(f(x,y) = 3x^2y^2 + 4xy^3 + 7y\) with respect to the first variable is \(\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x}f(x,y) = 6xy^2 + 4y^3.\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the metric space \((X, d_{X})\text{,}\) a nonempty subset \(E\) is termed path-connected if, for any two distinct points \(a, b \in E\text{,}\) a path \(p\colon [0,1] \to E\) exists such that \(p(0) = a\) and \(p(1) = b\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: You can walk from any point to any other point in a path-connected set without ever leaving the set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • In the metric space \((X, d_{X})\text{,}\) any path-connected subset of \(X\) is connected.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The topologist's sine curve is connected but not path-connected:

    \[ \{(0,0)\}\cup\{(x,\sin(1/x))\colon x>0\}. \]

    As \(x\to0^+\) the graph oscillates ever faster between \(-1\) and \(1\); the set is connected, but no path inside it reaches \((0,0)\).

  • The collection of line segments joining the origin to points \((1, 1/n)\) for all positive integers \(n\), together with the point \((1,0)\) is also connected but not path-connected.

    Segments from the origin to \((1,1/n)\) crowd towards the missing segment to \((1,0)\); only its endpoint \((1,0)\) belongs to the set, and no path inside the set reaches it.
