docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In a metric space \((X, d_{X})\), a path is a continuous function \(p\colon [0,1] \to X\). If for two points \(a, b \in X\), the path \(p\) satisfies \(p(0) = a\) and \(p(1) = b\), it is termed as a path from \(a\) to \(b\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A path is a continuous journey from one point to another within the space.

It is like drawing a curve without lifting your pencil, with the curve entirely contained in the space.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(p\) is a path from \(a\) to \(b\) and \(q\) is a path from \(b\) to \(c\), then it is possible to construct a path from \(a\) to \(c\) using \(p\) and \(q\). This is called the concatenation.
  • For any path \(p\) from \(a\) to \(b\), the reverse path \(p(1-t)\) is a path from \(b\) to \(a\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In Euclidean space, the function \(\boldsymbol{p}(t)=(1-t)\boldsymbol{a}+t\boldsymbol{b}\) is a path from \(\boldsymbol{a}\) to \(\boldsymbol{b}\).
  • The function \(\boldsymbol{p}(t)=(\cos(2\pi t),\sin(2\pi t))\) is a path from \((1,0)\) back to itself (a loop).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}\) be a sequence of functions \(f_n\colon X\to \mathbb{R}\) and \(f\colon X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be another function. We say that \((f_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}\) converges pointwise to \(f\) on \(X\) and write \(f_n\to f\text{,}\) if for every \(x \in X\text{,}\) \(\displaystyle \lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} f_n(x) = f(x)\text{.}\)

Each \(f_n\) is a Function, so fixing \(x\) gives an ordinary numerical sequence \(f_n(x)\). Its Limit of a Sequence is \(f(x)\); the required index may depend on this fixed \(x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Pointwise convergence means that for each fixed point, the function values get closer to a limit as the index goes to infinity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Pointwise convergence guarantees that the limit exists at each individual point.
  • Pointwise convergence does not preserve boundedness, limits/continuity, differentiability, or integrals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f_n(x) = \dfrac{n}{nx + 1}\) converges pointwise to \(f(x)=1/x\) on \((0,+\infty)\text{.}\)
  • \(f_n(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{x^2+1 / n}}\) converges pointwise to \(f(x)=|x|.\)

For each fixed \(x\), \(f_n(x)\to|x|\); at \(x=-1\) the values \(f_n(-1)\) (dots) increase to \(f(-1)=1\).

Point at a value \(x\): the numbers \(f_n(x)\) (right) enter the \(\varepsilon\)-band from some \(N(x)\) on. For \(x^n\) that \(N(x)\) grows without bound as \(x\to1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A polynomial on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a real-valued function that is a finite sum of monomials on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). The degree of a polynomial on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is defined as the maximum, over all its monomials with nonzero coefficient, of the total degree of each monomial (the zero polynomial is usually left without a degree).

With one variable this reduces to an ordinary Polynomial; with several variables the same finite-sum construction uses multivariate monomials.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A polynomial in several variables is a finite combination of monomials added together.

Its degree is the highest total degree among all the monomials that appear with nonzero coefficient.

The plotted polynomial \(p(x_1,x_2)=x_1^3-3x_1x_2^2\) is the sum of two monomials, each of total degree \(3\).

Drag the picture to turn it. \(x_1^3-3x_1x_2^2\) has degree \(3\); compare it with the degree-\(2\) examples, whose graphs are bowls and saddles.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The degree of the sum of two polynomials is at most the maximum of their degrees. The degree of the product of two polynomials is the sum of their degrees.
  • Polynomials are infinitely differentiable. All partial derivatives of all orders exist and are themselves polynomials (or zero).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x^2 + 2xy + y^2 + x + 1\) is a polynomial of degree 2. Its highest total degree comes from \(x^2\), \(xy\), and \(y^2\), all degree 2.
  • \(f(x,y) = x^3 + xy + y^2\) has degree 3 from the \(x^3\) term.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(a \in \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) A power series centred at \(a\) is expressed as \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\text{,}\) where \((c_n)_{n=0}^\infty\) is a sequence of real numbers, independent of \(x\text{.}\) We refer to \(c_n\) as the \(n\)-th coefficient of the power series.

Viewed as an Infinite Series of Functions, its \(n\)th summand is \(x\mapsto c_n(x-a)^n\). Convergence asks whether the partial sums of these functions have a limit at the chosen \(x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A power series is an infinite sum of power functions.

Raise \(N\): inside the shaded interval of convergence the partial sums settle on the sum; outside they run away.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The definition is formal: it does not say for which \(x\) the series converges. Every power series has a radius of convergence \(R\in[0,+\infty]\): it converges absolutely for \(|x-a|<R\) and diverges for \(|x-a|>R\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any polynomial is a special case of a power series, since the coefficients \(c_n\) are allowed to be zero.
  • \(1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\cdots\) is a power series.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a given power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\text{,}\) its radius of convergence \(R\) is a nonnegative real number or \(+\infty\) such that the series converges if \(|x-a|<R\) and diverges if \(|x-a|>R\text{.}\) The interval of convergence is the set of all values of \(x\) for which the series converges.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The radius of convergence tells you how far from the centre point a power series will reliably converge.

Each series converges for \(|x-a|<R\) and diverges for \(|x-a|>R\); what happens at the endpoints differs from series to series.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The convergence of \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) at \(x=a-R\) and \(x=a+R\) is to be determined case-by-case.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n(-2)^n (x-3)^n\) with \(R = 1/2\) centred at \(a = 3\), converges pointwise on \(\left(5/2, 7/2\right)\) and uniformly on any closed interval within it. Its convergence interval is \(\left(5/2, 7/2\right)\) since the series diverges at both endpoints.
  • The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{n^2} (x+2)^n\) with \(R = 0\) centred at \(a = -2\), converges solely at its centre \(x = -2.\)

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Consider the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) where \(a_n\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(a_n\ne0\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Let \(\displaystyle L=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right|\) when this limit exists (possibly as \(+\infty\)). Then:

  • If \(L < 1\text{,}\) the series converges. Moreover, \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_n|\) also converges.
  • If \(L > 1\text{,}\) the series diverges.
  • If \(L = 1\) or the limit does not exist, the test is inconclusive.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The ratio test states that a series converges if the limit of the ratio of consecutive terms is less than 1, and diverges if it is greater than 1.

\(\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\dfrac{n+1}{2n}\to L=\tfrac{1}{2}<1\). For \(n\ge3\), \(a_{n+1}\le\tfrac{2}{3}a_n\), so \(a_n\le a_3(\tfrac{2}{3})^{n-3}\) and \(\displaystyle \sum a_n\) converges by comparison.

Move \(x\): the ratios \(|a_{n+1}/a_n|\) (right) settle at \(L=|x-a|/R\). The series converges for \(L<1\) and diverges for \(L>1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • For the power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x - a)^n\) with eventually nonzero coefficients, the radius of convergence \(R\) can be found using \(\displaystyle R = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{c_{n}}{c_{n+1}} \right|\) if the limit exists or tends to infinity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n}{\mathrm{e}^n}\) is convergent since \(\displaystyle L=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{(n+1)/\mathrm{e}^{n+1}}{n/\mathrm{e}^n} \right| =\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{e}}<1\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{2^n}{n}\) diverges since \(\displaystyle L=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{2^{n+1}/(n+1)}{2^n/n} \right| =2>1\text{.}\)
  • When \(L=1\text{,}\) both convergent and divergent series exist, e.g., \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}\) diverges while \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}\) converges.
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\) converges for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}\) since \(\displaystyle R=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{(n+1)!}{n!} \right|=+\infty\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^n(x-3)^n\) converges for \(|x-3|<1/2\) since \(\displaystyle R=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{2^{n}}{2^{n+1}} \right|=\dfrac{1}{2}\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n!(x+1)^n\) diverges for all \(x\) except \(x=-1\) since \(\displaystyle R=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{n!} {(n+1)!}\right|=0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon E \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function where \(E \subseteq \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) We say:

  • \(f\) is real analytic at \(x=a\) if \(a\) is an interior point of \(E\) and there exists a power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) centred at \(a\) and an open interval \((a-r, a+r) \subseteq E\) (for some \(r > 0\)) where this series converges to \(f\text{.}\)
  • \(f\) is real analytic on \(E\) if \(E\) is an open set and \(f\) is real analytic at every point \(a \in E\text{.}\)

The results on Convergence of Power Series justify differentiating the local representation term by term inside its radius. Analyticity requires the resulting series to equal \(f\), not merely to exist formally.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A function is real analytic at a point if it can be represented by a power series that matches the function exactly in a small interval around that point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The convergence type here is not limited, but if we consider a closed subinterval of \((a-r,a+r)\text{,}\) then it is the uniform convergence.
  • Sums, products, and compositions of real analytic functions are also real analytic.
  • A real analytic function is always infinitely differentiable, and all of its higher-order derivatives are real analytic.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Almost all common functions are real analytic.
  • Most piecewise functions are not real analytic, though they can be even infinitely differentiable. For instance, the following function is a particular non-analytic but infinitely differentiable function.

Every derivative of \(f\) at \(0\) is \(0\), so its Taylor series at \(0\) is the zero series, yet \(f(x)>0\) for \(x>0\): \(f\) is infinitely differentiable but not real analytic at \(0\).

A real analytic function equals its Taylor series near each point \(a\). Move \(a\): the interval of convergence moves and changes size with it.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Consider the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) where \(a_n \in \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Let \(\displaystyle L = \limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{|a_n|}\), then:

  • If \(L < 1\text{,}\) the series converges. Moreover, \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_n|\) also converges.
  • If \(L > 1\text{,}\) the series diverges.
  • If \(L = 1\text{,}\) the test is inconclusive.

The \(n\)-th Root measures the geometric size of each term. The Limit Superior and Limit Inferior framework uses the largest limiting tail sizes, so the test can apply even when the root sequence has no ordinary limit.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The root test determines convergence by comparing the limit superior of the \(n\)-th root of the terms' absolute values to 1.

The \(n\)th roots \(|a_n|^{1/n}\) (right) approach \(L=|x-a|/R\); compare with \(1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The ordinary limit used in the ratio test may not exist. The root test above uses a limit superior, which always exists in \([0,+\infty]\), even when the root sequence has no ordinary limit.
  • The radius of convergence of a power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) is given by
\[ R=\frac{1}{\limsup\limits_{n\to\infty} |c_n|^{1/n}}. \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n}{\mathrm{e}^n}\) is convergent since \(\displaystyle L=\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{\left| \frac{n}{\mathrm{e}^n} \right|} = \frac{1}{\mathrm{e}}<1\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{2^n}{n}\) diverges since \(\displaystyle L=\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{\left|\frac{2^n}{n} \right|} = 2>1\text{.}\)
  • When \(L=1\text{,}\) both convergent and divergent series exist, e.g., \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}\) diverges while \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}\) converges.
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n(-2)^n (x-3)^n\) is convergent for \(|x-3|<\dfrac{1}{2}\) since \(R = \dfrac{1}{\limsup\limits_{n \to\infty}|n\left(-2\right)^{n}|^{1/n}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{n^2} (x+2)^n\) is divergent except at \(x=-2\) since \(R= \dfrac{1}{\limsup\limits_{n \rightarrow \infty}|2^{n^{2}}|^{1/n}}= 0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \((X,d_{X})\) be a metric space. A subset \(E\) of \(X\) is termed sequentially compact if for every sequence \((x_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) with each \(x_i \in E\text{,}\) there exists a convergent subsequence \((x_{i_j})_{j=1}^\infty\) that converges to a point \(x \in E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A set is sequentially compact if every infinite sequence drawn from it has a subsequence that converges to a point still inside the set.

It captures the idea that the set is "closed under taking limits of subsequences."

In the closed disc, the red subsequence converges to a point of \(E\). In the open disc, the illustrated sequence approaches a missing rim point, and every subsequence has that same limit outside \(E\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • In any metric space, a set is compact if and only if it is sequentially compact. This gives two equivalent ways to think about compactness: open covers or convergent subsequences.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The closed unit ball \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\in \mathbb{R}^n\colon \|\boldsymbol{x}\|\leq 1\}\) is sequentially compact. This fails in infinite dimensions.
  • Any finite set in any metric space is compact.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a metric space. The metrics \(d_p\) and \(d_q\) on \(X\) (two arbitrary metrics; the subscripts are only labels) are termed strongly equivalent, denoted \(d_p\approx d_q\), if positive constants \(a\) and \(b\) exist such that for any \(x,y \in X\),

\[ a \cdot d_p(x,y) \leq d_q(x,y) \leq b \cdot d_p(x,y). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Equivalent metrics measure distances in different scales but agree on which points are close or far apart.

On \(\mathbb{R}^2\), the illustrated Euclidean and taxicab distances satisfy \(d_2\le d_1\le\sqrt{2}\,d_2\). Consequently, \(B_{d_2}(\boldsymbol{x},r/\sqrt{2})\subseteq B_{d_1}(\boldsymbol{x},r)\subseteq B_{d_2}(\boldsymbol{x},r)\), so they induce the same open sets and convergent sequences.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The strong equivalence relation possesses symmetry (\(d_p\approx d_q\) if and only if \(d_q\approx d_p\)), reflexivity (\(d_p\approx d_p\)) and transitivity (if \(d_p\approx d_q\) and \(d_q\approx d_r\), then \(d_p\approx d_r\)).
  • Strongly equivalent metrics induce the same notion of convergence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any two \(p\)-metrics on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) are strongly equivalent.
  • The discrete metric, \(d_{\mathrm{disc}}\), is not strongly equivalent to any of the \(p\)-metrics.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The taxicab distance between points \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_n)\) in an \(n\)-dimensional real coordinate space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with fixed Cartesian coordinate system is:

\[ d_1(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|y_i-x_i|. \]

The taxicab norm, or known as \(\ell^1\) norm, of \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) is calculated as:

\[ \|\boldsymbol{x}\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|x_i|. \]

The coordinate sum defines a norm length, and subtracting two points gives a metric distance. Its triangle inequality follows by adding \(|x_i-z_i|\le|x_i-y_i|+|y_i-z_i|\) over the coordinates.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The taxicab distance represents the distance a taxi would travel between two points when restricted to cardinal directions (north, south, east, west) without moving diagonally or in any other curved path.

The red staircase has taxicab length \(d_1(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=5+4=9\). Any monotone staircase between the points has the same length, whereas the blue straight segment has Euclidean length \(d_2(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=\sqrt{5^2+4^2}\approx6.4\).

In the taxicab norm \(\|\boldsymbol x\|_1=|x_1|+|x_2|\) the unit circle is a diamond. Drag \(\boldsymbol x\): the \(1\)-norm is always at least the Euclidean norm.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The closed unit ball in the taxicab norm is an \(n\)-dimensional cross-polytope, e.g., a diamond in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and a regular octahedron in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The polynomial that emerges from Taylor's theorem is termed the \(k\)-th order Taylor polynomial for the function \(f\) at \(x=a\):

\[ \begin{aligned} P_{k}(x) &= f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \cdots\\ &\quad + \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k !}(x-a)^{k}. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• The \(k\)-th order Taylor polynomial of \(f\) captures the initial \(k+1\) terms of its Taylor series (given existence) centred at the same point.
  • If \(f\) is \(k\) times differentiable at \(a\text{,}\) then \(P_k\) is the unique polynomial of degree at most \(k\) with \(f(x)-P_k(x)=o\big((x-a)^k\big)\) as \(x\to a\text{;}\) in this sense it is the best polynomial approximation of order \(k\) near \(x=a\text{.}\)

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The \(k\)-th order Taylor polynomial and the function \(f\) have the same value and the same derivatives up to order \(k\) at \(x=a\text{:}\) \(P_k^{(j)}(a)=f^{(j)}(a)\) for \(j=0,1,\dots,k\text{.}\) Away from \(a\) they generally differ.
  • One can write a Taylor polynomial for a function just from its first few derivatives, but the full Taylor series exists if the function is smooth, and the full series converges to the function only if it's real analytic.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The 3rd order Taylor polynomial of \(\sin x\) around \(x=0\) is \(P_3(x) = x - \dfrac{x^3}{3!}\).

    The two panels compare Taylor polynomials of \(\sin x\) about \(0\). The cubic \(P_3\) on the right follows \(\sin x\) over a wider interval than the linear polynomial \(P_1\) on the left.

Raise the order \(k\) and move the centre \(a\): \(P_k\) matches \(f\) and its first \(k\) derivatives at \(a\), and fits over a wider range.

  • The 1st order Taylor polynomial of \(1/x\) around \(x = 1\) is \(P_1(x)=2-x\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(a\) be an interior point of \(E\subseteq \mathbb{R}\text{,}\) and let \(f\colon E\to\mathbb{R}\) be real analytic at \(x=a\text{.}\) Then, for some \(r>0\) with \((a-r,a+r)\subseteq E\), \(f\) has the power series expansion around \(x=a\):

\[ \begin{gathered} f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!} (x-a)^n\\ \text{for all } x \in (a-r,a+r), \end{gathered} \]

known as the Taylor series of \(f\) around \(x=a\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
If a function is so smooth that it behaves exactly like an infinite polynomial near a point, then that polynomial is built entirely from its derivatives at that point.

For \(\ln(1+x)\) and \(1/(1-x)\) the Taylor polynomials converge to \(f\) inside the shaded interval and not beyond it; for \(\mathrm{e}^x\) and \(\sin x\) everywhere.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The Taylor series centred at the origin is called the Maclaurin series.
  • For any smooth function you can write down its Taylor series around \(a\), but it need not converge to the function: it equals \(f\) on a neighbourhood of \(a\) if and only if \(f\) is real analytic at \(a\text{.}\) For example, \(f(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-1/x^2}\) for \(x\neq0\), \(f(0)=0\), is smooth, but its Taylor series at \(0\) is identically \(0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Taylor series of the natural exponential function at the origin:
\[ \displaystyle \mathrm{e}^x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!} = 1 + x + \dfrac{x^2}{2!} + \dfrac{x^3}{3!} + \cdots. \]
  • The generalized binomial expansion (binomial series) at the origin, which extends the binomial theorem to real exponents, valid for \(|x|<1\) and any real exponent \(\alpha\) (and for all \(x\) when \(\alpha\) is a nonnegative integer, since the series then terminates):
\[ \begin{aligned} &(1+x)^\alpha = \sum_{i=0}^\infty \binom{\alpha}{i} x^i \\ &\quad= 1 + \alpha x + \frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)}{2}x^2\\ &\qquad + \frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)(\alpha-2)}{6}x^3 + \cdots, \end{aligned} \]

where \(\displaystyle\binom{\alpha}{i}=\frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)\cdots(\alpha-i+1)}{i!}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(k \geq 1\) be an integer and assume that the function \(f\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is \(k\)-times differentiable (not necessarily real analytic) at \(x=a\text{.}\) There exists a function \(\displaystyle h_k \colon \mathbb{R} \to\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to a} h_k(x) = 0\) and

\[ \begin{aligned} f(x) &= f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \cdots\\ &\quad + \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k !}(x-a)^k + R_k(x) \end{aligned} \]

where \(R_k(x)= h_k(x)(x-a)^k\) is called the Peano form of the remainder.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
One can approximate a smooth function near a point using a polynomial, and the error term behaves like \((x-a)^k\) multiplied by something that tends to \(0\) as \(x\) approaches \(a\).

The right panel shows \(h_k(x)=R_k(x)/(x-a)^k\): it tends to \(0\) as \(x\to a\), which is the Peano form of the remainder.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Using the little-\(o\) notation, the statement in Taylor's theorem reads as \(R_k(x)=o((x-a)^k)\text{,}\) as \(x\to a\text{.}\) In this case, we have the \(k\)-th order Taylor expansion, whose polynomial part is the Taylor polynomial \(P_k(x)\):
\[ \begin{aligned} f(x) &= f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \cdots\\ &\quad + \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k !}(x-a)^{k}\\ &\quad + o((x-a)^{k}). \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathrm{e}^x=1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+h_2(x)x^2\), where \(\displaystyle h_2(x)=\sum_{n=3}^\infty \dfrac{x^{n-2}}{n!}\).
  • \(\dfrac{1}{1-x}=1+x+x^2+h_2(x) x^2\), where \(\displaystyle h_2(x)=\sum_{n=3}^\infty x^{n-2}\), for \(|x|<1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Two metrics \(d_p\) and \(d_q\) on a space \(X\) are termed (topologically) equivalent if they produce identical topology (the set of open subsets of \(X\)) on \(X\), i.e., a subset \(E \subseteq X\) is open with respect to \(d_p\) if and only if it's open under \(d_q\). This relationship is expressed as \(d_p \sim d_q.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Two metrics are topologically equivalent if they determine the same collection of open sets.

They may measure distances differently, but they agree on which points are close enough to be in the same open set.

Around every point of a \(d_p\)-ball fits a \(d_q\)-ball, and vice versa, so a set is \(d_p\)-open \(\iff\) it is \(d_q\)-open: the same topology.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • If two metrics are strongly equivalent, then they are topologically equivalent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• On the interval \((-\pi/2,\pi/2)\text{,}\) the metric \(d_{\tan}(x,y)=|\tan x-\tan y|\) is topologically equivalent to the absolute value metric, but they are not strongly equivalent: the ratio \(|\tan x-\tan y|/|x-y|\) is unbounded near \(\pm\pi/2\text{.}\)
  • The discrete metric is not topologically equivalent to any \(p\)-metrics.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A topology on a set \(X\), often denoted by \(\tau\), is a collection of subsets of \(X\) that satisfies the following properties:

  1. Both the empty set and the entire set \(X\) belong to \(\tau\).
  2. Any union of elements in \(\tau\) also belongs to \(\tau\).
  3. The intersection of any finite number of elements in \(\tau\) remains in \(\tau\).

The pair \((X,\tau)\) is called a topological space.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A topology is a collection of open sets that tells you which points are close to which without using a distance.

It is the most general setting for studying continuity and convergence.

\(\tau=\{\varnothing,\{a\},\{a,b\},X\}\) is a topology on \(X\): it contains \(\varnothing\) and \(X\) and is closed under unions and finite intersections (e.g. \(\{a\}\cup\{a,b\}=\{a,b\}\), \(\{a\}\cap\{a,b\}=\{a\}\)); the members of \(\tau\) are the open sets.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Metric spaces are topological spaces. Every metric space induces a topology where open sets are unions of open metric balls.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The trivial topology is the topology with the least possible number of open sets, namely the empty set and the entire space, i.e., \(\tau=\{\varnothing, X\}\).

docs.title: Total Derivative as a Linear Map
Definition
docs.text:
Let \(E\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\), let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon E\to\mathbb{R}^k\) be a function, let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\operatorname{int}E\), and let \(\boldsymbol{L}\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k\) be a linear transformation. We say that \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is (totally) differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_{0}\) with (total) derivative \(\boldsymbol{L}\) if, as \(\boldsymbol{x}\to\boldsymbol{x}_0\),

\[ \frac{\|\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})-\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)-\boldsymbol{L}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}_0)\|}{\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}_0\|}\to0. \]

The limit must hold however \(\boldsymbol{x}\) approaches \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), that is, along every convergent sequence \(\boldsymbol{x}_j\to\boldsymbol{x}_0\) with \(\boldsymbol{x}_j\neq\boldsymbol{x}_0\), not just along coordinate lines. It says that the relative error in the linear approximation tends to zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Total differentiability means the function can be approximated near the point by a linear transformation, with the error shrinking to zero faster than the distance to the point. The linear map \(\boldsymbol{h}\mapsto\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{h}\) is also called the differential of \(\boldsymbol{f}\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\); for \(n=k=1\) it is \(h\mapsto f'(x_0)h\), the one-variable differential \(\mathrm{d}y=f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\).

It is the multidimensional version of the one-variable fact that \(f\) is differentiable at \(x_0\) if and only if \(f(x_0+h)=f(x_0)+f'(x_0)h+o(h)\) as \(h\to0\) (sometimes called Newton's approximation).

The first-order approximation is \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h})=\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)+\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{h}+o(\|\boldsymbol{h}\|)\), where \(\boldsymbol{L}=\boldsymbol{Df}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\). Locally, \(\boldsymbol{f}\) acts like this linear map, so small squares become approximate parallelograms.

Move \(\boldsymbol x_0\) and zoom in: near \(\boldsymbol x_0\) the graph is almost the plane \(f(\boldsymbol x_0)+\mathrm{D}f_{\boldsymbol x_0}(\boldsymbol h)\), with an error that shrinks faster than \(\|\boldsymbol h\|\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For the function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\), its derivative, \(\mathrm{D} \boldsymbol{f}_{\boldsymbol{x}_0}\), is a \(k\times n\) matrix or an equivalent linear transformation from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}^k\).
  • \(\mathrm{D} \boldsymbol{f}_{\boldsymbol{x}_0}(\boldsymbol{h})\), where \(\boldsymbol{h}\) is an infinitesimal vector, provides an approximation of the shift in \(\boldsymbol{f}\) (a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^k\)) arising from the change \(\boldsymbol{h}\) in \(\boldsymbol{x}\) around \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\) (a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y) = (x^2,y^2)\) is differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}=(1,2)\) with the derivative \(\boldsymbol{L}(x,y) = (2x,4y)\).
  • The function \(f(x,y) = \sin(x^2+y)\) is differentiable at \((x,y)=(0,0)\) and the derivative is \(L(x,y)=y\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider metric spaces \((X,d_{X})\) and \((Y,d_{Y})\), and a function \(f\colon X\to Y\). We say \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \(X\) if, for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a \(\delta > 0\) such that for all \(x_1,x_2\in X\) with \(d_{X}(x_1,x_2)<\delta\), it holds that \(d_{Y}(f(x_1),f(x_2))<\varepsilon\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This is the general definition of uniform continuity where the metric functions are allowed to be potentially different metrics on possibly different spaces.

For a given \(\varepsilon>0\), the same \(\delta>0\) works at every point: \(d_{X}(x_1,x_2)<\delta\) implies \(d_{Y}(f(x_1),f(x_2))<\varepsilon\). Each \(\delta\)-ball is therefore mapped inside the \(\varepsilon\)-ball around its centre's image.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Any continuous function defined on a compact set is uniformly continuous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Every constant function is uniformly continuous regardless of the metrics.
  • Every function from a discrete space is uniformly continuous.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A function \(f\colon X \to \mathbb{R}\) with \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) is said to be uniformly continuous if, for every \(\varepsilon >0\text{,}\) there exists a \(\delta >0\) such that for all pairs of points \(x_1, x_2\in X\) with \(|x_1-x_2|<\delta\text{,}\) it holds that \(|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|<\varepsilon\text{.}\)

The same \(\delta\) controls all input pairs of the Function \(f\), rather than being selected separately for each point.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Uniform continuity means one fixed rule for “how small is small” works everywhere, while ordinary continuity may need different rules at different points.

For a fixed \(\varepsilon\) the right panel shows the largest admissible \(\delta\) at each \(x_0\). Uniform continuity means one positive \(\delta\) works everywhere; for \(1/x\) the admissible \(\delta\) shrinks to \(0\) near \(0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every uniformly continuous function is continuous, the converse doesn't necessarily hold.
  • \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \(X\) if and only if given two equivalent sequences \((x_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) and \((y_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) in \(X\) (that is, \(|x_n-y_n|\to0\) as \(n\to\infty\)), the sequences \((f(x_n))_{n=1}^\infty\) and \((f(y_n))_{n=1}^\infty\) are also equivalent.
  • A continuous function \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \((a, b)\) if and only if the right limit \(\displaystyle f(a^+)\) and the left limit \(\displaystyle f(b^-)\) both exist and are finite. In particular, a continuous function that is unbounded on a bounded interval \((a,b)\) is not uniformly continuous there; a bounded function can fail too, for example \(\sin(1/x)\) on \((0,1)\), which has no right limit at \(0\).
  • A differentiable function \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \((a,b)\) if \(f'\) is bounded. Boundedness of \(f'\) is sufficient, not necessary: \(\sqrt{x}\) is uniformly continuous on \((0,1)\) although its derivative is unbounded there. A typical failure on an unbounded domain is \(f(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) whose slope is unbounded.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=1/x\) is uniformly continuous on \((1,2)\), but not uniformly continuous on \((0,1)\).
  • The function \(g(x)=\sin x\) is uniformly continuous on all of \(\mathbb{R}\) (hence on any interval), since \(|\sin x_1-\sin x_2|\le|x_1-x_2|\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of functions defined on \(X \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) and \(f\colon X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be another function. We say that \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) converges uniformly to \(f\) on \(X\) and write \(f_n\rightrightarrows f\text{,}\) if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\text{,}\) there exists a positive integer \(N\) such that for all \(n > N\text{,}\) the inequality \(|f_n(x) - f(x) | < \varepsilon\) holds for all \(x \in X\text{.}\)

The objects converging are Function values on a common domain. A single index \(N\) must control the error at every input, which distinguishes uniform convergence from separate numerical limits.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Uniform convergence means that the function values get close to the limit at the same speed for all points, not one point at a time.

Uniform convergence \(f_n\to f\) means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\), the graph of \(f_n\) lies in the \(\varepsilon\)-tube around \(f\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Thus \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\) holds for all \(x\) at once, equivalently \(\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0\).

Uniform convergence asks for one \(n\) that puts the whole graph of \(f_n\) inside the \(\varepsilon\)-band. Compare \(\sin(nx)/n\) with \(x^n\) and the moving bump.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence.
  • Uniform convergence preserves boundedness and continuity (uniform limit theorem). On a closed bounded interval \([a,b]\) it preserves Riemann integrability and allows \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_a^b f_n=\int_a^b f\text{.}\) It does not preserve differentiability: for that, the derivatives \(f_n'\) must converge uniformly as well.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The sequence \(f_n(x) = x/n\) converges uniformly to \(f(x)=0\) on every bounded interval \([-R,R]\) (since \(|x/n|\le R/n\)), but only pointwise on \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\)
  • The functions \(f_n(x) = \dfrac{n}{nx + 1}\) on \((0,1]\) converge pointwise, but not uniformly, to \(f(x)=1/x\text{,}\) because \(|f_n(x)-1/x|=\dfrac{1}{x(nx+1)}\) is unbounded near \(0\) for every \(n\text{.}\) (On \([0,1]\) there is no pointwise limit at all, since \(f_n(0)=n\to\infty\text{.}\))

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
On a nonempty set \(X\), the uniform norm \(\|f\|_\infty\) of a bounded function \(f\colon X\to\mathbb{R}\) is defined as:

\[ \|f\|_\infty = \sup_{x \in X} |f(x)|. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The uniform norm is the supremum of the absolute value of the function over its entire domain.

The red segment marks the largest gap between \(f_n\) and \(f\): that is \(\|f_n-f\|_\infty\). Uniform convergence means it tends to \(0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
For possibly unbounded functions, the same supremum of the error \(|f_n-f|\) may be \(+\infty\); it is an extended error measure rather than a norm on the space of all functions. Uniform convergence means these errors eventually become finite and tend to zero.

  • A sequence of functions \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) converges uniformly to a function \(f\) on \(X\) if and only if:
\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \|f_n - f\|_\infty = 0. \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the function \(f\colon (0,+\infty) \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \(f(x) = \mathrm{e}^{-x}\), we have \(\|f\|_\infty = 1.\)
  • For the function \(g\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \(g(x) = \sin x\), we have \(\|g\|_\infty = 1.\)

docs.title: Union and Intersection of Closed Sets
Proposition
docs.text: For a metric space \((X,d)\) and a collection of closed subsets \((E_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) of \(X\), the countable intersection \(\displaystyle\bigcap_{i=1}^\infty E_i\) and the finite union \(\displaystyle \bigcup_{i=1}^k E_i\) are also closed.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Closed sets are preserved under finite unions and arbitrary intersections.

Infinite unions can break closedness.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both \(X\) and \(\varnothing\) are always closed (and also open).
  • In fact any intersection of closed sets, not just countably many, is closed. This holds for uncountable families as well.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty [-1/n, 1/n] = \{0\}\) is closed. Shrinking closed intervals collapse to a single closed point.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty [0, 1-1/n] = [0,1)\) is not closed. It is missing the endpoint \(1\).

docs.title: Union and Intersection of Open Sets
Proposition
docs.text: For a metric space \((X,d)\) and a collection of open subsets \((E_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) of \(X\), the countable union \(\displaystyle\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty E_i\) and the finite intersection \(\displaystyle \bigcap_{i=1}^k E_i\) are also open.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Open sets are preserved under finite intersections and arbitrary unions.

Infinite intersections can break openness.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both \(X\) and \(\varnothing\) are always open (and also closed).
  • In fact any union of open sets, not just countably many, is open. This holds for uncountable families as well.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty (0, 1-1/n) = (0,1)\) is open. Even though each interval misses the right endpoint, the union still does not include 1.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty (-1/n, 1+1/n) = [0,1]\) is closed. The intersection includes the endpoints 0 and 1, which are not interior points.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For a continuous function \(f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) and any \(\varepsilon > 0\text{,}\) there exists a polynomial \(P\colon [a, b]\to\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\|P-f\|_\infty < \varepsilon\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Any continuous function on a closed interval can be approximated as closely as desired by a polynomial.

Raise the degree \(n\) of the Bernstein polynomial until it lies within \(\varepsilon\) of \(f\) on all of \([0,1]\), even at the kink of \(|x-\tfrac12|\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Polynomials are dense in \(C^0([a,b])\) with respect to the uniform norm: every continuous function on \([a,b]\) is a uniform limit of polynomials.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any polynomial can be "approximated" by itself accurately.
  • Continuous functions, e.g., \(f(x)=\mathrm{e}^x\), over the entirety of \(\mathbb{R}\) aren't always uniformly approximable by polynomials.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Weierstrass function is defined as

\[ f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a^n \cos(b^n x) \]

where \(0<a<1\) and \(ab>1\text{.}\)

Each summand uses a Trigonometric Functions cosine with increasing frequency. The Infinite Series of Functions converges uniformly (by the Weierstrass \(M\)-test) because \(|a^n\cos(b^nx)|\le a^n\) and the geometric series converges for \(0<a<1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Weierstrass function is one of the most famous examples of continuous but nowhere differentiable functions. In the original paper, this function is defined as \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty a^n \cos(b^n \pi x)\) where  \(0<a<1\text{,}\) \(b\) is a positive odd number, and \(ab>1+\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\text{.}\)

The Weierstrass function is based on the earlier Riemann function \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{\sin(n^2 x)}{n^2}\text{,}\) which has also been called the Weierstrass function in some textbooks.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The Weierstrass function is continuous everywhere as long as \(0<a<1\text{.}\)
  • The Weierstrass function is nowhere differentiable if \(ab>1\text{.}\)

The figure plots the finite partial sum \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{8}a^n\cos(b^nx)\) with \(a=1/2\) and \(b=3\). The right panel magnifies the red window and illustrates the repeated roughness; the claim about the infinite limit function is stated above.

With \(0<a<1\) and \(ab>1\), add terms and zoom in: the graph keeps its wiggles at every scale, so it has no tangent anywhere.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^n} \cos(3^n x)\) is a particular Weierstrass function.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Suppose \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) is a sequence of bounded functions on \(X\) such that the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \|f_n\|_\infty\) converges. Then, the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\rightrightarrows f\text{.}\)

The Uniform Norm \(\|f_n\|_\infty\) is the smallest common upper bound on \(|f_n(x)|\) over all \(x\). Summability of these bounds is what makes the tail estimate independent of the input.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The bound \(|f_n(x)|\le M_n\) must hold for every \(x\in X\), with \(M_n\) independent of \(x\), and the numerical series \(\displaystyle \sum_n M_n\) must converge. For partial sums \(\displaystyle S_N=\sum_{n=1}^N f_n\), the same estimate controls every tail: \(\displaystyle |S_M(x)-S_N(x)|\le\sum_{n=N+1}^M M_n\) for all \(x\in X\) and \(M>N\). The right-hand side tends to zero independently of \(x\). Completeness of the real numbers gives a pointwise limit, and the common tail bound makes convergence uniform.

Here \(|f_n(x)|\le M_n=1/n^2\) for every \(x\). The tail bound \(\displaystyle \sum_{n>N}M_n\) is one band width for all \(x\) at once, which gives uniform convergence.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The limit function \(f\) is also bounded on \(X\).
  • Due to the uniform limit theorem, if each \(f_n\) is continuous, then the limit function \(f\) is continuous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• On \(X=\mathbb{R}\), take \(f_n(x)=2^{-n}\cos(3^nx)\). Since \(|\cos(3^nx)|\le1\) for every real \(x\), the bound \(|f_n(x)|\le M_n=2^{-n}\) holds simultaneously for all \(x\). The numerical series of bounds sums to \(1\), so the function series converges uniformly on \(\mathbb{R}\):
\[ \sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}|f(x)-S_N(x)|\le\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty 2^{-n}=2^{-N}. \]

For example, \(N=10\) makes the error at most \(2^{-10}=1/1024\) at every real \(x\), using the same number of terms everywhere.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an inequality constraint written as \(g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\le b_i\), the constraint is binding at a feasible point \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) if

\[ g_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=b_i. \]

It is nonbinding or slack at \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) if

\[ g_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)<b_i. \]

The same idea applies to constraints written in other equivalent sign conventions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A binding constraint is tight at the chosen point. A nonbinding constraint still has room left and does not directly limit the current choice.

At the illustrated optimum, \(g_1(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=3.9\) binds and has multiplier \(\lambda_1>0\), while \(g_2(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=2.2<3\) is slack and has \(\lambda_2=0\). In this example, relaxing the first constraint increases the maximum, whereas relaxing the second does not change it.

The constraint is binding when the optimum lies on the line \(x+y=b\) and slack when the peak is already feasible.

The function \(g_i\) evaluates the constrained quantity at the chosen point. Comparing that value with \(b_i\) through the defining inequality distinguishes equality at the boundary from strict slack inside the allowed region.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Only binding inequality constraints can carry nonzero multipliers in standard Kuhn-Tucker conditions.
  • The set of binding constraints is often called the active set.
  • Changing a nonbinding constraint slightly usually does not change the optimum locally.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(x\le 10\) and the optimum has \(x=10\), the constraint is binding.
  • If \(x+y\le 5\) and the chosen point is \((1,2)\), the constraint is nonbinding because \(1+2<5\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an equality-constrained problem with Lagrangian \(L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda})\) and constraint Jacobian \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\), the bordered Hessian matrix is the block matrix

\[ \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{0} & \boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\\ \boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)^{\top} & \boldsymbol{H}_xL(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast) \end{pmatrix}, \]

with the exact block orientation depending on whether gradients are written as rows or columns.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The bordered Hessian packages the constraint linearization and the objective curvature into one matrix for second-order constrained tests.

The constraint gradient borders the Hessian block; the determinant of the bordered matrix carries the second-order constrained test.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The grey \(m\times m\) zero block corresponds to the multiplier variables; the red \(m\times n\) border contains the constraint gradients.
  • The blue \(n\times n\) Hessian block is taken with respect to the choice variables, so the full matrix has size \((m+n)\times(m+n)\).
  • Determinants of selected bordered submatrices are used in bordered matrix tests.

For \(m<n\) equality constraints with independent gradients at a first-order candidate, the second-order sufficient conditions inspect the last \(n-m\) leading principal minors. Alternating signs starting with \((-1)^{m+1}\) give a strict local maximum; signs all equal to \((-1)^m\) give a strict local minimum. These tests check the curvature of \(L\) along directions tangent to the constraints.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For one constraint \(g(x,y)=0\), a common bordered Hessian has first row and column built from \(g_x\) and \(g_y\).
  • For two equality constraints in three variables, the bordered Hessian has a \(2\) by \(2\) zero block and a \(3\) by \(3\) Hessian block.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(Q(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{x}^{\top} \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\) with \(\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) symmetric, and let the independent linear constraint set be \(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{x}=0\) with \(\boldsymbol{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol{B})=m\). The bordered matrix is

\[ \boldsymbol{H}= \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{0}_m & \boldsymbol{B}\\ \boldsymbol{B}^{\top} & \boldsymbol{A} \end{pmatrix}. \]

Ignore the first \(2m\) leading principal minors. For \(k=2m+1,\ldots,m+n\):

  • If \((-1)^m\det(\boldsymbol{H}_k)>0\) for all relevant \(k\), then \(Q\) is positive definite on the constraint set.
  • If \((-1)^{k-m}\det(\boldsymbol{H}_k)>0\) for all relevant \(k\), then \(Q\) is negative definite on the constraint set.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The bordered matrix test checks curvature after linear constraints remove some directions. It is the constrained version of reading definiteness from determinant signs.

With one constraint in two variables, the sign of \(\det(\boldsymbol{H}_3)\) decides definiteness on the constraint set, matching the sign of the form along the highlighted line \(T\).

The quadratic form measures curvature only along directions satisfying the linear constraints. Full row rank of the constraint matrix ensures that the \(m\) constraint rows impose independent conditions; the bordered determinant rule uses this count.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Definiteness on the whole space can change after restricting to a constraint set.
  • For positive definiteness, all relevant signs match \((-1)^m\).
  • For negative definiteness, relevant signs alternate and the full determinant has sign \((-1)^n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The form \(x_1^2-x_2^2\) is indefinite on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) but positive on the line \(x_1=2x_2\).
  • When \(n=2\) and \(m=1\), there is just one relevant minor: \(\det \boldsymbol{H}<0\) gives positive definiteness of \(Q\) on the constraint line.
  • When \(n=3\) and \(m=1\), inspect \(\det(\boldsymbol{H}_3)\) and \(\det(\boldsymbol{H}_4)\) after ignoring the first two leading minors.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be an interval and let \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be a differentiable curve. Its velocity at \(t_0\) is

\[ \boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t_0)= \begin{pmatrix} \gamma_1'(t_0)\\ \vdots\\ \gamma_n'(t_0) \end{pmatrix}. \]

If \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is an open set containing \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(I)\) and \(f\colon B\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t_0)\in B\), then

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(f\circ\boldsymbol{\gamma})(t_0) &=\boldsymbol{D}f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t_0))\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t_0)\\ &=\boldsymbol{\nabla} f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t_0))^{\top}\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t_0). \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A curve describes motion through a multivariable state space. The chain rule says the value changes by combining the system's velocity with the local sensitivity of the function.

The chain rule gives \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t))\big|_{t=t_0}=\boldsymbol{\nabla} f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t_0))\cdot\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t_0)\). In the figure, the velocity has a positive component along the gradient, so \(f\) increases along the curve at \(t_0\). The grey circles are level sets of \(f\).

Move \(t\): the rate of change of \(f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t))\) (right) equals \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t))^\top\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t)\), the gradient dotted with the velocity.

A path assigns a position to each parameter value. Composing it with \(f\) restricts \(f\) to that motion; differentiating the composition pairs the derivative of \(f\) with the path velocity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The derivative of \(f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t))\) is the total derivative of \(f\) applied to the velocity of \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}\).
  • If the velocity is a unit vector, the formula is a directional derivative.
  • The curve case is the one-dimensional input version of the multivariable chain rule.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) and \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)=(t,2t)\), then \((f\circ\boldsymbol{\gamma})'(t)=10t\).
  • If \(f(x,y)=xy\) and \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)=(\mathrm{e}^t,t^2)\), then \((f\circ\boldsymbol{\gamma})'(t)=\mathrm{e}^t(t^2+2t)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an inequality constraint written as \(c_i(\boldsymbol{x})\le 0\) (for example \(c_i=g_i-b_i\) for a constraint \(g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\le b_i\)) with multiplier \(\lambda_i\ge 0\), complementary slackness is the condition

\[ \lambda_i c_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=0. \]

Equivalently, either the constraint is binding or its multiplier is zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Complementary slackness says that a constraint can matter through its multiplier only when it is actually tight.

On the left, the binding constraint holds back the maximum, with \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} f=\lambda\boldsymbol{\nabla} c\), \(\lambda>0\), and \(c=0\). On the right, the optimum lies in the interior and the multiplier is zero. The grey curves are objective level sets and the blue region is feasible.

Move \(b\) and the peak: either the constraint binds, or its multiplier is \(0\), so the product \(\lambda\,(b-g(\boldsymbol{x}^*))\) is always \(0\).

The inequality fixes the sign of the slack. A strictly negative constraint value forces its multiplier to zero because their product must vanish; equality permits a nonzero multiplier.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(c_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)<0\), then \(\lambda_i=0\).
  • If \(\lambda_i>0\), then \(c_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=0\).
  • The condition is part of the Kuhn-Tucker system for inequality-constrained optimization.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(x\le 4\) is written as \(x-4\le 0\) and the optimum has \(x=3\), then the multiplier must be \(0\).
  • If a multiplier for \(x\le 4\) is positive, then the optimum must satisfy \(x=4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex. A function \(f\colon C\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex if for all \(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in C\) and all \(\lambda\in[0,1]\),

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &f(\lambda \boldsymbol{x}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{y})\\ &\quad\le\lambda f(\boldsymbol{x})+(1-\lambda)f(\boldsymbol{y}). \end{aligned} \]

It is concave if the inequality is reversed.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A convex function lies below the straight interpolation of its values. A concave function lies above that interpolation.

The two graphs illustrate the segment test: on a convex domain \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), apply the defining inequality to every segment joining \(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in C\). Reversing the inequality gives concavity; equivalently, \(f\) is concave if and only if \(-f\) is convex. For a twice continuously differentiable function on an open convex domain, the Hessian test checks positive semidefiniteness for convexity and negative semidefiniteness for concavity.

Along the segment from \(\boldsymbol{y}\) to \(\boldsymbol{x}\) (right), a convex function stays below the chord and a concave one above it.

Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\): for a convex \(f\) the surface along the segment stays below the chord between \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) and \(f(\boldsymbol{y})\).

A convex domain keeps the interpolated input inside the domain, so its function value is defined. The convexity inequality then compares this output with the same weighted interpolation of the endpoint outputs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For convex functions, every local minimum is a global minimum.
  • For concave functions, every local maximum is a global maximum.
  • If \(f\) is strictly convex, it has at most one minimizer on \(C\); if \(f\) is strictly concave, it has at most one maximizer on \(C\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) is convex on \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
  • The function \(u(x,y)=\log x+\log y\) is concave on \((0,\infty)^2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex if for every \(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in C\) and every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\),

\[ \lambda \boldsymbol{x}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{y}\in C. \]

Equivalently, the whole line segment between any two points of \(C\) lies inside \(C\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A convex set has no inward gaps when viewed along straight lines. Moving directly between two feasible points stays feasible.

Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\) inside the set and move \(\lambda\): a set is convex when every such segment stays inside. Find a segment that leaves the L-shape.

Points of real coordinate space are represented by vectors. Their weighted sum parametrizes the straight segment; convexity requires every such point, including both endpoints, to stay in the set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Intersections of convex sets are convex.
  • Euclidean open balls, closed balls, half-spaces, and affine subspaces are convex. The same ball conclusion holds for norm-induced metrics, but not for arbitrary metrics.
  • A feasible region described by linear equality and weak linear inequality constraints is convex.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The set \(\{(x,y)\colon x+y\le 1\}\) is convex because it is a half-space.
  • The unit disk \(\{(x,y)\colon x^2+y^2\le 1\}\) is convex, but the unit circle \(\{(x,y)\colon x^2+y^2=1\}\) is not.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
In a parametric problem, the value function is the optimized objective value

\[ F(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(\boldsymbol{\alpha});\boldsymbol{\alpha}), \]

where \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\) is an optimizer. For equality constraints, define

\[ L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\mu};\boldsymbol{\alpha})=f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\alpha})+\sum_j\mu_jh_j(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\alpha}). \]

If smooth optimizer and multiplier functions satisfy the first-order conditions, then

\[ \frac{\partial F}{\partial\alpha_\ell}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\alpha_\ell}\big(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}),\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha});\boldsymbol{\alpha}\big). \]

For mixed constraints, the same formula holds with the Lagrangian including the binding inequalities and equality constraints, provided the relevant bordered Hessian is nonsingular and the active set is smooth. In the special equality case \(h_j(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\alpha_j-\widetilde h_j(\boldsymbol{x})\) with \(f\) independent of \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\), the multiplier is the shadow price:

\[ \frac{\partial F}{\partial\alpha_j}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\widetilde\mu_j(\boldsymbol{\alpha}). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The envelope theorem computes how the best attainable value changes when a parameter changes. It avoids separately differentiating every movement of the optimizer.

In the illustrated example, the feasible choices do not depend on \(\alpha\), and the value function \(V(\alpha)=\max_x f(x;\alpha)\) (written \(F\) in the theorem above) is the upper envelope of the grey curves obtained by fixing \(x\). At \(\alpha_0\), it touches the curve for \(x^\ast(\alpha_0)\) and shares its slope: \(V'(\alpha_0)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha}(x^\ast(\alpha_0);\alpha_0)\). The theorem above gives the corresponding formula when the constraints depend on the parameter.

The derivative of the optimal value \(F(\alpha)\) equals the partial derivative of the Lagrangian with respect to \(\alpha\) at the optimum, here the multiplier \(\mu\).

The equality-constraint Lagrange method supplies the stationarity equations. Applying the implicit function theorem to those equations and the constraints can give locally smooth optimizer and multiplier functions when the relevant bordered Hessian is nonsingular. The chain-rule terms involving optimizer movements then cancel by stationarity and differentiated feasibility.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The value function records the optimum as a function of parameters.
  • The envelope derivative is the direct parameter derivative of the Lagrangian at the optimal solution.
  • A shadow price is the marginal value of relaxing a constraint in the stated equality-constraint setup.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x;\alpha)=\alpha x-x^2\), the envelope derivative is \(x^\ast(\alpha)\).
  • In utility maximization with income as a parameter, the multiplier on the budget equation measures marginal utility of income.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In an equation system \(\boldsymbol{F}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=0\), the variables in \(\boldsymbol{x}\) are called exogenous variables if they are treated as freely chosen inputs. The variables in \(\boldsymbol{y}\) are called endogenous variables if the equation system is used to solve for them as functions of \(\boldsymbol{x}\).

When possible, the implicit function theorem gives a local function \(\boldsymbol{g}\) such that

\[ \boldsymbol{F}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}))=0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Exogenous variables are the knobs set from outside the system. Endogenous variables are the quantities the system determines in response.

The model takes the exogenous variables as inputs and solves for the endogenous variables. Under the local invertibility assumptions of the implicit function theorem, \(m\) equations determine \(m\) endogenous variables locally once the inputs are fixed. The split is a modelling choice: prices are endogenous in an equilibrium model but exogenous for a price-taker.

The local function assigns endogenous outputs to exogenous inputs. The partial Jacobian with respect to the endogenous variables is the block whose invertibility lets the implicit function theorem solve for those outputs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The distinction depends on how the equation system is being used, not only on the symbols.
  • The implicit function theorem requires the partial Jacobian with respect to the endogenous variables to be invertible in the square case.
  • Comparative statics studies how endogenous variables change when exogenous variables are perturbed, that is, the derivatives of the local function \(\boldsymbol{g}\) above.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(x+y=10\), if \(x\) is chosen externally, then \(y=10-x\) is endogenous.
  • In supply and demand equilibrium, a tax can be exogenous while price and quantity are endogenous equilibrium variables.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, and let \(f,g_i,h_j\) be continuously differentiable on \(A\). For minimization, write the inequalities as \(g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\le0\); for maximization, write them as \(g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\ge0\). With equalities \(h_j(\boldsymbol{x})=0\), define the generalized Lagrangian

\[ \begin{aligned} \Lambda(\boldsymbol{x},\lambda_0,\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\mu}) &= \lambda_0 f(\boldsymbol{x})+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\\ &\quad+\sum_j\mu_j h_j(\boldsymbol{x}). \end{aligned} \]

If \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) is a local constrained optimum, then there exist multipliers with \(\lambda_0\in\{0,1\}\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\), and \((\lambda_0,\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\mu})\neq0\) such that stationarity, feasibility, and complementary slackness hold.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This method avoids a separate regularity check by adding a multiplier on the objective itself. The extra case captures points where the active constraints are degenerate.

The illustrated feasible arc satisfies \(h(\boldsymbol{x})=c\) and \(g(\boldsymbol{x})\le3.1\). Both constraints bind at \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\), where the objective gradient is a combination of the active constraint gradients with the appropriate multiplier signs. The theorem above specifies the normalization and regularity requirements for the multipliers.

The mixed-constraint method is recovered when the objective multiplier can be normalized to one. The nondegenerate constraint qualification rules out an abnormal candidate with zero objective multiplier: independence of the active constraint gradients would then force every multiplier to vanish.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\lambda_0=1\), the regular first-order necessary conditions are recovered.
  • If \(\lambda_0=0\), the condition signals linear dependence among active constraint gradients.
  • The method keeps nonregular feasible points inside the theorem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a regular optimum, choosing \(\lambda_0=1\) gives the usual Lagrangian conditions.
  • If active constraint gradients are linearly dependent, a solution may appear with \(\lambda_0=0\) and nonzero constraint multipliers.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(f\colon A\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\in A\).

  • \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) is a global maximum if \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\ge f(\boldsymbol{x})\) for all \(\boldsymbol{x}\in A\).
  • \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) is a global minimum if \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\le f(\boldsymbol{x})\) for all \(\boldsymbol{x}\in A\).

The extremum is strict if the inequality is strict for all \(\boldsymbol{x}\in A\setminus\{\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A global extremum compares the candidate with every feasible point. Strictness means there is no other feasible point with the same optimal value.

In the figure, the global minimum occurs at the boundary point \(0\) and the global maximum at \(c\). The points \(a\) and \(b\) are only a local maximum and minimum, respectively, because their comparisons use a neighbourhood rather than the whole feasible set.

On the square \([-2,2]^2\) the largest and smallest values may sit on the boundary rather than at a critical point.

The extreme value theorem on compact sets gives an existence condition: a continuous function on a nonempty compact feasible set attains both extrema. The definition itself does not guarantee attainment on an arbitrary set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A strict global maximum or minimum has a unique optimizer.
  • A continuous function on a compact feasible set attains both a global maximum and a global minimum.
  • A global extremum is automatically local when neighbourhoods inside the feasible set are considered.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=-(x^2+y^2)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\), \((0,0)\) is a strict global maximizer.
  • For \(f(x,y)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\), every point with \(x=0\) is a global minimizer.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be a scalar-valued function whose second-order partial derivatives exist at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in E\). The Hessian matrix of \(f\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &\boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\\ &=\begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1^2}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) & \cdots & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1\partial x_n}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_n\partial x_1}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) & \cdots & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_n^2}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) \end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} \]

The entry in row \(i\) and column \(j\) is the second partial derivative with respect to \(x_i\) and \(x_j\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Hessian collects all second-order bending information of a scalar function at one point. It is the multivariable analogue of the second derivative in one-variable calculus.

The blue diagonal entries are the pure second partials, measuring curvature along the coordinate axes. The mixed partials appear in symmetric pairs when \(f\) is \(C^2\). When \(f\) is \(C^2\) on an open neighbourhood of \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), the second-order approximation is \(f(\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h})=f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)+\boldsymbol{\nabla} f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\cdot \boldsymbol{h}+\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{h}^{\top} \boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}+o(\|\boldsymbol{h}\|^2)\). At a stationary point, positive or negative definiteness gives a strict local minimum or maximum, and an indefinite Hessian gives a saddle; semidefinite cases can be inconclusive.

Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\): the Hessian collects the second-order partial derivatives there, and its eigenvalues describe how the level curves bend.

Move \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) and read \(\boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\): at the marked critical points its definiteness matches the shape of the surface.

Arranging the second derivatives in a matrix makes curvature along a displacement accessible through the quadratic form \(\boldsymbol{h}^{\top}\boldsymbol{H}_f\boldsymbol{h}\). For a \(C^2\) function, this is the second-order term in the local Taylor approximation, up to its factor \(1/2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
For the second-order tests below, assume \(f\) is \(C^2\) on an open neighbourhood of \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) and \(\boldsymbol{\nabla}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\boldsymbol{0}\). Mere existence of the Hessian at one point is insufficient.

  • If \(f\) is \(C^2\) near \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), then the Hessian is symmetric.
  • At a critical point (for differentiable \(f\) the same as a stationary point, \(\boldsymbol{\nabla}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\boldsymbol{0}\)), a positive definite Hessian gives a strict local minimum.
  • At a critical point, a negative definite Hessian gives a strict local maximum.
  • At a critical point, an indefinite Hessian gives a saddle point.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+2xy+3y^2\), the Hessian is \(\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&6\end{pmatrix}\) at every point.
  • For \(f(x,y)=x^3+2xy^2-y^3\), the Hessian at \((1,1)\) is \(\begin{pmatrix}6&4\\4&-2\end{pmatrix}\).

docs.title: Hessian Test for Convexity and Concavity
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and open, and let \(f\colon C\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable.

Then \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is positive semidefinite for every \(\boldsymbol{x}\in C\).

The function \(f\) is concave on \(C\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is negative semidefinite for every \(\boldsymbol{x}\in C\).

If \(\boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is positive definite for every \(\boldsymbol{x}\in C\), then \(f\) is strictly convex. If \(\boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is negative definite for every \(\boldsymbol{x}\in C\), then \(f\) is strictly concave.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Hessian test turns the geometric question of bending upward or downward into a matrix definiteness check at every point of the domain.

For \(-x^2-xy-y^2\) the Hessian is negative definite everywhere, so the function is strictly concave. Other examples fail the test somewhere.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Positive semidefinite Hessian everywhere is equivalent to convexity under the stated smoothness and convex-domain assumptions.
  • Negative semidefinite Hessian everywhere is equivalent to concavity under the same assumptions.
  • Positive definiteness everywhere is sufficient for strict convexity, but not necessary in every case.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\), \(\boldsymbol{H}_f=2\boldsymbol{I}\), so \(f\) is strictly convex.
  • For \(f(x,y)=-(x^2+y^2)\), \(\boldsymbol{H}_f=-2\boldsymbol{I}\), so \(f\) is strictly concave.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A higher-order partial derivative is obtained by differentiating a partial derivative again with respect to one or more variables. For example, for \(f\colon A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\),

\[ f_{x_i x_j x_k}(\boldsymbol{a})= \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_k} \right) \right)(\boldsymbol{a}) \]

is a third-order partial derivative, when all indicated derivatives exist. In this notation the derivative written closest to \(f\) (here \(\partial/\partial x_k\)) is taken first; many texts instead read subscripts from left to right, so that \(f_{xy}=(f_x)_y\text{.}\) For \(C^3\) functions both readings give the same value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Higher-order partial derivatives measure how earlier rates of change themselves change as one moves in chosen coordinate directions.

The rows hold the partials of order \(1\), \(2\) and \(3\). \(f_{x_ix_jx_k}=\partial_{x_i}\big(\partial_{x_j}(\partial_{x_k}f)\big)\): there are \(n^k\) partials of order \(k\) in \(n\) variables. For \(C^k\) functions the order of differentiation does not matter, so many of them coincide.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Second-order partial derivatives form the Hessian matrix when they exist.
  • Third-order partial derivatives can be arranged in a three-dimensional array.
  • Continuity assumptions are usually needed before changing the order of differentiation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2y^3\), \(f_{xy}=6xy^2\) and \(f_{xyy}=12xy\).
  • For \(f(x,y,z)=xyz^2\), \(f_{xyz}=2z\) and \(f_{xzz}=2y\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(f\) have continuous partial derivatives up to order \(k\) on an open neighbourhood of \(\boldsymbol{a}\). Then any two \(k\)th-order partial derivatives that differentiate with respect to the same variables the same number of times are equal at \(\boldsymbol{a}\).

For third-order derivatives this means, for example,

\[ \begin{aligned} f_{xyz}(\boldsymbol{a})&=f_{xzy}(\boldsymbol{a})\\ &=f_{yxz}(\boldsymbol{a})=f_{yzx}(\boldsymbol{a})\\ &=f_{zxy}(\boldsymbol{a})=f_{zyx}(\boldsymbol{a}) \end{aligned} \]

whenever the required third-order partial derivatives are continuous near \(\boldsymbol{a}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
When the function is smooth enough, only the number of times each direction is used matters, not the order in which the differentiations are performed.

The top row shows the eight formal third-order partials in two variables. For a \(C^3\) function, they fall into four groups according to how often each variable is used, for example \(f_{xxy}=f_{xyx}=f_{yxx}\). More generally, symmetry reduces the \(n^k\) ordered partials of a \(C^k\) function to at most \(\binom{n+k-1}{k}\) distinct values.

The differentiability class \(C^k\) packages the hypothesis that all partial derivatives through order \(k\) exist and are continuous. This regularity permits repeated interchange of the order of differentiation; existence of derivatives alone is insufficient.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The second-order case is the usual symmetry of mixed partial derivatives.
  • For a sufficiently smooth scalar function, the third derivative tensor is symmetric under permutations of its indices.
  • Without the needed continuity assumptions, mixed partials can fail to agree.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y,z)=x^2yz^3\), the derivatives \(f_{xyz}\), \(f_{xzy}\), and \(f_{zyx}\) agree because \(f\) is a polynomial.
  • For \(f(x,y)=\mathrm{e}^{xy}\), \(f_{xxy}=f_{xyx}=f_{yxx}\) at every point because all partial derivatives are continuous.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
In a system \(\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=0\), the variables \(\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) are treated as exogenous and \(\boldsymbol{y}\in\mathbb{R}^m\) as endogenous. For \(\boldsymbol{G}\colon A\to\mathbb{R}^m\), define the partial Jacobians \(\boldsymbol{D}_x\boldsymbol{G}\) and \(\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{G}\) by differentiating with respect to the \(\boldsymbol{x}\)-block and \(\boldsymbol{y}\)-block.

Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\) be open and let \(\boldsymbol{G}\colon A\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be \(C^1\). Suppose \((\boldsymbol{x}_0,\boldsymbol{y}_0)\in A\), \(\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\boldsymbol{y}_0)=0\), and

\[ \det(\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\boldsymbol{y}_0))\neq 0. \]

Then there is a neighbourhood \(B\) of \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) and a \(C^1\) function \(\boldsymbol{\varphi}\colon B\to\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \(\boldsymbol{\varphi}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\boldsymbol{y}_0\) and \(\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\varphi}(\boldsymbol{x}))=0\) for all \(\boldsymbol{x}\in B\). After shrinking \(B\) if necessary, there is a neighbourhood \(W\) of \(\boldsymbol{y}_0\) such that, for each \(\boldsymbol{x}\in B\), \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{\varphi}(\boldsymbol{x})\) is the only solution of \(\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=0\) in \(W\). Moreover,

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{\varphi}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\\ &=-(\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\boldsymbol{y}_0))^{-1}\boldsymbol{D}_x\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\boldsymbol{y}_0). \end{aligned} \]

For one equation in two variables, this reduces to \(\varphi'(x_0)=-G_x(x_0,y_0)/G_y(x_0,y_0)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The theorem says that a regular system of equations can locally be solved for the variables that must adjust. It also gives the local response of those adjusting variables when the chosen variables change.

For the circle \(G(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1=0\), the point \((x_0,y_0)=(0,1)\) has \(G_y(x_0,y_0)=2\ne0\). In a neighbourhood of that point, the circle is the graph \(y=g(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}\), and \(g'(x)=-x/y\). The theorem above gives the corresponding derivative formula for systems of equations.

Move along \(x^2+y^2=1\): wherever \(D_yG\ne0\) the curve is locally a graph \(y=\varphi(x)\) with slope \(-D_xG/D_yG\). At \(y=0\) this fails.

The Jacobian contains the first-order effects of the equation variables. Its endogenous block must be invertible to solve locally for changes in the endogenous variables; a singular block does not meet the theorem's hypothesis.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The determinant condition says the endogenous block is locally pinned down by the equations.
  • The theorem gives local existence, differentiability, and a derivative formula.
  • The one-equation case is the familiar slope formula for an implicit curve.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(G(x,y)=y-x^2\), the theorem gives \(y=\varphi(x)=x^2\) because \(D_yG=1\).
  • For \(G(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1\) near \((0,1)\), the theorem gives the upper circle locally as a function of \(x\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A linear constraint system

\[ \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b} \]

with \(\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has independent constraints if the rows of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) are linearly independent, equivalently

\[ \operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{A}=m. \]

For nonlinear equality constraints \(g_1(\boldsymbol{x})=0,\ldots,g_m(\boldsymbol{x})=0\), the corresponding local condition at \(\boldsymbol{a}\) is that the gradients \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} g_1(\boldsymbol{a}),\ldots,\boldsymbol{\nabla} g_m(\boldsymbol{a})\) are linearly independent.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Independent constraints each remove a genuinely new direction. Dependent constraints repeat information and can make multiplier tests misleading.

On the right, the rows of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) are dependent and \(\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{A}=1\). The corresponding parallel lines either have no common solution or coincide along a whole line. On the left, the two independent constraints have rank \(2\) and meet at one point.

The rank counts independent rows. Equality to \(m\) means that no constraint equation is an algebraic consequence of the others; for nonlinear constraints the same check applies to their gradients at the chosen point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(m\) independent equality constraints in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the linearized feasible directions (the null space of the constraint matrix or Jacobian) form an \((n-m)\)-dimensional space, by the rank-nullity theorem.
  • Independence is a rank condition on the constraint Jacobian.
  • Nondegenerate constraint qualification is the nonlinear optimization version of this idea.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The constraints \(x+y=1\) and \(2x+2y=2\) are dependent because the second repeats the first.
  • The constraints \(x+y=1\) and \(x-y=0\) are independent because the matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\) has rank \(2\).
