docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable near \(\boldsymbol{a}\), and write \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{a})\) for its \(m\times n\) Jacobian matrix at \(\boldsymbol{a}\).

If \(\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{a})=n\) and \(n\le m\), then \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is locally injective near \(\boldsymbol{a}\).

If \(\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{a})=m\) and \(m\le n\), then \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is locally surjective near \(\boldsymbol{a}\).

If \(n=m\) and \(\det \boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{a})\neq 0\), then \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is locally bijective near \(\boldsymbol{a}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Full rank of the Jacobian tells which local behaviour survives under linearization: no collapsing for full column rank, no missing nearby outputs for full row rank, and a local inverse in the square case.

In the top example, \(n=1\le m=2\) and \(\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}=1\). Distinct nearby inputs have distinct images, illustrating local injectivity.

In the bottom example, \(m=1\le n=2\) and \(\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{D}f=1\). The map covers a whole interval of nearby target values, illustrating local surjectivity.

Local injectivity and surjectivity describe neighbourhoods, rather than the entire domain and codomain. Full column rank prevents nearby inputs from sharing an output; full row rank permits every sufficiently nearby output to be reached.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The square case is the multivariable inverse function theorem.
  • Full column rank gives a locally one-to-one parametrized surface or curve.
  • Full row rank means nearby target values can be reached by nearby inputs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\boldsymbol{f}(t)=(t,t^2)\), \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(t)=(1,2t)^{\top}\) has rank \(1\), so the curve is locally injective.
  • For \(f(x,y)=x+y\), \(\boldsymbol{D}f=(1\ 1)\) has rank \(1\), so the map is locally surjective onto \(\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and let \(f\) and the finitely many constraint functions \(g_i\) be \(C^1\) on \(A\). For the maximization problem

\[ \begin{aligned} &\max_{\boldsymbol{x}\in A} f(\boldsymbol{x})\\ &\text{subject to}\quad g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\le b_i,\qquad x_h\ge0, \end{aligned} \]

define the Kuhn-Tucker Lagrangian

\[ \widetilde L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda})=f(\boldsymbol{x})+\sum_i\lambda_i(b_i-g_i(\boldsymbol{x})). \]

Assume the nondegenerate constraint qualification holds for all active inequalities, including the active bounds \(-x_h\le0\): their gradients at the candidate point are linearly independent. At such a regular local maximum, there exists \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast\ge0\) such that

\[ \begin{gathered} \frac{\partial \widetilde L}{\partial x_h}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast)\le0,\\ x_h^\ast\frac{\partial \widetilde L}{\partial x_h}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast)=0,\qquad x_h^\ast\ge0, \end{gathered} \]

and

\[ \begin{gathered} \frac{\partial \widetilde L}{\partial \lambda_i}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast)\ge0,\\ \lambda_i^\ast\frac{\partial \widetilde L}{\partial \lambda_i}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast)=0,\qquad \lambda_i^\ast\ge0. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Nonnegative variables can be either interior or stuck at the boundary. The Kuhn-Tucker conditions encode that boundary logic together with ordinary inequality slackness.

In this maximization example, \(x_1^\ast>0\) gives \(\partial L/\partial x_1=0\), while \(x_2^\ast=0\) gives \(\partial L/\partial x_2\le0\) and \(x_2^\ast(\partial L/\partial x_2)=0\). The inequality \(g(\boldsymbol{x})\le b\) is slack, so its multiplier is \(\lambda=0\); only the nonnegativity of \(x_2\) binds. The objective would increase by moving below the \(x_1\)-axis, but that move is infeasible.

At a corner two constraints bind at once, each with its own nonnegative multiplier.

These conditions specialize the inequality-constrained maximization method to coordinate restrictions. Treating \(x_h\ge0\) as inequalities gives a zero derivative for a positive coordinate and a nonpositive derivative at a coordinate fixed at zero, with the stated maximization convention.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(x_h^\ast>0\), the derivative condition for that variable becomes equality.
  • If a multiplier is positive, the corresponding ordinary inequality constraint is binding.
  • The conditions are necessary at regular local maxima.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(x_h^\ast>0\), then \(x_h^\ast\partial\widetilde L/\partial x_h=0\) forces \(\partial\widetilde L/\partial x_h=0\).
  • If \(\lambda_i^\ast>0\), then \(\partial\widetilde L/\partial\lambda_i=0\), so the constraint is binding.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an optimization problem with equality constraints \(h_i(\boldsymbol{x})=0\) and inequality constraints \(g_j(\boldsymbol{x})\le 0\), a Kuhn-Tucker Lagrangian is an expression of the form

\[ \begin{aligned} L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\mu}) &= f(\boldsymbol{x}) +\sum_i \lambda_i h_i(\boldsymbol{x})\\ &\quad+\sum_j \mu_j g_j(\boldsymbol{x}), \end{aligned} \]

with sign restrictions such as \(\mu_j\ge 0\) or \(\mu_j\le 0\) depending on the maximization or minimization convention.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Kuhn-Tucker Lagrangian brings the objective and all active constraint pressures into one stationarity expression.

At the illustrated constrained maximum, the gradient points outwards, towards the infeasible unconstrained maximum. Writing the constraints as \(g_i( oldsymbol{x})\le b_i\) and using the maximization convention \(L=f-\sum_i\lambda_i(g_i-b_i)\) with \(\lambda_i\ge0\), the multipliers satisfy \(\displaystyle oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)=\sum_i\lambda_i oldsymbol{ abla} g_i( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\), and \(\lambda_i(g_i( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)-b_i)=0\). Any slack inequality has multiplier zero.

At the optimum \( oldsymbol{ abla} f\) is a nonnegative multiple of the gradients of the binding constraints.

This extends the Lagrangian function by including inequality residuals. Their multiplier signs depend on how the residual and optimization direction are written; complementary slackness prevents a strictly slack constraint from contributing a nonzero multiplier.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Equality multipliers are usually unrestricted in sign.
  • Inequality multipliers have sign restrictions tied to the chosen convention.
  • Complementary slackness connects each inequality multiplier to whether its constraint is binding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For maximizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(g(x)\le 0\), one common convention uses \(L=f-\mu g\) with \(\mu\ge 0\).
  • For a nonnegativity condition \(x_i\ge 0\), the Kuhn-Tucker system may include a multiplier attached to that boundary condition.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A Lagrange multiplier is an auxiliary variable attached to a constraint in a Lagrangian. For equality constraints \(h_j(\boldsymbol{x})=c_j\), a typical course convention writes

\[ L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\mu})=f(\boldsymbol{x})+\sum_{j=1}^m\mu_j(c_j-h_j(\boldsymbol{x})). \]

At a regular constrained optimum, the multipliers make the gradient of the objective a linear combination of the gradients of the active constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A multiplier records how a constraint enters the first-order trade-off at a candidate optimum. In parameterized problems, it can also measure the marginal value of relaxing a constraint.

At the illustrated optimum, \( oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)=\mu oldsymbol{ abla} h( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)\), so the level set of \(f\) is tangent to the constraint curve. The figure maximizes \(f( oldsymbol{x})=-(x_1-3)^2-(x_2-2.5)^2\), whose level sets are circles about \((3,2.5)\), subject to \(x_1+x_2=3\). The optimum is \( oldsymbol{x}^\ast=(1.75,1.25)\), where \( oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)=(2.5,2.5)=2.5\, oldsymbol{ abla} h( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)\), so \(\mu=2.5\). Under the sensitivity assumptions stated for the envelope theorem, \(\mu=\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}c\) measures the marginal value of changing the constraint level. In the figure, the optimal value for level \(c\) is \(V(c)=- frac{1}{2}(5.5-c)^2\), and \(V'(3)=2.5=\mu\).

Move the point until the arrows \( oldsymbol{ abla} f\) and \( oldsymbol{ abla} h\) line up (both are drawn to the same scale). The factor between them is the multiplier \(\mu\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Equality multipliers may be positive, negative, or zero.
  • Inequality multipliers have sign restrictions under the course convention.
  • In the envelope theorem, some multipliers can be interpreted as shadow prices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Maximize \(xy\) subject to \(x+y=10\). With \(L(x,y,\mu)=xy+\mu(10-x-y)\), stationarity gives \(y-\mu=0\) and \(x-\mu=0\), so \(x=y=\mu\); the constraint then gives \(x=y=5\) and \(\mu=5\), with maximum \(25\). Raising the budget from \(10\) to \(11\) raises the maximum to \(5.5^2=30.25\), an increase of \(5.25\approx\mu\): the multiplier is the marginal value of the budget.
  • Minimize \(x^2+y^2\) subject to \(x+y=1\). For \(L(x,y,\mu)=x^2+y^2+\mu(1-x-y)\), stationarity gives \(2x-\mu=0\) and \(2y-\mu=0\), so \(x=y=\mu/2\). The constraint gives \(\mu=1\) and \(x=y=\tfrac{1}{2}\), with minimum value \(\tfrac{1}{2}\). For level \(c\) the minimum is \(c^2/2\), whose derivative at \(c=1\) is \(1=\mu\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a constrained optimization problem with objective \(f\) and equality constraints \(h_j(\boldsymbol{x})=c_j\), a Lagrangian function is an auxiliary function that combines the objective and the constraints with multiplier variables. Under the course convention for equality constraints,

\[ L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\mu})=f(\boldsymbol{x})+\sum_{j=1}^m \mu_j(c_j-h_j(\boldsymbol{x})). \]

For inequality constraints, the same idea is used with sign conventions chosen so that multiplier restrictions match the direction of the inequality.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Lagrangian rewrites a constrained problem as one expression whose stationary points encode both the objective trade-off and the constraint equations.

At the illustrated candidate \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\), the gradients of \(f\) and \(h\) are parallel. At the orange point they are not, so moving along \(h(\boldsymbol{x})=c\) can improve \(f\). The differentiability and rank assumptions for the multiplier test are stated in the equality-constraint method.

Setting all partial derivatives of \(L(x,y,\mu)\) to zero recovers both the tangency condition and the constraint itself.

The Lagrangian is a function of both the decision variables and the multipliers. Partial differentiation with respect to a multiplier recovers its constraint residual; differentiation with respect to a decision variable gives the corresponding stationarity equation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Differentiating with respect to the multiplier variables recovers the constraints.
  • Differentiating with respect to the choice variables gives the first-order balance between objective gradients and constraint gradients.
  • Changing the sign convention changes multiplier signs, but not the underlying candidate points when handled consistently.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\max xy\) subject to \(x+y=10\), one convention uses \(L(x,y,\mu)=xy+\mu(10-x-y)\).
  • For \(\min x^2+y^2\) subject to \(x+y=1\), one can use \(L(x,y,\mu)=x^2+y^2+\mu(1-x-y)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon A\to B\) be a function. A left inverse of \(f\) is a function \(\ell\colon B\to A\) such that

\[ \ell\circ f=\operatorname{id}_A. \]

A right inverse of \(f\) is a function \(r\colon B\to A\) such that

\[ f\circ r=\operatorname{id}_B. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A left inverse undoes the function after the function is applied. A right inverse gives a way to hit every target value.

The left inverse sends each image point back to its original input; it can take arbitrary values on unused points of \(B\). The right inverse chooses one preimage for every point of \(B\).

The equations use composition: applying \(\ell\) after \(f\) must recover the identity function on the input set for a left inverse. A right inverse instead makes applying \(f\) after \(r\) recover the identity on the output set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A function has a left inverse only if it is injective.
  • A function has a right inverse only if it is surjective, assuming the usual choice of a preimage for every output.
  • A two-sided inverse is both a left inverse and a right inverse.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The inclusion \(\boldsymbol{i}\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^2\), \(\boldsymbol{i}(t)=(t,0)\), has a left inverse \(\ell(x,y)=x\).
  • The projection \(p\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\), \(p(x,y)=x\), has a right inverse \(\boldsymbol{r}(t)=(t,0)\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon A\to\mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\operatorname{int}(A)\) with \(\boldsymbol{b}_0=\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\).

  • \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is locally injective at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) if nearby equations \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{b}\) have at most one nearby solution.
  • \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is locally surjective at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) if nearby equations \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{b}\) have at least one nearby solution.
  • \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is locally bijective at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) if nearby equations \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{b}\) have exactly one nearby solution.

If \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is \(C^1\), then (see the Jacobian rank theorem) full column rank of \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) implies local injectivity, full row rank implies local surjectivity, and square full rank implies local bijectivity.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
These local properties describe whether nearby outputs have no duplicate inputs, no missing inputs, or exactly one input. The Jacobian rank gives the local linear signal for these behaviours.

The function \(f(x)=x^2\) is locally bijective near \(x_0=1\), where \(f'(1)=2\ne0\): each value close to \(f(1)\) has exactly one preimage close to \(1\). At the fold \(x_0=0\), nearby values instead have two preimages or none.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Full column rank gives local uniqueness of nearby solutions.
  • Full row rank gives local existence of nearby solutions.
  • If \(n=m\) and \(\det(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0))\neq0\), the function is locally bijective at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The map \(f(x,y)=x\) is locally surjective from \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) at every point.
  • The map \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)=(x,y,x+y)\) is locally injective because its Jacobian has full column rank.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(f\colon A\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\in A\).

  • \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) is a local maximum if there is a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) such that \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\ge f(\boldsymbol{x})\) for all \(\boldsymbol{x}\in U\cap A\).
  • \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) is a local minimum if there is a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) such that \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\le f(\boldsymbol{x})\) for all \(\boldsymbol{x}\in U\cap A\).

The extremum is strict if the inequality is strict for all nearby feasible points other than \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A local extremum is best only against nearby feasible alternatives. It may or may not be globally best.

The red level sets decrease in value as one moves away from the local maximum, while the blue ones increase away from the local minimum. Only nearby feasible points in \(U\cap A\) are compared. An interior local extremum of a \(C^1\) function is stationary, but the Hessian may be inconclusive when it is semidefinite.

The marked critical points are classified by their Hessians: with the colours of the legend for minima, maxima and saddles.

Marked points are critical points, classified by the Hessian; move \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) onto one and the tangent plane becomes horizontal.

An open metric ball can specify the neighbourhood: choose a radius \(r>0\) and compare the candidate only with feasible points less than \(r\) away. Intersecting the ball with the feasible set also covers candidates on its boundary.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Interior local extrema of differentiable unconstrained problems must satisfy a first-order necessary condition.
  • Second-order conditions use the Hessian to classify critical points when possible.
  • Local extrema need not be unique and need not be global.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\), \((0,0)\) is a strict local minimum.
  • For \(f(x)=x^3-3x\), \(x=-1\) is a local maximum and \(x=1\) is a local minimum.

docs.title: Method of Lagrange for Constrained Minimization
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, and let the objective \(f\) and all constraint functions \(g_i,h_j\) be continuously differentiable on \(A\). For

\[ \begin{aligned} &\min_{\boldsymbol{x}\in A} f(\boldsymbol{x})\\ &\text{subject to}\quad g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\ge b_i,\quad h_j(\boldsymbol{x})=c_j, \end{aligned} \]

the course convention writes the inequality part as \(b_i-g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\le0\) and defines

\[ \begin{aligned} L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\mu})&=f(\boldsymbol{x})+\sum_i\lambda_i(b_i-g_i(\boldsymbol{x}))\\ &\quad+\sum_j\mu_j(c_j-h_j(\boldsymbol{x})). \end{aligned} \]

If \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) is a local constrained minimizer, then either nondegenerate constraint qualification (NDCQ) fails or there are multipliers satisfying

\[ \begin{gathered} \boldsymbol{\nabla}_xL=0,\quad \lambda_i^\ast(g_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)-b_i)=0,\\ g_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\ge b_i,\quad h_j(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=c_j,\quad \lambda_i^\ast\ge0. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
For minimization, the inequality is written so the same nonnegative multiplier convention can be used. The resulting conditions are still only a candidate filter.

In the illustrated minimization problem, \(g_i( oldsymbol{x})\ge b_i\) and the nonnegative multipliers satisfy \(\displaystyle oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)=\sum_i\lambda_i oldsymbol{ abla} g_i( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)+\sum_j\mu_j oldsymbol{ abla} h_j( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) and \(\lambda_i(g_i( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)-b_i)=0\). At the boundary optimum, the gradient points into the feasible side. Equivalently, one can maximize \(-f\) under the same constraints.

For \(\min x^2+y^2\) on \(x+y=c\) the smallest level circle touching the line marks the optimum, with \( oldsymbol{ abla} f=\mu oldsymbol{ abla} h\) there.

The mixed-constraint method separates equality multipliers from signed inequality multipliers. Passing from maximization to minimization requires the residual convention written above; multiplier signs cannot be copied without checking that convention.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sign of the inequality term in the Lagrangian depends on the feasible side of the constraint.
  • Nonbinding inequalities have zero multipliers.
  • Equality multipliers remain unrestricted.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\min \mathrm{e}^{x-y}\) subject to \(x^2+y^2\ge4\), use \(L=\mathrm{e}^{x-y}+\lambda(4-x^2-y^2)\).
  • If \(x+y>1\) at a local minimizer subject to \(x+y\ge1\), complementary slackness forces the multiplier on that constraint to be zero.

docs.title: Method of Lagrange for Equality Constraints
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open. Consider

\[ \begin{aligned} &\max_{\boldsymbol{x}\in A} f(\boldsymbol{x})\\ &\text{subject to}\quad h_j(\boldsymbol{x})=c_j,\ j=1,\ldots,m, \end{aligned} \]

with \(C^1\) data and \(m<n\). Define

\[ L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\mu})=f(\boldsymbol{x})+\sum_{j=1}^m\mu_j(c_j-h_j(\boldsymbol{x})). \]

If \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) is a local maximum or minimum subject to the constraints, then either nondegenerate constraint qualification (NDCQ) fails at \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) or there exists \(\boldsymbol{\mu}^\ast\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that

\[ \boldsymbol{\nabla} L(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\mu}^\ast)=0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A regular equality-constrained optimum must be a critical point of the Lagrangian. Nonregular feasible points are kept as candidates rather than thrown away.

At the illustrated candidate \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\), the gradients of \(f\) and \(h\) are parallel. At the orange point they are not, so moving along \(h(\boldsymbol{x})=c\) can improve \(f\). The stationarity and rank assumptions for the multiplier test are given above.

Slide the point along \(x+y=c\): \(f\) is largest where its level curve touches the line, which is where \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} f\) is a multiple \(\mu\boldsymbol{\nabla} h\) of the constraint normal.

Only points on the line \(x+y=c\) count: the red curve is \(f\) restricted to the constraint, and its highest point is the constrained maximum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The theorem gives necessary, not sufficient, conditions.
  • Stationarity in the multiplier variables recovers the equality constraints.
  • Equality constraints can be written on either side because they have no direction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Maximizing \(xy\) subject to \(x+y=10\) gives \(L=xy+\mu(10-x-y)\).
  • Minimizing \(x^2+y^2\) subject to \(x+y=1\) uses the same equality-constrained stationarity method.

docs.title: Method of Lagrange for Inequality-Constrained Maximization
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, and let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_k\colon A\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable. Consider

\[ \begin{aligned} &\max_{\boldsymbol{x}\in A} f(\boldsymbol{x})\\ &\text{subject to}\quad g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\le b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,k. \end{aligned} \]

The course convention writes \(b_i-g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\ge0\) and defines

\[ L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda})=f(\boldsymbol{x})+\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i(b_i-g_i(\boldsymbol{x})). \]

If \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) is a local constrained maximizer, then either nondegenerate constraint qualification (NDCQ) fails or there exists \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast\) such that

\[ \begin{gathered} \boldsymbol{\nabla}_xL(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast)=0,\\ \lambda_i^\ast(g_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)-b_i)=0,\\ \lambda_i^\ast\ge0,\qquad g_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\le b_i. \end{gathered} \]

The condition \(\lambda_i^\ast(g_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)-b_i)=0\) is complementary slackness.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Inequality constraints are directional, so multiplier signs and slackness matter. A nonbinding constraint has slack and therefore contributes no multiplier force at a regular candidate.

At the illustrated constrained maximum, the gradient points outwards, towards the infeasible unconstrained maximum. The multipliers satisfy \(\displaystyle oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)=\sum_i\lambda_i oldsymbol{ abla} g_i( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\), and \(\lambda_i(g_i( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)-b_i)=0\). Any slack inequality has multiplier zero.

Drag the peak of \(f\): if it is feasible the constraint is slack and \(\lambda=0\); otherwise the optimum sits on the line and \( oldsymbol{ abla} f=\lambda oldsymbol{ abla} g\) with \(\lambda>0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A binding constraint satisfies \(g_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=b_i\).
  • A nonbinding constraint has zero multiplier by complementary slackness.
  • The theorem gives necessary, not sufficient, conditions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\max xy\) subject to \(x+y\le10\), the Lagrangian is \(xy+\lambda(10-x-y)\).
  • If no inequality is binding at a local maximum, all inequality multipliers are zero and the unconstrained stationarity condition returns.

docs.title: Method of Lagrange for Mixed Constraints
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, and let the objective \(f\) and all constraint functions \(g_i,h_j\) be continuously differentiable on \(A\). Consider

\[ \begin{aligned} &\max_{\boldsymbol{x}\in A} f(\boldsymbol{x})\\ &\text{subject to}\quad g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\le b_i,\quad h_j(\boldsymbol{x})=c_j. \end{aligned} \]

The course convention defines

\[ \begin{aligned} L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\mu}) &=f(\boldsymbol{x})+\sum_i\lambda_i(b_i-g_i(\boldsymbol{x}))\\ &\quad+\sum_j\mu_j(c_j-h_j(\boldsymbol{x})). \end{aligned} \]

If \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) is a local constrained maximizer and the binding inequalities are indexed by \(i_1,\ldots,i_\ell\), then either

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{D}(g_{i_1},\ldots,g_{i_\ell},h_1,\ldots,h_m)(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\\ &\quad<\ell+m, \end{aligned} \]

or there exist multipliers satisfying stationarity, complementary slackness, inequality feasibility, equality feasibility, and \(\lambda_i^\ast\ge0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Mixed problems combine exact equations with one-sided restrictions. The first-order candidate conditions combine equality stationarity with inequality sign and slackness rules.

The illustrated feasible arc satisfies \(h(\boldsymbol{x})=c\) and \(g(\boldsymbol{x})\le3.1\). Both constraints bind at \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\), where the objective gradient is a combination of the active constraint gradients with the appropriate multiplier signs. The theorem above specifies the normalization and regularity requirements for the multipliers.

The equality-constraint method contributes unrestricted multipliers for the equalities. The inequality-constrained maximization method contributes nonnegative multipliers and complementary slackness for the inequalities. Both kinds enter the same stationarity equation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Only inequalities require nonnegative multipliers.
  • Only binding inequalities are included in the active NDCQ matrix.
  • All equality constraints must hold exactly.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\max xy\) subject to \(x+y\le10\) and \(x-y=0\), the method uses one nonnegative multiplier and one unrestricted multiplier.
  • If an inequality is nonbinding at the solution, its multiplier is zero and it is not part of the active rank test.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), let \(\boldsymbol{g}\colon A\to B\), and let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon B\to\mathbb{R}^k\). If \(\boldsymbol{g}\) is differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\operatorname{int}(A)\), \(\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\in\operatorname{int}(B)\), and \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\), then \(\boldsymbol{f}\circ \boldsymbol{g}\) is differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) and

\[ \boldsymbol{D}(\boldsymbol{f}\circ \boldsymbol{g})(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}_0))\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}_0). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Local changes pass through the inner map first and then through the outer map. This is why the derivative matrices multiply in the same order as the composition acts on changes.

The local linear approximations compose in the same order as the maps. Near \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), the derivative of \(\boldsymbol{f}\circ \boldsymbol{g}\) is the product of the \(k\times m\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}_0))\) and the \(m\times n\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\); reversing that order is generally invalid.

The Jacobian matrices represent the derivatives as linear maps. Their ordered product first applies the derivative of the inner function and then the derivative of the outer function; reversing the order is generally invalid and can even give incompatible dimensions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol{g}\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^k\), then the product has size \(k\times n\).
  • If both maps are continuously differentiable near the relevant points, their composition is continuously differentiable near \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol{g}(x,y)=(x+y,xy)\) and \(f(u,v)=u^2+v\), then \(\boldsymbol{D}(f\circ \boldsymbol{g})=\boldsymbol{D}f(\boldsymbol{g})\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}\).
  • If \(\boldsymbol{g}(t)=(t,t^2)\) and \(f(x,y)=x+y\), the formula gives the curve derivative \(1+2t\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon A\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be \(C^1\), and let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in A\) with \(\boldsymbol{y}_0=\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\). If

\[ \det(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0))\neq0, \]

then there exists an open neighbourhood \(V\subseteq A\) of \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) such that \(\boldsymbol{f}|_V\colon V\to \boldsymbol{f}(V)\) is bijective. The image \(f(V)\) is an open neighbourhood of \(\boldsymbol{y}_0\). Its inverse is \(C^1\) and

\[ \boldsymbol{D}(\boldsymbol{f}|_V^{-1})(\boldsymbol{y}_0)=\left(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\right)^{-1}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An invertible Jacobian makes the function locally reversible. Near the reference point, outputs can be used to recover inputs smoothly.

The conclusion is local bijectivity: neighbourhoods are chosen so that the restricted map is one-to-one and reaches every point of its local image. It does not assert a global inverse on the original domain.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The determinant condition is the square full-rank condition.
  • The derivative of the local inverse is the inverse matrix of the original derivative.
  • The theorem can be derived from the implicit function theorem and vice versa.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)=(\mathrm{e}^x\cos y,\mathrm{e}^x\sin y)\), the determinant is \(\mathrm{e}^{2x}\), so the map is locally invertible everywhere.
  • For \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)=(x^2,y)\) at \((0,0)\), the determinant is \(0\), so the theorem does not apply there.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be sufficiently smooth near \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) and let \(\boldsymbol{h}\) be a small displacement. The first-order Taylor approximation is

\[ f(\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h})\approx f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)+\boldsymbol{D}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}. \]

If \(f\) is \(C^2\) near \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), the second-order approximation is

\[ \begin{aligned} f(\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h})&\approx f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)+\boldsymbol{D}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}\\ &\quad+\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{h}^{\top} \boldsymbol{H}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}. \end{aligned} \]

The first correction uses local slope, and the second correction uses local curvature.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Taylor approximations replace a complicated function near a point by simpler local information. The linear term estimates the immediate change, and the quadratic term corrects for bending.

The figure follows the line \(\boldsymbol{x}_0+t\boldsymbol{h}\) for a fixed direction \(\boldsymbol{h}\). Its first-order approximation is \(f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)+t\boldsymbol{D}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}\); the second-order approximation adds \(\frac{1}{2}t^2\boldsymbol{h}^{\top}\boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}\). As \(t\to0\), the errors are \(o(|t|)\) under differentiability and \(o(t^2)\) under the \(C^2\) hypothesis.

Compare both approximations along a line through \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) (right). Under the smoothness assumptions, the Hessian term improves the order of the local error as the displacement tends to zero.

Compare the first-order approximation (the tangent plane) with the second-order one, \(f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)+\boldsymbol{D}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}+\tfrac12\boldsymbol{h}^\top \boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}\), near \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\).

The Jacobian of a scalar-valued function is a row matrix, so multiplying it by the displacement gives the first-order scalar change. The Hessian contributes the quadratic correction when the \(C^2\) hypothesis holds.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a real-valued function, \(\boldsymbol{D}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}=\boldsymbol{\nabla} f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)^{\top} \boldsymbol{h}\).
  • If \(f\) is \(C^2\), then the Hessian is symmetric and the second-order term is a quadratic form.
  • At a critical point, the quadratic term is the first potentially nonzero correction. It may also vanish, in which case higher-order information is needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+xy+y^2\) at \((0,0)\), the second-order approximation is exact.
  • For \(f(x,y)=\mathrm{e}^{x+y}\) at \((0,0)\), the second-order approximation is \(1+x+y+\frac{1}{2}(x+y)^2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Write the constraint map as \(\boldsymbol{h}=(h_1,\ldots,h_m)\). For equality constraints \(h_1(\boldsymbol{x})=c_1,\ldots,h_m(\boldsymbol{x})=c_m\), the nondegenerate constraint qualification is satisfied at \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) if

\[ \operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{h}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast))=m. \]

With inequality constraints, the same rank condition is applied to the gradients of the binding inequality constraints together with the equality constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
NDCQ says the active constraints are locally independent. If it fails, some constraint may be redundant or the feasible set may have a singular shape.

On the left, the constraints cross transversally and \(\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{h}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=2=m\), so the qualification holds. On the right, they touch with parallel gradients and \(\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{h}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=1<m\), so it fails.

The Jacobian collects the constraint gradients as rows. Its rank equals the number of active constraints exactly when these rows are independent, excluding a nonzero linear relation between their first-order effects.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• When NDCQ holds, the regular Lagrange necessary conditions apply at a constrained local optimum.
  • If NDCQ fails, the point remains a candidate that must be checked separately.
  • For inequality problems, nonbinding inequalities are not included in the active rank check.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(h(x,y)=x+y\), NDCQ holds at every point because the gradient is nonzero.
  • For \(h_1(x,y)=x+y\) and \(h_2(x,y)=2x+2y\), NDCQ fails because the gradients are dependent.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A parametric constrained optimization problem is an optimization problem whose objective, constraints, or feasible set depend on a parameter. A typical equality-constrained maximization problem has the form

\[ \begin{aligned} &V(s)=\max_{\boldsymbol{x}} f(\boldsymbol{x},s)\\ &\text{subject to}\quad g(\boldsymbol{x},s)=0. \end{aligned} \]

The parameter \(s\) is not optimized over; it changes the problem being solved.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A parametric problem asks how the best choice and best value move when outside conditions change.

In the figure, the parameter \(s\) sets the constraint level \(h(\boldsymbol{x})=s\), and \(V(s)=\max\{f(\boldsymbol{x})\colon h(\boldsymbol{x})=s\}\). The blue lines show different feasible sets, the grey circles are level sets of \(f\), and the dashed path follows the corresponding optima \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast(s)\).

The parameter \(c\) is not chosen by the optimizer: changing it changes the problem, and the optimum moves along with it.

At a fixed parameter value, the equality-constraint Lagrange method handles the equality example. If inequalities are present, the inequality-constrained maximization method also imposes multiplier signs and complementary slackness. Only after solving each fixed-parameter problem does one study how its optimizer and value change.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The optimal value as a function of the parameter is the value function.
  • Envelope theorems give derivatives of the value function without fully differentiating the optimizer.
  • Constraint multipliers often measure the marginal value of relaxing parameterized constraints.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A firm may maximize profit over inputs while the wage rate is a parameter.
  • A consumer may maximize utility over bundles while income is a parameter in the budget constraint.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{F}\colon A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p+q}\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be differentiable, and write the variables as \((\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\) with \(\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\in\mathbb{R}^q\). The partial Jacobians of \(\boldsymbol{F}\) are the blocks

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{D}_x\boldsymbol{F}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})&\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p},\\ \boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{F}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})&\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times q}. \end{aligned} \]

Together they form the full Jacobian:

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{F}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\\ &=\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol{D}_x\boldsymbol{F}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})&\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{F}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A partial Jacobian isolates how an equation system responds to one chosen block of variables while the other block is held fixed.

The Jacobian splits as \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{F}=(\boldsymbol{D}_x\boldsymbol{F}\mid \boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{F})\), with \(m=3\), \(p=2\), and \(q=3\) in the figure. Under the implicit function theorem's assumptions, an invertible square block \(\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{F}\) lets one solve locally for \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x})\), with \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}=-(\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{F})^{-1}\boldsymbol{D}_x\boldsymbol{F}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Partial Jacobians are the matrix version of holding some variables constant in partial differentiation.
  • The implicit function theorem uses the partial Jacobian with respect to the variables being solved for.
  • Block notation makes comparative statics formulas easier to write and remember.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(F(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1\), \(D_xF=2x\) and \(D_yF=2y\).
  • For \(\boldsymbol{F}(x_1,x_2,y)=(x_1+y,x_2y)\), \(\boldsymbol{D}_x\boldsymbol{F}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&y\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{F}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\x_2\end{pmatrix}\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) and let \(I=\{i_1,\ldots,i_k\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The principal submatrix \([\boldsymbol{A}]_I\) keeps the rows and columns indexed by \(I\), and its principal minor is \(\det([\boldsymbol{A}]_I)\). The \(k\)-th leading principal submatrix is \(\boldsymbol{A}_k=[\boldsymbol{A}]_{\{1,\ldots,k\}}\), and its determinant \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}_k)\) is the \(k\)-th leading principal minor.

If \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is symmetric, Sylvester's criterion states:

  • \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is positive definite if and only if \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}_k)>0\) for all \(k=1,\ldots,n\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is negative definite if and only if \((-1)^k\det(\boldsymbol{A}_k)>0\) for all \(k=1,\ldots,n\).
  • Positive and negative semidefinite cases require all principal minors with the corresponding sign pattern.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Principal minors are determinant snapshots of matched rows and columns. Sylvester's criterion uses their signs to test definiteness without directly computing eigenvalues.

Change the symmetric matrix: positive leading minors give a positive definite form (one colour everywhere); a negative \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}_2)\) shows both colours.

Each principal submatrix is a square matrix formed by retaining the same index set for rows and columns. This matching of indices distinguishes principal minors from arbitrary minors and is essential to the symmetric-matrix definiteness criterion.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Leading principal minors are enough for positive and negative definiteness.
  • Semidefinite cases require checking all principal minors.
  • The criterion applies to symmetric matrices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\), the leading minors are \(2\) and \(3\), so \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is positive definite.
  • For \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&-3\end{pmatrix}\), the alternating sign test shows negative definiteness.

docs.title: Quadratic Form on a Constraint Set
Definition
docs.text:
Let \(q(\boldsymbol{h})=\boldsymbol{h}^{\top} \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{h}\) be a quadratic form and let a differentiable equality constraint system \(\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{0}\) have linearized direction space

\[ T=\{\boldsymbol{h}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{a})\boldsymbol{h}=0\}. \]

The quadratic form is positive definite on the constraint set at \(\boldsymbol{a}\) (that is, on the constraint directions \(T\), not on the feasible set \(\{\boldsymbol{g}=\boldsymbol{0}\}\) itself) if

\[ \boldsymbol{h}^{\top} \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{h}>0 \]

for every nonzero \(\boldsymbol{h}\in T\). Negative definiteness on the constraint set is defined similarly with \(\boldsymbol{h}^{\top} \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{h}<0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Under constraints, curvature only matters in directions that are feasible to first order. The same matrix can look indefinite overall but decisive on the allowed directions.

The form \(q(\boldsymbol{h})=\boldsymbol{h}^{\top} \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{h}\) is indefinite on the full space but positive definite on the tangent line \(T\) drawn. A constrained second-order test examines this restricted curvature rather than every direction in the ambient space.

Only the directions \(\boldsymbol{h}\) with \(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{h}=0\) (the highlighted line \(T\)) count. Turn the constraint: an indefinite form can be definite along the allowed line.

An independent linear constraint system identifies the linearized directions left free by the constraints. The test considers only its null space: curvature in a forbidden direction cannot decide whether the objective improves along feasible motion.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Under the full-row-rank regularity condition, the kernel \(T\) is the tangent space of the equality constraint set. Active inequality constraints generally lead to a cone of feasible directions instead.
  • Constrained second-order tests study the Hessian of the Lagrangian on the feasible direction space.
  • Bordered matrix tests are determinant-based ways to check this restricted definiteness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(q(h_1,h_2)=h_1^2-h_2^2\) with constraint \(h_2=0\), the restricted form is positive definite.
  • For \(q(h_1,h_2)=h_1^2-h_2^2\) with constraint \(h_1=0\), the restricted form is negative definite.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon A\to B\) be a function and let \(S\subseteq A\). The restriction of \(f\) to \(S\) is the function

\[ f|_S\colon S\to B, \qquad f|_S(x)=f(x). \]

Only the domain is changed; the rule used to compute the value is the same.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A restriction focuses the same function on a smaller feasible set. This is the formal move behind optimizing a function subject to constraints.

\(f|_S(x)=f(x)\) for \(x\in S\subseteq A\); properties can change with the domain: \(f|_S\) may be injective or bounded even when \(f\) is not, and its extrema are constrained extrema of \(f\).

The circle \(S\) (in the plane) lifts to a closed curve on the graph: that curve is the graph of \(f|_S\), plotted against \(t\) on the right. Turn the picture and change the radius.

The original function supplies the assignment rule. For an equality constraint \(g(\boldsymbol{x})=c\), choose its level set as the restricted domain, keeping the objective unchanged while limiting admissible inputs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The restricted function can have extrema that the unrestricted function does not have.
  • A constraint set often defines the domain of the restricted objective.
  • Properties such as injectivity can change after restriction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x,y)=x+y\) restricted to the circle \(x^2+y^2=1\) becomes an objective on that circle only.
  • The function \(f(x)=x^2\) is not injective on \(\mathbb{R}\), but its restriction to \([0,\infty)\) is injective.

docs.title: Prerequisites

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) and let \(\boldsymbol{a}\in A\). The point \(\boldsymbol{a}\) is a saddle point if it is a stationary point but is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum.

In many two-variable examples, every sufficiently small neighbourhood of \(\boldsymbol{a}\) contains points where \(f\) is larger than \(f(\boldsymbol{a})\) and points where \(f\) is smaller than \(f(\boldsymbol{a})\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A saddle point is a flat-looking candidate where the function rises in some directions and falls in others.

The figure shows \(f(\boldsymbol{x})=x_1^2-x_2^2\) and its level sets. At the origin, \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} f(0)=0\) and \(\boldsymbol{H}_f(0)=\operatorname{diag}(2,-2)\) is indefinite, so the stationary point is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum. Every neighbourhood contains both higher and lower values.

At the nondegenerate saddles shown here (where the Hessian is invertible), \(f\) increases in some directions and decreases in others, and the Hessian is indefinite. A saddle can also have a zero Hessian, as for \(f(x,y)=x^4-y^4\) at the origin.

Turn the surface: at a saddle point the tangent plane is horizontal, yet \(f\) rises in some directions and falls in others.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An indefinite Hessian at a critical point is the standard second-order signal for a saddle point.
  • A zero gradient alone does not imply an extremum.
  • Some saddle points require higher-order information because the Hessian test can be inconclusive.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2-y^2\), \((0,0)\) is a saddle point because values increase along the \(x\)-axis and decrease along the \(y\)-axis.
  • For \(f(x,y)=xy\), \((0,0)\) is a saddle point because \(xy\) takes positive and negative values arbitrarily close to the origin.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k\) be a function and let \(x_i,x_j\) be coordinate variables. A second-order partial derivative is obtained by differentiating a first-order partial derivative again:

\[ \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j\partial x_i} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} \left( \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_i} \right). \]

When \(i\neq j\), this is called a mixed partial derivative or cross partial derivative.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A second-order partial derivative measures how one first-order rate of change changes as another input is varied. Mixed partial derivatives compare changes across two different coordinate directions.

The expression \(\partial^2\boldsymbol{f}/(\partial x_j\partial x_i)\) means differentiating first with respect to \(x_i\) and then with respect to \(x_j\). For a scalar-valued function, the \(n^2\) ordered second partials form its Hessian. For a vector-valued function, each scalar component has its own Hessian. Pure partials measure curvature along an axis; mixed partials measure how a slope changes in another coordinate direction and agree in symmetric pairs when \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is \(C^2\).

The entries of \(\boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) are the second-order partial derivatives at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\); drag the point to see them change.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If the relevant mixed partial derivatives are continuous near a point, then their order may be exchanged.
  • Second-order partial derivatives form the entries of the Hessian matrix for scalar-valued functions.
  • Second-order information is the basic input for local curvature and extrema tests.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+xy+y^2\), \(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\partial x}=1\) and \(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\partial y}=1\).
  • For \(f(x,y)=x^2y^3\), \(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\partial y}=6xy^2\) and \(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2}=6x^2y\).

docs.title: Second-Order Sufficient Conditions for Constrained Optimization
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\mu})\) be the Lagrangian of a \(C^2\) constrained problem. Consider a first-order candidate \((\boldsymbol{x}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\mu}^\ast)\) at which the multiplier of every binding inequality constraint is nonzero. Collect the binding inequality constraints and all equality constraints in \(\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{x})\), let \(r\) be the number of active constraints (written \(m\) on the bordered Hessian page, where all constraints are equalities), and assume that their gradients at \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) are linearly independent (nondegenerate constraint qualification, NDCQ). The relevant bordered Hessian, with \(\boldsymbol{D}^2_{xx}L\) the Hessian of \(L\) with respect to \(\boldsymbol{x}\), is

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &\boldsymbol{H}^\ast\\ &=\begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{0}_r & \boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\\ \boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)^{\top} & \boldsymbol{D}^2_{xx}L(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\mu}^\ast) \end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} \]

Inspect the last \(n-r\) leading principal minors after ignoring the first \(2r\) leading minors. The candidate is a strict local constrained maximizer if these minors alternate in sign and the last one has sign \((-1)^n\). It is a strict local constrained minimizer if these minors all have sign \((-1)^r\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The bordered Hessian checks curvature only along feasible directions. It is the constrained counterpart of using the Hessian in an unconstrained second-order test.

In the figure, the level set of \(f\) touches the constraint curve \(h(\boldsymbol{x})=c\) at the first-order candidate \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\), where \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} f\) is parallel to \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} h\). The orange arrows mark tangent directions \(T=\{\boldsymbol{v}\colon\boldsymbol{D}h(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\boldsymbol{v}=0\}\). Under the theorem's assumptions, negative curvature \(\boldsymbol{v}^{\top} \boldsymbol{D}^2_{xx}L(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\mu}^\ast)\boldsymbol{v}<0\) for every nonzero feasible tangent direction gives a strict local constrained maximum; positive curvature gives a strict local constrained minimum. For multiple active constraints, use \(T=\ker \boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) and the bordered-Hessian sign test above.

The mixed-constraint Lagrange method supplies the first-order candidate and its multipliers. The second-order test then examines the Lagrangian curvature on the feasible tangent directions, under the strict active-multiplier and regularity hypotheses stated above.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Only binding inequality constraints and equality constraints enter the relevant bordered Hessian.
  • The nonzero multipliers on binding inequality constraints are part of the theorem, so check them before applying the test. If a binding inequality has a zero multiplier, the test does not apply.
  • The theorem gives sufficient conditions for strict local constrained optima.
  • Zero or semidefinite cases can be inconclusive.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• With one equality constraint in two variables, the relevant bordered Hessian is a three-by-three matrix.
  • For a maximization problem with three variables and one active constraint, the final relevant determinant must have sign \((-1)^3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a constrained optimization problem, a shadow price is the marginal change in the optimal value when a constraint is relaxed slightly. Under the usual regularity assumptions and sign conventions, this marginal change is represented by the associated Lagrange multiplier.

For a constraint written as \(g(\boldsymbol{x})=b\), one commonly has

\[ \frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}b}=\lambda \]

or the corresponding sign-adjusted version determined by the Lagrangian convention.

For a linear program the same quantity is the shadow price in linear programming, read off the optimal simplex tableau and valid over a right-hand-side range.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A shadow price measures how valuable a little extra room in a constraint would be at the optimum.

Change \(c\): the optimal value \(V(c)\) (right) rises with slope \(\mu\), the value of one more unit of the constrained resource.

The value function gives the optimized objective for each resource level \(b\). Its derivative measures the marginal improvement after reoptimizing the decision variables; differentiating the objective while holding those variables fixed would be a different quantity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A positive shadow price means relaxing the constraint raises the optimal value under the chosen convention.
  • A zero shadow price often corresponds to a nonbinding inequality constraint.
  • The sign depends on whether the constraint is written as a resource, residual, or equality condition.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If one more unit of a resource increases maximum profit by \(3\), the shadow price of that resource is \(3\).
  • If a budget constraint is slack, its shadow price is typically \(0\) because a small increase in the budget does not improve the optimum.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n o\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable at \( oldsymbol{a}\), and suppose \( oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{a}) eq oldsymbol{0}\). Among all unit vectors \( oldsymbol{u}\), the directional derivative

\[ D_{ oldsymbol{u}} f( oldsymbol{a})= oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{a})^{ op} oldsymbol{u} \]

is maximized when

\[ oldsymbol{u}= rac{ oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{a})}{\| oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{a})\|}. \]

The maximum value is \(\| oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{a})\|\), and the minimum value is \(-\| oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{a})\|\) in the opposite direction.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The gradient points in the direction where the function rises fastest. Its length tells how fast the best immediate rise is.

For a unit vector \( oldsymbol{u}\) at angle \( heta\) to the gradient, \(D_{ oldsymbol{u}}f( oldsymbol{a})=\| oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{a})\|\cos heta\): the rate is largest at \( heta=0\), most negative at \( heta=\pi\), and zero at \( heta=\pi/2\), along the level set.

Turn the unit vector \( oldsymbol{u}\): \(D_{ oldsymbol{u}}f( oldsymbol{a})= oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{a})^ op oldsymbol{u}\) (right) is largest when \( oldsymbol{u}\) points along \( oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{a})\), with value \(\| oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{a})\|\).

From \( oldsymbol{x}_0\) the red path always moves along \( oldsymbol{ abla} f\), the direction of steepest ascent, and crosses the level curves at right angles.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The result follows from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.
  • The direction of steepest descent is \(- oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{a})/\| oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{a})\|\).
  • If \( oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{a})= oldsymbol{0}\), then every directional derivative is zero and there is no unique steepest direction from first-order information.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) at \((1,2)\), \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} f=(2,4)\), so the steepest ascent direction is \((1,2)/\sqrt{5}\).
  • For \(f(x,y)=3x-y\) at any point, \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} f=(3,-1)\), so the steepest ascent direction is \((3,-1)/\sqrt{10}\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in E\), and let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon E\to\mathbb{R}^k\). If the two mixed second-order partial derivatives

\[ \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j\partial x_i} \quad\text{and}\quad \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_i\partial x_j} \]

exist on a neighbourhood of \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) and are continuous at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), then

\[ \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j\partial x_i}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) = \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_i\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
When a function is smooth enough, differentiating first in one coordinate direction and then in another gives the same result as doing those two steps in the opposite order.

The order of differentiation does not matter: if both mixed partials exist and are continuous at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), they coincide there. Consequence: the Hessian of a \(C^2\) function is symmetric. Example: \(f=x_1^2x_2\) has \(f_{x_1x_2}=f_{x_2x_1}=2x_1\).

Twice continuous differentiability is a convenient sufficient hypothesis ensuring the displayed mixed partials are continuous. The stated theorem only needs the specified mixed partials locally; it should not be read as saying every weaker existence assumption implies symmetry.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A \(C^2\) function automatically satisfies the hypotheses of the theorem for second-order mixed partial derivatives.
  • For scalar-valued \(C^2\) functions, the Hessian matrix is symmetric.
  • The same idea extends to higher-order partial derivatives when the required higher-order derivatives are continuous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2y+\mathrm{e}^{xy}\), the mixed derivatives \(f_{xy}\) and \(f_{yx}\) agree at every point because the function is smooth.
  • For \(f(x,y,z)=xyz^2\), the derivatives \(f_{xz}\) and \(f_{zx}\) both equal \(2yz\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{D}^k f(\boldsymbol{a})\) be the \(k\)th derivative of a scalar function at \(\boldsymbol{a}\), viewed as a \(k\)-linear map. Its contraction with a displacement \(\boldsymbol{h}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is

\[ \boldsymbol{D}^k f(\boldsymbol{a})[\boldsymbol{h},\ldots,\boldsymbol{h}]. \]

In a Taylor polynomial, the corresponding \(k\)th-order contribution is

\[ \frac{1}{k!}\boldsymbol{D}^k f(\boldsymbol{a})[\boldsymbol{h},\ldots,\boldsymbol{h}]. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A derivative tensor is useful once it is evaluated on a concrete displacement. Contraction turns the stored derivative information into the actual Taylor correction in that direction.

\(\boldsymbol{D}^3f(\boldsymbol{a})=\big(f_{x_ix_jx_k}(\boldsymbol{a})\big)_{i,j,k}\) has \(n^3\) entries (here \(n=2\): a \(2\times2\times2\) cube, front \(k=1\), back \(k=2\)), symmetric under any permutation of \((i,j,k)\) for \(C^3\) \(f\). Contraction with \(\boldsymbol{h}\), \(\displaystyle \boldsymbol{D}^3f(\boldsymbol{a})[\boldsymbol{h},\boldsymbol{h},\boldsymbol{h}]=\sum_{i,j,k}f_{x_ix_jx_k}(\boldsymbol{a})\,h_ih_jh_k\), gives the cubic Taylor term \(\tfrac{1}{3!}\boldsymbol{D}^3f(\boldsymbol{a})[\boldsymbol{h},\boldsymbol{h},\boldsymbol{h}]\).

The third-order derivative tensor is the case \(k=3\): inserting the displacement in all three slots and summing over its indices produces one scalar cubic contribution, with coefficient \(1/3!\) in the Taylor formula.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(k=2\), the contraction is the quadratic form \(\boldsymbol{h}^{\top} \boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{a})\boldsymbol{h}\).
  • For \(k=3\), the contraction sums all third partial derivatives weighted by three components of \(\boldsymbol{h}\).
  • The factorial corrects for repeated counting in the Taylor expansion.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol{H}=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&6\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\boldsymbol{h}=(u,v)\), then \(\boldsymbol{D}^2f(\boldsymbol{a})[\boldsymbol{h},\boldsymbol{h}]=2u^2+6v^2\).
  • For \(f(x,y)=x^3+xy^2\) at the origin and \(\boldsymbol{h}=(u,v)\), the third-order contraction is \(6u^3+6uv^2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a scalar function \(f\colon A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) with third-order partial derivatives continuous on an open neighbourhood of \(\boldsymbol{a}\) (that is, \(f\) is \(C^3\) there), the third-order derivative tensor is the array

\[ \boldsymbol{D}^3 f(\boldsymbol{a})=\left(f_{x_i x_j x_k}(\boldsymbol{a})\right)_{i,j,k=1}^n. \]

It represents the trilinear map

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &\boldsymbol{D}^3 f(\boldsymbol{a})[\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{w}]\\ &=\sum_{i,j,k=1}^n f_{x_i x_j x_k}(\boldsymbol{a})u_i v_j w_k. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The third derivative tensor stores all third-order curvature information in the same way that the Hessian stores all second-order curvature information.

\(\boldsymbol{D}^3f(\boldsymbol{a})=\big(f_{x_ix_jx_k}(\boldsymbol{a})\big)_{i,j,k}\) has \(n^3\) entries (here \(n=2\): a \(2\times2\times2\) cube, front \(k=1\), back \(k=2\)), symmetric under any permutation of \((i,j,k)\) for \(C^3\) \(f\). Contraction with \(\boldsymbol{h}\), \(\displaystyle \boldsymbol{D}^3f(\boldsymbol{a})[\boldsymbol{h},\boldsymbol{h},\boldsymbol{h}]=\sum_{i,j,k}f_{x_ix_jx_k}(\boldsymbol{a})\,h_ih_jh_k\), gives the cubic Taylor term \(\tfrac{1}{3!}\boldsymbol{D}^3f(\boldsymbol{a})[\boldsymbol{h},\boldsymbol{h},\boldsymbol{h}]\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(n\) variables, the raw array has \(n^3\) entries.
  • If the third partial derivatives are continuous, many entries are equal by symmetry.
  • Taylor's third-order term is obtained by feeding the displacement vector into the tensor three times.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^3+xy^2\), entries include \(f_{xxx}=6\), \(f_{xyy}=2\), and \(f_{yyy}=0\).
  • For \(f(x,y,z)=xyz\), all mixed third partials with one \(x\), one \(y\), and one \(z\) equal \(1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(E\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) be open and let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon E\to\mathbb{R}^k\) be a function.

The function \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is continuously differentiable, or \(C^1\), on \(E\) if all first-order partial derivatives of \(\boldsymbol{f}\) exist on \(E\) and are continuous on \(E\).

The function \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is twice continuously differentiable, or \(C^2\), on \(E\) if all second-order partial derivatives of \(\boldsymbol{f}\) exist on \(E\) and are continuous on \(E\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A continuously differentiable function changes smoothly enough that its first local rates of change do not jump. A twice continuously differentiable function has the same smooth behaviour one derivative level deeper.

A function is \(C^1\) on an open set \(E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) when all its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous, and it is \(C^2\) when all its second partial derivatives are also continuous. Thus \(C^2\subseteq C^1\subseteq C^0\). The Hessian tests and second-order Taylor formula above use \(C^2\) regularity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A \(C^1\) function on an open set is totally differentiable at every point of that set.
  • A \(C^2\) scalar function has symmetric mixed second derivatives.
  • Polynomials and the usual elementary smooth functions are \(C^2\) on the interior of their domains.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x,y)=x^2+\sin y\) is \(C^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
  • The function \(f(x)=|x|\) is not \(C^1\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), because it is not differentiable at \(0\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and let \(f\colon A\to\mathbb{R}\).

If \(f\) is \(C^1\) and has a local extremum at an interior point \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\), then

\[ \boldsymbol{D}f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=(0,\ldots,0). \]

If \(f\) is \(C^2\), then a local maximum has \(\boldsymbol{H}f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) negative semidefinite and a local minimum has \(\boldsymbol{H}f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) positive semidefinite. Conversely, if \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) is a critical point, a negative definite Hessian gives a strict local maximum, a positive definite Hessian gives a strict local minimum, and an indefinite Hessian gives a saddle point.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
At an interior unconstrained optimum, first-order movement must disappear. The Hessian then describes the local curvature when the second-order information is decisive.

Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) to a point where \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} f=0\); the Hessian there separates minima, maxima and saddles.

At a critical point \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=0\) and the tangent plane is flat; the Hessian \(\boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) decides whether the surface bends up, down or both ways.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• First-order stationarity is necessary but not sufficient.
  • Semidefinite Hessians can make the second-order test inconclusive.
  • An indefinite Hessian at a critical point means the point is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\), the Hessian is positive definite and the origin is a strict local minimum.
  • For \(f(x,y)=x^2-y^2\), the Hessian is indefinite and the origin is a saddle point.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a parametric optimization problem, the value function assigns to each parameter value the optimized objective value. For example,

\[ V(s)=f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast(s),s) \]

when \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast(s)\) solves the problem at parameter \(s\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The value function records the best achievable outcome after the decision variables have been chosen optimally.

\(V(s)=f(x^\ast(s),s)=\max_{x} f(x,s)\) is the best value attainable at \(s\): its graph is never below any single curve \(s\mapsto f(x,s)\) with \(x\) fixed (grey) and touches the curve of \(x^\ast(s)\); here \(V(s)=s^2\), for instance \(V(2)=f(x^\ast(2),2)\) with \(x^\ast(2)=2\).

Each \(c\) gives a new optimum; the right panel plots the optimal value \(V(c)\) against \(c\).

A global maximum or minimum determines the best feasible objective at each parameter value. When several optimizers attain it, they give the same value; recording only a local optimum would not in general define the global value function.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The value function depends on parameters, not directly on arbitrary feasible choices.
  • Envelope theorems provide formulas for derivatives of value functions under regularity conditions.
  • A value function can be nonsmooth if the optimizer changes abruptly or constraints switch status.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(V(I)\) is the maximum utility attainable with income \(I\), then \(V\) is a value function.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be a differentiable curve, that is, a path parametrized by an interval \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) rather than by \([0,1]\). If each component \(\gamma_i\) is differentiable at \(t_0\), then the velocity vector of \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}\) at \(t_0\) is

\[ \boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t_0)= \begin{pmatrix} \gamma_1'(t_0)\\ \vdots\\ \gamma_n'(t_0) \end{pmatrix}. \]

The velocity is the tangent vector to the curve at the point \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t_0)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The velocity vector records the instantaneous direction and rate of motion along an already chosen path.

For the differentiable curve \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)=(\gamma_1(t),\ldots,\gamma_n(t))\), the vector \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t_0)=(\gamma_1'(t_0),\ldots,\gamma_n'(t_0))\) is its velocity and \(\|\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t_0)\|\) is its speed. If the velocity is nonzero, the tangent line is \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t_0)+s\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t_0)\), \(s\in\mathbb{R}\).

The velocity \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t)\) is tangent to the curve; its components are the derivatives of the coordinates, and its length is the speed.

A path assigns the position at time \(t\). Its componentwise derivatives measure how each coordinate of that position changes; collecting them in order gives the tangent vector.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Velocity is computed component by component.
  • If \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t_0)\neq 0\), then \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t_0)\) gives a tangent direction to the image of the curve.
  • The speed of the curve is \(\|\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t_0)\|\) when a norm is being used.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)=(t,t^2)\), the velocity is \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t)=(1,2t)\), so at \(t=1\) the curve passes through \((1,1)\) with velocity \((1,2)\).
  • For \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)\), the velocity is \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t)=(-\sin t,\cos t)\), which is tangent to the unit circle.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For random variables \(X\), \(Y\) and \(Z\) with \(\mathbb{E}|Y|<\infty\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X,Z]\mid Z]=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z]. \end{aligned} \]

This is Adam's Law with \(Z\) kept as background information. Conditioning on \((X,Z)\) retains all the information in \(Z\), and no independence assumption is needed.

Taking \(Y=\indicator_{A}\) for an event \(A\), letting \(X\) encode a finite or countable partition \(\{B_i\}\) and letting \(Z\) indicate an event \(C\) gives LOTP with extra conditioning: once we condition on \(C\), we treat \(C\) as the new background information and apply the ordinary LOTP inside that conditional world. Assume \(\mathbb{P}(C)>0\) and omit terms with \(\mathbb{P}(B_i\cap C)=0\). For the remaining terms, \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i,C)\) means \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i\cap C)\). The events \(B_i\) still form a partition, but all probabilities are now computed under the assumption that \(C\) has occurred:

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(A\mid C) &= \sum_i \mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i,C)\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid C). \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Average out the extra information while retaining the background information. The retained conditional mean is unchanged.

Let \(Y=X+Z\), where \(X\) is independent of \(Z\) and takes \(1\) and \(3\) with equal probability. Averaging \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X,Z]=X+Z\) over \(X\) while keeping \(Z\) fixed gives \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X,Z]\mid Z]=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z]=2+Z\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For integrable \(Y\), \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X,Z]\mid Z]=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z]\) almost surely.
  • Taking \(Y\) as an event indicator and \(X\) as a partition label yields total probability with extra conditioning.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(Y=X+Z\), \(X\) is independent of \(Z\), and \(\mathbb{E}X=2\), then \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X,Z]\mid Z]=2+Z\).
  • If \(Z\) is constant, the identity reduces to \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]]=\mathbb{E}Y\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) with \(\mathbb{E}|Y|<\infty\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]]=\mathbb{E}[Y]. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Averaging the conditional average recovers the original average. Conditioning simplifies a calculation while keeping its final unconditional answer.

For \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(10,X)\), the conditional mean is \(10X\). Averaging over \(X\) gives \(\mathbb{E}[Y]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]]=\int_0^1 10x\,\mathrm{d}x=5\).

\(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]\) is the centre of each group; averaging these with the probabilities \(\mathbb{P}(X=x)\) gives \(\mathbb{E}Y\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For discrete \(X\), \(\displaystyle \mathbb{E}Y=\sum_x\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]p_X(x)\); for density \(X\), use the corresponding integral.
  • Conditioning on more information first and then on less gives the conditional expectation given the smaller information: \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X,Z]\mid Z]=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z]\) (Adam's law with extra conditioning).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(10,X)\), then \(\mathbb{E}Y=\mathbb{E}[10X]=5\).
  • If \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) and \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(X)\), then \(\mathbb{E}Y=\mathbb{E}X=1/2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) and \(X\) be random variables defined on one probability space, that is, one sample space with one probability function. The sequence \(X_n\) converges almost surely to \(X\) if

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(\lim_{n\to\infty}X_n=X)=1. \end{aligned} \]

The set of outcomes on which \(X_n\) does not converge to \(X\) need not be empty, but it must have probability zero. This is written as \(X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.} X\). One also says that \(X_n\) converges to \(X\) with probability one, abbreviated w.p.1.

For each outcome outside the exceptional null set, the Limit of a Sequence is taken for the numerical values \(X_n(\omega)\); the probability-one condition refers to the set of outcomes where that limit equals \(X(\omega)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Outside a set of outcomes of probability zero, the entire sequence converges point by point along each outcome’s sample path.

The diagram follows \(X_n=\indicator_{\{U<1/n\}}\) for three outcomes of \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\). Each path equals \(1\) while \(n<1/U\) and is \(0\) thereafter. Every outcome with \(U>0\) converges, so \(X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}0\).

Almost-sure convergence is about whole paths: each simulated path of \(\bar X_n\) settles at \(\mu\). The red dot marks the last time a path leaves the band.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability.
  • Changing any of the variables on a common event of probability zero does not change almost-sure convergence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\) is finite almost surely and \(X_n=X/n\), then \(X_n\to0\) on every outcome where \(X\) is finite, so convergence is almost sure.
  • For a single \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(X_n=\indicator_{\{U<1/n\}}\), each outcome with \(U>0\) eventually has \(X_n=0\), so \(X_n\to0\) almost surely.
