docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be a real \(m\times n\) matrix and \(p=\min(m,n)\). The matrix \(A^{\top}A\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite, so its eigenvalues are real and nonnegative; order them \(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n\ge0\). The singular values of \(A\) are

\[ \reflow \begin{gathered} \sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i}\quad(i=1,\ldots,p),\\ \sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_p\ge0. \end{gathered} \]

They are the diagonal entries of \(\Sigma\) in the singular value decomposition \(A=U\Sigma V^{\top}\). Some texts list only the positive ones, or all \(n\) values; the positive singular values are the same under every convention.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Singular values measure stretching. A matrix maps the unit sphere onto an ellipsoid whose semi-axis lengths are the singular values: \(\sigma_1\) is the largest factor by which \(A\) lengthens a unit vector, and zero singular values mark directions that are collapsed.

The figure uses the first example below, \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\). Both eigenvalues are \(1\), yet the unit circle is stretched into an ellipse with semi-axes \(\sigma_1\approx1.618\) and \(\sigma_2\approx0.618\). The blue and red unit vectors on the left are the directions that land on these semi-axes (eigenvectors of \(A^{\top}A\)), and every length \(\|A\boldsymbol{x}\|\) with \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=1\) lies between \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_1\).

Turn \(\boldsymbol{x}\) around the unit circle with \(\varphi\): \(\|A\boldsymbol{x}\|\) ranges between \(\sigma_2\approx0.618\) and \(\sigma_1\approx1.618\), although both eigenvalues of the shear are \(1\). Change the entries of \(A\) to compare other matrices.

Nonnegativity of \(\lambda_i\) comes from \(\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}A^{\top}A\boldsymbol{x}=\|A\boldsymbol{x}\|^2\ge0\), with \(\|\cdot\|\) the Euclidean norm.

Singular values are not the absolute values of the eigenvalues, except for special matrices such as symmetric ones. They exist for rectangular matrices, are always real and nonnegative, and do not change under orthogonal transformations of either side, whereas eigenvalues can be complex and are defined only for square matrices.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(A^{\top}A\) and \(AA^{\top}\) have the same nonzero eigenvalues, so \(A\) and \(A^{\top}\) have the same singular values; either product may be used, whichever is smaller.
  • The number of positive singular values equals the rank of \(A\).
  • \(\sigma_1=\max_{\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=1}\|A\boldsymbol{x}\|\), the spectral (operator) norm \(\|A\|_2\). If \(m\ge n\), \(\sigma_n=\min_{\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=1}\|A\boldsymbol{x}\|\).
  • Via the trace: \(\sigma_1^2+\cdots+\sigma_p^2=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\top}A)=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2\) (squared Frobenius norm).
  • For square \(A\), the determinant satisfies \(|\det A|=\sigma_1\cdots\sigma_n\), so \(A\) is invertible if and only if \(\sigma_n>0\).
  • Symmetric \(A\): \(\sigma_i=|\lambda_i(A)|\) after reordering. Orthogonal \(Q\): all singular values equal \(1\). Scaling: the singular values of \(cA\) are \(|c|\sigma_i\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Eigenvalues versus singular values. \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) has both eigenvalues equal to \(1\). But \(A^{\top}A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\) has trace \(3\) and determinant \(1\), so eigenvalues \(\tfrac{3\pm\sqrt{5}}{2}\) and

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} \sigma_1&=\tfrac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\approx1.618,\\ \sigma_2&=\tfrac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}\approx0.618. \end{aligned} \]

Checks: \(\sigma_1\sigma_2=1=|\det A|\) and \(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2=3=1^2+1^2+0^2+1^2\).

A \(2\times3\) matrix. For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}\) the smaller product is \(AA^{\top}=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\), so \(\sigma_1=\sqrt{2}\), \(\sigma_2=1\); the \(3\times3\) matrix \(A^{\top}A\) has eigenvalues \(2,1,0\). The maximal stretch is attained at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1,0,1)^{\top}\): \(A\boldsymbol{x}=(\sqrt{2},0)^{\top}\), of length \(\sqrt{2}=\sigma_1\). The rank is \(2\), the number of positive singular values.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(x^*\) be an equilibrium of \(x'(t)=f\big(x(t)\big)\), where \(x'(t)=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)\).

  • \(x^*\) is stable if solutions that start close to \(x^*\) stay bounded near it: for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(\delta>0\) such that \(|x(0)-x^*|<\delta\) implies \(|x(t)-x^*|<\varepsilon\) for all \(t\geq0\).
  • \(x^*\) is (locally) asymptotically stable if it is stable and, in addition, \(x(t)\to x^*\) as \(t\to\infty\) for every \(x(0)\) close enough to \(x^*\).
  • \(x^*\) is unstable if it is not stable.

Linearization test. If \(f\) is continuously differentiable near \(x^*\), then

  • \(f'(x^*)<0\) implies that \(x^*\) is locally asymptotically stable;
  • \(f'(x^*)>0\) implies that \(x^*\) is unstable;
  • \(f'(x^*)=0\) gives no conclusion.

In Math V, stable means that solutions stay bounded (near the equilibrium); if, in addition, every nearby solution converges to the equilibrium, it is asymptotically stable.

Beyond the course

Many textbooks call the \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) notion above Lyapunov stability. Math V does not use that name; it simply says stable.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Near \(x^*\), the Taylor polynomial of degree 1 gives \(f(x)\approx f'(x^*)(x-x^*)\), so the deviation \(y=x-x^*\) approximately obeys \(y'=f'(x^*)\,y\), with solution \(y(0)\mathrm{e}^{f'(x^*)t}\). A negative derivative makes small deviations decay; a positive one makes them grow. Graphically: \(x^*\) is asymptotically stable when \(f\) crosses zero from positive to negative.

The figure shows the logistic example below, \(x'=f(x)=x(1-x)\). The sign of \(f\) gives the direction of motion on the \(x\)-axis: to the right where \(f>0\), to the left where \(f<0\). At \(x^*=0\) the graph crosses zero upwards, \(f'(0)=1>0\), and nearby solutions move away; at \(x^*=1\) it crosses downwards, \(f'(1)=-1<0\), and nearby solutions move towards it from both sides.

Choose \(f\) and drag \(x(0)\) close to each equilibrium: solutions return when \(f'(x^*)<0\) and move away when \(f'(x^*)>0\). For \(-x^3\), \(x^3\) and \(x^2\) the test is inconclusive, as \(f'(0)=0\), yet the three outcomes differ.

The continuous-time criterion is a sign condition, \(f'(x^*)<0\). The discrete-time criterion is a size condition: \(|a|<1\) for the linear equation \(x_{t+1}=ax_t+b\) (see stability of a scalar difference equation), and, by the same linearization, \(|g'(x^*)|<1\) for a fixed point of \(x_{t+1}=g(x_t)\) with \(g\) continuously differentiable. Mixing the two is a common error.

Stability in the test is local: it says nothing about initial values far from \(x^*\). Asymptotic stability also requires the limit at infinity \(\lim_{t\to\infty}x(t)=x^*\); bounded motion near \(x^*\) is not enough.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(x'=ax+b\) with \(a\neq0\), \(x(t)-x^*=\mathrm{e}^{at}\big(x(0)-x^*\big)\): the equilibrium \(x^*=-b/a\) is globally asymptotically stable if \(a<0\) and unstable if \(a>0\).
  • For \(x'=0\) every point is an equilibrium that is stable but not asymptotically stable.
  • When \(f'(x^*)=0\), all three outcomes occur: \(x'=-x^3\) (asymptotically stable), \(x'=x^3\) (unstable) and \(x'=x^2\) (unstable, although solutions starting below \(0\) approach it).
  • For linear systems, the analogue is that all eigenvalues must have negative real part; see linear vector ODE and stability of higher-order ODEs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Logistic equation. \(x'=x(1-x)\), so \(f(x)=x-x^2\) and \(f'(x)=1-2x\). At \(x^*=0\), \(f'(0)=1>0\): unstable. At \(x^*=1\), \(f'(1)=-1<0\): locally asymptotically stable. Near \(1\), deviations shrink roughly like \(\mathrm{e}^{-t}\).

Linear with forcing. \(x'=-0.5x+3\) has \(x^*=6\) and \(a=-0.5<0\), so \(x^*\) is asymptotically stable. From \(x(0)=10\): \(x(t)=6+4\mathrm{e}^{-0.5t}\) and \(x(2)=6+4\mathrm{e}^{-1}\approx7.47\).

Inconclusive test. For \(x'=-x^3\), \(f'(0)=0\). Yet \(x\,x'=-x^4<0\) for \(x\neq0\), so \(|x(t)|\) decreases, and indeed \(x(t)\to0\): the equilibrium is asymptotically stable although the test is silent.

docs.title: Stability of Solutions of Higher-Order ODEs
Proposition
docs.text:
Consider the linear ordinary differential equation (ODE) with constant real coefficients

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &x^{(n)}(t)+a_{n-1}x^{(n-1)}(t)+\dots\\ &\quad+a_1x'(t)+a_0x(t)=g(t), \end{aligned} \]

with \(x'(t)=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)\) and characteristic equation \(p(r)=r^n+a_{n-1}r^{n-1}+\dots+a_0=0\). For the homogeneous equation (\(g\equiv0\)):

  1. Every solution satisfies \(x(t)\to0\) as \(t\to\infty\) if and only if every root of \(p\) has negative real part. The equation is then called asymptotically stable.
  2. If some root has positive real part, some solutions are unbounded: the equation is unstable.
  3. If all roots have real part \(\leq0\), all solutions are bounded on \([0,\infty)\) if and only if every root with real part \(0\) is simple; the equation is then called stable. A repeated root on the imaginary axis gives unbounded terms such as \(t\) or \(t\cos\beta t\).

For constant \(g\equiv c\) with \(a_0\neq0\), every solution tends to the equilibrium \(c/a_0\) if and only if all roots have negative real part.

In Math V, stable means that all solutions stay bounded, and asymptotically stable that they all converge (case 1). A simple root on the imaginary axis therefore gives a stable equation that is not asymptotically stable.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
By the general solution of a linear ODE, every homogeneous solution is a combination of terms \(t^j\mathrm{e}^{rt}\), one family for each root \(r=\alpha+\mathrm{i}\beta\). With Euler's formula, \(|t^j\mathrm{e}^{rt}|=t^j\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t}\): the oscillation \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\beta t}\) has modulus \(1\), and only \(\alpha\) decides growth or decay. Exponential decay beats any polynomial factor \(t^j\), so \(\alpha<0\) is enough.

The figure places the characteristic roots of the examples below in the complex plane. The roots \(-1,-2\) of \(x''+3x'+2x=4\) lie in the shaded half-plane \(\operatorname{Re} r<0\), so every solution converges. The simple roots \(\pm2\mathrm{i}\) of \(x''+4x=0\) lie on the imaginary axis: solutions stay bounded but do not decay. The roots \(1\pm2\mathrm{i}\) of \(x''-2x'+5x=0\) lie to the right, and the double root \(0\) of \(x''=0\) lies on the axis but is repeated; both give unbounded solutions.

Move \(a_1\) and \(a_0\) and watch the roots against the shaded half-plane: while both have negative real part, every solution tends to \(x^*=c/a_0\) whatever \(x(0)\) and \(x'(0)\); with roots on the imaginary axis the oscillation never dies out.

The criterion is the continuous-time counterpart of stability of an equilibrium: writing the equation as a first-order system, the roots are the eigenvalues of the companion matrix, and "negative real part" plays the role of \(f'(x^*)<0\). For difference equations the boundary is the unit circle \(|\lambda|=1\), not the imaginary axis; see stability of a scalar difference equation.

Typical mistakes: requiring only real roots to be negative and ignoring complex ones; treating purely imaginary roots as stable in the asymptotic sense; and concluding stability from positive coefficients alone when \(n\geq3\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Order 2: \(x''+a_1x'+a_0x=0\) is asymptotically stable if and only if \(a_1>0\) and \(a_0>0\) (the roots have sum \(-a_1\) and product \(a_0\)).
  • For any \(n\), positive coefficients \(a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}\) are necessary for asymptotic stability, but not sufficient when \(n\geq3\).
  • Stability is a property of the homogeneous part and does not depend on \(g\): all solutions \(x=x_p+x_h\) satisfy \(x(t)-x_p(t)\to0\) if and only if all roots have negative real part.
  • The same test applies to the first-order system form: its companion matrix has the roots of \(p\) as eigenvalues, as for the linear vector ODE.

Beyond the course

Many textbooks state the Routh-Hurwitz criterion, which decides from the coefficients alone whether all roots have negative real part. It is not part of Math V.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Asymptotically stable with forcing. \(x''+3x'+2x=4\): roots \(-1,-2\), and the particular solution is \(x_p=2\). Every solution \(2+c_1\mathrm{e}^{-t}+c_2\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\) tends to \(2\).

Pure oscillation. \(x''+4x=0\): roots \(\pm2\mathrm{i}\), solutions \(c_1\cos2t+c_2\sin2t\) are bounded but do not tend to \(0\): stable, not asymptotically stable.

Growing oscillation. \(x''-2x'+5x=0\): \(r=1\pm2\mathrm{i}\), solutions \(\mathrm{e}^{t}(c_1\cos2t+c_2\sin2t)\): unstable, matching \(a_1=-2<0\).

Double root at zero. \(x''=0\): \(r=0\) twice, solutions \(c_1+c_2t\), unbounded: unstable although no root has positive real part.

Positive coefficients are not enough. \(r^3+r^2+r+1=(r+1)(r^2+1)\) has roots \(-1,\pm\mathrm{i}\). All coefficients are positive, yet the simple roots \(\pm\mathrm{i}\) lie on the imaginary axis: stable, not asymptotically stable.

docs.title: Stability of a System of Linear Difference Equations
Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be a real \(n\times n\) matrix and consider the system \(\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t+\boldsymbol{b}\) with constant \(\boldsymbol{b}\in\mathbb{R}^n\). The following are equivalent:

  1. every eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(A\), real or complex, satisfies \(\lvert\lambda\rvert<1\);
  2. \(A^t\to O\) as \(t\to\infty\);
  3. for every \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) the solution of the homogeneous system satisfies \(\boldsymbol{x}_t=A^t\boldsymbol{x}_0\to\boldsymbol{0}\).

In that case \(1\) is not an eigenvalue, the equilibrium \(\boldsymbol{x}^*=(I-A)^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}\) is unique, and every solution converges to it: the equilibrium is (globally) asymptotically stable.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The deviation from equilibrium evolves as \(\boldsymbol{x}_t-\boldsymbol{x}^*=A^t(\boldsymbol{x}_0-\boldsymbol{x}^*)\). For a diagonalizable matrix it is a sum of terms \(c_i\lambda_i^t\boldsymbol{p}_i\), and each dies out exactly when the modulus \(\lvert\lambda_i\rvert\) is below \(1\). In general the Jordan normal form adds factors \(t^j\), which do not change the conclusion. This is the matrix version of the scalar criterion \(\lvert a\rvert<1\).

The figure plots the eigenvalues of the three examples below. The first matrix has the single eigenvalue \(0.5\) (green), inside the unit circle, so the system is asymptotically stable. The second has \(-0.5\) inside but \(1.5\) outside (red), and one eigenvalue outside is enough for instability. The third has \(0.7\) inside and \(1\) on the circle (orange): solutions stay bounded and converge, but not to a single equilibrium.

Change the entries of \(A\) and watch its eigenvalues: while every modulus is below \(1\) the iterates converge to \(\boldsymbol{x}^*=(I-A)^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}\) from any \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\); push one eigenvalue outside the circle and they diverge.

Complex eigenvalues must be included: a conjugate pair \(\rho \mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\theta}\) produces rotations whose size is multiplied by \(\rho\) each period. A common mistake is to inspect the entries of \(A\) instead of its eigenvalues; small diagonal entries do not imply stability unless \(A\) is triangular.

In Math V, asymptotic stability means that all solutions converge, which needs all eigenvalues strictly inside the unit circle. The weaker notion, stable, means that all solutions stay bounded; it holds if and only if all \(\lvert\lambda\rvert\le1\) and every eigenvalue with \(\lvert\lambda\rvert=1\) has equal algebraic and geometric multiplicity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If some eigenvalue has \(\lvert\lambda\rvert>1\), solutions starting on its eigenvector (or its real invariant plane, for a complex pair) grow without bound; solutions starting in the span of the generalized eigenvectors with \(\lvert\lambda\rvert<1\) still converge.
  • Eigenvalues with \(\lvert\lambda\rvert=1\) exclude asymptotic stability: \(\lambda=1\) gives constant modes, \(\lambda=-1\) a two-cycle, a nonreal pair a rotation of constant size.
  • For \(n=2\): both eigenvalues lie inside the unit circle if and only if \(\lvert\det A\rvert<1\) and \(\lvert\operatorname{tr}A\rvert<1+\det A\) (the determinant and trace are the product and sum of the eigenvalues).
  • Necessary condition for any \(n\): \(\lvert\det A\rvert<1\), since \(\lvert\det A\rvert=\prod_i\lvert\lambda_i\rvert\).
  • A scalar equation of order \(k\) is (asymptotically) stable if and only if its companion matrix is, since the eigenvalues are the characteristic roots (higher-order equation).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Asymptotically stable, not diagonalizable. \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0\\0.25&0.5\end{pmatrix}\), \(\boldsymbol{b}=(1,1)^{\top}\). The only eigenvalue is \(0.5\), so the system is asymptotically stable. Solving \((I-A)\boldsymbol{x}^*=\boldsymbol{b}\) gives \(\boldsymbol{x}^*=(2,3)^{\top}\); check: \(A\boldsymbol{x}^*+\boldsymbol{b}=(1+1,\,0.5+1.5+1)^{\top}=(2,3)^{\top}\). Here \(A^t=0.5^t\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0.5t&1\end{pmatrix}\), and \(0.5^{t}\cdot0.5t\to0\) despite the factor \(t\).

Small diagonal, unstable. \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&1\\1&0.5\end{pmatrix}\) has \(\operatorname{tr}A=1\), \(\det A=-0.75\) and eigenvalues \(1.5\) and \(-0.5\). Unstable; the \(2\times2\) test agrees, since \(\lvert\operatorname{tr}A\rvert=1\not<0.25=1+\det A\).

Boundary case. For \(\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t\) with the column-stochastic matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}0.9&0.2\\0.1&0.8\end{pmatrix}\) of a two-state Markov chain the eigenvalues are \(1\) and \(0.7\). Solutions converge, but to a limit that depends on \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) (a multiple of \((2,1)^{\top}\)), so the zero solution is not asymptotically stable. It is stable: both eigenvalues are simple and \(\lvert\lambda\rvert\le1\), so all solutions stay bounded.

docs.title: Stability of a Scalar Difference Equation
Proposition
docs.text:
Consider the linear difference equation of order \(k\) with constant coefficients and constant right-hand side

\[ x_{t+k}+a_{k-1}x_{t+k-1}+\cdots+a_0x_t=b, \]

with characteristic polynomial \(p\) and \(p(1)\ne0\), so that \(x^*=b/p(1)\) is the unique equilibrium. The equilibrium is called (globally) asymptotically stable if every solution converges to \(x^*\), whatever the initial values. This holds if and only if every characteristic root \(r\) satisfies \(\lvert r\rvert<1\).

  • First order, \(x_{t+1}=a x_t+b\) with \(a\ne1\): asymptotically stable if and only if \(\lvert a\rvert<1\).
  • Second order, \(x_{t+2}+a_1x_{t+1}+a_0x_t=b\): asymptotically stable if and only if \(\lvert a_0\rvert<1\) and \(\lvert a_1\rvert<1+a_0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The deviation \(x_t-x^*\) solves the homogeneous equation, so it is a combination of terms \(t^j r^t\). Each term tends to \(0\) exactly when the modulus \(\lvert r\rvert\) is below \(1\); the polynomial factor \(t^j\) from a repeated root cannot prevent decay. One root with \(\lvert r\rvert\ge1\) is enough to spoil convergence for some initial values.

The figure shows the first example below, \(x_{t+1}=-0.8x_t+9\) with \(x_0=0\). Because \(a=-0.8\) is negative, \(x_t\) jumps to alternate sides of \(x^*=5\); because \(\lvert a\rvert<1\), the distance \(\lvert x_t-x^*\rvert=5(0.8)^t\) shrinks every period, so the path stays inside the dashed envelope \(5\pm5(0.8)^t\) and converges to \(5\).

Move \(a\) across \(\pm1\) and follow the cobweb: each period multiplies the distance to \(x^*\) by \(|a|\), so every starting value \(x_0\) converges when \(|a|<1\) and moves away when \(|a|>1\).

The definition quantifies over all initial values. An unstable equation can still have particular solutions that converge, namely those whose coefficients on the large roots happen to be zero.

In Math V, asymptotic stability (all solutions converge) requires all roots strictly inside the unit circle. The equation is called stable when all solutions stay bounded: all roots satisfy \(\lvert r\rvert\le1\) and those with \(\lvert r\rvert=1\) are simple. Such roots give solutions that neither grow nor die out, so the equation is stable but not asymptotically stable. Compare the continuous-time criterion for the stability of an equilibrium of an ordinary differential equation, where decay requires \(f'(x^*)<0\) (negative real parts for linear systems) rather than a modulus below \(1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For the first-order equation, \(x_t=x^*+a^t(x_0-x^*)\). For \(0<a<1\) the approach is monotone, for \(-1<a<0\) it is a damped oscillation, for \(\lvert a\rvert>1\) the path diverges unless \(x_0=x^*\), and for \(a=-1\) it is a two-cycle.
  • A pair of simple nonreal roots \(\rho \mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\theta}\) gives oscillations with amplitude proportional to \(\rho^t\): damped if \(\rho<1\), constant if \(\rho=1\), explosive if \(\rho>1\).
  • Necessary conditions for asymptotic stability: \(\lvert a_0\rvert<1\) (since \(\lvert a_0\rvert=\prod_i\lvert r_i\rvert\)) and \(p(1)>0\).
  • The speed of convergence is set by the largest root modulus \(\max_i\lvert r_i\rvert\).
  • If \(p(1)=0\), \(r=1\) is a root, there is no unique equilibrium and the equation is not asymptotically stable.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Damped oscillation. \(x_{t+1}=-0.8x_t+9\) has \(x^*=9/1.8=5\) and \(x_t=5+(-0.8)^t(x_0-5)\). From \(x_0=0\): \(x_1=9\), \(x_2=1.8\), approaching \(5\) from alternating sides. Asymptotically stable, since \(\lvert-0.8\rvert<1\).

Asymptotically stable with complex roots. \(x_{t+2}-x_{t+1}+0.5x_t=0\): here \(a_0=0.5\), \(a_1=-1\), and \(\lvert a_0\rvert<1\), \(\lvert a_1\rvert=1<1.5\). Directly: \(r=\tfrac{1\pm\mathrm{i}}{2}\) with \(\lvert r\rvert=\tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\approx0.707<1\).

Unstable, yet some solutions converge. \(x_{t+2}-2.5x_{t+1}+x_t=0\) has roots \(2\) and \(0.5\); the test fails because \(\lvert a_0\rvert=1\). The general solution \(c_1 2^t+c_2(0.5)^t\) diverges unless \(c_1=0\); for instance \(x_0=2\), \(x_1=1\) gives \(x_t=2(0.5)^t\to0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A system of differential equations consists of \(n\) first-order differential equations for \(n\) unknown functions \(x_1(t),\dots,x_n(t)\). For \(i=1,\dots,n\),

\[ x_i'(t)=f_i\big(t,x_1(t),\dots,x_n(t)\big), \]

where \(x_i'(t)=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x_i}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)\). With the state vector \(\boldsymbol{x}(t)=\big(x_1(t),\dots,x_n(t)\big)^{\top}\) it reads \(\boldsymbol{x}'(t)=\boldsymbol{f}\big(t,\boldsymbol{x}(t)\big)\). The system is linear if

\[ \boldsymbol{x}'(t)=A(t)\,\boldsymbol{x}(t)+\boldsymbol{b}(t) \]

for an \(n\times n\) matrix function \(A(t)\) and a vector function \(\boldsymbol{b}(t)\); it is coupled if some \(x_i'\) depends on some \(x_j\) with \(j\neq i\). An initial value problem prescribes the whole vector \(\boldsymbol{x}(t_0)\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A system describes several interacting quantities, such as two competing populations or prices in linked markets. In the linear case the matrix product \(A\boldsymbol{x}\) packs all couplings into one coefficient matrix; the entry \(a_{ij}\) measures how \(x_j\) affects the rate of change of \(x_i\).

The figure shows the coupled example below in the \((x_1,x_2)\) plane. Along the eigenvector \((1,1)^{\top}\) (blue, \(\lambda=3\)) solutions move outwards like \(\mathrm{e}^{3t}\), along \((1,-1)^{\top}\) (red, \(\lambda=-1\)) they move inwards like \(\mathrm{e}^{-t}\), and every other solution (grey) combines the two. The green curve is the solution with \(\boldsymbol{x}(0)=(3,1)^{\top}\): it comes in near the \((1,-1)^{\top}\) line and then leaves in the \((1,1)^{\top}\) direction. Neither coordinate can be solved on its own, but in eigenvector coordinates the two motions separate.

Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) and move \(t\): the component along \((1,1)^T\) grows like \(e^{3t}\) and the component along \((1,-1)^T\) decays like \(e^{-t}\), so every orbit off the line of \((1,-1)^T\) eventually leaves along \((1,1)^T\).

Every scalar equation of order \(n\) is a first-order system in disguise: with \(y_1=x\), \(y_2=x'\), ..., \(y_n=x^{(n-1)}\) the equation \(x^{(n)}=f(t,x,\dots,x^{(n-1)})\) becomes \(y_1'=y_2,\ \dots,\ y_{n-1}'=y_n,\ y_n'=f(t,y_1,\dots,y_n)\). For a second-order differential equation this gives a two-dimensional system. So first-order systems are the general framework, and one theory covers all orders.

Coupling is what makes systems harder than \(n\) separate scalar equations. For constant, diagonalizable \(A\) the eigenvalues and eigenvectors remove it: a coordinate change along eigenvectors turns the system into decoupled scalar equations. A common error is to solve each row as if the other variables were constants. The discrete-time counterpart is the system of linear difference equations \(\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a linear system with continuous \(A(t),\boldsymbol{b}(t)\) on an interval \(I\), each initial value problem has exactly one solution on \(I\).
  • If \(\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{0}\) and \(A\) is constant and diagonalizable, \(A=PDP^{-1}\) (diagonalization), then \(\boldsymbol{y}=P^{-1}\boldsymbol{x}\) satisfies \(\boldsymbol{y}'=D\boldsymbol{y}\), i.e. \(y_i'=\lambda_iy_i\), so \(y_i(t)=y_i(0)\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_it}\).
  • In that case \(\boldsymbol{x}(t)=\sum_i c_i\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_it}\boldsymbol{v}_i\), with \(\boldsymbol{v}_i\) the columns of \(P\); for any constant \(A\), \(\boldsymbol{x}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{At}\boldsymbol{x}(0)\) with the matrix exponential.
  • The companion matrix of \(x''+a_1x'+a_0x=0\) is \(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-a_0&-a_1\end{pmatrix}\), with characteristic polynomial \(\lambda^2+a_1\lambda+a_0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Coupled linear system. \(x_1'=x_1+2x_2\), \(x_2'=2x_1+x_2\), so \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\). Eigenpairs: \(A(1,1)^{\top}=3(1,1)^{\top}\) and \(A(1,-1)^{\top}=-(1,-1)^{\top}\). Hence

\[ \boldsymbol{x}(t)=c_1\mathrm{e}^{3t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}+c_2\mathrm{e}^{-t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}. \]

With \(\boldsymbol{x}(0)=(3,1)^{\top}\): \(c_1+c_2=3\), \(c_1-c_2=1\), so \(c_1=2\), \(c_2=1\) and \(\boldsymbol{x}(t)=\big(2\mathrm{e}^{3t}+\mathrm{e}^{-t},\ 2\mathrm{e}^{3t}-\mathrm{e}^{-t}\big)^{\top}\).

Reduction of order. \(x''+3x'+2x=0\) becomes, with \(y_1=x\), \(y_2=x'\), the system \(\boldsymbol{y}'=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-2&-3\end{pmatrix}\boldsymbol{y}\), whose eigenvalues \(-1,-2\) are the roots of \(r^2+3r+2\).

Decoupled system. \(x_1'=-x_1\), \(x_2'=4x_2\) has diagonal \(A\) and solution \(\big(x_1(0)\mathrm{e}^{-t},\ x_2(0)\mathrm{e}^{4t}\big)^{\top}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A system of linear difference equations (first order, constant coefficients) is

\[ \boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t+\boldsymbol{b}_t,\qquad t=0,1,2,\ldots, \]

where \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is the state vector, \(A\) is a fixed real \(n\times n\) matrix and \((\boldsymbol{b}_t)\) is a given sequence of forcing vectors. It is homogeneous if \(\boldsymbol{b}_t=\boldsymbol{0}\) for all \(t\). For every initial vector \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) the unique solution is

\[ \boldsymbol{x}_t=A^t\boldsymbol{x}_0+\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}A^{t-1-s}\boldsymbol{b}_s. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Entry \(a_{ij}\) says how much variable \(j\) today contributes to variable \(i\) in the next period. The system is the vector form of the first-order linear difference equation: the number \(a\) becomes the matrix \(A\), and \(a^t\) becomes the matrix power \(A^t\).

The figure plots the population-shares example below. Writing \(\boldsymbol{x}_0=(1,0)^{\top}\) in the eigenvector basis, the component along \((2,1)^{\top}\) (\(\lambda=1\)) never changes, while the component along \((1,-1)^{\top}\) (\(\lambda=0.7\)) is multiplied by \(0.7\) each period. So the iterates move along the dashed line through \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) in direction \((1,-1)^{\top}\), with steps shrinking by the factor \(0.7\), towards \(\boldsymbol{x}^*=(2/3,1/3)^{\top}\) on the blue eigenvector line.

Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) or change the entries of \(A\): in eigenvector coordinates each component is multiplied by its own eigenvalue every period. With the default matrix the component for \(\lambda=0.7\) dies out and the iterates settle on the eigenvector line of \(\lambda=1\).

Powers of \(A\) are hard to read off directly, which is where eigenvalues and eigenvectors come in. If \(A\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda\boldsymbol{p}\), then \(A^t\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda^t\boldsymbol{p}\): along an eigenvector the system behaves like a scalar equation. When \(A\) has \(n\) independent eigenvectors, write \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) in that basis and each component evolves separately. This is diagonalization applied to dynamics.

Any scalar higher-order equation can be written as such a system with a companion matrix, so the system covers every linear constant-coefficient difference equation. A common mistake is to compute \(A^t\) entrywise, as if \((A^t)_{ij}=a_{ij}^t\); this is only true for diagonal matrices.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(A=PDP^{-1}\) with \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)\), then \(A^t=PD^tP^{-1}\) and the homogeneous solution is \(\boldsymbol{x}_t=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i\lambda_i^t\boldsymbol{p}_i\) with \(\boldsymbol{c}=P^{-1}\boldsymbol{x}_0\).
  • For a nondiagonalizable \(A\), the Jordan normal form adds terms \(t^j\lambda^t\) (\(\lambda\ne0\)) for \(0\le j<\) the size of the Jordan block.
  • With constant forcing \(\boldsymbol{b}\), an equilibrium solves \((I-A)\boldsymbol{x}^*=\boldsymbol{b}\); it is unique if and only if \(1\) is not an eigenvalue of \(A\). Then \(\boldsymbol{x}_t-\boldsymbol{x}^*=A^t(\boldsymbol{x}_0-\boldsymbol{x}^*)\).
  • Nonreal eigenvalues of the real matrix \(A\) come in conjugate pairs and produce oscillating real solutions.
  • The long-run behaviour is governed by the eigenvalues of largest modulus; see stability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Diagonalizable system. Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\), with eigenvalues \(3,1\) and eigenvectors \(\boldsymbol{p}_1=(1,1)^{\top}\), \(\boldsymbol{p}_2=(1,-1)^{\top}\). For \(\boldsymbol{x}_0=(3,1)^{\top}=2\boldsymbol{p}_1+\boldsymbol{p}_2\),

\[ \boldsymbol{x}_t=2\cdot3^t\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}. \]

Check: \(\boldsymbol{x}_1=A\boldsymbol{x}_0=(7,5)^{\top}=(6+1,\,6-1)^{\top}\).

Population shares. Each period \(10\%\) of region 1 moves to region 2 and \(20\%\) of region 2 moves to region 1: \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0.9&0.2\\0.1&0.8\end{pmatrix}\). The eigenvalues are \(1\) (eigenvector \((2,1)^{\top}\)) and \(0.7\) (eigenvector \((1,-1)^{\top}\)). From \(\boldsymbol{x}_0=(1,0)^{\top}=\tfrac{1}{3}(2,1)^{\top}+\tfrac{1}{3}(1,-1)^{\top}\),

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{x}_t&=\tfrac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}+\tfrac{1}{3}(0.7)^t\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\\ &\to\begin{pmatrix}2/3\\1/3\end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} \]

Check: \(\boldsymbol{x}_1=(0.9,0.1)^{\top}\) both ways. This is a two-state Markov chain written for column vectors.

docs.title: Actuarial notation
docs.text:
The term angle \(\angl{n}\) means an \(n\)-year term. Its horizontal bar and right-hand stroke mark the duration, while the variable \(n\) keeps its usual mathematical font.

Symbol Meaning Markdown formula \(v\), \(d\), \(\delta\) Discount factor \(v=(1+i)^{-1}\), discount rate \(d=1-v\) and force of interest \(\delta=\log(1+i)\) at annual effective interest \(i\) $v$, $d$, $\delta$ \(\ddot a_{\angl{n}}\) Annuity certain, payable in advance $\ddot a_{\angl{n}}$ \(\ddot a_{x:\angl{n}}\) Temporary life annuity-due $\ddot a_{x:\angl{n}}$ \(\bar a_{x:\angl{n}}\) Continuous temporary life annuity $\bar a_{x:\angl{n}}$ \(A_{x:\angl{n}}\) Endowment insurance, annual settlement $A_{x:\angl{n}}$ \({}_{u\mid}\ddot a_x\) Deferred life annuity-due ${}_{u\mid}\ddot a_x$ \({}_np_x\), \({}_nq_x\) Survival and death probabilities ${}_np_x$, ${}_nq_x$ \({}_nE_x\) Pure endowment factor ${}_nE_x$ \({}^{2}A_x\) Second moment of whole life insurance present value ${}^{2}A_x$ \(l_{[x]+t}\) Select-table survivors after duration \(t\) $l_{[x]+t}$

Payment timing and benefit conditions are defined on each concept page. A bar above \(a\) or \(A\) indicates continuous payments or settlement at death; the two dots on \(a\) indicate payments in advance.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The actuarial present value (APV) of an insurance cash flow is the expectation of its random present value \(Z\): \(\operatorname{APV}=\mathbb{E}[Z]\), when integrable. For a benefit \(b(T_x)\) paid at death under constant force of interest \(\delta\), \(Z=b(T_x)\mathrm{e}^{-\delta T_x}\). Define \(v=(1+i)^{-1}\) and \(\delta=\log(1+i)\) for annual effective interest \(i>-1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The payment timing is uncertain even when the benefit amount is fixed. Discount each possible payment first, then average over the mortality model.

The figure uses the Examples case. The payment of 100 at time 5 is made only if \(T_x>5\); carrying it back to time 0 multiplies it by the discount factor \(v^5=(1.04)^{-5}\) and by the survival probability \({}_5p_x=0.9\). The result, \(100(1.04)^{-5}(0.9)\approx73.97\), is the expectation of a present value that equals \(100v^5\) with probability \(0.9\) and \(0\) otherwise.

Move \({}_np_x\), \(n\) and \(i\): the payment is discounted by \(v^n\) and then weighted by the survival probability. The APV is the mean of the two possible present values of \(Z\).

The future lifetime \(T_x\) determines when a death benefit is paid. Its density weights the discounted benefit in the integral below; for a survival payment, the event \(T_x>t_k\) determines whether that payment occurs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A nonnegative benefit paid at death has APV \(\int_0^\infty b(t)v^tf_x(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\).
  • For payments \(b_k\) at fixed times \(t_k\) conditional on survival, APV is \(\displaystyle \sum_k b_kv^{t_k}{}_{t_k}p_x\).
  • Scaling benefits by \(B\) scales APV by \(B\) and variance by \(B^2\).
  • A net single premium covers expected discounted benefits under the chosen basis; expenses and risk loading require additional treatment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: A payment of 100 at time 5 with survival probability \(0.9\) and \(i=0.04\) has APV \(100(1.04)^{-5}(0.9)\approx73.97\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a life aged \(x\) with future lifetime \(T_x\), define \({}_tp_x=\mathbb{P}(T_x>t)\) and \({}_tq_x=\mathbb{P}(T_x\le t)\) for \(t\ge0\). The deferred death probability is

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} {}_{u|t}q_x&=\mathbb{P}(u<T_x\le u+t)\\ &={}_up_x-{}_{u+t}p_x. \end{aligned} \]

Here \(u\ge0\) is the deferment and \(t\ge0\) the subsequent coverage period. An omitted left-hand duration means one year: \(p_x={}_1p_x\), \(q_x={}_1q_x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
These symbols encode the age, waiting period and coverage period of a survival event. Reading those three parts prevents confusion between dying within a period and surviving until it begins.

The figure uses the Examples values for a life aged 40. The blue arrows are the survival events \(T_{40}>5\) and \(T_{40}>10\); the red interval is the deferred death event \(5<T_{40}\le10\), open at 5 and closed at 10. Surviving past time 5 means either surviving past time 10 or dying in \((5,10]\), so \({}_{5|5}q_{40}={}_5p_{40}-{}_{10}p_{40}=0.98-0.95=0.03\), a probability measured from age 40.

Move \(u\) and \(t\): \({}_{u|t}q_x\) is the drop of the survival curve from \(u\) to \(u+t\), while \({}_tq_{x+u}\) divides that drop by \({}_up_x\). The defaults give \({}_{5|5}q_{40}=0.03\).

The multiplication rule for conditional probability explains survival over successive periods: first survive to duration \(t\), then survive another \(u\) years given attained age \(x+t\). This gives \({}_{t+u}p_x={}_tp_x{}_up_{x+t}\) whenever the first survival probability is positive.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \({}_tp_x+{}_tq_x=1\).
  • \({}_{t+u}p_x={}_tp_x\,{}_up_{x+t}\).
  • \({}_{u|t}q_x={}_up_x\,{}_tq_{x+u}\) when survival to \(x+u\) has positive probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \({}_5p_{40}=0.98\) and \({}_{10}p_{40}=0.95\), then \({}_{5|5}q_{40}=0.03\). This is an unconditional probability at age 40, not the conditional five-year death probability at age 45.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An annuity certain makes specified payments independently of survival. For \(n\) annual unit payments, the annuity-due pays at \(0,\ldots,n-1\), whereas the annuity-immediate pays at \(1,\ldots,n\). With annual discount factor \(v=(1+i)^{-1}\) at interest rate \(i\), their present values are \(\displaystyle \ddot a_{\angl{n}}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}v^k\) and \(\displaystyle a_{\angl{n}}=\sum_{k=1}^nv^k\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This is the deterministic building block for life annuities, such as the whole life annuity-due. The due/immediate distinction describes payment timing, not uncertainty.

The figure uses the Examples case with \(v=0.9\) and \(n=3\). Each red arrow is a unit payment, and the number below it is its present value \(v^k\). The annuity-due pays at times \(0,1,2\) and is worth \(1+0.9+0.81=2.71\). The annuity-immediate makes the same three payments one year later, so every present value, and hence the total, is multiplied by \(v\): \(a_{\angl{3}}=0.9(2.71)=2.439\).

Change \(v\) and \(n\): each arrow shrinks to its present value \(v^k\). The immediate row is the due row moved one year later, so \(a_{\angl{n}}=v\,\ddot a_{\angl{n}}\).

Because these payments are certain, their actuarial present value equals their ordinary discounted value. The geometric series formula evaluates the finite sums of powers of \(v\) and gives the closed forms below.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With \(d=1-v\ne0\), \(\ddot a_{\angl{n}}=(1-v^n)/d\) and \(a_{\angl{n}}=v\ddot a_{\angl{n}}\).
  • A continuous unit-rate annuity has value \(\bar a_{\angl{n}}=(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\delta n})/\delta\), with limit \(n\) at \(\delta=0\).
  • Paying \(1/m\) in advance every \(1/m\) year gives \(\displaystyle m^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{mn-1}v^{k/m}\).
  • At positive interest, the infinite-duration versions (\(n\to\infty\)) are called perpetuities, with \(\ddot a_{\angl{\infty}}=1/d\) and \(a_{\angl{\infty}}=v/d=1/i\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: At \(v=0.9\), three unit payments in advance have value \(1+0.9+0.81=2.71\). Moving all payments one year later gives \(0.9(2.71)=2.439\).

docs.title: Constant Force Within a Year of Age
Definition
docs.text: For integer age \(x\), constant-force interpolation, also called the constant force of mortality (CFM) assumption, takes \(\mu_{x+s}=\mu_x^*\) for \(0\le s<1\). If the annual survival probability is \(p_x>0\), the required force is \(\mu_x^*=-\log p_x\). Different years may have different forces.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Survival declines exponentially within each annual interval. A piecewise constant force can match all integer-age entries without assuming one exponential lifetime distribution over every age.

The figure takes \(p_{60}=0.9\) from the Examples. Under CFM the force is flat at \(\mu_{60}^*=-\log0.9\approx0.105\) throughout the year; the shaded area up to \(s\) is \(s\mu_{60}^*\), so \({}_sp_{60}=\mathrm{e}^{-s\mu_{60}^*}=0.9^s\). The dashed curve is the uniform distribution of deaths (UDD) force \(q_{60}/(1-sq_{60})\), which rises from \(0.100\) to about \(0.111\). Both forces have area \(-\log0.9\) over the whole year, so they agree at \(s=1\), but at \(s=\tfrac{1}{2}\) CFM gives \(\sqrt{0.9}\approx0.94868\) and UDD gives \(0.95\).

Change \(p_{60}\) and \(s\): the flat force \(\mu^*_{60}=-\log p_{60}\) gives \({}_sp_{60}=p_{60}^s\), while the dashed UDD force rises. Both have the same area over the year, so the two curves meet only at \(s=0\) and \(s=1\).

A life table supplies \(p_x=l_{x+1}/l_x\). Integrating a constant force of mortality gives exponential survival within the year; matching its one-year value to \(p_x\) determines \(\mu_x^*=-\log p_x\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \({}_sp_x=p_x^s\) and \(l_{x+s}=l_xp_x^s\) for \(0\le s\le1\).
  • Within one interval, \({}_tp_{x+s}=p_x^t\) for \(s+t\le1\).
  • For an interval crossing an integer age, multiply survival probabilities for its successive pieces.
  • CFM and UDD agree at integer ages but generally differ at fractional ages.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(p_{60}=0.9\), half-year survival is \(\sqrt{0.9}\approx0.94868\) under CFM, compared with \(0.95\) under UDD.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A continuous life annuity pays at rate one per year while the annuitant is alive. Its present value is \(Y=\int_0^{T_x}\mathrm{e}^{-\delta t}\,\mathrm{d}t\), and its actuarial present value (APV) is \(\bar a_x=\mathbb{E}[Y]\). A temporary version stops at \(\min(T_x,n)\) instead.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Continuous payments provide a tractable idealization of a frequent payment stream. Payment rate one means an amount \(dt\) over an interval of length \(dt\), not a unit payment at every instant.

The figure uses the Examples values \(\lambda=0.02\) and \(\delta=0.03\). At time \(t\) the benefit rate 100 is discounted by \(v^t=\mathrm{e}^{-0.03t}\) and is paid only if the annuitant is alive, which has probability \({}_tp_x=\mathrm{e}^{-0.02t}\), so the expected discounted rate is \(100\mathrm{e}^{-0.05t}\). The shaded area under this curve is \(100\bar a_x=100/(\lambda+\delta)=2000\).

Change \(\lambda\) and \(\delta\): the APV is the area under \(100v^t{}_tp_x\), \(100/(\lambda+\delta)=2000\) at the defaults, and \(\bar A_x+\delta\bar a_x=1\). Drag the probe to see \(Y=(1-v^{T_x})/\delta\) rise with the lifetime.

The whole life annuity-due values annual survival-contingent payments by a sum. Here a payment rate replaces those individual payments, so survival-weighted discount factors are integrated over time. The force of mortality determines \({}_tp_x\); a constant force \(\lambda\) gives \(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\), producing the closed form below.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\bar a_x=\int_0^\infty v^t{}_tp_x\,\mathrm{d}t\) and \(\bar a_{x:\angl{n}}=\int_0^n v^t{}_tp_x\,\mathrm{d}t\).
  • For \(\delta\ne0\), \(Y=(1-v^{T_x})/\delta\) and \(\bar A_x+\delta\bar a_x=1\).
  • At constant force of mortality \(\lambda>0\) and force of interest \(\delta\ge0\), \(\bar a_x=1/(\lambda+\delta)\).
  • At zero interest, \(Y=T_x\) and the APV is the complete expectation of life.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: At \(\lambda=0.02\) and \(\delta=0.03\), a continuous benefit rate of 100 per year has APV \(100/0.05=2000\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The curtate future lifetime of a life aged \(x\) is \(K_x=\lfloor T_x\rfloor\), the number of complete future years lived. It takes values \(0,1,2,\ldots\). Under the continuous lifetime assumption,

\[ \mathbb{P}(K_x=k)={}_kp_x-{}_{k+1}p_x={}_kp_xq_{x+k}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Annual insurance payments often depend on the year of death rather than its exact time. A death after 3.7 years has \(K_x=3\) and an end-of-year death payment at time 4.

Each year \([k,k+1)\) of the time axis is labelled with the value of \(K_x\) for a death inside it. The life in the figure ends at \(T_x=3.7\), inside the shaded year \([3,4)\), so \(K_x=3\) and an end-of-year death payment is made at \(K_x+1=4\). The position of the death within the year is discarded: \(\mathbb{P}(K_x=3)\) is the probability that the death falls anywhere in the shaded year.

Move \(T_x\): every death in the year \([k,k+1)\) gives \(K_x=k\), and the bar over that year has area \(\mathbb P(K_x=k)={}_kp_x-{}_{k+1}p_x\), the area under the density over the same year.

Taking the floor of future lifetime \(T_x\) records only completed years. The actuarial survival and death probabilities at successive integer durations give the probability of death during year \(k\): survive \(k\) years, then die before the next anniversary.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\{K_x\ge k\}=\{T_x\ge k\}\) for integer \(k\); strict versus weak inequalities have the same probability under continuous lifetimes.
  • \(\displaystyle \mathbb{E}[K_x]=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}{}_kp_x\).
  • \(\displaystyle \mathbb{E}[K_x^2]=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(2k-1){}_kp_x\), when finite.
  • A mass function for \(K_x\) gives probabilities; a density for \(T_x\) does not.

docs.title: Examples

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A unit annual life annuity-due deferred \(u\) years, for integer \(u\ge0\), begins payments at time \(u\) conditional on survival and then continues while the annuitant lives. Its present value is \(\displaystyle Y=\sum_{k=u}^{\infty}v^k\indicator_{\{T_x>k\}}\), and its actuarial present value (APV) is denoted \({}_{u|}\ddot a_x=\mathbb{E}[Y]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A pension can be viewed as an annuity whose first payment waits until retirement. Survival to retirement and discounting both affect its issue-date value.

The figure uses the Examples case: a unit pension for a life aged 40, deferred \(u=20\) years (the time axis is broken between 2 and 19). No payments are made before time 20. From then on, unit payments are made while the annuitant is alive; for an annuitant alive at age 60 they are worth \(\ddot a_{60}=12\) at time 20. Multiplying by \({}_{20}E_{40}=0.3\), which discounts over 20 years and allows for survival to age 60, gives \({}_{20|}\ddot a_{40}=3.6\) at issue.

Move \(u\): no payment is made before time \(u\), and \({}_{u|}\ddot a_{40}={}_uE_{40}\ddot a_{40+u}=\ddot a_{40}-\ddot a_{40:\angl{u}}\). The defaults give \({}_{20}E_{40}\approx0.30\) and \(\ddot a_{60}\approx12.0\), close to the Examples.

The pure endowment factor \({}_uE_x\) discounts the start date and accounts for survival to it. Conditional on reaching age \(x+u\), the remaining payments form a whole life annuity-due, with value \(\ddot a_{x+u}\) at that date. This gives the first identity below. Alternatively, remove the first \(u\) payments from a whole life annuity-due at age \(x\): those payments form a temporary life annuity, giving the second identity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
\[ \begin{aligned} {}_{u|}\ddot a_x&={}_uE_x\ddot a_{x+u},\\[4pt] {}_{u|}\ddot a_x&=\ddot a_x-\ddot a_{x:\angl{u}}. \end{aligned} \]
  • The first identity follows by writing \({}_{u+j}p_x={}_up_x{}_jp_{x+u}\) in the payment sum.
  • For a deferred annuity-immediate, specify that the first payment is at \(u+1\); the factorization uses \(a_{x+u}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \({}_{20}E_{40}=0.3\) and \(\ddot a_{60}=12\), a unit pension starting at age 60 has issue-date APV \(0.3(12)=3.6\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A death insurance deferred \(u\) years pays only for a death after duration \(u\). For a unit deferred whole life benefit paid at death, \(Z=v^{T_x}\indicator_{\{T_x>u\}}\), with actuarial present value (APV) \({}_{u|}\bar A_x=\mathbb{E}[Z]\). The discount is from the original issue date, not from the end of the deferment.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The insured must first survive the waiting period. Conditional on doing so, the remaining contract is a whole life insurance issued at the older age.

The figure uses the Examples case with \(u=5\). A death in the grey waiting period pays nothing; a death after time 5, such as the one marked, pays 1 at \(T_x\). For a life alive at age \(x+5\) the remaining cover is a whole life insurance worth \(\bar A_{x+5}=0.4\), and multiplying by \({}_5E_x=0.7\) brings it back to the issue date: \({}_{5|}\bar A_x=0.28\).

Move the deferment \(u\): deaths before \(u\) pay nothing, and \({}_{u|}\bar A_x={}_uE_x\bar A_{x+u}\). At constant force \(\bar A_{x+u}=0.4\) for every \(u\); here \({}_5E_x=e^{-0.25}\approx0.779\) rather than the Examples' \(0.7\).

The pure endowment factor \({}_uE_x=v^u{}_up_x\) values survival to the end of the waiting period. Multiplying it by the death-insurance APV at age \(x+u\) brings that conditional later contract back to the original issue date.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \({}_{u|}\bar A_x=v^u{}_up_x\bar A_{x+u}={}_uE_x\bar A_{x+u}\).
  • Whole life APV equals term APV over \(u\) years plus the \(u\)-year deferred whole life APV.
  • The same factorization applies to annual settlement for integer \(u\).
  • A deferred term policy additionally ends coverage after a finite period.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \({}_5E_x=0.7\) and the unit whole life APV at age \(x+5\) is \(0.4\), the deferred contract has APV \(0.7(0.4)=0.28\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An \(n\)-year endowment insurance pays a unit benefit at death within the term or at time \(n\) on survival. With immediate death settlement, \(Z=v^{\min(T_x,n)}\). With annual death settlement and integer \(n\), \(Z=v^{\min(K_x+1,n)}\). The actuarial present values (APVs) \(\mathbb{E}[Z]\) are denoted \(\bar A_{x:\angl{n}}\) and \(A_{x:\angl{n}}\), respectively.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Every lifetime leads to a payment. The uncertainty concerns when that payment occurs, up to the fixed maturity time.

The figure plots the present value \(Z=v^{\min(T_x,n)}\) against \(T_x\) for \(n=10\) and \(\delta=0.03\), so \(v=\mathrm{e}^{-0.03}\). A death before time 10 gives \(v^{T_x}\), which falls from 1 to \(\mathrm{e}^{-0.3}\approx0.741\); survival to time 10 gives the fixed maturity value \(v^{10}=\mathrm{e}^{-0.3}\). Every outcome lies between these two values, and with \(\lambda=0.02\) the mean is the Examples value \(\mathbb{E}[Z]\approx0.76392\).

Change \(n\), \(\lambda\) and \(\delta\): the APV is the term area plus the point mass \({}_nE_x\) at \(n\), and every outcome of \(Z=v^{\min(T_x,n)}\) lies between \(v^n\) and 1.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• APV equals the APV of an \(n\)-year term insurance plus \({}_nE_x\).
  • Death and survival benefits occur on disjoint events; their product is zero. Their covariance is generally negative, not zero.
  • To calculate the second moment, square each discounted payment on its own event. Do not add component variances without a covariance term.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: At \(\lambda=0.02\), \(\delta=0.03\) and \(n=10\), immediate death-or-survival APV is \(0.4(1-\mathrm{e}^{-0.5})+\mathrm{e}^{-0.5}\approx0.76392\).

docs.title: Complete and Curtate Expectation of Life
Definition
docs.text: The complete expectation of life at age \(x\) is \(\mathring e_x=\mathbb{E}[T_x]\), whereas the curtate expectation is \(e_x=\mathbb{E}[K_x]\). Their \(n\)-year term versions are \(\mathbb{E}[\min(T_x,n)]\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\min(K_x,n)]\), respectively.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The complete quantity includes fractions of the final year. The curtate quantity counts only completed years. A term expectation stops accumulating lifetime after a fixed horizon.

The figure uses the Examples force \(\lambda=0.1\), so \({}_tp_x=\mathrm{e}^{-0.1t}\) (drawn up to \(t=30\)). The area under the curve is \(\mathring e_x=10\). The bars have width one and take the height \({}_kp_x\) at the right end of each year, so their total area is \(e_x=\sum_{k\ge1}{}_kp_x\approx9.508\). The red gaps between the bars and the curve are the fractional final years that the curtate count drops; here they total about \(0.492\), within the bound \(0\le\mathring e_x-e_x\le1\).

Change \(\lambda\): \(\mathring e_x\) is the area under \({}_tp_x\), \(e_x\) the total area of the unit bars, and the red gaps add up to less than 1. Switch on the term version to stop both at \(n\) years.

The curtate future lifetime \(K_x\) counts complete future years. Summing its tail probabilities therefore gives the curtate expectation, whereas integrating the tails of \(T_x\) includes the final fractional year.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathring e_x=\int_0^{\infty}{}_tp_x\,\mathrm{d}t\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\min(T_x,n)]=\int_0^n{}_tp_x\,\mathrm{d}t\).
  • \(\displaystyle e_x=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}{}_kp_x\) and \(\displaystyle \mathbb{E}[\min(K_x,n)]=\sum_{k=1}^n{}_kp_x\) for integer \(n\).
  • When expectations are finite, \(0\le\mathring e_x-e_x\le1\). Under uniform distribution of deaths (UDD) at integer age the difference is \(1/2\).
  • \(\mathbb{E}[T_x^2]=2\int_0^\infty t\,{}_tp_x\,\mathrm{d}t\) when finite.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: At force \(\lambda=0.1\), the complete expectation is 10 years, while the curtate expectation is \(1/(\mathrm{e}^{0.1}-1)\approx9.508\) years.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Under the course's absolutely continuous survival model, the force of mortality at attained age \(x+t\) (the age reached \(t\) years after age \(x\)) is

\[ \mu_{x+t}=\frac{f_x(t)}{S_x(t)}=-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\log S_x(t), \]

where \(S_x(t)>0\) and the derivative exists. Equivalently, it is the limit of \(\mathbb{P}(t<T_x\le t+h\mid T_x>t)/h\) as \(h\downarrow0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Mortality is measured per unit of time among those still alive. The force can exceed one; it is a rate and must be multiplied by a short duration to approximate a probability.

The figure uses the Examples force \(0.02\), so \(S_x(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-0.02t}\). At \(t=20\) the tangent to \(S_x\) has slope \(-f_x(20)\). Dividing the height \(S_x(20)\) by this rate of decline gives the time the tangent needs to reach zero, \(S_x(20)/f_x(20)=1/\mu_{x+20}=50\) years, so a high force means a tangent that is steep relative to the height of the curve. Because this force is constant, the tangent at any \(t\) reaches zero 50 years later.

Move \(t\) and \(\lambda\): the tangent to \(S_x\) at \(t\) has slope \(-f_x(t)\) and reaches zero after \(S_x(t)/f_x(t)=1/\mu_{x+t}\) years. Switch to Makeham's law and watch \(1/\mu_{x+t}\) shrink as the attained age rises.

Here \(T_x\) is future lifetime, \(S_x(t)\) is its survivor function, and \(f_x(t)\) is its probability density function. Dividing the density by the probability of still being alive expresses a death rate among survivors rather than among all lives originally insured.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \({}_tp_x=\exp(-\int_0^t\mu_{x+s}\,\mathrm{d}s)\) and \(f_x(t)={}_tp_x\mu_{x+t}\).
  • A constant force \(\lambda>0\) gives \({}_tp_x=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\), an exponential future lifetime.
  • An increasing force means that the death rate among survivors rises with time survived (positive duration dependence); a decreasing force means that it falls (negative duration dependence).
  • For a finite force at \(x\), \({}_hq_x=\mu_xh+o(h)\), with little-\(o\) notation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: At constant force \(0.02\) per year, the one-year death probability is \(1-\mathrm{e}^{-0.02}\approx0.01980\), rather than exactly \(0.02\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a life currently aged \(x\ge0\), the future lifetime \(T_x\) is the remaining time until death, conditional on being alive at age \(x\). If \(T_0\) denotes age at death and \(S_0(x)=\mathbb{P}(T_0>x)>0\), then

\[ \mathbb{P}(T_x>t)=\frac{S_0(x+t)}{S_0(x)},\qquad t\ge0. \]

The course assumes an absolutely continuous lifetime distribution. Thus \(T_x\) is a continuous random variable, not a single number; its mean \(\mathbb{E}[T_x]\) is the expected future lifetime.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The model updates the lifetime distribution when a person survives to a specified age. Two people at different ages generally have different remaining-lifetime distributions.

The figure uses the uniform example: the blue line is \(S_0(y)=1-y/100\), and the dashed red line is \(\mathbb{P}(T_{60}>t)\) drawn at attained age \(60+t\). Conditioning on survival to 60 rescales the remaining part of \(S_0\) by \(1/S_0(60)\), so the new curve starts again at 1 and still reaches 0 at age 100; at age 70 it equals \(S_0(70)/S_0(60)=0.3/0.4=0.75\).

Move \(x\) and \(t\): \(\mathbb P(T_x>t)=S_0(x+t)/S_0(x)\) rescales the rest of \(S_0\) so that it starts again at 1. Under a constant force the rescaled curve is the newborn's curve once more.

The survivor function \(S_0\) gives survival from birth. By conditional probability, survival another \(t\) years given survival to age \(x\) is \(S_0(x+t)/S_0(x)\), which is the remaining-lifetime survivor function.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Writing \(S_x(t)=\mathbb{P}(T_x>t)\), conditioning gives \(S_x(t+u)=S_x(t)S_{x+t}(u)\) whenever the conditioning probability is positive.
  • The density is \(f_x(t)=-S_x'(t)\) almost everywhere.
  • A distribution of \(T_x\) that does not depend on \(x\) is a special property of a constant force of mortality (the memoryless property), not a general assumption.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \(T_0\) is uniform on \((0,100)\), a survivor aged 60 has \(T_{60}\) uniform on \((0,40)\). Their probability of surviving another 10 years is \(30/40=0.75\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a policy still in force at duration \(t\), let \(Z_t\), \(H_t\) and \(Y_t\) be present values at time \(t\) of future benefits, expenses and premium income. The gross future loss is \(L_t^g=Z_t+H_t-Y_t\). The net loss omits expenses. All quantities refer to the policy conditional on its being in force at \(t\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The insurer faces random future obligations and random future premium income. Positive loss means future outgo exceeds income; negative loss means a future surplus.

The figure takes the realized scenario from the Examples: benefits \(Z_t=100\) and expenses \(H_t=5\) make up the outgo bar, premium income \(Y_t=80\) the income bar, and the gap between their tops is \(L_t^g=105-80=25\). A different realized lifetime would change all three bars, which is why \(L_t^g\) is a random variable rather than a number.

Actuarial present value averages a random discounted cash flow. In contrast, \(Z_t\), \(H_t\) and \(Y_t\) retain the realized uncertainty; their conditional expectations, rather than the realized values themselves, enter an expected policy liability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The time-\(t\) discount origin differs from the issue-date discount origin.
  • A policy ended by death before \(t\) does not have an in-force future-loss distribution at \(t\).
  • The course normally measures the loss after any benefit at \(t\) but before the premium at \(t\). Annuity timing must be specified separately.
  • An equivalence premium gives \(\mathbb{E}[L_0^g]=0\) only under the same valuation and expense basis.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If the future benefit present value (PV) is 100, expense PV 5 and premium-income PV 80 in a realized scenario, the gross future loss is 25. These realized quantities need not equal their expectations.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An annual life annuity-due with an \(n\)-year guarantee pays at times \(0,\ldots,n-1\) irrespective of survival. Payments at \(n,n+1,\ldots\) are made only while the annuitant survives. After an early death, guaranteed payments continue to the designated recipient.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The guarantee protects against losing the entire payment stream through early death. It converts the first part into an annuity certain and leaves a deferred life annuity afterwards.

In the figure the solid arrows at times \(0,\ldots,4\) form the annuity certain; they are paid even when death \(T_x\) falls inside the guarantee period, as marked. The dashed arrows from time 5 are paid only on survival and form the deferred life annuity. With the numbers from the Examples, the actuarial present value (APV) is \(4.5+8=12.5\).

Move \(n\): the first \(n\) payments ignore survival and form \(\ddot a_{\angl{n}}\), the rest form \({}_{n|}\ddot a_x\). The defaults give about \(4.5+8=12.5\), above \(\ddot a_x\) without a guarantee.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• APV is \(\ddot a_{\angl{n}}+{}_{n|}\ddot a_x\).
  • With the same unit payment and timing, APV is at least that of a whole life annuity-due without a guarantee.
  • The guarantee is not the same as a temporary annuity: a temporary annuity stops on death, while guaranteed payments do not.
  • Beneficiary and payment-timing conventions must be stated in the contract.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If five certain payments have present value (PV) \(4.5\) and the five-year deferred life annuity has APV \(8\), the guaranteed contract has APV \(12.5\).

docs.title: Death Benefits Payable at Fractional-Year Boundaries
Definition
docs.text: A unit death benefit payable at the end of the \(1/m\)-year interval of death is paid at \(\tau_m=\lceil mT_x\rceil/m\), for a positive integer \(m\). Its actuarial present value (APV) is \(A_x^{(m)}=\mathbb{E}[v^{\tau_m}]\). Mortality is continuous, so death exactly on a payment boundary has probability zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Settlement at frequency \(m\) leaves a waiting time of less than \(1/m\) year after death. Refining to a frequency that is an integer multiple of \(m\) cannot increase the waiting time for any death. An arbitrary higher frequency need not reduce every realized wait because its calendar grid may not contain the earlier grid. Unlike an annuity payable \(m\) times a year, this is one benefit payment, not \(m\) instalments of \(1/m\).

The figure shows the example with death at \(T_x=2.13\). With quarterly settlement the benefit is paid at the next quarter-year mark, \(\tau_4=\lceil 4\times2.13\rceil/4=2.25\), so the wait is less than \(1/4\) year; with annual settlement it is paid at the end of the year of death, time 3.

Move \(m\) and drag the probe \(T_x\): the benefit waits until the next \(1/m\)-year mark, so \(A_x^{(m)}\) rises towards \(\bar A_x\) as \(m\) grows. With \(m=4\), a death at \(2.13\) is paid at \(2.25\).

Whole life insurance provides the same death benefit with either annual or immediate settlement. The fractional-year version changes the settlement grid. Under uniform distribution of deaths (UDD), the fraction of the year lived is uniform and independent of the year of death, allowing within-year discounting to be averaged separately.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle A_x^{(m)}=\sum_{k=0}^\infty v^{(k+1)/m}({}_{k/m}p_x-{}_{(k+1)/m}p_x)\).
  • As \(m\to\infty\), \(A_x^{(m)}\to\bar A_x\) for nonnegative interest.
  • Under UDD in each year and \(i>0\), \(A_x^{(m)}=[i/i^{(m)}]A_x\), where \(i^{(m)}=m((1+i)^{1/m}-1)\).
  • The continuous limit is \(\bar A_x=(i/\delta)A_x\) under UDD, with \(\delta=\log(1+i)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For quarterly settlement (\(m=4\)), death at \(T_x=2.13\) leads to payment at time 2.25. Annual settlement would pay at time 3.

docs.title: Variance of an Insurance Present Value
Definition
docs.text: For a discounted insurance benefit \(Z\), its variance is \(\mathbb{E}[Z^2]-(\mathbb{E}[Z])^2\), provided the second moment is finite. For a unit benefit paid once on event \(D\) at time \(\tau\), \(Z=\mathrm{e}^{-\delta\tau}\indicator_D\) and \(Z^2=\mathrm{e}^{-2\delta\tau}\indicator_D\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The second moment uses twice the force of interest because the discount factor is squared. Mortality and the covered event stay the same.

For the Examples case (constant force of mortality \(\lambda=0.02\)), the actuarial present value (APV) of unit whole life insurance valued at force of interest \(s\) is \(\lambda/(\lambda+s)\), the blue curve. The first moment is its value at \(\delta=0.03\), namely \(0.4\); the second moment is its value at \(2\delta=0.06\), namely \(0.25\), which lies above \((\bar A_x)^2=0.16\). The gap \(0.25-0.16=0.09\) is the variance.

Change \(\lambda\), \(\delta\) or the contract: \(\mathbb E[Z^2]\) is the same APV evaluated at force \(2\delta\), and the green gap between it and \((\mathbb E[Z])^2\) is \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)\).

Actuarial present value gives the first moment of the discounted benefit. Its variance also needs the APV of the squared payment, evaluated with the squared discount factor; the first moment alone does not determine risk.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a unit benefit, a second-moment symbol such as \({}^2\bar A_x\) means valuation at force \(2\delta\), not \((\bar A_x)^2\).
  • If annual effective interest is \(i\), the double-force equivalent rate is \((1+i)^2-1\), not \(2i\).
  • For benefit \(B\), the second moment is multiplied by \(B^2\).
  • If benefits vary with time, both the benefit function and the discount factor must be squared.

docs.title: Examples

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Under compound interest at annual effective interest rate \(i>-1\), an amount \(1\) invested at time \(0\) grows to \((1+i)^t\) at time \(t\ge0\) (in years). Equivalently, a payment of \(1\) at time \(t\) has present value \(v^t\) at time \(0\), where

\[ \begin{aligned} v&=(1+i)^{-1}&&\text{(discount factor)},\\ d&=1-v&&\text{(discount rate)},\\ \delta&=\log(1+i)&&\text{(force of interest)}. \end{aligned} \]

Here \(\log\) is the natural logarithm, so \((1+i)^t=\mathrm{e}^{\delta t}\) and \(v^t=\mathrm{e}^{-\delta t}\). The present value of payments \(c_k\) at times \(t_k\) is \(\sum_kc_kv^{t_k}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The four quantities \(i\), \(v\), \(d\) and \(\delta\) describe one and the same interest basis; knowing any one of them fixes the others. They differ in what they measure:

  • \(i\) is interest paid at the end of the year on \(1\) invested at the start;
  • \(d=iv=i/(1+i)\) is the same interest paid at the start of the year: borrowing \(1\) repayable in a year, one receives \(v=1-d\) now;
  • \(\delta\) is the instantaneous growth rate, \(\delta=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\log\big((1+i)^t\big)\), and it is what turns discounting into an exponential function \(\mathrm{e}^{-\delta t}\) for payments at any real time \(t\).

The figure places the rates of the first and third examples, all for the same basis \(i=0.04\), on one number line. They are different ways of quoting the same interest, so they are close but ordered: \(d<\delta<i^{(12)}<i\), as in the Key Results. The nominal rate \(i^{(m)}\) equals \(i\) for \(m=1\) and approaches \(\delta\) as \(m\to\infty\); at \(m=12\) it is already within \(0.00007\) of \(\delta\).

Over one year \(1\) grows to \(1+i\), while \(v\) grows to \(1\): \(i\) is the interest at the end of the year and \(d\) the same interest at the start, and the dashed tangent at \(t=0\) has slope \(\delta\). Raise \(m\): the nominal rate \(i^{(m)}\), the slope of the chord over the first \(1/m\) of a year, falls from \(i\) towards \(\delta\), and the nominal discount rate \(d^{(m)}\) rises from \(d\) towards it. Raise \(i\) to see the gaps more clearly, or set the basis by \(\delta=0.03\) to reproduce the second example.

Discounting moves money back in time. Insurance pages multiply each possible payment by \(v^t\) first and then weight it by a survival or death probability; the result is an actuarial present value. When the payments are certain, as in an annuity certain, only the discounting step remains.

The force of interest plays the same role for money as the force of mortality plays for survival. If the force varies over time as \(\delta(s)\), the discount factor to time \(t\) is \(\exp\big(-\int_0^t\delta(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\big)\), just as \({}_tp_x=\exp\big(-\int_0^t\mu_{x+s}\,\mathrm{d}s\big)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(d=iv=i/(1+i)\) and \(i=d/(1-d)\); \(\delta=-\log v=-\log(1-d)\); and \(i-d=id\).
  • If interest is paid \(m\) times a year at the nominal rate \(i^{(m)}\), the rate per period is \(i^{(m)}/m\), and equivalence with \(i\) means \((1+i^{(m)}/m)^m=1+i\), so \(i^{(m)}=m\big((1+i)^{1/m}-1\big)\). As \(m\to\infty\), \(i^{(m)}\to\delta\).
  • Similarly, the nominal discount rate \(d^{(m)}\) deducts \(d^{(m)}/m\) at the start of each \(1/m\) year, with \((1-d^{(m)}/m)^m=v=1-d\), so \(d^{(m)}=m\big(1-v^{1/m}\big)\). As \(m\to\infty\), \(d^{(m)}\to\delta\) as well.
  • For \(i>0\) and \(m>1\): \(d<d^{(m)}<\delta<i^{(m)}<i\). For small rates all of them are close: \(\delta=i-\tfrac{1}{2}i^2+\cdots\).
  • Level payments of \(1\) at times \(0,1,\ldots,n-1\) have present value \(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}v^k=(1-v^n)/d\) by the geometric series formula; a continuous payment stream at rate \(c(t)\) has present value \(\int_0^\infty c(t)\mathrm{e}^{-\delta t}\,\mathrm{d}t\).
  • Rates over other periods follow by compounding, not by proportion: the effective rate for \(h\) years is \((1+i)^h-1\), so a half-year rate is \((1+i)^{1/2}-1\), not \(i/2\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
From \(i\) to the rest. At \(i=0.04\):

\[ \begin{aligned} v&=1/1.04\approx0.961538,\\ d&=0.04/1.04\approx0.038462,\\ \delta&=\log1.04\approx0.039221. \end{aligned} \]

A payment of \(100\) in five years has present value \(100v^5=100(1.04)^{-5}\approx82.19\). Weighted by a survival probability of \(0.9\), this gives the \(73.97\) of the actuarial present value example.

From \(\delta\) to the rest. Several Life Insurance examples use a constant force \(\delta=0.03\). Then \(v=\mathrm{e}^{-0.03}\approx0.970446\), \(d=1-\mathrm{e}^{-0.03}\approx0.029554\) and \(i=\mathrm{e}^{0.03}-1\approx0.030455\); as expected, \(d<\delta<i\).

A nominal monthly rate. At \(i=0.04\), the equivalent monthly rate is \(1.04^{1/12}-1\approx0.0032737\), so \(i^{(12)}\approx12(0.0032737)\approx0.039285\). It lies between \(\delta\approx0.039221\) and \(i=0.04\). The ratio \(i/i^{(12)}\approx1.0182\) is the UDD adjustment for monthly settlement on the page on death benefits payable at fractional-year boundaries. The matching nominal discount rate is \(d^{(12)}=12\big(1-1.04^{-1/12}\big)\approx0.039157\), just below \(\delta\).

Ten payments in advance. At \(i=0.04\), payments of \(1\) at times \(0,1,\ldots,9\) are worth \(\ddot a_{\angl{10}}=(1-v^{10})/d=(1-1.04^{-10})/0.038462\approx8.4353\), compared with \(10\) undiscounted.

docs.title: Life Annuities Payable Several Times a Year
Definition
docs.text: A life annuity payable \(m\) times a year pays instalments of \(1/m\) at intervals of \(1/m\) year while the annuitant survives. The due version starts at time zero and has actuarial present value (APV) \(\displaystyle \ddot a_x^{(m)}=m^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^\infty v^{k/m}{}_{k/m}p_x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The annual benefit rate stays one as frequency changes. Fractional-age survival must be calculated from a continuous mortality model or an explicit table interpolation rule.

The figure compares \(m=1\) and \(m=4\) for an annuitant who dies at time \(T_x=2.4\) (an illustrative value). Both pay at annual rate 1, but the annual annuity-due pays 1 at times \(0,1,2\), a total of 3, while the quarterly one pays \(1/4\) at times \(0,1/4,\ldots,9/4\), ten instalments totalling \(2.5\). Grey arrows are instalments that are not paid because the annuitant has died.

Raise \(m\): instalments of \(1/m\) every \(1/m\) year bring \(\ddot a_x^{(m)}\) down towards the continuous \(\bar a_x\). Switch the survival model to compare exponential (constant force) with linear (UDD) survival within each year.

The whole life annuity-due is the annual-payment case \(m=1\). Fractional payment dates require survival probabilities between integer ages: uniform distribution of deaths (UDD) interpolates these linearly, whereas constant force of mortality (CFM) within each year of age interpolates exponentially. Thus the same annual table can give different fractional-payment values.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The immediate version starts at time \(1/m\), so \(a_x^{(m)}=\ddot a_x^{(m)}-1/m\).
  • A temporary due version with integer term \(n\) stops its sum at \(mn-1\).
  • Under suitable finiteness conditions, the limit as \(m\to\infty\) is the continuous life annuity.
  • UDD and CFM can produce different values from the same annual table. Woolhouse's formula, an approximation of \(\ddot a_x^{(m)}\) from annual annuity values, is outside the course scope.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: An annuity paying monthly at annual rate 1200 pays 100 at each payment date. Its APV is \(\displaystyle 100\sum_{k\ge0}v^{k/12}{}_{k/12}p_x\) for payments in advance.

docs.title: Equivalence Principle for Life Insurance Premiums
Definition
docs.text: The equivalence principle chooses a premium so that expected discounted premium income equals expected discounted benefits and, for gross valuation, expenses. Let \(Z\) be the benefit present value (PV), \(H\) the expense PV and \(Y\) the PV of a unit premium stream. For a level premium \(P\), the gross equation is \(P\mathbb{E}[Y]=\mathbb{E}[Z+H]\). Net valuation omits \(H\); the resulting level premium is the net level premium, and "net" always means that expenses and loadings are excluded.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This balances expected cash flows at issue under a specified mortality and interest basis. It does not guarantee that every policy or every portfolio has zero realized loss.

With the numbers from the Examples, the net premium \(P=4\) makes \(P\,\mathbb{E}[Y]=4\times10\) equal \(\mathbb{E}[Z]=40\), and the gross premium \(P=4.5\) makes \(4.5\times10=45\) equal \(\mathbb{E}[Z+H]=40+5\). The bars balance in expectation only; a realized policy can still produce a profit or a loss.

Move the trial premium \(P\): the orange gap is \(\mathbb E[L_0^g]\), which vanishes where income \(P\,\mathbb E[Y]\) meets the outgo. Add a premium-related expense share \(r\) and the outgo line tilts, so it must be solved together with \(P\).

Premiums paid annually in advance while the policyholder is alive form a whole life annuity-due. Its actuarial present value (APV) is the expected present value of one unit of premium each year, explaining the denominator \(\ddot a_x\) in the whole-life premium formula.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\mathbb{E}[Y]>0\) and expenses do not themselves depend on \(P\), \(P=\mathbb{E}[Z+H]/\mathbb{E}[Y]\).
  • An annual net whole life premium payable in advance while alive is \(P=A_x/\ddot a_x\) for unit annual-settlement death benefit.
  • If premiums are payable for at most \(n\) years, the denominator is \(\ddot a_{x:\angl{n}}\).
  • Premium-related expenses must remain in the equation and be solved together with \(P\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If expected benefit PV is 40 and the unit premium-stream APV is 10, the net annual premium is 4. Expenses with APV 5, independent of the premium, raise the gross premium to 4.5.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For annual unit whole life insurance with actuarial present value (APV) \(A_x\), conditioning on the first year gives the valuation recursion

\[ A_x=vq_x+vp_xA_{x+1}, \]

where \(v\) is the annual discount factor and \(p_x=1-q_x\). The first term represents death during the year; the second represents survival followed by the remaining contract.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A long contract can be valued one year at a time. This also explains why product decompositions have both financial and survival discount factors.

The figure follows the Examples. From age \(x\) the life either dies within the year with probability \(q_x=0.02\), and the benefit 1 is paid at time 1, or survives with probability \(p_x=0.98\) and then holds a contract worth \(A_{x+1}=0.4\) at time 1. Weighting the two time-1 values by their probabilities and discounting by \(v=0.95\) gives \(A_x=0.95(0.02\times1+0.98\times0.4)=0.3914\).

For endowment insurance, survival through the first year leaves an endowment contract with one fewer year. At zero remaining term the survival payment is due immediately, explaining the terminal value \(A_{x:\angl{0}}=1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Let \(A_{x:\angl{n}}\) denote annual-settlement unit \(n\)-year endowment APV. Then \(A_{x:\angl{n}}=v[q_x+p_xA_{x+1:\angl{n-1}}]\), with \(A_{x:\angl{0}}=1\).
  • Annual term insurance uses the same recursion but a terminal value of zero.
  • Backward numerical valuation requires a terminal age or a justified tail treatment.
  • The recursion concerns conditional values at successively older ages, not independent new policies.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A life table specifies survivor numbers \(l_x\) at ages \(x\) for a hypothetical cohort with a chosen initial size, the radix. Annual deaths are \(d_x=l_x-l_{x+1}\). Within the mortality model represented by the table, for \(l_x>0\),

\[ {}_tp_x=\frac{l_{x+t}}{l_x},\qquad q_x=\frac{d_x}{l_x}. \]

Fractional ages require an interpolation assumption if only integer-age entries are supplied.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The table expresses a survival model through cohort counts. Its numbers may be modelled or estimated; the displayed ratios do not remove sampling or projection uncertainty.

The figure follows the cohort in the Examples. Of \(l_{60}=1000\) lives, \(d_{60}=20\) die before age 61, so \(q_{60}=20/1000=0.02\); after five years \(l_{65}=900\) remain, so \({}_5p_{60}=900/1000=0.9\). Every probability is a ratio of table entries, which is why rescaling the radix leaves it unchanged.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \({}_{u|t}q_x=(l_{x+u}-l_{x+u+t})/l_x\).
  • Scaling all entries by the same positive constant leaves survival probabilities unchanged.
  • A population table and an insured-life table can differ through selection. Choose the table appropriate to the covered population.
  • Use table ratios only when a table is given or a corresponding table model has been specified.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Makeham's law specifies the force of mortality at age \(y\ge0\) as \(\mu_y=A+Bc^y\). In the standard increasing-age model, \(A\ge0\), \(B>0\) and \(c>1\). These constants determine both an age-independent component and an exponentially increasing age component.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The constant term allows a background mortality rate, while the exponential term models increasing mortality at older ages. This is a model assumption, not a universal law of human mortality.

The figure plots the Examples parameters \(A=0.001\), \(B=0.0001\) and \(c=1.1\) on a logarithmic vertical scale. At young ages \(\mu_y\) stays close to the constant \(A\) (dashed orange); at older ages it follows the Gompertz term \(Bc^y\), a straight line on this scale because \(\log(Bc^y)\) is linear in \(y\). At age 40 the two parts give \(\mu_{40}\approx0.00553\).

Change \(A\), \(B\) and \(c\): on the logarithmic scale \(\mu_y\) follows the constant \(A\) at young ages and the straight Gompertz line \(Bc^y\) later; the defaults give \(\mu_{40}\approx0.00553\). Move \(x\) and \(t\) to read \({}_tp_x\) and \(f_x(t)={}_tp_x\mu_{x+t}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a life aged \(x\),

    \[ {}_tp_x=\exp\left[-At-\frac{Bc^x(c^t-1)}{\log c}\right]. \]

    Here \(\log\) is the natural logarithm, because \(\int_0^tBc^{x+s}\,\mathrm{d}s=Bc^x(c^t-1)/\log c\); a base-10 logarithm would give the wrong survival probability.

  • Setting \(A=0\) gives the Gompertz form.

  • Mortality depends on attained age \(x+t\), so the starting age must be retained in calculations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(A=0.001\), \(B=0.0001\) and \(c=1.1\), the force at age 40 is \(0.001+0.0001(1.1)^{40}\approx0.00553\). The survival formula integrates this changing force over the entire future interval.
