docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The prospective gross policy value at duration \(t\) is \(V_t=\mathbb{E}[L_t^g\mid\text{policy in force at }t]\). Equivalently, it is the expected time-\(t\) present value (PV) of future benefits and expenses minus the expected time-\(t\) PV of future premiums, under the selected valuation basis and timing convention, provided the in-force event has positive probability and the future loss is integrable.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The value measures the expected remaining liability of an active policy. It changes as the insured ages and as benefits and premium payments approach or pass.

The figure looks forward from duration \(t\) with the numbers from the Examples. Premiums already paid (grey) play no part; given that the policy is in force, future premiums have expected value 30 at time \(t\) and future benefits and expenses 50, so \(V_t=50-30=20\). The arrows are schematic: the figure fixes only the two expected totals, not individual cash flows.

Move \(t\) and switch the contract: \(V_t\) is the expected remaining benefits minus the expected remaining premiums, \(0\) at issue under the equivalence premium. It climbs to \(1000\) at maturity for the endowment and returns to \(0\) at the end of a term policy.

The future loss random variable supplies \(L_t^g=Z_t+H_t-Y_t\). Conditional expectation given an event describes averaging after information is fixed; here the information is that the policy remains in force at \(t\). Averaging the remaining net outgo under that condition gives the policy value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(V_t+\mathbb{E}[Y_t\mid\text{in force}]=\mathbb{E}[Z_t+H_t\mid\text{in force}]\).
  • Net policy values omit expenses and use the corresponding net premium.
  • A value at issue is zero under matching equivalence assumptions; this need not hold at later durations or after a change of basis.
  • An expected-liability value is not, by itself, a complete capital requirement for adverse outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If expected remaining benefits and expenses are 50 and expected remaining premiums are 30, the prospective policy value is 20 at the specified valuation time.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A unit pure endowment pays at time \(n\ge0\) only if the life aged \(x\) survives to that time. Its present value is \(Z=v^n\indicator_{\{T_x>n\}}\), and its actuarial present value (APV) is denoted \({}_nE_x=v^n{}_np_x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The insurer pays for survival rather than death. The factor \({}_nE_x\) combines financial discounting with the probability that the later payment is due.

The figure uses the example below: \(i=0.05\), \({}_{10}p_x=0.8\) and a benefit of 1000 at \(n=10\). Only the upper scenario, \(T_x>10\), triggers a payment; the lower one ends with nothing paid. Discounting the payment by \(v^{10}\) and weighting it by the survival probability \(0.8\) gives the APV \(1000\,v^{10}{}_{10}p_x\approx491.13\). Because only these two outcomes exist, \(Z\) is a scaled Bernoulli variable, which is where \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=v^{2n}{}_np_x(1-{}_np_x)\) comes from.

Change \(n\), \({}_np_x\) and \(i\): the APV is \(Bv^n{}_np_x\), and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=B^2v^{2n}{}_np_x(1-{}_np_x)\) is largest at \({}_np_x=\tfrac12\).

The actuarial survival and death probabilities supply \({}_np_x\), the probability that the survival benefit is payable. Multiplying that probability by the discounted amount \(v^n\) gives the APV, while the two possible payment values give its variance.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For benefit \(B\), APV is \(Bv^n{}_np_x\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=v^{2n}{}_np_x(1-{}_np_x)\) for a unit benefit.
  • \({}_{n+m}E_x={}_nE_x\,{}_mE_{x+n}\) when conditioning on survival is defined.
  • A pure endowment is the survival component of an endowment insurance.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A select mortality model records both age at selection and elapsed duration since selection. Write \(q_{[x]+s}\) for the one-year death probability of a life selected at age \(x\) and observed \(s\) years later. After a specified select period \(r\), the ultimate rate depends only on attained age: \(q_{[x]+s}=q_{x+s}\) for \(s\ge r\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Underwriting can make newly selected lives differ from other lives of the same age. The model keeps that duration effect until the assumed select period ends.

Each row of the table belongs to an age at selection and each column to a duration since selection; with select period \(r=2\) the third column holds the ultimate rates, which depend on attained age only. A life selected at 40 moves along its row, \(q_{[40]}=0.005\) and \(q_{[40]+1}=0.007\), then continues in the ultimate column with \(q_{42}=0.01\) and later \(q_{43},\ldots\), so \({}_3p_{[40]}=0.995(0.993)(0.99)=0.97815465\) as in the example. The shaded cells all concern attained age 42 but hold different rates, \(q_{[42]}\), \(q_{[41]+1}\) and \(q_{42}\), because those lives were selected at different ages.

A life table normally indexes annual mortality by attained age. A select table adds the age at selection and duration since selection; after the select period, valuation returns to the ordinary attained-age table.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \({}_kp_{[x]}=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-q_{[x]+j})\) for integer \(k\).
  • Use select rates before duration \(r\) and ultimate rates afterwards.
  • Brackets identify selection age, not attained age. A life selected at 40 and now aged 42 is \([40]+2\).
  • The disappearance of selection after \(r\) is a modelling convention, not evidence that all real selection effects vanish.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For a two-year select period with \(q_{[40]}=0.005\), \(q_{[40]+1}=0.007\) and ultimate \(q_{42}=0.01\), three-year survival is \(0.995(0.993)(0.99)=0.97815465\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A unit \(n\)-year temporary life annuity pays while the life survives, for at most \(n\) payments. For integer \(n\ge1\), the due version has payments at \(0,\ldots,n-1\) and the immediate version at \(1,\ldots,n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The term limits payment duration even if the annuitant lives longer. The final immediate payment requires survival to time \(n\), whereas the due version starts with a certain payment at time zero.

The figure uses the example values \(n=2\), \(v=0.95\), \({}_1p_x=0.9\) and \({}_2p_x=0.8\). Each red arrow is a unit payment conditional on survival, labelled with its contribution \(v^k{}_kp_x\) to the actuarial present value (APV); the grey arrows are whole life payments that the term cuts off. The due version keeps the certain payment at time \(0\) and stops before \(n\), giving \(1.855\); the immediate version starts at time \(1\) and includes the payment at \(n=2\), which needs survival to \(n\), giving \(1.577\). Their difference, \(1-0.95^2(0.8)=0.278\), is \(1-{}_2E_x\).

Move \(n\), \(v\) and the survival model: the due version pays at \(0,\ldots,n-1\) and the immediate one at \(1,\ldots,n\), and they differ by \(1-{}_nE_x\). The defaults reproduce \(1.855\) and \(1.577\).

Truncating the payment sum of a whole life annuity-due after times \(0,\ldots,n-1\) gives the due version. Truncating a whole life annuity-immediate after times \(1,\ldots,n\) gives the immediate version. The identity involving endowment insurance uses the same stopping time: an annual death-or-survival payment occurs at \(\min(K_x+1,n)\), and the discounted annuity payments before it form a finite geometric sum. Taking expectations yields \(d\ddot a_{x:\angl{n}}=1-A_{x:\angl{n}}\), where \(d=1-v\) and \(A_{x:\angl{n}}\) is the annual-settlement endowment APV.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \ddot a_{x:\angl{n}}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}v^k{}_kp_x\) and \(\displaystyle a_{x:\angl{n}}=\sum_{k=1}^nv^k{}_kp_x\).
  • \(\ddot a_{x:\angl{n}}-a_{x:\angl{n}}=1-{}_nE_x\).
  • For \(d=1-v\ne0\), \(d\ddot a_{x:\angl{n}}=1-A_{x:\angl{n}}\), where \(A_{x:\angl{n}}\) is annual-settlement endowment APV.
  • The whole life annuity is the limit as the term increases, when finite.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An \(n\)-year term insurance pays a death benefit only if death occurs within the coverage period \([0,n)\). A unit benefit paid at death has present value \(Z=v^{T_x}\indicator_{\{T_x<n\}}\). For integer \(n\) and annual settlement, \(Z=v^{K_x+1}\indicator_{\{K_x<n\}}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The contract provides protection during a fixed term and pays nothing on survival to its end. The death condition and settlement time must both be specified.

With constant force \(\lambda=0.02\) and \(\delta=0.03\), the death density is \(f_x(t)=0.02\mathrm{e}^{-0.02t}\) and \(v^t=\mathrm{e}^{-0.03t}\), so the integrand is \(0.02\mathrm{e}^{-0.05t}\). The whole area under this curve is the whole life actuarial present value (APV) \(\lambda/(\lambda+\delta)=0.4\); the 10-year term contract keeps only the red part left of the cutoff \(n=10\), which is \(0.4(1-\mathrm{e}^{-0.5})\approx0.15739\), as in the example. The grey remainder, \(0.4\mathrm{e}^{-0.5}\approx0.24261\), belongs to deaths after the term. Moving the cutoff to the right adds area, which is why the APV increases with the term.

Move the term \(n\): the APV keeps only the red area of \(v^tf_x(t)\) before \(n\), \(0.4(1-e^{-0.5})\approx0.15739\) at the defaults, and it grows with the term.

Whole life insurance covers deaths at every future duration. Restricting its death-payment integral or annual payment sum to the first \(n\) years gives the term contract; deaths after the cutoff contribute zero.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Immediate-payment APV is \(\int_0^n v^tf_x(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\).
  • Annual-settlement APV is \(\displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}v^{k+1}{}_kp_xq_{x+k}\).
  • At constant force of mortality \(\lambda>0\) and force of interest \(\delta\ge0\), the immediate APV is \(\lambda[1-\mathrm{e}^{-(\lambda+\delta)n}]/(\lambda+\delta)\).
  • Increasing the term increases APV for a nonnegative fixed benefit.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(\lambda=0.02\), \(\delta=0.03\) and \(n=10\), the unit APV is \(0.4(1-\mathrm{e}^{-0.5})\approx0.15739\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The uniform distribution of deaths (UDD) assumption is \({}_sq_x=sq_x\) for integer age \(x\) and \(0\le s\le1\). If imposed in every subsequent year, the fractional part \(R_x=T_x-K_x\) is uniform on \((0,1)\) and independent of \(K_x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Within each year of age, deaths are spread uniformly rather than concentrated at particular dates. The assumption gives a rule for interpolating an integer-age life table.

Under UDD the survival curve within a year of age is a straight line between the table values at integer ages: with \(q_{60}=0.1\), \({}_sp_{60}=1-0.1s\) falls from \(1\) to \(0.9\). The probability of surviving from 60.5 to 60.75 is the ratio of the two marked heights, \(0.925/0.95\approx0.97368\), as in the example. The vertical axis starts at \(0.88\), so the drop is magnified. The line has constant slope, but relative to the shrinking survival level that slope grows, so \(\mu_{60+s}=q_{60}/(1-sq_{60})\) increases within the year.

Change \(q_{60}\), \(s\) and \(t\): under UDD \({}_sp_{60}\) is a straight line, \({}_tp_{60+s}=[1-(s+t)q_{60}]/[1-sq_{60}]\) and the force \(q_{60}/(1-sq_{60})\) rises. The dashed curves show constant force for comparison.

The curtate future lifetime \(K_x\) identifies the year of death, and \(R_x=T_x-K_x\) identifies the fraction lived within it. The uniform distribution assumption makes this fraction uniform on \((0,1)\). As independent random variables, \(R_x\) and \(K_x\) permit separate averaging of fractional-year timing and the death year under UDD throughout the model.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(l_{x+s}=l_x-sd_x=(1-s)l_x+sl_{x+1}\).
  • \(\mu_{x+s}=q_x/(1-sq_x)\) where the denominator is positive.
  • For \(0\le s\le s+t\le1\), \({}_tp_{x+s}=[1-(s+t)q_x]/[1-sq_x]\).
  • UDD does not mean constant force within a year; its force of mortality increases when \(q_x>0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A varying life annuity pays predetermined amounts \(b_k\ge0\) at times \(t_k\) conditional on survival. Its present value is \(\displaystyle Y=\sum_k b_kv^{t_k}\indicator_{\{T_x>t_k\}}\). For continuous rate \(b(t)\), replace the sum by \(\int_0^{T_x}b(t)v^t\,\mathrm{d}t\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The indicator specifies eligibility for each payment. This representation handles increasing, decreasing and stepped benefits without treating them as separate probability models.

The figure draws the example \(Y=1+2v\indicator_{\{T_x>1\}}\) with \(v=0.95\) and \(p_x=0.9\). The arrow lengths show the different scheduled amounts, and the survival indicator decides whether the second one is paid: \(Y=2.9\) with probability \(0.9\) and \(Y=1\) with probability \(0.1\). Hence \(\mathbb{E}[Y]=2.71\), and since only the second payment is random, \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=(1.9)^2(0.9)(0.1)=0.3249\).

The whole life annuity-due is recovered by setting unit payments at integer dates. An indicator random variable switches each scheduled amount on only when the life survives to its date. Joint survival events explain the dependence between payments in the second-moment calculation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The actuarial present value (APV) is \(\displaystyle \sum_k b_kv^{t_k}{}_{t_k}p_x\), or \(\int_0^\infty b(t)v^t{}_tp_x\,\mathrm{d}t\) for continuous payments.
  • Survival indicators at different dates are dependent. Their joint probability is \({}_{\max(t_j,t_k)}p_x\).
  • Thus \(\displaystyle \mathbb{E}[Y^2]=\sum_{j,k}b_jb_kv^{t_j+t_k}{}_{\max(t_j,t_k)}p_x\), when finite.
  • Do not calculate annuity variance by assuming independent annual payments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure's example \(Y=1+2v\indicator_{\{T_x>1\}}\) is worked out above: APV \(2.71\) and variance \(0.3249\).

Increasing annuity-due. Payments \(1,2,3\) at times \(0,1,2\), with \(v=0.95\), \(p_x=0.9\) and \({}_2p_x=0.8\). The APV is \(1+2(0.95)(0.9)+3(0.95)^2(0.8)=1+1.71+2.166=4.876\). The present value takes three values: \(Y=1\) if \(T_x\le1\) (probability \(0.1\)), \(Y=2.9\) if \(1<T_x\le2\) (probability \(0.1\)), and \(Y=2.9+3(0.95)^2=5.6075\) if \(T_x>2\) (probability \(0.8\)). So \(\mathbb{E}[Y^2]=0.1+0.841+25.155245=26.096245\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=26.096245-4.876^2\approx2.3209\). Treating the payments as independent would give only about \(1.4978\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A varying death benefit is specified by a deterministic payment rule \(b(t)\ge0\). For payment at death, \(Z=b(T_x)v^{T_x}\); for annual settlement, \(Z=b(K_x+1)v^{K_x+1}\). A compound reversionary bonus increases the insured benefit by a fixed proportion at specified vesting dates (the dates on which each bonus becomes a guaranteed part of the benefit).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The mortality model determines whether and when payment occurs; the benefit rule determines its amount. Write the vesting convention explicitly before valuing a bonus.

The figure draws the example: a compound reversionary bonus of 2% vests at each completed anniversary, so the benefit in force is 1 in the first year, \(1.02\) in the second and \((1.02)^k\) after \(k\) anniversaries. Death at \(T_x=3.4\) comes after three anniversaries, so the benefit is \((1.02)^3\); with end-of-year settlement it is paid at \(K_x+1=4\), giving \(Z=(1.02)^3v^4\). This is the course formula \(Z=v^{K_x+1}(1+j)^{K_x}\) with \(j=0.02\) and \(K_x=3\): the mortality model decides when the payment is made, and the bonus rule decides its size.

Whole life insurance provides the death time and its payment convention. Replacing the unit benefit by \(b(T_x)\), or by \(b(K_x+1)\) for annual settlement, weights the same death-payment probabilities by the specified benefit schedule.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The immediate-settlement actuarial present value (APV) is \(\int_0^\infty b(t)v^tf_x(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\).
  • Annual APV is \(\displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^\infty b(k+1)v^{k+1}{}_kp_xq_{x+k}\).
  • For annual anniversary bonuses at rate \(j\ge0\), base benefit 1 and end-of-year death settlement, the course uses \(Z=v^{K_x+1}(1+j)^{K_x}\).
  • At-death settlement needs its own rule for partial-year bonuses; do not infer one from annual settlement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With a 2% bonus vested only on completed anniversaries, death at time 3.4 gives benefit \((1.02)^3\). If settlement is at the end of the death year, discount this amount by \(v^4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A unit annual whole life annuity-due pays at the beginning of each year while the life aged \(x\) is alive, including a certain payment at issue. Its present value is \(\displaystyle Y=\sum_{k=0}^{K_x}v^k\) and actuarial present value (APV) is \(\ddot a_x=\mathbb{E}[Y]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Each annual payment is a pure endowment for its payment date. A longer lifetime increases the number of payments, whereas a death benefit is generally discounted more heavily when death occurs later.

For a fixed lifetime the annuity-due is no longer random: payments are made at \(0,1,\ldots,K_x\) while the life is alive, and the payment that would be due at \(K_x+1\) falls after death at \(T_x\). These \(K_x+1\) payments form an annuity certain, so \(Y=\sum_{k=0}^{K_x}v^k=(1-v^{K_x+1})/d\). The randomness of \(Y\) comes only from \(K_x\), which is why \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\) reduces to \(\operatorname{Var}(v^{K_x+1})/d^2\).

Change \(v\) and \(q\): each arrow is the expected present value \(v^k{}_kp_x\) of the payment at \(k\), and \(A_x+d\,\ddot a_x=1\) throughout. At \(v=0.95\) and \(q=0.0351\), \(A_x\approx0.4\) and \(\ddot a_x\approx12\).

For a realized curtate future lifetime \(K_x\), the payments at \(0,\ldots,K_x\) have the same discounted sum as an annuity certain with \(K_x+1\) payments; its geometric-sum formula gives \(Y=(1-v^{K_x+1})/d\) with \(d=1-v\). To average over possible lifetimes, write each payment using an indicator random variable: the payment at time \(k\) is made only on survival to \(k\). Its expected discounted value is \(v^k{}_kp_x\), so adding these expectations gives the APV sum below.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \ddot a_x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}v^k{}_kp_x\).
  • For \(d=1-v\ne0\), \(Y=(1-v^{K_x+1})/d\), so \(A_x+d\ddot a_x=1\), where \(A_x\) is the APV of whole life insurance with annual settlement.
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\operatorname{Var}(v^{K_x+1})/d^2\) when finite.
  • One-year recursion: \(\ddot a_x=1+vp_x\ddot a_{x+1}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \(A_x=0.4\) and \(d=0.05\), the unit annuity APV is \((1-0.4)/0.05=12\). This uses annual death settlement for \(A_x\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A unit annual whole life annuity-immediate pays at times \(1,2,\ldots\) only while the annuitant survives. Its present value is \(\displaystyle Y^*=\sum_{k=1}^{K_x}v^k\) and actuarial present value (APV) is \(\displaystyle a_x=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}v^k{}_kp_x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
There is no guaranteed initial payment. Compared with the corresponding life annuity-due, the contract omits exactly the payment at time zero.

In the figure the life dies between \(K_x\) and \(K_x+1\). The annuity-immediate makes the same survival-contingent payments as the annuity-due except the certain one at time \(0\), so \(Y^*=Y-1\) for every lifetime and the two have the same variance. Shifting the whole due stream by one year, \(vY\), instead pays at \(1,\ldots,K_x+1\): its last payment (orange) falls after death, so \(v\ddot a_x\) is generally larger than \(a_x\).

Change \(v\) and \(q\): the immediate row drops only the payment at 0, so \(a_x=\ddot a_x-1\). The shifted row \(v\,\ddot a_x\) keeps each payment's earlier survival condition, and its orange parts would be paid after death.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(Y^*=Y-1\), so \(a_x=\ddot a_x-1\) and both present values have the same variance.
  • \(a_x=vp_x\ddot a_{x+1}\) by conditioning on survival to the first payment.
  • Multiplying \(\ddot a_x\) by \(v\) alone is generally wrong: moving a survival-contingent payment also changes its survival condition.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If the annuity-due APV is 12, the matching annuity-immediate APV is 11. Their variance is equal because the omitted initial payment is deterministic.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A unit whole life insurance pays on death whenever it occurs. For immediate payment its present value is \(Z=v^{T_x}\) and actuarial present value (APV) is \(\bar A_x\). For payment at the end of the year of death, \(Z=v^{K_x+1}\) and APV is \(A_x\), where \(v=(1+i)^{-1}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The contract covers the entire remaining lifetime. Its value depends on whether settlement occurs at death or later at an annual boundary.

The figure follows one illustrative lifetime with death at \(T_x=3.4\), so \(K_x=3\) complete years are lived. Immediate settlement pays at the moment of death, with present value \(Z=v^{T_x}=v^{3.4}\); annual settlement waits until the end of the year of death, \(K_x+1=4\), with \(Z=v^{K_x+1}=v^4\). Since \(T_x\le K_x+1\) for every lifetime, the immediate payment is never later, which is why \(\bar A_x\ge A_x\) when interest is nonnegative.

Change \(\lambda\) and \(\delta\): \(\bar A_x=\lambda/(\lambda+\delta)\) is the red area under \(v^tf_x(t)\). Drag the probe along \(T_x\), and switch on end-of-year settlement (\(m=1\)) to see \(A_x\le\bar A_x\).

The curtate future lifetime \(K_x\) determines the annual settlement date \(K_x+1\). For immediate settlement, the force of mortality converts the survival probability into the death density \({}_tp_x\mu_{x+t}\) used in the APV integral.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\bar A_x=\int_0^\infty v^t{}_tp_x\mu_{x+t}\,\mathrm{d}t\).
  • \(\displaystyle A_x=\sum_{k=0}^\infty v^{k+1}{}_kp_xq_{x+k}\).
  • For nonnegative interest, \(\bar A_x\ge A_x\) because immediate settlement is earlier.
  • At constant force of mortality \(\lambda>0\) and force of interest \(\delta\ge0\), \(\bar A_x=\lambda/(\lambda+\delta)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(\lambda=0.02\) and \(\delta=0.03\), a benefit of 100 paid at death has APV \(100(0.02/0.05)=40\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Adverse selection arises when one side of a transaction has private information, a type such as quality or risk, that affects the other side's value of trading, and the terms of trade cannot depend on that type. Because the uninformed side can only condition on the conditional expectation of the type among those willing to trade, a given price or contract is accepted disproportionately by the types that are worse for the uninformed side. As a result, some mutually beneficial trades do not take place.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The word "adverse" refers to the selection, not to the people: those who accept a given offer are, on average, the ones the offer-maker would least like to trade with. In the market for lemons, a seller of a good car does not want to sell at an average price; a low-risk customer does not want to pay an average premium. When they withdraw, the average type among those who remain gets worse, which lowers the acceptable price further.

Adverse selection concerns hidden information that exists before the contract (who you are). It differs from moral hazard, which concerns hidden actions taken after the contract (what you do).

Game-theoretically, the uninformed party's offer and the informed party's type-contingent acceptance rule are equilibrium strategies of a game with incomplete information, for example a Bayesian Nash equilibrium. The inefficiency is a property of equilibrium, not of irrational play. Remedies change the information structure: inspections, warranties, screening by menus of contracts, or signals sent by the informed side, as in a signalling game.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• At a price \(p\) that every type accepts, the uninformed side's value is the unconditional mean; at a price only low types accept, it is the mean conditional on low quality.
  • Trade with high types survives only if their share is large enough; below a threshold, only the worst types trade.
  • With a continuum of types the process can unravel completely, so that no trade occurs at any positive price.
  • The outcome is generally not Pareto efficient: high-quality trades with positive gains are lost.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Used cars, buyer makes the offer. A seller's car is high quality (\(H\)) with probability \(0.4\) and low (\(L\)) with probability \(0.6\). Values in thousands of euros:

seller buyer \(L\) 4 6 \(H\) 10 12

The buyer makes a take-it-or-leave-it offer \(p\); each seller type accepts if and only if \(p\) is at least her own value.

  • \(p=10\) (both accept): buyer's expected value \(0.4\cdot12+0.6\cdot6=8.4\), payoff \(8.4-10=-1.6\).
  • \(p=4\) (only \(L\) accepts): payoff \(0.6\cdot(6-4)=1.2\).
  • Any \(p\in(4,10)\) is accepted only by \(L\) and pays less than \(p=4\); any \(p<4\) pays 0.

The buyer offers 4 and only lemons trade, although each high-quality car is worth 2 more to the buyer than to the seller. Pooling at 10 would be optimal if and only if \(12\mu+6(1-\mu)-10\ge2(1-\mu)\), i.e. \(\mu\ge\tfrac{3}{4}\), where \(\mu\) is the share of high quality.

The figure plots the buyer's expected payoff against the offer \(p\), with the seller values 4 and 10 marked as dashed thresholds. Raising \(p\) above 4 only pays more to the same low-quality sellers, so the payoff falls along \(0.6(6-p)\); at \(p=10\) the high types join, but the pooled value \(8.4\) is below the price, so the payoff jumps only to \(-1.6\). The best offer is \(p=4\), where only lemons trade.

Move the offer \(p\): the payoff peaks at \(4\), where only lemons sell. Raise the share \(\mu\) of high-quality cars past \(\tfrac34\) and offering \(10\) becomes best.

Insurance. Equal numbers of low-risk (loss 100 with probability \(0.1\)) and high-risk (probability \(0.5\)) customers are willing to pay 15 and 55. The break-even pooled premium is \(0.5\cdot10+0.5\cdot50=30>15\), so low risks drop out and the premium must rise to at least 50: only high risks are insured.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
Let \(\Gamma\) be a finite extensive-form game of perfect information (every information set is a single node).

  1. Take a decision node all of whose immediate successors are terminal nodes. Choose an action that maximizes the payoff of the player who moves there.
  2. Replace that node by a terminal node carrying the payoffs of the chosen action.
  3. Repeat steps 1–2 until the root has been processed.

The actions chosen at all decision nodes, including nodes that are not reached, form a profile of strategies, the backward-induction solution. The path from the root through the chosen actions is the backward-induction outcome.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Each player is treated as a rational agent who, whenever she moves, best responds to what she correctly predicts later movers will do. The last mover's choice needs only her own rationality; the second-to-last mover's choice requires that she knows the last mover is rational, and so on. For long games the argument therefore relies on common knowledge of rationality, and in games such as the centipede game experimental behaviour departs from the prediction.

The method needs a last move. In infinite-horizon games, such as infinitely repeated games, there is no last node, and equilibria are checked instead with the one-stage deviation principle.

A common error is to report only the outcome. The solution is a full strategy profile: it states what each player would do at every node, including nodes that the solution itself avoids.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In a finite game of perfect information, the backward-induction profile is a subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium, and every pure-strategy SPNE arises from backward induction with some tie-breaking (Zermelo, Kuhn).
  • Consequently every finite game of perfect information has a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium.
  • If no player has the same payoff at two different terminal nodes, there are no ties and the solution is unique.
  • With ties, each choice among the maximizing actions gives a (possibly different) SPNE.
  • For games with imperfect information, generalized backward induction replaces each smallest subgame by the payoffs of one of its Nash equilibria and continues.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Entry game. Out gives \((0,2)\) to (entrant, incumbent); after In, Accommodate gives \((1,1)\) and Fight \((-1,-1)\). At the incumbent's node, \(1>-1\), so she accommodates. Replacing the node by \((1,1)\), the entrant compares \(1\) (In) with \(0\) (Out) and enters. Solution: (In, Accommodate).

Three-move centipede. Player 1 chooses Stop, giving \((1,0)\), or Continue. Player 2 then chooses Stop, \((0,2)\), or Continue. Player 1 finally chooses Stop, \((3,1)\), or Continue, \((2,4)\).

  • Node 3 (player 1): \(3>2\), Stop; replace by \((3,1)\).
  • Node 2 (player 2): Stop gives \(2\), Continue gives \(1\); Stop. Replace by \((0,2)\).
  • Node 1 (player 1): Stop gives \(1\), Continue gives \(0\); Stop.

Solution: player 1 plays (Stop, Stop), player 2 plays Stop, outcome \((1,0)\). Both \((3,1)\) and \((2,4)\) give both players strictly more, so the outcome is not Pareto efficient.

The figure solves the centipede from right to left. Step 1 compares \(3\) with \(2\) at player 1's last node and replaces it by \((3,1)\); step 2 lets player 2 compare \(2\) with \(1\) and replaces her node by \((0,2)\); step 3 lets player 1 compare \(1\) with \(0\) at the root. The highlighted Stop branches are the chosen actions at all three nodes, which together form the backward-induction solution, although only the first is reached.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Battle of the Sexes is a two-player normal-form game in which each player chooses \(O\) or \(F\) (traditionally opera or football). Both players want to choose the same option, but player 1 prefers that they meet at \(O\) and player 2 that they meet at \(F\); failing to coordinate gives both the lowest payoff. The standard numerical version:

\(O\) \(F\) \(O\) \(2,1\) \(0,0\) \(F\) \(0,0\) \(1,2\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Battle of the Sexes is a coordination game with a conflict of interest. Matching is good for both, but the two ways of matching split the gains differently. It models situations such as two firms choosing a common technical standard, each preferring its own.

Each point is a payoff pair \((v_1,v_2)\) from the table. The two pure equilibria (filled green) are both far better than miscoordination at \((0,0)\), but player 1 prefers \((O,O)\) with \((2,1)\) and player 2 prefers \((F,F)\) with \((1,2)\), so neither point is better for both. The mixed equilibrium of Week 2 (open circle, see Key Results) gives each player \(\tfrac{2}{3}\); both pure equilibria lie in the shaded quadrant of pairs that are higher for both players, which is the sense in which the mixed equilibrium is Pareto dominated by each of them.

The game has more than one Nash equilibrium, and the theory alone does not say which one is played. Each pure equilibrium is self-enforcing once both players expect it, but nothing in the payoffs tells the players which of the two to expect. Common knowledge of rationality does not help either: no strategy is strictly dominated, so dominance reasoning eliminates nothing. In practice coordination may come from convention, communication or the order of moves.

Each player's best response is to do what the other does, so the right choice depends entirely on the belief about the other player. This is the opposite of the Prisoner's Dilemma, where finking is best whatever the other does. And unlike in the Prisoner's Dilemma, the equilibria here are efficient: the problem is not that equilibrium play wastes payoff, but that the players disagree about which equilibrium to play.

Read the blue graph as player 1's best reply to the probability \(q\) that player 2 goes to \(O\): she chooses \(O\) when \(q>\tfrac{1}{3}\) and \(F\) when \(q<\tfrac{1}{3}\), as in the example below. The red graph does the same for player 2, with threshold \(p=\tfrac{2}{3}\). Where the graphs meet, both players best respond: at the pure equilibria \((O,O)\) and \((F,F)\), and at the mixed equilibrium of Week 2. Change \(a\) (player 1's payoff at \((O,O)\), player 2's at \((F,F)\)) and \(b\) (the other way round): the thresholds move, but both pure equilibria remain.

Compare it with two other \(2\times2\) games. In Matching Pennies (Week 2) one player wants to match and the other to mismatch, so there is no pure equilibrium at all. In the chicken game both have two pure equilibria and one mixed equilibrium, but in chicken each player wants to do the opposite of the other, while here each wants to do the same.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The pure Nash equilibria are \((O,O)\) and \((F,F)\); the two mismatches are not equilibria.
  • The best responses are \(BR_1(O)=O\), \(BR_1(F)=F\), \(BR_2(O)=O\) and \(BR_2(F)=F\).
  • No player has a dominant strategy and no strategy is strictly dominated, so iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies removes nothing.
  • Both pure equilibria are Pareto efficient and cannot be ranked against each other: player 1 prefers \((O,O)\) and player 2 prefers \((F,F)\). Both give the same total payoff, \(3\).
  • In a pure coordination game, where both players prefer the same matched outcome, one equilibrium would Pareto dominate the other; in Battle of the Sexes neither does.

Looking ahead:

  • With mixed strategies (Week 2) there is exactly one further Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies: player 1 plays \(O\) with probability \(\tfrac{2}{3}\) and player 2 plays \(O\) with probability \(\tfrac{1}{3}\), giving each an expected payoff of \(\tfrac{2}{3}\). It is Pareto dominated by both pure equilibria.
  • If player 1 moves first and player 2 observes the move (Week 3), the unique subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium leads to \((O,O)\): the first mover gets her preferred outcome.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Pure equilibria. Check best responses cell by cell. Against \(O\), player 1 prefers \(O\) (\(2>0\)); against \(F\), she prefers \(F\) (\(1>0\)). Player 2 likewise wants to match player 1 (\(1>0\) against \(O\), \(2>0\) against \(F\)). The cells where both players are best responding are \((O,O)\) and \((F,F)\). At \((O,F)\) either player gains by switching, so it is not an equilibrium.

A belief decides the choice. If player 1 believes that player 2 goes to \(O\) with probability \(q\), her expected payoffs are \(2q\) from \(O\) and \(1-q\) from \(F\). She prefers \(O\) exactly when \(2q>1-q\), that is, \(q>\tfrac{1}{3}\). Even a fairly small chance that player 2 comes to the opera is enough, because player 1 gains more from meeting there.

The mixed equilibrium (Week 2). Let \(p\) be player 1's probability of \(O\) and \(q\) player 2's. By the indifference principle, each player's mixture makes the other indifferent:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{player 1: }&2q=1\cdot(1-q)\;\Rightarrow\;q=\tfrac{1}{3},\\ \text{player 2: }&1\cdot p=2(1-p)\;\Rightarrow\;p=\tfrac{2}{3}. \end{aligned} \]

Each player expects \(\tfrac{2}{3}\), less than the worse of her two pure-equilibrium payoffs. The players miscoordinate with probability \(\tfrac{2}{3}\cdot\tfrac{2}{3}+\tfrac{1}{3}\cdot\tfrac{1}{3}=\tfrac{5}{9}\).

Sequential version (Week 3). Suppose player 1 chooses first and player 2 observes the choice. Player 2's strategies are pairs (reply to \(O\), reply to \(F\)). By backward induction she replies \(O\) to \(O\) (\(1>0\)) and \(F\) to \(F\) (\(2>0\)), the strategy \(OF\). Anticipating this, player 1 compares \(2\) from \(O\) with \(1\) from \(F\) and chooses \(O\). The SPNE is \((O,OF)\) with outcome \((O,O)\) and payoffs \((2,1)\). The profile \((F,FF)\) is still a Nash equilibrium with outcome \((F,F)\), but it rests on player 2's non-credible threat to choose \(F\) after \(O\).

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
Let \((\sigma,\mu)\) be an assessment: a strategy profile \(\sigma\) and a system of beliefs \(\mu\). For an information set \(h\) and a node \(x\in h\), write \(\mathbb{P}_\sigma(x)\) for the probability that play reaches \(x\) when Nature moves according to the common prior and players follow \(\sigma\). If \(\mathbb{P}_\sigma(h)=\sum_{y\in h}\mathbb{P}_\sigma(y)>0\), beliefs are consistent with Bayes' rule at \(h\) when, for every \(x\in h\),

\[ \mu(x)=\frac{\mathbb{P}_\sigma(x)}{\sum_{y\in h}\mathbb{P}_\sigma(y)}. \]

Two types. Suppose an entrant is competitive (\(C\)) with prior probability \(p\) and weak (\(W\)) with probability \(1-p\), and type \(C\) enters with probability \(q_C\) and type \(W\) with probability \(q_W\). If \(q_C\,p+q_W\,(1-p)>0\), the incumbent's belief after observing entry is

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} \mu&=\mathbb{P}(C\mid\text{entry})\\ &=\frac{q_C\,p}{q_C\,p+q_W\,(1-p)}. \end{aligned} \]

If \(q_C\,p+q_W\,(1-p)=0\), entry is off the equilibrium path and the formula places no restriction on \(\mu\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This is Bayes' rule applied to the nodes of an information set: the prior over types is updated with the probability that each type takes the observed action. The denominator is the total probability of the observed action, by the law of total probability.

The figure draws the mixed-strategy example below. The widths of the two strips are the prior probabilities \(p=0.2\) and \(1-p=0.8\), and the shaded height in each strip is that type's entry probability, \(q_C=1\) and \(q_W=\tfrac{1}{2}\). Observing entry means play is somewhere in the shaded area, of total size \(0.2+0.4=0.6\); the posterior \(\mu\) is the share of that area belonging to type \(C\), namely \(\tfrac{1}{3}\).

Change \(q_W\): the posterior \(\mu\) is type \(C\)'s share of the shaded entry area. Set \(q_C=q_W\) and it equals the prior; set \(q_W=0\) and it jumps to \(1\).

The new element compared with Year-1 probability is that the "likelihoods" \(q_C,q_W\) are not given by nature but chosen in equilibrium: they come from the players' strategies, possibly a mixed strategy. Beliefs and strategies are therefore determined jointly, and a change in one type's behaviour changes what the other side infers.

A common mistake is to apply the formula at an information set that is reached with probability zero, or to conclude that off-path beliefs must equal the prior. Neither is implied: Bayes' rule simply has nothing to say there.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If all types take the observed action with the same probability (\(q_C=q_W>0\)), the posterior equals the prior: \(\mu=p\). This is the pooling case.
  • If only one type takes the action (\(q_C>0=q_W\)), then \(\mu=1\); if \(q_C=0<q_W\), then \(\mu=0\). This is the separating case.
  • If the action is taken with probability \(0\) by all types, \(\mu\) is unrestricted by Bayes' rule.
  • For \(0<p<1\) and a positive denominator, the posterior is nondecreasing in \(q_C\) and nonincreasing in \(q_W\); it is strictly monotone in both when \(q_C>0\) and \(q_W>0\).
  • In a perfect Bayesian equilibrium, Bayes' rule is required at every information set reached with positive probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Pure strategies. Prior \(p=\frac{1}{2}\). If both types enter, \(\mu=\frac{1\cdot0.5}{1\cdot0.5+1\cdot0.5}=0.5\). If only \(C\) enters, \(\mu=\frac{0.5}{0.5+0}=1\).

Mixed strategy. Prior \(p=\frac{1}{5}\). Type \(C\) always enters (\(q_C=1\)) and type \(W\) enters with probability \(q_W=\frac{1}{2}\). Then

\[ \mu=\frac{1\cdot0.2}{1\cdot0.2+0.5\cdot0.8}=\frac{0.2}{0.6}=\frac{1}{3}. \]

Entry raises the probability of a competitive entrant from \(0.2\) to \(\frac{1}{3}\), because type \(W\) enters less often than type \(C\).

Inverse use. If the incumbent must hold belief \(\mu=\frac{1}{3}\) after entry with \(p=\frac{1}{5}\) and \(q_C=1\), the weak type's entry probability solves \(\frac{0.2}{0.2+0.8\,q_W}=\frac{1}{3}\), giving \(q_W=\frac{2p}{1-p}=\frac{1}{2}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A (static) Bayesian game is a tuple

\[ \big\langle N,\ \{A_i\}_{i\in N},\ \{\Theta_i\}_{i\in N},\ \{v_i\}_{i\in N},\ p\big\rangle, \]

where \(N=\{1,\dots,n\}\) is the set of players, \(A_i\) is player \(i\)'s action set, \(\Theta_i\) is her set of types, \(v_i\colon A\times\Theta\to\mathbb{R}\) gives her payoff \(v_i(a;\theta)\) for action profile \(a\in A=\times_jA_j\) and type profile \(\theta\in\Theta=\times_j\Theta_j\), and \(p\) is a common prior on \(\Theta\). The timing is: Nature draws \(\theta\) from \(p\); each player learns her own \(\theta_i\); players choose actions simultaneously; payoffs are \(v_i(a;\theta)\). All components of the tuple are common knowledge. A pure strategy is a map \(s_i\colon\Theta_i\to A_i\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A Bayesian game extends a normal-form game to private information. Without types there would be nothing a player knows that the others do not; with types, each player must think about what every possible type of every opponent would do.

The figure follows the timing in the definition. Nature draws \(\theta\) from the common prior \(p\); player 1 sees only \(\theta_1\) and player 2 only \(\theta_2\), and the dashed line between the two rows marks that neither sees the other's type. Each action is produced by a strategy \(s_i\) applied to the player's own type, while the payoff \(v_i(a;\theta)\) can depend on the whole type profile, shown by the dashed arrow from Nature.

Given strategies \(s_{-i}\) of the others, type \(\theta_i\) evaluates action \(a_i\) by her interim expected payoff

\[ \sum_{\theta_{-i}}p(\theta_{-i}\mid\theta_i)\,v_i\big(a_i,s_{-i}(\theta_{-i});\theta_i,\theta_{-i}\big). \]

Two misunderstandings are common. First, a strategy is not the action actually taken; it must specify what each type would do, because the others' optimal choices depend on all of them. Second, payoffs may depend on the others' types as well as one's own (interdependent values, as with car quality in the market for lemons); "private values" is the special case \(v_i(a;\theta_i)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With finite sets, player \(i\) has \(|A_i|^{|\Theta_i|}\) pure strategies.
  • If every \(\Theta_i\) is a singleton, the Bayesian game is an ordinary normal-form game of complete information.
  • The equilibrium concept is the Bayesian Nash equilibrium: each type best responds given her beliefs.
  • The game can equivalently be drawn as an extensive-form game in which Nature moves first, the Harsanyi transformation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Contribution game. Two neighbours, \(N=\{1,2\}\), choose \(A_i=\{C,D\}\) (contribute or decline). A shared good worth 1 to each is provided if at least one contributes; contributing costs \(\theta_i\). So

\[ v_i(a;\theta)=\indicator_{\{a_1=C\text{ or }a_2=C\}}-\theta_i\,\indicator_{\{a_i=C\}}. \]

Types are \(\Theta_i=\{\tfrac{1}{4},2\}\), drawn independently with probability \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) each. Each player has \(2^2=4\) pure strategies. A high-cost type gets \(1-2=-1\) from contributing and at least 0 from not contributing, so \(D\) is a strictly dominant action for her, whatever the other does. The low-cost type's choice depends on what she expects the other to do; this is solved on the Bayesian Nash equilibrium page.

Auctions. In a sealed-bid auction each bidder's type is her valuation, her action is a bid, and payoffs depend on all bids; see the first-price auction.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a Bayesian game \(\langle N,\{A_i\},\{\Theta_i\},\{v_i\},p\rangle\), a profile of pure strategies \(s^*=(s_1^*,\dots,s_n^*)\) with \(s_i^*\colon\Theta_i\to A_i\) is a Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE) if for every player \(i\), every type \(\theta_i\) with \(p(\theta_i)>0\) and every action \(a_i\in A_i\),

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &\sum_{\theta_{-i}}p(\theta_{-i}\mid\theta_i)\,v_i\big(s_i^*(\theta_i),s_{-i}^*(\theta_{-i});\theta\big)\\ &\quad\ge\sum_{\theta_{-i}}p(\theta_{-i}\mid\theta_i)\,v_i\big(a_i,s_{-i}^*(\theta_{-i});\theta\big). \end{aligned} \]

That is, each type's prescribed action is a best response to the other players' type-contingent strategies, given that type's beliefs. Mixed BNE are defined in the same way with mixed actions for each type.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A BNE is a Nash equilibrium in which "player" is replaced by "player-type". Each type maximizes a conditional expectation of her payoff given her own type, and the expectation is taken over the others' types and hence over their type-dependent actions. Players need not know what the others will actually do; they know the others' strategies, the maps from types to actions.

The condition is imposed type by type (interim), but it is equivalent to an ex ante condition: \(s^*\) is a BNE if and only if it is a Nash equilibrium of the normal-form game whose strategies are the maps \(s_i\) and whose payoffs are ex ante expected payoffs \(\sum_\theta p(\theta)v_i(s(\theta);\theta)\), provided every type has positive probability. Maximizing an average with positive weights is the same as maximizing each term.

A common mistake is to check only the type that is "actually realized". Every type must be optimizing, because the other players' incentives depend on what the unrealized types would do.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If every \(\Theta_i\) is a singleton, a BNE is a Nash equilibrium of the underlying game.
  • A finite Bayesian game has at least one BNE, possibly in mixed strategies, by the Nash existence theorem applied to the ex ante game.
  • If an action is strictly dominant for a type that has positive probability, that type plays it in every BNE.
  • In a BNE of a game with a sequential structure, off-path behaviour need not be optimal; sequential versions such as perfect Bayesian equilibrium add this.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Contribution game. Each player \(i\in\{1,2\}\) chooses \(C\) (contribute) or \(D\) (decline); the good (worth 1 to each) is provided if at least one contributes; contributing costs \(\theta_i\in\{\tfrac{1}{4},2\}\), independently low with probability \(q\).

  1. High-cost type: \(C\) gives \(1-2=-1\), \(D\) gives at least 0, so she plays \(D\).
  2. Low-cost type: \(C\) gives \(1-\tfrac{1}{4}=\tfrac{3}{4}\). \(D\) gives 1 times the probability that the other contributes, which is at most \(q\), because the other's high type never contributes.
  3. With \(q=\tfrac{1}{2}\): \(D\) gives at most \(\tfrac{1}{2}<\tfrac{3}{4}\), so the low type contributes.

The unique BNE is \(s_i^*(\tfrac{1}{4})=C\), \(s_i^*(2)=D\) for both players; the good is provided with probability \(1-\tfrac{1}{4}=\tfrac{3}{4}\).

Changing the prior. The profile in step 3 remains a BNE if and only if \(q\le\tfrac{3}{4}\). For \(q>\tfrac{3}{4}\) a low-cost type would rather free-ride on the other's low type; then, for example, "only player 1's low type contributes" is a BNE (player 2's low type gets \(q>\tfrac{3}{4}\) from \(D\), and player 1's low type gets \(\tfrac{3}{4}>0\) from \(C\)).

The figure fixes the other player's strategy at the candidate profile, so that her low type contributes and her high type declines. A low-cost type then gets \(1-\tfrac{1}{4}=\tfrac{3}{4}\) from \(C\) and \(q\) from \(D\). At \(q=\tfrac{1}{2}\) the \(C\) line lies above the \(D\) line, which is step 3; the shaded region \(q\le\tfrac{3}{4}\) is where the profile remains a BNE, and to the right of the threshold declining and free-riding pays more.

Move the prior \(q\) past \(\tfrac34\): declining then pays the low-cost type more than contributing, and the profile stops being a BNE. A lower contribution cost moves the threshold \(1-\theta_i\) to the right.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a Bertrand duopoly two firms sell an identical (homogeneous) product and simultaneously choose prices \(p_1,p_2\ge0\). Both have the same constant marginal cost \(c>0\), and market demand \(D(p)\) is continuous and nonincreasing with \(D(c)>0\) (for example \(D(p)=\max\{(a-p)/b,0\}\) with \(a>c\)). Consumers buy from the cheaper firm, and split equally at equal prices:

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &v_1(p_1,p_2)\\ &=\begin{cases} (p_1-c)\,D(p_1) & \text{if } p_1<p_2,\\ \tfrac{1}{2}(p_1-c)\,D(p_1) & \text{if } p_1=p_2,\\ 0 & \text{if } p_1>p_2, \end{cases} \end{aligned} \]

and symmetrically for firm 2. Prices are continuous, so \(S_i=[0,\infty)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
With identical products, a slightly lower price captures the whole market. When both firms charge the same price above cost, undercutting by a small amount roughly doubles a firm's sales at almost the same margin. This undercutting pressure drives prices down to marginal cost.

The figure uses the example below, \(D(p)=100-p\) and \(c=10\), and fixes the rival's price at \(p_2=40\). Matching the rival gives firm 1 half the market, a profit of \(900\); any price just below \(40\) gives the whole market and a profit close to \(1800\); any price above \(40\) sells nothing. The open circle at \(1800\) is never reached, which is why no best "just below" price exists, and repeating this argument at every common price above \(c\) pushes the equilibrium down to \(p_1^*=p_2^*=c\).

With \(p_2=40\), move \(p_1\) towards \(40\) from below: the profit approaches \(1800\) but drops to \(900\) at the tie. Lower \(p_2\) towards \(c\) and the gain from undercutting shrinks to nothing.

The result, two firms already pricing as under perfect competition, is called the Bertrand paradox. It contrasts with the Cournot duopoly, where quantity competition gives a price above cost: the choice of strategic variable (price or quantity) changes the prediction. The paradox disappears with differentiated products, capacity limits or repeated interaction (see repeated game, Week 4).

A common error is to look for an equilibrium with a small positive margin, "just below" the rival. With continuous prices there is no best "just below" price, so best responses can fail to exist (see the best-response correspondence).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The unique Nash equilibrium is \(p_1^*=p_2^*=c\); both firms earn zero profit.
  • Proof by cases (the argument for \(p_2<p_1\) is symmetric):
    • \(p_1=p_2=p>c\): either firm gains by undercutting. If \(D(p)>0\), a price slightly below \(p\) raises its profit from \(\tfrac{1}{2}(p-c)D(p)\) to almost \((p-c)D(p)\); if \(D(p)=0\), a price slightly above \(c\) gives a positive profit.
    • \(c<p_1<p_2\): firm 2 earns \(0\) and can earn a positive profit by pricing slightly above \(c\) (and below \(p_1\)).
    • \(c=p_1<p_2\): firm 1 earns \(0\) and can earn a positive profit by pricing slightly above \(c\) but below \(p_2\).
    • \(p_1<c\) with \(p_1\le p_2\): firm 1 makes a loss and gains by raising its price above \(p_2\).
    • \(p_1=p_2=c\): lowering the price gives a loss and raising it gives zero sales; no deviation helps.
  • In equilibrium each firm's strategy is a best response but is not strictly better than every alternative: any \(p_i>c\) also gives zero against \(p_j=c\).
  • With a discrete price grid of step \(h>0\) (for example cents) that contains \(c\), and \(D(c+h)>0\), both \((c,c)\) and \((c+h,c+h)\) are Nash equilibria; the latter because deviating to \(c\) gives \(0<\tfrac{1}{2} h\,D(c+h)\), and every other deviation gives zero or a loss.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Let \(D(p)=100-p\) and \(c=10\).

Undercutting. At \(p_1=p_2=40\), each firm earns \(\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot30\cdot60=900\). Firm 1 deviating to \(39.99\) earns \(29.99\cdot60.01\approx1799.70\), so \((40,40)\) is not an equilibrium.

At cost. At \(p_1=p_2=10\), each earns \(0\). Raising to \(12\) sells nothing and still earns \(0\); lowering to \(9\) earns \((9-10)\cdot91=-91\). Neither firm can gain, so \((10,10)\) is the equilibrium.

Comparison. The Cournot equilibrium with the same demand and cost has price \(40\) and profit \(900\) per firm; Bertrand gives price \(10\) and profit \(0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The best-response correspondence of player \(i\) assigns to every profile of the other players' strategies \(s_{-i}\in S_{-i}\) the set of player \(i\)'s best responses:

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &BR_i(s_{-i})\\ &=\{s_i\in S_i\colon v_i(s_i,s_{-i})\ge v_i(s_i',s_{-i})\\ &\qquad\text{for every } s_i'\in S_i\}\\ &=\arg\max_{s_i\in S_i}v_i(s_i,s_{-i}). \end{aligned} \]

A correspondence is a rule that assigns to each point a set, which may contain several elements or be the empty set. If \(BR_i(s_{-i})\) contains exactly one element for every \(s_{-i}\), the correspondence is an ordinary function, called a best-response function (or reaction function).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The correspondence summarizes all of player \(i\)'s optimal reactions in one object. Several strategies can be optimal against the same \(s_{-i}\) when payoffs tie, which is why a set is used rather than a single value.

The figure draws Example 3 below: above each rival price \(p_2\) it shows the whole set \(BR_1(p_2)\). For \(p_2<c\) the set is the open region above the diagonal, at \(p_2=c\) it is the vertical ray \([c,\infty)\), and for \(p_2>p^m\) it is the single point \(p^m\), where the correspondence behaves like a function. For \(c<p_2\le p^m\) nothing is drawn above the axis, because the set of best responses is empty.

Move the rival price \(p_2\) and read off \(BR_1(p_2)\) above it: a region for \(p_2<c\), a ray at \(p_2=c\), nothing between \(c\) and \(p^m\), and the single point \(p^m\) beyond.

A frequent mistake is to report only one maximizer when several tie; a Nash equilibrium can then be missed. A second is to assume \(BR_i(s_{-i})\) is always nonempty: in games with infinite strategy sets the supremum of the payoff may not be attained.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A profile \(s^*\) is a Nash equilibrium if and only if \(s_i^*\in BR_i(s_{-i}^*)\) for every \(i\in N\).
  • For two players with interval strategy sets, the Nash equilibria are the intersection points of the graphs of \(BR_1\) and \(BR_2\) drawn in the same \((s_1,s_2)\) plane.
  • If \(S_i\) is finite, \(BR_i(s_{-i})\) is nonempty for every \(s_{-i}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
1. Ties. Suppose player 1 has strategies \(U\), \(M\), \(D\) and, against player 2's strategy \(L\), receives \(1\), \(3\), \(3\). Then \(BR_1(L)=\{M,D\}\), a two-element set.

2. Cournot reaction functions. In a Cournot duopoly with price \(100-q_1-q_2\) and unit cost \(10\),

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} BR_1(q_2)&=\max\Big\{\frac{90-q_2}{2},\,0\Big\},\\ BR_2(q_1)&=\max\Big\{\frac{90-q_1}{2},\,0\Big\}. \end{aligned} \]

Both are single-valued. Their intersection solves \(q_1=(90-q_2)/2\) and \(q_2=(90-q_1)/2\), so \(q_1=q_2=30\).

3. Bertrand: an empty set. In a Bertrand duopoly with identical products, unit cost \(c\), demand \(D(p)=\max\{(a-p)/b,0\}\) with \(a>c\), and monopoly price \(p^m=(a+c)/2\):

  • \(BR_1(p_2)=(p_2,\infty)\) if \(p_2<c\) (any price that sells nothing);
  • \(BR_1(p_2)=[c,\infty)\) if \(p_2=c\) (profit is \(0\) at best);
  • \(BR_1(p_2)=\varnothing\) if \(c<p_2\le p^m\): firm 1 wants to price just below \(p_2\), but no largest price below \(p_2\) exists;
  • \(BR_1(p_2)=\{p^m\}\) if \(p_2>p^m\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a normal-form game \(\langle N,\{S_i\},\{v_i\}\rangle\), fix the other players' strategies \(s_{-i}\in S_{-i}\). A strategy \(s_i\in S_i\) is a best response of player \(i\) to \(s_{-i}\) if, for every \(s_i'\in S_i\),

\[ v_i(s_i,s_{-i})\ge v_i(s_i',s_{-i}). \]

More generally, if player \(i\) holds a belief \(\pi_i\), a probability distribution over \(S_{-i}\) (finite here), then \(s_i\) is a best response to \(\pi_i\) if it maximizes the expected payoff \(\sum_{s_{-i}\in S_{-i}}\pi_i(s_{-i})\,v_i(s_i,s_{-i})\) over \(S_i\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A best response is what a rational agent does once a belief about the others has been formed: the opponents' play is treated as given and the player solves an ordinary maximization problem. With a probabilistic belief this is expected payoff maximization.

The figure uses the matrix of Example 1 below. If player 2's belief puts probability \(\pi_2(T)\) on \(T\), her expected payoffs are \(3-2\pi_2(T)\) from \(L\), \(1+\pi_2(T)\) from \(M\) and \(0\) from \(R\). The best response is the strategy on the highlighted upper envelope: \(L\) while \(\pi_2(T)<\tfrac{2}{3}\) and \(M\) above \(\tfrac{2}{3}\), where the two lines cross, with both optimal at \(\tfrac{2}{3}\); \(R\) is never a best response. At the belief \(0.4\) of Example 2 the comparison is \(2.2\) against \(1.4\).

Move player 2's belief \(\pi_2(T)\): the best response is the strategy on the green upper envelope, switching from \(L\) to \(M\) at \(\tfrac23\). Raise \(R\)'s payoffs to see when it, too, becomes a best response.

A best response is defined relative to \(s_{-i}\); it changes when \(s_{-i}\) changes. If the belief is wrong, the chosen strategy may not be optimal against what is actually played. Nash equilibrium is the situation in which every player best responds to the strategies the others actually use.

Best responses need not be unique: with ties, all maximizers are best responses, collected in the best-response correspondence \(BR_i(s_{-i})\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(S_i\) is finite, a best response exists for every \(s_{-i}\). If \(S_i\) is compact and \(v_i(\cdot,s_{-i})\) is continuous, existence follows from the extreme value theorem on compact sets; otherwise a best response may fail to exist (undercutting in a Bertrand duopoly).
  • A strictly dominated strategy is never a best response, to any \(s_{-i}\) or any belief.
  • A strictly dominant strategy is the unique best response to every \(s_{-i}\).
  • If \(S_i\) is an interval and \(v_i(\cdot,s_{-i})\) is differentiable and concave, every interior point satisfying the first-order condition \(\partial v_i/\partial s_i=0\) is a best response; if no interior point satisfies it, check the endpoints.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
1. Matrix game. Payoffs \((v_1,v_2)\):

\(L\) \(M\) \(R\) \(T\) \(2,1\) \(3,2\) \(0,0\) \(B\) \(1,3\) \(1,1\) \(4,0\)

Player 1 compares down each column: the best response to \(L\) is \(T\) (\(2>1\)), to \(M\) is \(T\) (\(3>1\)), to \(R\) is \(B\) (\(4>0\)). Player 2 compares along each row: the best response to \(T\) is \(M\) (\(2>1>0\)), to \(B\) is \(L\) (\(3>1>0\)).

2. Belief. If player 2 believes player 1 plays \(T\) with probability \(0.4\) and \(B\) with probability \(0.6\), the expected payoffs are \(L\): \(0.4\cdot1+0.6\cdot3=2.2\), \(M\): \(0.4\cdot2+0.6\cdot1=1.4\), \(R\): \(0\). The best response to this belief is \(L\).

3. Cournot. In a Cournot duopoly with price \(100-q_1-q_2\) and unit cost \(10\), firm 1's profit is \((90-q_1-q_2)q_1\). Setting the derivative \(90-2q_1-q_2\) equal to zero gives \(q_1=(90-q_2)/2\); since the second derivative is \(-2<0\), this is a maximum, and against \(q_2=20\) the best response is \(q_1=35\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The chicken game is a symmetric two-player normal-form game in which each player chooses \(S\) (swerve, yield) or \(T\) (go straight, stand firm), and each player's payoffs satisfy

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} v_i(T,S)&>v_i(S,S)\\ &>v_i(S,T)>v_i(T,T). \end{aligned} \]

Standing firm is best if the other yields, yielding is best if the other stands firm, and mutual standing firm is the worst outcome. A standard numerical version:

\(S\) \(T\) \(S\) \(0,0\) \(-1,1\) \(T\) \(1,-1\) \(-3,-3\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Chicken is an anti-coordination game: each player wants to do the opposite of the other. It models standoffs such as two drivers heading for each other, price wars, or a confrontation in which backing down is costly but collision is disastrous. In biology the same structure is called the hawk–dove game.

In the figure \(p\) and \(q\) are the probabilities with which players 1 and 2 choose \(T\) in the table above. Player 1's best response \(BR_1\) is \(T\) (\(p=1\)) when \(q<\tfrac{1}{3}\), \(S\) (\(p=0\)) when \(q>\tfrac{1}{3}\), and any \(p\) when \(q=\tfrac{1}{3}\); player 2's \(BR_2\) is the mirror image. Because each player wants the opposite of the other, both curves step downwards and cross three times: at the two pure equilibria and at the mixed equilibrium \((\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{3})\).

Raise the crash cost \(c\) and watch the mixed equilibrium \(q=w/(w+c-\ell)\) fall towards \(0\); with \(c<\ell\), standing firm becomes dominant and only \((T,T)\) remains.

Compare it with the Prisoner's Dilemma. There, defecting is best whatever the other does, so there is a single equilibrium. In chicken, no action is dominant, \((T,T)\) is worse than being the one who yields, and the game has three equilibria. The theory alone does not say which one is played; the two pure equilibria require the players to know who yields.

Chicken is a standard example for purification: if each player's toughness, that is the payoff from standing firm, is slightly private, the mixed equilibrium can be reinterpreted as pure behaviour by different types, and the game becomes a Bayesian game.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The pure Nash equilibria are \((S,T)\) and \((T,S)\); \((S,S)\) and \((T,T)\) are not equilibria.
  • There is exactly one further Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies, symmetric, in which each player chooses \(T\) with the probability that makes the other indifferent.
  • No action is strictly dominated, so iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies removes nothing.
  • The mixed equilibrium is Pareto-dominated by \((S,S)\), which is not an equilibrium: it is not Pareto efficient.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Mixed equilibrium in the table above. Let the opponent play \(T\) with probability \(q\). By the indifference principle, \(S\) yields \(-q\) and \(T\) yields \((1-q)-3q=1-4q\); equating gives \(q=\tfrac{1}{3}\). By symmetry each player plays \(T\) with probability \(\tfrac{1}{3}\), and each earns \(-\tfrac{1}{3}\).

  • The crash \((T,T)\) occurs with probability \(\tfrac{1}{9}\).
  • Both players get \(0>-\tfrac{1}{3}\) at \((S,S)\), which confirms the Pareto comparison.
  • In the pure equilibria the payoffs are \((-1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\).

General parameters. With \(v_i(S,S)=0\), \(v_i(T,S)=w>0\), \(v_i(S,T)=-\ell<0\) and \(v_i(T,T)=-c\) with \(c>\ell\), indifference gives \(-\ell q=w(1-q)-cq\), so \(q=w/(w+c-\ell)\). A more costly crash (larger \(c\)) lowers the probability of standing firm. The table above has \(w=1\), \(\ell=1\), \(c=3\), so \(q=1/3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(E\) be a fact (an event) concerning the players \(N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) of a game. Define the levels of knowledge recursively:

  • \(K^1(E)\): every player knows \(E\) (mutual knowledge);
  • \(K^{m+1}(E)\): every player knows that \(K^m(E)\) holds, for \(m=1,2,\ldots\)

The fact \(E\) is common knowledge among the players if \(K^m(E)\) holds for every \(m\ge1\): everyone knows \(E\), everyone knows that everyone knows \(E\), and so on at every finite level.

Common knowledge of rationality is the case where \(E\) is the statement "every player is a rational agent".

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
In game theory a player's best choice depends on what the others will do, which depends on what they believe, including what they believe about this player. Common knowledge closes this chain of "beliefs about beliefs" by assuming that every level holds.

The figure draws each level as a smaller set of situations: a situation where \(K^2(E)\) holds also satisfies \(K^1(E)\) and \(E\), but not the other way round. Further levels \(K^3(E),K^4(E),\ldots\) would be drawn as more boxes inside \(K^2(E)\); common knowledge is what lies inside all of them. The labels follow Example 1 below: rationality of player 2 alone deletes \(R\), knowing that player 2 is rational lets player 1 delete \(B\), and the second level lets player 2 delete \(L\).

The main misunderstanding is to treat common knowledge as "everyone knows". Mutual knowledge \(K^1(E)\) does not imply \(K^2(E)\): each player may know \(E\) without knowing that the others know it.

Two standard assumptions use the concept. In a static game of complete information the players, strategy sets and payoff functions are common knowledge. Common knowledge of rationality justifies iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (Key Results).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Common knowledge of \(E\) implies \(K^m(E)\) for every \(m\); no finite level \(K^m(E)\) implies common knowledge.
  • Deleting a strictly dominated strategy in round \(1\) needs only rationality of its owner. A deletion in round \(k\) needs rationality together with \(k-1\) levels of "everyone knows that ..." about rationality. Common knowledge of rationality therefore supports the whole elimination process, for as many rounds as needed.
  • Common knowledge of rationality does not by itself select a Nash equilibrium: in Battle of the Sexes no strategy is eliminated, and players can still fail to coordinate.
  • In a Bayesian game (Week 5) the common prior over types is assumed to be common knowledge.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
1. Levels of rationality. Player 1 chooses \(T\) or \(B\), player 2 chooses \(L\), \(M\) or \(R\); payoffs are \((v_1,v_2)\).

\(L\) \(M\) \(R\) \(T\) \(2,1\) \(3,2\) \(0,0\) \(B\) \(1,3\) \(1,1\) \(4,0\)
  • Player 2 is rational: \(R\) is strictly dominated by \(M\) (\(2>0\) and \(1>0\)), so \(R\) is not played.
  • Player 1 is rational and knows player 2 is rational: without \(R\), \(T\) beats \(B\) \((2>1,\ 3>1)\).
  • Player 2 is rational, knows player 1 is rational, and knows that player 1 knows player 2 is rational: given \(T\), \(M\) beats \(L\) \((2>1)\).

The prediction \((T,M)\) uses rationality plus two levels of knowledge about rationality.

2. Private versus public. Each of two players is told privately that a meeting is at 9:00. Both know the time (\(K^1\)), but neither knows that the other knows. If the time is announced to both together, each sees the other hear it, and the time becomes common knowledge.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a game with types \(\theta\in\Theta=\Theta_1\times\cdots\times\Theta_n\), a common prior is a single probability distribution \(p\) on \(\Theta\) that is common knowledge among the players and from which every player's beliefs are derived. Player \(i\) of type \(\theta_i\) (with \(p(\theta_i)>0\)) holds the conditional belief

\[ p(\theta_{-i}\mid\theta_i)=\frac{p(\theta_i,\theta_{-i})}{\sum_{\theta'_{-i}}p(\theta_i,\theta'_{-i})}, \]

where \(\theta_{-i}\) denotes the types of the other players. For finite type spaces, \(p\) is a joint probability mass function of the type profile.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The common prior assumption says that players differ in what they know, not in how they interpret the world: any difference in beliefs comes from different private information. Each type's belief is the conditional probability of the others' types given her own, obtained from \(p\) by Bayes' rule.

The figure shows the correlated example below as one table that both players read. Player 1 of type \(a\) knows she is in the outlined row and rescales it by its total \(0.5\), giving \(p(x\mid a)=0.8\); player 2 of type \(x\) knows she is in the dashed column and rescales it by \(0.6\), giving \(p(a\mid x)=\tfrac{2}{3}\). Different types end up with different beliefs only because they condition on different parts of the same \(p\).

This is what lets a Bayesian game be written as one game with Nature moving first, the Harsanyi transformation: Nature draws \(\theta\) from \(p\), and everyone knows that it does.

When types are correlated, a player's own type is informative about the others', so different types of the same player hold different beliefs; using the marginal distribution of \(\theta_{-i}\) in that case is a frequent error. Only independent types give every type the same belief (Key Results).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Beliefs consistent with a common prior satisfy \(p(\theta_i)\,p(\theta_{-i}\mid\theta_i)=p(\theta)\) for all \(i\) and \(\theta\).
  • With independent types, \(p(\theta)=\prod_jp_j(\theta_j)\) and \(p(\theta_{-i}\mid\theta_i)=p(\theta_{-i})\) for every type \(\theta_i\): all types of player \(i\) hold the same belief, the product of the others' marginals.
  • Not every belief system comes from a common prior: two players without private information who assign different probabilities to the same event cannot share one. More generally (Aumann's agreement theorem), under a common prior, posteriors about an event that are common knowledge must be equal.
  • Under a common prior, a type's expected payoff is computed with \(p(\cdot\mid\theta_i)\); the ex ante expected payoff averages these with weights \(p(\theta_i)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Correlated types. Let \(\Theta_1=\{a,b\}\), \(\Theta_2=\{x,y\}\) and

\(x\) \(y\) \(a\) \(0.4\) \(0.1\) \(b\) \(0.2\) \(0.3\)

The entries sum to 1. Type \(a\) has \(p(a)=0.5\) and believes \(p(x\mid a)=0.4/0.5=0.8\); type \(b\) believes \(p(x\mid b)=0.2/0.5=0.4\). Player 2 has \(p(x)=0.6\), \(p(y)=0.4\), so type \(x\) believes \(p(a\mid x)=0.4/0.6=\tfrac{2}{3}\) and type \(y\) believes \(p(a\mid y)=0.1/0.4=\tfrac{1}{4}\).

Independent types. If each \(\theta_i\in\{\tfrac{1}{4},2\}\) with probability \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) independently, \(p(\theta)=\tfrac{1}{4}\) for each of the four profiles and every type believes the other is low-cost with probability \(\tfrac{1}{2}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a common-value auction the object has the same value \(v\) for every bidder, but no bidder knows \(v\). Each bidder \(i\) privately observes a signal \(\theta_i\) that is informative about \(v\), and her payoff from winning at price \(p\) is \(v-p\). Bidder \(i\)'s expected value therefore depends on the other bidders' signals as well as on her own.

A two-bidder example with this structure has \(v=\theta_1+\theta_2\), where bidder \(i\) observes only her own component \(\theta_i\), and \(\theta_1,\theta_2\) are independent.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The contrast with a private-value auction is about information, not about who values the object more. With private values, learning a rival's signal would not change one's own valuation; with a common value it would. Classic examples are drilling rights to an oil field of unknown size, or a jar of coins whose total is estimated by eye.

Because the value is shared, winning is itself informative: a bidder wins in a symmetric equilibrium when her signal is the highest, which is bad news about the others' signals. A rational bidder therefore bids on the basis of the conditional expectation of \(v\) given her signal and given that she wins (or, in a second-price auction, given that she is just tied). Ignoring this produces the winner's curse.

Truthful bidding results for private values do not carry over directly. In a second-price auction the case argument for bidding "one's value" fails, because one's value is not known; the equilibrium bid must instead be computed as a Bayesian Nash equilibrium.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In a symmetric equilibrium with increasing bids, \(\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_i]\) overstates what a bidder can expect when she wins; the relevant quantity is \(\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_i,\ i\text{ wins}]\).
  • For \(v=\theta_1+\theta_2\) with \(\theta_i\) i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\): the symmetric BNE of the second-price auction is \(b(\theta)=2\theta=\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_1=\theta_2=\theta]\), and that of the first-price auction is \(b(\theta)=\theta\).
  • In that example both formats give expected revenue \(\frac{2}{3}\).
  • The Dutch–first-price equivalence holds with common values; the English–second-price equivalence can fail with three or more bidders, because drop-out prices reveal signals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Take \(v=\theta_1+\theta_2\) with \(\theta_1,\theta_2\) independent and uniform on \([0,1]\).

Second-price. Let bidder 2 bid \(2\theta_2\). Bidder 1 with signal \(x\) who bids \(b\le2\) wins when \(\theta_2<b/2\) and pays \(2\theta_2\), so her expected payoff \(\mathbb{E}[u]\) (written \(u\) because \(v\) is the common value) is

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[u]&=\int_0^{b/2}\big(x+y-2y\big)\,\mathrm{d}y\\ &=\int_0^{b/2}(x-y)\,\mathrm{d}y. \end{aligned} \]

The integrand is positive for \(y<x\) and negative for \(y>x\), so the payoff is maximized at \(b/2=x\), i.e. \(b=2x\). Revenue is \(2\,\mathbb{E}[\min(\theta_1,\theta_2)]=2\cdot\frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}\).

First-price. Let bidder 2 bid \(\theta_2\). Bidder 1 with signal \(x\) bidding \(b\le1\) wins when \(\theta_2<b\), with expected payoff

\[ \mathbb{E}[u]=\int_0^{b}(x+y-b)\,\mathrm{d}y=xb-\tfrac{1}{2}b^2, \]

maximized at \(b=x\). Revenue is \(\mathbb{E}[\max(\theta_1,\theta_2)]=\frac{2}{3}\).

Numbers. With \(x=0.6\), \(\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_1=0.6]=1.1\), but \(\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_1=0.6,\ \theta_2<0.6]=0.6+0.3=0.9\). The first-price bid \(0.6\) leaves an expected margin of \(0.3\) when winning.

The figure fixes bidder 1's signal at \(x=0.6\), so the value is \(0.6+\theta_2\). Averaged over all \(\theta_2\) it is \(1.1\), but in the first-price equilibrium bidder 1 wins only in the shaded region \(\theta_2<0.6\), where the average value is \(0.9\). A bid computed from \(1.1\) would overpay on average, which is the winner's curse; the equilibrium bid \(0.6\) sits \(0.3\) below the conditional value.

Move the bid \(b\): a winning bid means \(\theta_2<b\), so it buys only the green average value. The naive bid \(1.1\) overpays, while \(b=x=0.6\) maximizes the expected payoff.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a Cournot duopoly two firms produce a homogeneous good and simultaneously choose quantities \(q_1,q_2\ge0\). In the standard linear version:

  • the market price is given by the inverse demand \(P(q_1+q_2)=\max\{a-b(q_1+q_2),\,0\}\) with \(a>0\), \(b>0\);
  • each firm has constant marginal cost \(c\) with \(0\le c<a\), so its cost is \(c\,q_i\);
  • firm \(i\)'s payoff is its profit \(v_i(q_1,q_2)=\big(P(q_1+q_2)-c\big)q_i\).

This is a static game of complete information with strategy sets \(S_i=[0,\infty)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Each firm's profit depends on the rival's quantity through the common price: more output by the rival lowers the price and makes one's own output less valuable. A firm's best response therefore falls as the rival's quantity rises.

The figure uses the numbers below (\(a=100\), \(b=1\), \(c=10\)). Firm 1's reaction line \(q_1=(90-q_2)/2\) gives its profit-maximizing output for each \(q_2\), and firm 2's line \(q_2=(90-q_1)/2\) does the same with the roles swapped; both slope downwards because a larger rival output lowers one's own best output. The only point on both lines is \((30,30)\), where each quantity is a best response to the other, so it is the Nash equilibrium.

Drag the profile \(s\): the orange arrows point to each firm's best response to the other's quantity, and they vanish only at \((30,30)\). Change \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) to move the equilibrium \(q^*=(a-c)/(3b)\).

The equilibrium is found by computing both best responses and solving them together, which is the definition of a Nash equilibrium applied to continuous strategies. Taking the partial derivative of \(v_i\) with respect to the firm's own quantity, holding the rival's fixed, is the key step; differentiating the sum or the rival's quantity is a common error.

The equilibrium lies between monopoly and perfect competition: the firms together produce more than a monopolist, but less than the competitive output at which price equals marginal cost.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Best response (first-order condition \(a-c-2bq_i-bq_j=0\), with \(\partial^2v_i/\partial q_i^2=-2b<0\)):
\[ BR_i(q_j)=\max\Big\{\frac{a-c-bq_j}{2b},\,0\Big\}. \]
  • Unique Nash equilibrium: \(q_1^*=q_2^*=\dfrac{a-c}{3b}\), total output \(Q^*=\dfrac{2(a-c)}{3b}\), price \(P^*=\dfrac{a+2c}{3}\), profit \(\dfrac{(a-c)^2}{9b}\) per firm.
  • A monopolist would produce \(Q^m=\dfrac{a-c}{2b}\); perfect competition gives \(Q^c=\dfrac{a-c}{b}\); so \(Q^m<Q^*<Q^c\).
  • If each firm produced \(\dfrac{a-c}{4b}\) (half the monopoly output), each would earn \(\dfrac{(a-c)^2}{8b}>\dfrac{(a-c)^2}{9b}\), but this is not an equilibrium: each firm's best response to \(\dfrac{a-c}{4b}\) is \(\dfrac{3(a-c)}{8b}\). The equilibrium is not Pareto efficient for the firms.
  • With \(n\) identical firms the symmetric equilibrium is \(q_i^*=\dfrac{a-c}{(n+1)b}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Numbers. Let \(a=100\), \(b=1\), \(c=10\), so \(P=100-q_1-q_2\) when \(q_1+q_2\le100\) and \(P=0\) otherwise.

  • Profit: \(v_1=(90-q_1-q_2)q_1\); the first-order condition \(90-2q_1-q_2=0\) gives \(BR_1(q_2)=(90-q_2)/2\) for \(q_2\le90\).
  • By symmetry \(q_2=(90-q_1)/2\). Solving this system of linear equations: \(q_1=(90-(90-q_1)/2)/2\), so \(4q_1=90+q_1\) and \(q_1=30\).
  • Hence \(q_1^*=q_2^*=30=(100-10)/3\), \(P^*=40\), profit \(30\cdot30=900\) each.
  • Check: against \(q_2=30\), producing \(31\) gives \((29)(31)=899\) and producing \(29\) gives \((31)(29)=899\), both below \(900\).
